the sueet nesse of his goodnesse in spiritualls may sometimes passe
away so farre, that we can make out nothing ofit to our selves,
nor see the good of any promise that belongs tous. And then
indeed, our melsare is passed away as a cloud.
Jub having thus given us a description of the terrours and trou¬
bles which fell upon his spirit, proceeds to shew their sad effects
both upon his inward and outward man.

0158.head: Ghap. 30. An Expofition upon the Bookee ef JOR. Vers.16"

body.t: And non my soule is powred out upon me; the dayes
of affliction have taken hold upon me.
My bones are pierced in the night season: and my
sinems take no rest.
N the former verse Jab opened the troubles of his mind, ter¬
Frors pursued or persecuted his soule, his principal one: in this
16th, as also in the 17th and 18th verses, we have a description
of the paines and languishments of his body, together with their
effects upon his spirit; and at the r9ch verse we have the result
of all; in which as in a glasse we may see in what plight and
pickle Job was, or to what he was reduced by all these sufferings,
He hath cast me into the mire, and I am become like dust and
asbes.
Verf. 16. And now my soule is powred out apen mee.
And now, that is, things being come to this passe, or to this
extreamity, the waters of trouble being swell’d and growne thus
high, Now my soule is pomred out upon me. At the 15th verse he
sayd, Terrours pursued my seule as the mind; here he saith, my
soule is pomred out upon mee. This powring out of his soule upon
him, was not only a consequent, but an effect of that terrible pur¬
suite which was made aster his soule.
In the Original, there are two different words used in these
two places, both which wee, in our translation, render soule.
Tob used a very peculiar word in the former verse, to expresse
his soule by, calling it in strictnes of reading, his chiefe or
principal one; but in this verse he useth a word of a more large
and Common signification to the same purpose, which therefore
in Scripture is rendred under various notions.
First, Sometimes no more is intended by it then the breath
of a man; which is an effect of life; Mans breath (that is, his
life) is in his nestrils; He that hath breath in his nostrils, lives,
rand to have our breath in our nostrils, notes the frailtie of our
lives.

0159.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Boke ef IOB. Verf.16.

body.t: Secondly, The word imports not only breath, but life, which
is the spring of breath. God saith ( Job 2.6.) Behold he is in
thine hand, lut spare his life, or breath, (we render it soule.)
David praying for deliverance from his Enemy, useth this argu¬
ment, (Psal. 7. 2.) Least he teare my soule lihe a Lion, reming
it in pieces, while there is none to deliver. ¶It is not in the power
of all the Lions or tyrants, in the world to touch the soule of
man; when they have kild the body, they have no more to doe;
but when he saith, least they tear my soule, the meaning is, lest the
take away my life; As it he had sayd, They seck to destroy me,
they thirst after my blood, I see nothing else nill quench their bloody
thirst, Therefore O Lord deliver me. So’tis said of Rachel in tra¬
vell with child (Gen. 35. 18.) It came to passe as her soule wa¬
departing, ( for shee dyed) that is, as her lite was departing, or
as she was dying, that sue called his name Benoni.
Thirdly, The word notes any creature endued with a sensi¬
tive life. In which generall sence Moses gives it (Gen. 1.24.)
And God said, let the carth bring forth the living creature (or
soule) after his kind, cattel and creeping thing, &c.
Fourthly, “Tis put for the whole man, consisting of soule ard
body (Gen. 12. 5.) And Abram teoke Sarah his mife, and Lot
his Brothers son, and all the substance that they had gathered, and
the soules that they had gotten in Charan, and they ment forth,
xc.
Fifthly, It sometimes signifies a Carkasse, or a dead body,
a body from which the soule is departed ( Levit. 19. 28.) Te
hall not mabe any cutting in your flest for the dead, or for a soule.
We finde the word againe in that sence ( Numb. 5. 2.) Com¬
mand the children of Israel that they put out of the Campe every
leper, and every one that hath an issue, and mhosoever is defiled by
the dead. So ( Hag. 2.13.) Ifone that is uncleane by a dead bo¬
dy touch any of these, &c. It may seeme very strange that the
same word should signifie life and a dead body, yet it doth, for
this reason ( say some) chat we might remember that life and
soule belong to the dead bodyes of men, or that even a dead bo¬
dy shall be raised againe by the power of God to life, and re¬
married ( after that long separation) to the soule in the morn¬
ing of the resurrection.
Sixthiy, This xord imports appetite, defire, vill, luit, which.

0160.head: Chap.30. An Exposition upon the Book ef JoR. Verf.16.

body.t: are acts of the soule. ( Psal. 27. 12.) Deliver mee not ouer anto
the mill (or lust) of mine enemies. The word is, Deliver mee not
cver to the soule of mine enemies; that is, deliver mee not over to
such a soule as hath onely vill and lust, without reason to direct
either its resolutions or actions by. Solomon applyeth it also to
that inferiour faculty, sensuall appetite, (Prov. 23. 2.) uben
theu sittest to cate mith a ruler, confider diligently what is before
thee, and put a knife to thy tbroat, if thou be a man given to appetite,
if thou be a man that hast a soule, that is, a soule made up of or
Master'd by appetite. The Hebrew strictly taken is thus rendred,
If thou art a Master of the soule or appetite. And the text vould
run wel in that plaine sence, as if Solomon had fayd, If thou art a
Master of, or canst rule and command, thy soule or appetite, then
shew it by thy moderation in eating, or by checking thy appetite
when thou sittest at the rulers Table. But we render it, and so
doe most of the learned translaters, as a phrase signifying a man
very apt to be Master’d by his appetite. In which sence the word
is rendred againe (Pro. 22.24.) Mabe no friendship with an
angry man: the Hebrew is with a Master of anger, we render it
according to the scope and exigence of the place, mith an angry
man, that is, with a man who is apt to be Master’d and overcome
with anger, or (as we commonly expresse it) vith a man who
hath no command ot his passions. Thus in the Scripture first al¬
ledged, the text nece ssirates that meaning of the phrase, which
our translation holds out, if thou art a man given to ( soule or)
appetite: As if Solomon had sayd, If thou hast an appetite which
thou canst not vell rule, thou hadst need looke well to it at all
times, but then especially when thou sittest with the ruler. Ru¬
lers have full Tables, and many when they are at them, in stead of
putting a knife to their throates by abstinence, put a knife to their
throates by their intemperance, and so while they fill their bel¬
lyes, destroy their lives, and cut their oun throates. When men
are famisht with want of food, we usually say, their throates are
cut without a knife; and so are theirs who over-feed themsel ves.
But to returne to the poynt for which this passage in the Pro¬
verbes was instanc’d in; Namely, to shew that the word by which
tob expresseth his soule, fignifieth among other things, meere
will, lust or appetite.
When Tob saith, Ay soule is pemred out apon mee, we may
Firá,
take the word soule two wayes.

0161.head: Chap.30. An Exposstion upon the Book of JOB. Verf.

body.t: First, For life (my soule is pomred out upon mee) that is, I am
ready to dye; I am wasted, I am spent, my spirits are even gone,
I am neere expiring, my life is ready to be poured out as water
upon the ground, which cannot be gathered up againe.
Secondly, We may expound it by that which is the strength
of the soule, Courage and Cheatfulnesse under affliction; my
soule, that is, my spirit, my strengch, yea my patience, are all neere
spent and gone, exhausted and poured out; I have been so long
worried and wearied with these afflictions, that l can hold out no
longer. Thus the Lord made a gracious promise to his afflicted
people (Isa 57. 16) I will not contend for ever, neither will I
be alwayes wroth: for tue spirit sould faile before me, and the soules
mhich I have made; that is, the soules wbich I have made will be
even unmade, as to their joyes, comforts, and courage, they will
utterly fayle, or as Job saith, be powred out.
My soule is powred eut.
There is an Elegancy in that Expressi on (poured out) the word
is applyed to water, wine, or any liquid; and to poure out, in
Scripture, notes abundance, or the giving forth of much in quan¬
tity or degree. The Lord saich in that great and g orious pro¬
mise (pel 2. 28.) It shall come to passe in the latter dayes that I
nill powre out of my spirit upon all flesh; that is, Believers in those
latter dayes shall have plenty of the spirit; not dews and drops
only, distilling upon them, but showers and mighty raines, cven
flouds of the Spirit, both in gifts and graces. So that promise is
expressed by another Prophet, ( Isa. 44.3) I will powre water
unon him that is thirsty, and fluds upen the dry ground, (which is
thus explain'd in the latter part of the same verse) I wilt powre
my Spirit upon thy sesd, and my blessing upon thine eff-spring.
So that when Job saith (my soule is poured out) he would tell us
that he was abundant in those sorrowes and troubles of spirit,
his soule was so much poured out, that there was scarce any
thing, scarce a drop of his soule lest within. That's the difference
betueen God, powring out of himselse, and his pouring out the
creature,or the creatures pouring out it selfe. When God powrs
out himselfe, that is, bis gifts and blessings he poures out abun¬
dantly, and though he powres out so much as fils the creature,
yet hou much soever he poures out, he doth not at all empey

0162.head: Chap.30. Ax Expositim upon the Boake of JO 2. Vers.16.

body.t: himfelfe man wasteth and emptieth his own stocke by powring
out, but God doth net: man may poure out till nothing’s lest;
for his is but the fullnesse of a vessel, how full soever he is: but
God powres out as a fountaine, and therefore is alwayes full,
Tob migut well say, my soule is pomred out, his soule was once a
vessel or a cisterne sull of strength, life, livelines, Joy and Com¬
fort, but his long sufferings and afflictions had almost emptied
and drawne him dry to the very bottome. Ais all, or all his,
soule and all was powred out; He had onty so much soule left
him as would serve him to tell others, that he had scarce any
soule left, My soule is powred eut.
Yet further, this phrase of powring out, may beare a threefold
Consideration.
Fust, The Greeke Scholiast understands this effusion or pow¬
ring out, of the irresolution and unset lednes of Tobs mind, what
to doe, or what course to take for his own reliese in, or delive¬
rance from his troubles. When a man knows not where to pitch,
what to resolve on, his soule is (asit were) dissolved and pow¬
red out. And when a man comes to a setlednes of purpose in any
poynt, the severall powers of his soule are (upon the matter)
gathered up and knit together againe.
Secondiy, To poure out the soule, is in Scripture language,
to be much in prayer. As prayer is called in Scripture ihe lifting
up ef the foule to God ( Psal. 25. 1.) so the powring out of the
foule before God. When that much grieved and gracious wo¬
man Hannah was praying, Ely thought she had been distemper'd
with wine; How long milt thou be drunker? put away thy winc
from thec. The good woman answered, No my Lord, I am a
moman of a sorromfull spirit, I have drunk neither vine nor strorg
drinbe, but have powred out my soule before the Lord, (1 Sam. 1.
14.) that is, I have prayed, yea I have prayed much and ear¬
nestly. Prayer is a powring out of the soule, especially, earnest,
important, fervent prayer. So in the confession of sin, the soule
is poured out in sorrous, and in supplication for supply of wants,
the soule is powred out in desires, and in faith. Thus œe are ex¬
horted to pray at once in faith and fervency, (Psal.62. 8.)
Trust in him at all times, ye people pomre eut your hearts before
him; that is, pray to him, and pray to him abundantiy, pray to
him earnestly, let your soules goe forth in your supplications.

0163.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Rooke of I02. Verf. 16,

body.t: When David was in great distresse, he saith, (Psal. 142. 2.)
I powred out my Complaint before him, I shemed before him my trou¬
bles: that is, I prayed unto him with all my soule, or I prayed
my very foule unto him. ( Lament. 2. 18, 19.) Their heart
Cryed unto the Lord, &c. Arise, Cry out iu the night: in the be¬
giuning of the matches powre out thine heart like mater befere the
face of the Lord: lift up thy hands toward him. So then, prayet
may be called a powring out of the soule or heart to God, and
sit is so, for two reasons.
First, Because when Saints are in great trouble or straits of
any kind, then their hearts are enlarged, and they open their
Nhole mind to God, they keep nothing back: they tell him of
all their doubts, desires, hopes, feares sins, they tell him of all
their temptations, sorrows, and afflictions: when all comes out,
there is a pouring out of the heart.
Secondiy, It is called a powring out of the heart, not onsy
because of the abundance of matter uttered in prayer, but be
cause of the fervency and earnestnesse of the Spirit in prayer,
when prayer comes not forth droppingly, droopingly, sleepily,
dreamingly, or drousily, but with a mighty force, with strong
affections, like a flood or torrent, when ’tis a morhing or in¬
wrought prayer, then the soule is powred forth; Then we may be
sayd not only to pray much, but to be much in prayer. It is an
easie matter to powre out words in prayer, but it is a hard mat¬
ter, yea without the Spirit an impossible matter, to poure out the
soule, the heart before the Lord in prayer; yea there are many
that powre out tears before God, and yet povre not out their
hearts and soules before God in prayer. In this sence, doubtles,
Iobs soule was poured out upon him. The Apostle James (Chap.
13.) gives this direction; Is any man afflicted? let him pray.
Tob was not only a man afflicted, but much and greatly afflict ed
therefore, surely, he (being God) did not only pray, but he prayed
much and greatly in his affliction.
Thirdly, This phrase of powring out the soule, may import
a neernes to death, or a giving up of the ghost. A dying man
poureth out his soule; Thus the woman spake in her petition to
David for the returne of Abspalom, (2 Sam. 14. 14.) We must
necdi dy, and be as mater spilt upon the ground woich cannot be ga¬
thered up againe. The body is lihe an empty vessel when once the

0164.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Bock of JOE. Verf. 16.

body.t: soule is departed, or spilt like water upon the ground. So the
word is used (Lam. 2. 12.) Where the Prophet describing the
extreame famine in Jerusalem saith, The children and the suck¬
lings smoon in the stretts, they cry to their mothers, where is Corne
and wine? (O what a sad Condition were they in, when they
said, where is Corne and mine?) when they smooued as the wound¬
ed in the streets of the Citie, when their soule was poœred out into
their mothers bosome. Poore Children cryed out, O where's
bread? We at this day have bread enough, and to spare, (blessed
be God) but it was not so with Jerusalem in that day; O mo¬
mother u here's wine? wherés bread cryed the poore children?
and then they swooned even as the wounded in the streets, and
were ready to powre eut their soules into their mothers bo¬
some; that is, they were ready to dye and expire for want of
bread. Thus also Jobs soule was powred out, he was ready to
swoon and to dye; so he tells us uith much livelines and quick¬
nesse both of speech and spirit (Chap. 17.1.) Ay breath is cor¬
rupt, my dayes are extiuct, the graves are ready for me. All which
expressions doe buc reach this interpretation of his complaint in
the present text, My soule is powred eut npon mee.
Now though the two former expositions of these words, as
they import; first, the uosetlednes and unresolvednes of soba spi¬
rit what to dot, or secondly, his set lednes and utmost resolution
co vent his soule in prayer, that God would both shew him what
to doe, and helpe him to doe it in that extremity, (though. I say,
both these openings of the text carry a faire respect to it) yet
conceave this last or third most proper and sutable to it, And
therefore
Hence note.
Man is a poore fraile creature, a britle creature, he quichl
fayles and faints under his burden.
IfGod doe but touch him, and leave him under the hand of
an affliction, present ly he feels his very soule ready to be powred
out upon him. The flesh of man, that is, his naturall estate as man,
is grasse, that is, like grasse, the grasse let alone will quickly wi¬
ther, but usually the grasse is cut or eaten doune before it wi¬
thers many are cropt in their greenenes, or in the height and
flourish of outward prosperity, their soule is powred out.

0165.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Book of IOR. Verf. 16.

body.t: Man at his best estate is altogether vani y. Which is both ex¬
plained and urged further in the words following.
The dayes of affliction have taken hold upon mes.
Or, affliction dayes.
Man hath his dayes of Consolation, and his dayes of afflicti¬
on, his dayes of peace, and his dayes of trouble, his good dayes,
and his bad dayes, in this world. The text may be rendred ei¬
ther Tue dayes of affliction (as we) or, as others, the dayes of bu¬
mil ation, the dayes of pressing domne, the dayes of laying lon, (All
this the word signifies) these sad and darke dayes have taken
hold upon mec.
To tabe hold, is properly the act of a living Creature, of man
especially, when he seizeth, apprehends, or attacheth any thing
or person. And it notes not bare holding, but holding fast and
sure; Mr. Broughton translates, Affliction dayes hove caughi met;
As if he had sayd, I had hope to escape them, but they have been
too nimble for me; they have caught me, as the hound doth tbe
hare, or a snare the bird. The vulgar translation saith, The dayes
of affliction have p ssest mee: Holding notes Having and posses¬
fing. As inour Law-formes of Conveyance or Lease, To have
and to hold, is to pofsesse either for terme of yeares, or for ever.
Thus Job speaks as it he had been wholly delivered into the hand
of affliction, and were fully possessed by it; or as if he were under
the dominion, rule, and pouer of affliction, as bis Lord and Ma¬
Rer. The Seaventy render it shortly; The dayes of affliction bave
mesi they have me in their pouer, I am bound under them:
our reading atraines the same sence, The dayes ef affliction have
taben hold upon mee.
Hence note.
Affliction hath its day.
The dayes of affliction are dayes appoynted, dayes set out by
God. As there are dayes wherein Gou uill have us afflict our
selves, ( Esay 22. 13.) In that day the Lord called to mourning,
and to fasting, and unto sackeleth, and unto asbes, that is, The provi¬
dences of God to his people in that day had that vovre in them,
and did ( as it were) call aloud upon them, to mourne, to fast,

0166.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Booke of JOE. Verf.16.

body.t: to repent in sackeloath and ashes. Fasting dayes, are selse-af¬
flicting dayes, or as Moses calls them ( Levit. 16.29.) Soule¬
afficting dares. Now (I say) As God appoints us dayes where¬
in to affl ct our selves; so God appoynts dayes, wherein he will
afflict us. All the dayes of our lives are measured or set out unto
us, and they are of two sorts; First, Affliction dayes; Secondly,
Consolation dayes, as was shewed before. Sorrow and joy take up
and divide allour dayes between them. The life of man is a kind
of Chicquer morbe, there’s white and black, and more black then
white, that’s onr present state. Jacob said of the day es of his life,
They mere few, and they were evill, ( Gen. 47. 2.) As his dayes
were not many considered in themielves, and few compared with
some of his ancestors, so they were evill with respect to his mani¬
fold afflictions; and he gave the denomination of his few dayes
by evill, because the most or major part of his dayes were in that
sence evill. And usually the troubles of our life are most, they
are more and greater then our Comforts, they out-number and
out-weigh them as to outwards. The Saints indeed have inward
Joy in their outward sorrowes and tribulations, but their tribu¬
lations and sorrowes appeare more, or are more visible then
their joyes.
Secondly, In that he calls them dayes of affliction,
Observe,
Affictions may Continue long, or a great while, not enli for¬
day, but for dares.
Though that be a truth (Psal. 30.5.) Sorrow endures for a
night, bat soy cometh in the morning; The Lord often makes such
fuddaine changes, yet we are not to understand it strict ly, as if
this were the meaning, that they who have sorrow in the even¬
ing, shall at the next break of day have Joy, or, that as soone as
the day returnes, their comforts shall returne too.But the mean¬
ing is this, after sorrow they shall have Joy, as fure as the morn¬
ing followes the night. A righteous mans troubles, tryalls and
sorrowes may abide many naturall dayes and nighes with him;
he may fiod (as fob did, Chap. 7.3.) himselfe made to pessesse
moneths of vanitie, and not only a night of wearinesse, but (as he
there spenhes) wearisome niglus eppointed to him. The scope and
meaning of that text in-ihe Rsalme is only this, The righteous

0167.head: Chap.30. An Exposition upon the Bocke ef JOB. Verf.

body.t: fhall have a succession of Joy after sorrow, their sorrow shall not
be perpetuall, nor abide for ever. As the rod of the wiched shall
not (Psal. 125. 3.) so God will not let his rod rest upon the
lot of the righteous. Though their night of sorrow Continue
many dayes and weeks, yea moneths and yeares, yet they shall
have a morning of Joy. Solomon saith of the meere worldly man,
(Eccl. 5. 17.) All his dayes he eateth in darknes, and he hath
much sorrow and wrath mith his sicknes. And as through his vexa¬
tious cares in getting and keeping the things of the world, he
deprives himselfe of all comfort in the use of them all the dayes
of his life, so when he dyeth, he goes to the generation of his fa¬
thers, they (that is, both he and they) suall never see light,
(Psal. 49. 19.) Thus in this life a wicked mans night of trouble
runs through all his dayes, for all his daves he eateth in darknes,
through the darknes of his own spirit ard practice; and the life
to come, (through the rlghteous judgement of God) will be to
him as one everlasting night, for he shall never see (that is, en¬
joy) light. But heres the comfort of the righteous, that if their
affliction dayes are many, yet they are but dayes of affl ction,
they shall not feele an eternity of affliction. Saiuts have afflicti¬
on dayes, The miched have an Eternitie of affliction; no affliction
shall enter into the Eternity of Saints, The whole eternity of the
wicked shail be affliction. When once believers have done uith
dayes, chey have done with sorrowes all temoshall be wiped
not only off from but out of their eyes: The very spring of teares
fhali be dry ed up for ever, and they delivered not only from
actuall sorrow, but from the possibility of it. Tis but uhile our
lives are measured by dayes, that the dayes of the godly are
darkned with clouds or nights of trouble.
Thirdly, In that Tob speanes of affliction dayes taking hold
of him.

de ne usaroani"
Affliction will come in its time, in its season or day.
When the day appointed gomes, affliction vill come. Af¬
Hiction dayes will as certainly come, as our birth. day came, or as
our death-day is coming, and there is one and the same reason of
all, even because they are all appointed. All the changes of our
dayes, our dayes of Joy and oùr daves of foron, our feafrdayca
COIR TTA

0168.head: Chap.30. An Exposition upon the Bok ef JOR. Verf.16,

body.t: and our fast dayes; The dayes wherein wee eate the fat and
drink the sweet; and the dayes wherein we drinke teares, and
feed upon ashes, are under an unchangeable appoyntment:
there’s no avoyding them, they uill come, they will take hold of
us, and possesse us. David saith of the wicked man, (Psal.37.13.)
Tee Lord shall laugh at bim; Why? for he seeth that his day is
Coming: the wicked man pleaseth himfelfe in his prosperous
condition, then he laughs and rejoyceth; and then the Lord
laughs at him. None have such cause to mourne as they, at uhom
God laughs. God laughs at the wicked man, and why ? because
he sees a day of blacknes, a day of Clouds and darknes, a day of
gloomines and thick darknes ( as the Prophet Joel speakes) thit
is, a day of great trouble coming justly upon him: the Lord sees
that a blacke day is Coming upon the wicked man, which will
turne all his plots against the righteous ( in the hoped successe of
which he reloyced) upon his oun head. Now as some ungodly
men have specially appoimed black dayes coming upon them in
this world for ruine and destruction; so the godly have dayes of
affliction appointed them for tryall and correction: Nor doth
the best of Saints know how soone such a day may come upon
him: Now it is a day of health with a godly man, but a day of
sicknes may quickly come upon him; now it is a day of riches,
but a day of poverty may quickly come upon him;now it is a day
of credit or honour in the world, but a day of disgrace and re¬
proach from the world may be coming, and quickly come upon
him. It is said (Psal.37. 18.) The Lord bnoweth the dayes of the
upright; That is, he knowes what kind of dayes or times they
fhall live in and passe thorough. He knoues not only what na¬
turall, but what providentiall dayes fhall goe over their heads,
what changes they shall be in, or meet with while they are pas¬
sing through this world. Looke what troubles the Lord knowes
will come upon any day, they wisl come at their day as sure as the
day cometh.
Fourthly, job doth not only fay that dayes of affliction came
apon him, but they tooke hold upon him.
Hence note,
wuen affliction comes, it tabes bold, it tabes fast hold, and mil
nt le ue ge til Gadgivut leavr.

0169.head: Chap.30. An Exposition upon the Book of JOB. Verf. 17.

body.t: Affliction doth not only strike but sticke and take hold by or¬
der from God; It cannot touch us without commission, and
when commission'd it vill tahe hold, fast hold ofus and will not
let us goe. It is said Concerning the Heathenish Idolatrous
Princes and people of those lands which the Children of Israel
were to possesse; Tht people shal heare, and be afraid: sorrows
shall take hold ef the Inbabitants of Palestina, (Exod.15.14.) The
report of what God had done against the Egyptians, made those
remoter Nations tremble, and sorrow tooke them prisoners long
before they were slaine by the sword. And what the Scripture
speakes in that place of the wicked and uncircumcised Nations,
The same David saith of himselfe (Psal. 116.3.) The sorrows
of death Compassed mee about: and the paines of hell gat hold upon
mee. The originall word is, found mee, as we put in the Margin;
they found him, as an Officer or Sergeant finds a person that he
is sent out to attach or arrest, who no sooner finds him, but he
takes hold of him, or (as we say) take him into Custody. And
when Warrants are sent out to take a man, who keeps out of the
way, the returne is, Non est Inventus, the man is not found, he
cannot be met with or taken hold of. Davids paines quiçkly
found him, and having found him they gat hold of him, fuch
finding is so certainly and suddainly folloued with taking hold,
and holding uhat is taken, that one word in the Hebrew serves
to expresse both acts. When God sends out troubles and afflicti¬
ons as Officers to attach any man, they will find him, and find¬
ing him, they will take hold of him. The dayes of affliction uill
take hold, There's no striving, no strugling with them, no getting
out of their hands. These divine Purse vants wil neither be persua¬
ded nor bribed to let you goe, till God speake the word, till God
say deliver him, release him: Till God send his uarrant to have
the Prison dore opened, and the poore soule set free from afflicti¬
on, he hath no reliefe, no helpe for it.
Affliction having thus taken hold of fob, he tells us in the
next verse, how hardly it used him.
Vers. 17. Ay bones are pierced in the nighte season: and m
siuens tate no rest.
These words are a description of fobi bodily sicknes (accord¬
ing to the letter of the text) such is the malignity of some vio-

0170.head: Chap.30. An Expofition mpon the Booke of JOR. Vers.17.

body.t: lent diseases, that they not only corrode the flesh, but enter into
the very bones; my bones are pierced. The word properly signifies
strength, And because bones are the strongest part of a man,
(bones are to the body, as Timber rafters, posts and pillars to the
house, the strength of it) therefore our bones and our strength are
significantly expressed by the same word. Pob speakes of his
bones, to shew that the strength of his body was invaded and
chaken, and by his bones, he intends his whole body in the best
strength of it; which ( some conceive) he callech his bones for
this reason also, because his body uas so wasted and consumed,
that he had nothing lest but bones, or he was nothing, but, anit
were, a shaliton or pack of bones.He could scarce say, his flesh
was pierced, he having little or none to pierce. Tob usech the
same Elegancy in setting forth or aggravating the extremity of
his sufferings (Chap.7. 15.) My soule chuseth death rather then
life; so we translate, but the Hebrew is, rather then my benes;
As if he had said, I had rather die then live in a body wasted to
skin and bones; It is more eligible with me to lay my boues downe iu
the grave, tloen to beare them up and donne xpon the carth, I live
mith a company of bare bones, and it were better for me te die then
to live in the flesn and have nont, or te live xith consaming pining
dying flesh, Thus here, My bones are pierced, my paines and sor¬
rows haye worne me to the bones.
Yet further and more particularly, uhen Job saith; Ay benet
are pierced within me in the night season. There are foure things
in the words of this complaint, which exceedingly highten his
sorrowes, and might wel give him cause to say, that dayes of af¬
fliction had taben hold upon bim.
First, In that he had not only paine in his flesh, but in his ve¬
ry bones. When in Scripture, the bones are spoken of as being in
paine, it notes very great dolour and paine; for as the bones lie
within the flesh, and are hard to come at, or to be reached by
paine, so they are very hard and may seeme impregnable against
all paine: When, therefore paine pierceth the bones, it must
needs be a very sharpe and powerfull paine. Hence that grievous
cry, ( Pfal. 31 10) Heare O Lord, bave mercy upon mee; for
my life is spent mith griefe, and my yeares mith sighing: my-strength
faileth because of mine Iniquity, aud my bones are censumed; that
is, my forrow is no common forrow, 'cis great and deepe, it pier

0171.head: Chap. 30. An Exposttion upon the Booke of JOE. Verf. 17.

body.t: eeth my bones. Thus king Hez ebiah describes his extream sick¬
nesse (Isn? 38. 13.) I rechoned till morning, that as a Lion so wilt
he break all my bones; nor that he thought God would indeed
crush his bones, but thereby he uould set out the violence of his
sicknesse, which he made full account would make an end of him
before the morning were over or at an end, even as when a feirce
hunger bitten Lion teares the flesh and cracks the bones of a
poore sheepe or lambe. And thus Elihu describes his sick man,
(Chap. 33. 19) He is chastened with paine upon his bed, aud the
multitude of his bones nith strong paine; That is, his whole body,
or all his bones are chastned, and heis pained in every ovnt and
part of his body. The breaking of the bones, and troubie upon
the bones, import not only the forest sufferige of the body, but
ot the soule also. When Dauia would tell us how eacredingiy
he was grieved sor his sinne, he prages (Psal. 518) Mute me
to heart j'y and gladnes that the bunes mhich thou nast broken may
rejoyce. When we breaxs the commandements of God by sin¬
ning 'tis no marvaile (and when’tis with Godly forrow to re¬
pentance’tis a mercy) if God breake our bones with sorrow for
our sins, that is, if he bring us to the deepest sence of his displea¬
sure, and of our own folly for our sins; even as if he had broken
our bones upon the wheele, or dif jognted them with a racke.
Heart breakings are more painfull then bone- breakings, and are
therefore expressed by breaking the bones, because that to sence
is most painsull. David prayes againe in the same Rhetoricall
straine ( Pfal. 6. 2.) O Lord heale me, for my boues are vexed.
It was the healing of his soule which he prayed for, and the trou¬
ble which he had for wounding it, he calls the vexing of his
bones. ( Psal. 102. 3.) Afy dayes are Consumed libe smoke, and
my bones are burnt up as an hearth. So in that prophecy of
Christs sorrowes. ( Psal.22. 14.) All my bones were out ef joynt.
(Psal. 32.3.) While I hept silence my bones waxed old, &c. What
doe all these texts speake, but the sorrow of a soule pained under
the apprehensions of divine wrath for sin, either our own, or of
others, as the case of Christ was.
So on the contrary, when God is said to make the bones fatt,
it notes mueh mercy, or mercy all over. The Prophet puts this
among the promises to them that keep a fast Indeed (I/a. 58.11.)
The Lord shall guide thee Continually, and satitfie thy soule in

0172.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Book of JOB. Vers.17.

body.t: drought, and make fat thy bones; As if he had sayd, Feare not
leanenes or wasting of thy body with fasting, for God will make
fat thy bones, that is, he will comfort thee, and fill thee uith Joy
both of soule and body. And when the Lord would expresse his
greatest care over any one of his people, tis said. He koepeth all his
bones, not one of them is broken, (Psal.34.20) When all our boue¬
praise God (as David said his should, Psal.35 10.) and say, Lord,
wbo is like unto thee! O how wel is it with us? and when all our
bones mourne before God, who can tell how ill’tis with us? and
hence those things which have the greatest efficacy in affl cting
and refreshing, or doe most exquisitely affect the sense, whethes
with paine or pleasure, are compared to oyle which pierceth the
bones. There’s the oyle of gladnesse, (Psal. 45. 7.) and there's
the oyle of sorrow, (Psal. 109. 18.) As he Clotheth himselfe
mith cursing, so let it come upon him, let it come into his bowels like
water, and lite oyle into bis benes: The curse soakes into the bones
like oyle, not to supple and strengthen them as oyle doth, but
to vexe and torment them, as a curse doth. The curse enters the
bones like oyle, secretly and powerfully, but it workes like it
selfe sorrowfully and painefully.
Secondly, To aggravate his affliction, Job doth not say this
or that bone of mine was pierced, but my bones are pierced, that is,
all my bones. If a man have an ache in one of his bones, if he
have but one broken bone, or but one bone out of joynt, he will
find paine enough: but uhen all his bones are broken, he is no¬
thing but paine. Job laments that all his bones were pierced, as
if they had been but one bone. The original is more cleare to
this sence, which may be thus rendered, Every one of my bones art
shagen; a verbe plural being joyned with a Noune singular, is di¬
stributive to every one in particular. Jobs fle sh was so smitten
with soares, that his uhole body looked like one continued soare;
and his bones were so universally pierced, as if indeed he had
but one bone to be pierced. He had not the bone of a little toe
or finger free.
Thirdly, Tob doth not say, all his bones were pained, but they
vere all pierced; some read it, broken: the Seaventy render, my
bones are burnt; As if he had sayd, I feele a fire in my bones,
which sucks and dries up the moysture and marrow of them.
The piercing of the bones must needs be a most gricvous paine,

0173.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Book of I0E. Vers, 17.

body.t: for though the bone it selfe hath no sense, yet the membranes
and mufles that are next the bones, are of a more exquisite sense,
then the flesh in any part or member of the body. Therefore to
pierce the bones, cannot but cause the greatest bodily paine suffe¬
rable or imaginable. When the Apostle would set forth the sad
and sore troubles both of body and soule, which they wbo mill
be rich draw upon themselves, he saith (1 Tim. 6. 10.) Ther
have pierced themselves through mith many sorromes.
Fourthly, When Job saith, Ay bones are pierced
In the night season.
There's another aggravation of his paine and griefe. These
words, in the night season, fhew more then the long continuance
of his paine, even the uncessantnesse of his paine. As if he had
said, The night which usually gives refresting to man, was so farre
from afforaing me any, that then I nas mest restlesse. It hightens
our affliction, when it comes or stayes upon us in that season
which is appointed for repose. Some can sleepe away much of
their paine and sorrow, but Teb had sorrow in the night, in stead
of sleepe. Slèepe is the best medicine for wearines, it conquers
our cares, and gives at least some truce from the assaults of sor-
row. The labour and travell of the day weares out, spends and
wasts our strength, but in the night we rest, and recruit or re¬
paire our strength againe. Now if the night be spent in tortu¬
ring paines, how doth our strength (pend? to what a Condition
is such a poore soule brought, whose very bones take no rest in
the night season! Here’s a fourth aggravation ot jobs affliction;
First, it was in his bones; Secondly, in all his bones; Thirdly, it
pierced his bones; and Fourthly, it was upon him in the night
season; when others went to rest, he tooke none; His paines
stayed upon him day and night. Thus the lamenting Prophet
labours to ketpe the sorrows of the Captive lewes awake ( Lam.
2.18,19.) Let teares run downe like a river day and night, give
tby selfe no rest let not the apple of thine eye cease, arise cry out in¬
the night, in the beginning of the waiches poure eut thine hiart lik¬
mater before the face of the Lord.
Further, V hereas we seeme to understand that his paine was
it, which pierced his bones, some read it thus, He hath pierced my¬
bones, that is, the Lord hath commanded these dayes of afflicti¬

0174.head: Chap. 30. An Expofition upon the Booke ef JOB. Vers.1

body.t: on, or the affliction of these dayes to pierce my bones, even in
the night season.
Againe, Others thus; The night pierceth my bones; The let¬
ter of the Original is clearest for this reading: As if he had sayd,
I feele more paine in the night then in the day. The day paineth
my flesh, but the night pierceth my bones. ( Mr. Broughton tran¬
stites,) The night pierceth my benes from me; we say, in me, The
Hebreu is, From above me; as ascribing all his paines to God,
who had afflicted him from heaven, or from on high.
And my sinews tabe no rest.
Some read my nerves, others, my veines, many my pusses tabe
no rest : The Hebrew is, They lie not downe, or slcepe not. The
pulse signifies the nature ot the disease: Physicians learne much
of the state of the whole body by the pulse. Now, saith fob, my
pulse, my sineus take no rest. When the pulse beats high, and
quicke, as if it were in a rage, then certainly the patient is in a
very great distemper. Now, The pulse useth to move more tem¬
perately in the night, when the heate is drawne into the inward
parts, yet Job (it seemes) by reason of his great inflammation,
and the accutenes of his disease, found his pulse as quicke in the
hight as in the day, and the pulse being so restlesse, he could
take no rest.
There is yet another reading, which I shall touch a little, and
so shut up the exposition of this verse. For whereas wee say,
my sinems, that saith, they that eat mee take no rest : Which is ex¬
plained two wayes.
First, For the wormes or lice which bred in his putrified
flesh, which we may suppose as troublesome as the malice of thé
Devill could make them: As if he had said, The vermine mhich
are fenerated in my mounds and soares, take no rest, nor mill they
suffer me to tabe any, they lie almayes biing, and working, and
gnaving, as if they would eate me up. Hom then can I tete
Secondly, Others, by these Eaiers, understard his i&-willess
and detractors. They eat up a man, who slander anc speake evill
of him, these eat up a mans credit, or good name. And these (saith
Job according to this exposition) give mee no rest; I am conti¬
nually followed hy men, ahofe tongues are fes on file, víeia

0175.head: Chap.30. An Exposition upon the Booke ef JOB. Verf.

body.t: malice is restlesse; no wonder then if my reputation be smoakt
and smother’d, scorcht & almost consumed to ashes, among those
who know or beleeve no more nor better of mee, then these men
report, who are alwayes reporting evill of me. They that thus
eate me, who would eate up and devoure my honour and inno.
cency at a morsel, are hungry still, and will not give over eating;
They that eate me tabe no rest. This is an undeniable truth, de¬
tractors eat, yea swallom up the reputation ef the ixnocent But I
shall not stay upon these readings, which are but farre fetcht and
forraine conjectures.
I close and conclude with our own translation, wbich plainly
holds forth, that Tob was now come to the urmost strecch and
Extremity of affliction, His bones mere pierced mitbin him in the
nigot season, and his sinews took ne rest. He had a continuall fe¬
ver, a burning heate feeding upon the vitalls of his body, while
his soule wes powred out upon him.
Hence note.
Tue best of men are subject io the morst extreamities, both ef
soule and body.
Tub was not only afflicted, but extreamely afflicted, not only
was his body smitten but his soule, and not his soule only but his
body. He hath bis load both upon flesh end Spirit, both with¬
out and within, or as the Apostle expr sseth it in his own case,
(2 Cor. 7. 5.) Without nere figótings, within were snares.
At the 15 th verse, we read of terrours pursuing his soule; and at
the 16th ( he saith) bis soule nas pomred out upon him, affliction
dayes tooke hold of him; in this 17th verse, His bones were pier¬
ced in the night season, and his sinens tooke no rest. What could
be added ( and doubtlesse if Satan had knowne of any thing he
would have added it) to make him yet more miserable! There
was but one thing more ( and that Satan could not adde) the
wrath of God mingled with his sufferings, which might have
added to his misery, and yet he had a share, as to present appre¬
hensions, of that also. Now, when paines of body, aud terrours of
soule meet together, then’tis full sea with affliction; then’tis an af¬
fliction day indeed. Though the body be extreamly afflicted and
pained, yet if the soule be free; if there be no darts of darknesse
sticking chere, a man may beare up with it, and abide it; as Sole¬

0176.head: Chap.30. An Exposition upen the Bort ef JOE. Verf.17.

body.t: mon tells us, (Pro. 18. 4.) The spirit of a man xill sustaine hir
I firmities: that is, the sicknesses and weaknesses, the paines and
troubles which fall upon his outward man. Though a man have
many sores and sorrows upon his flesh, yet he maybe borne up
by the strength of his spirit under them all. For though I like not
at all those vaine opinions of some ancient Philosophers, who
held and pretended to maintaine, That the paines of the body
were nothing to the soule, or that the soule was not at all af¬
flicted with or concern’d in them; yet this is a noble solid truth,
that the soule being serene and free, will, to admiration, support
the body, with a patient and insuperable resolution, under the
greatest body ly paines and pressures. And if a man having his
spirit wounded, hath yet his body and world ly estate untoucht,
this is some kinde of ease or reliefe to him, though (I confesse)
a very small one; but when the mind is troubled, and the body
diseased, when at once the spirit of a man is wounded, and all
outuard comforts scatter’d, who can tell the sadnesse of that
mans condition! yet as all these evills possibly may, so they of.
ten actually have met and center’d in the same man, and he wor¬
thily reckoned among the best of men.
Let them therefore Consider the goodnesse of God, who
though they have affl ction dayes of many kindes, yet have not
affliction dayes of both or of all kinds:As few have ever attained
Jobs graces, so few have ever felt Jobs tryalls, either as to kind
and number, or as to degree and measure at the same time. It
may be your bodyes are sickly and pained, but are you made a
heape of bones? are your bones pierced? are your sinews rest¬
lesse? or if your affliction pierceth to the bones, yet are your
spirits wounded? is the peace of your soules broken? if you
have quietnes there, and all be wel within, you are within a little
of well. Tis sparing mercy when our affliction dayes leave some¬
what whole and untoucht, but’tis great mercy when in affliction
dayes our best part, our soule is left whole and untoucht; Tis
sparing mercy when all sorts of sorrowful evils come not at once,
or alltogether, especially when ( though we have many, yet) we
are alltogether freed from the evills of inward terror, and of à
troubled conscience, which are worst of all.

0177.head: Chap.30. An Exposition upon the Book of IO B. Verf. 18.

body.t: Ey the great force of my disease, is my garment chan¬
ged: it bindeth me about as the collar of my coat.
He hath cast me into the mire, and I au become like
dust and ashes.
I ery unto thee, and thou doest not hear me: I stand
up, and thou regardest me not.
N the former verse Job shewed both the extremity and un¬
T cessantnesse of his sicknesse; Hu bones mere pierced in the
night season, and his sinems took no rest. In this 18 h and in the 19th
verse, he furcher prosecutes the same sad argument, adding that in
the zoth which made it yet more sad, the remedilessness of it.
I cry unto thee, aud thou doest not heare me: I stand up, and thou
regardest me not. I am left forlorne to sinke or swimme, it bootes
me not to call for helpe, for I finde none, I am neither heard nor
helped.
Vers. 18. By the great force of my discase, i my garment chan¬
ged: it bindeth me about as the collar of my coate.
Those words, my disease, are not exprest in the Hebrew, and
therefore the text hath a twofold rendring by way of supply.
First, Some referring it unto God, read the text thus, By the
greatnes of the force or power ( that is, of God in afflicting me
ù my garment changed; And’tis a truth, that although God af-
flicteth his own people in measure, and doth not suffer his wl ole
displeasure to arise against them, yet he puts forth force and
pouer in the afflicting of his own people, as well as in destroying
of the wicked, or his utter enemies.
But secondly, wee and severall others, ( referring this effect to
his disease, which also was from God, as Job acknowledged, and
so both readings meete in one sence) render, by the great force of
my diseafe, is my garment changed. Diseases are our weaknesses,
and they weaken us, yet they are of great force or power and
therefore force may wel be ascribed to them. Some diseases ap¬
peare but littie, and worke slowiy, or lingringly, other diseases

0178.head: Chap.30. An Expofition upon the Bocke of JOR. Verl.18.

body.t: risé high, worke fiercely, and appeare in power; they have a
power in them, an irrefistible power, they come, like an armed
man, and then (as pob speakes) by their great force, they make
great changes. The force of a discase beares downe, yea beates
downe the force of the body, and casteth it first on the bed, and
then into the grave, No man is able to stand before the force of
diseases. Mighty Gyants, even the mightiest sons of Anake
have been overthrowne by them, such is their force; They who
have been too strong for all men, may quickly mecte with theit
match, and feele a disease too strong for them. By the great force
of my disease ( saith fob)
is my garment changed.
As the disease had an effect upon his body; so his body had
an effect upon his garment. But is it not strange that Job under
a deadly disease should complaine about his garment As if a man
that hath received a stabb with a dagger, or is thrust through the
body with a sword, should thinke rather of the hole that is made
in his coate, then of the wound which is made in his flesh: yet
thus Job speakes, By the great force of my disease, is my garment
changed; He doth not say my body is weakned and changed, or
I am brought to deaths-doore but, my garment ir changed; yet
while he speakes of his garment, he meanes more then his gar¬
ment, when he saith, My garment is changed, he intends the
change of his whole body which wore that garment onlyto
shew how great a charge it wrougnt upon his body, he tells us of
a change upon his very garment. As if he had said, The lorts
that are upon my body run continually, and have changed net only
my garment of flesb, but the garment which covers my flesh. O con¬
sider in mhat a pichle I am, mho have so vehement a disease brouen
out upon my body, that you may see it in my garment. Judge, I pray,
mhat a change my poore body hath suffered br the change of my Gar¬
ment. And his garment might be changed in a double respect.
First, In respect of the colour of it, his garment was (asit
were) new died in the gore and filth that issued from his ulce¬
rous soares it vras once a pure and faire garment, but then pol¬
luted, and (as some give the illustration ) his garment had put en
another garment. His garment was covered over uith that loath¬
some purulent matter, uhich was digested in and flowed out of

0179.head: Chap. 30. Ax Exposition upon the Booke ef JOR. Verf. 18.

body.t: those boiles and botches with which Satan (having obtained
leave from God) smote him from the sole of his foote unto his
crewne, (Chap. 2.7.
Secondly, Wee may take these words not as implying a
change upon his garment, but his change of garments. In which
sence the word is used (1 Kings 22. 30) where; the king of Is
rael said unto Jehoshaphat, I mil disguise my selfe and enter into
the battel; that is, I will change my habit, or pnt off that royall
apparrel which I usually weare as a King, and put on such as
shall not signifie who or what I am. A disguise is most usually
made by change of garments; though we often change our gar¬
ments, and not to disguise our selves. Now, when Jub saith,
By the great force of my discase, is my garment changed; his mean¬
ing may be this; My disease is so effensive both to my selfe and
others, that I am forced to shist or change my garments often.
Change of Garments is a refreshing to the body, but to be ne¬
cessitated to change our garments, that we may keepe our selves
sweet and cleane is a signe of a noysome ly diseased and putrified
body. Surely in this sence Tub had cause enough to say, By the
great force of my disease, ie my garment changed. Hence take two
Cautions.
First, Boast not ef your bodilz strength er force. There is no
standing before the face of a disease. As the men of Samaria said
concerning Jenu (2 Kings 10. 4) Behold tmo kings stood not be¬
fore him, bow then can me stard? Thus any man may lay concern¬
ing any strong sicknesse or disease, behold no king no man of
might was ever able to stand before it how then can I? Ler not
the strong man boast of his strength, for as bodyly strength is a
thing of so low a forme, that it is not worth the boasting in,
how long so ever it continueth in its best perfection, so it is a
thing of no long continuance: Though a mars hight be as the
Cedars of Lebanon, and his ftrer gth as the Oakes of Bashan, yet
the force of a disease will pull him downe, or roote him up;
And as it may doe so to any strong man, so usually it doth so to¬
thole soonest who trust in or boast of their strength.
Secondly, Boast not ef your garments Be not proud of your
apparrell, God can send you a sore that shall change the colour
and staine the beauty of them let them who change their gar¬
ments osten in wantonnesse and delicacy, or for vaine ostenrati¬

0180.head: Chap.30. An Expofition upon the Bock of JO B. Verf. 18.

body.t: on, remember, and tremble while they remember, that God can
make them change their garments for the very stench, and noy¬
somnesse of them; He can give prison-garments, instead of pride¬
garments: and sick bed-garments, instead of feasting-garments.
As he gracioussy gives the garments of praise for the spirit of hea¬
vinesse tothe meeke and humble, ( Isa. 61.3.) so he righte¬
oussy gives the garment of heavinesse to those who have a spi¬
rit of pride, or a proud spirit. Take heed you abuse not your
goodly costly cloathing and garments, as a flag of vanity, lest
you provoke the Lord to cloath you with raggs or filthy gar¬
ments. When Joshua the High-Priest mas cloat hed with filthy gar¬
ments, and stood before the Angel ( that is, Christ in the vision,
Zech.3.3.) we read in the Ath verse, how He (that is, Christ the
Angel) ansmered and spake unto those that stood before him, saying,
Tabe away the filthy garments from him. And unto him he said, 1
have caused thine iniquity to passe from thee, and I will cloath thet
with change of raiment. As Christ in rich mercy takes away the
filthy garments of his people, both of sin and misery or afflicti¬
on, ( such were those with which Jushua was cloathed) and gives
them change of raiment, that is, pardon through his blood and
righteousnesse, as also outward peace and prosperity. So Christ
in much wrath takes away the pompous garments, the purple
and fine linnen, with which the wicked either men or women arc
cloathed, ( themselves being cloathed with wickednesse) and
gives them fisthy garments; or as another Prophet speakes,
Isa. 3. 24.) It comes to passe that in stead of sweet smel, there is
a stench, and in stead of a girdle a rent, and in stead of wel set hayre
baldnes, and in stead of a stomacher a girding mith sackeloath, and
burning in stead of beauty.
The vulgar translation saith ( as inthe former verse) Througb
the multitude efithem is my garment consumed; That is, The mul¬
titude of lice or vermine that breed in my garment, is so great
that my garment is changed, or consumed, and even eaten up by
them. As Jobs sicknes possibly brought this change of his gar¬
ment upon him; so the sin of many bath certainly doneit; They
who through pride would not suffer the least spot or dust upon
their garments, have had their garments, yea and their skin too
caten up with lice. Those diseases are indeed full of force, which
breed and bring forth these uncouth forces, whole armyes and

0181.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Bock of IOR. Vert. 18.

body.t: fivarmes of lice and vermine ( of which me have many examples
in the Histories of Gods severest Judgements upon the cruel per¬
secuters of his people, and such was that upon Herod for his
pride, Acts 12. 23. Those diseases (Isay) are full of force,
which bring forth such forces) to eate up the flesh and change
the Garment. By the great force ef my disease, is my garment
changed:
It bindetb me about as the collar of my coate.
Some read here also, he bindeth, &c. that is, God bindeth me
about with sores, ( making me but one sore) even as the collar
of my coate bindeth my coate. We translate well, It; that is,
the disease, or the sicknesse bindes me about, as the collar of my
coate; it girts and houlds me, as a close and over. close collar doth
the necke. Tob alludes in this expression to the frequent well
knowne fashion of the garments of those times and places where¬
in he lived, which had no seame ( such was Christs coat, Job.19.
23.) but were one whole piece woven from the top througheut,
only they had a collar, through which the head was put, and so
hung loose about the body. As the collar bindes the upper part
of the coate or garment; so it bindes the neck of him that weares
it. Thus Tobs disease bound him about, as the collar of his coate;
he was strait ly bound by it. Mr. Broughton translates, as the edge
of my coate girdes me; but whether the one or the other word be
used, the sence is the same; his disease stuck close to him, and gir¬
ded him in as the upper-edge, ( which must needs be the collar)
or his coate.
Hence note.
We can neitber beare bodr̃iy discases and distempers wirb ease,
nor cast them off easily.
How many are bound about with or made prisoners to a dis¬
ease, sicknes holds us fast, we cannot get our neches out of that
collar when we will. Then
First, Be thankfull for health continued; health is a great bles¬
sirg, the prince of temporall blessings, though ue little prize it,
or give the Lord glory by serving him withit. They who fecle
paine, and are under the arrest of sicknesse, would give much and
even spend (as that womanin the Gospel did) all that they have

0182.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Booke ef JOR. Vers.i8.

body.t: upon Physicians and medicines, to get ease and cure; whereas
they who are well and strong doe seldome (and then for the most
part but formally) give thankes forit, or goe to the expence of
a due praise to God forit.
Secondly, Because ( the body being subject to so many dis.
eases and sicknesses) the outward man (though insencibly) de¬
cayeth day by day, we should looke after an increase of the inner
man day by day; that as our bodies decline towards the grave,
so our soules may incline and grow up towards heaven. And that
when we lay downe these earthly tabernacles in the dust, we may
doe it in a fullnes of hope to receive them againe from the dust,
freed and exonerated from all those sicknesses and diseases, which
now bind us about, like the collar of our coate, and (as Job pro¬
ceeds in the report of his sad condition) make us like dust, before
we goe to the dust.
Vers. 19. He hath cast me into the mire, and I am become hite
dust and ashes.
This verse is the utmost line of mortality on this side death
and the grave, when a living man sticks in the mire, and lookes
like dust and ashes, we can hardly tell whether we should reckon
him among the living or the dead, yet to this exigence was Tob
reduc’d.
He hath cast me into the mire.
The word which we translate, to cast, signifieth also to teach,
and therefore some render the text, He (that is, God ] hath
taught me in the mire. There is no state ( in this life) so bad
therein God cannot teach us to be better. He often makes the
dunghil or mire our school, and there he instructs us. That's a ve¬
ry spirituall sence. When God sends his into the dirty and miery
places of affliction, he sends them to learne some lesson or other
which they would not understand in the faire pastures of their
prosperity. Are they sick? he teacheth them in the mire of sick¬
nesse, to looke after soule-health. Are they in the mire of po¬
verty? he teacheth them in their poverty to looke aster the true
riches. They are happy who learne how to cleanse themselves
chough in the mire, uho get instruction by correction.

0183.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon tbe Boske ef JO B. Verf.

body.t: But rather the word (as we give it) signifieth, to cast domne,
and to cast downe with strength; so that though the other be
a more spirituall sence, yet this is a more proper and commodi¬
ous sense in this place. He hath cast me into the mire. What
mire ?Tis usuall in Scripture to signifie any state of great adver¬
sity by mire. David acknowledged the goodnesse of God in his
deliverance from trouble under this Notion ( Psal. 40 2.) He

under the same metaphor he bewayles his trouble (Psal. 69.2)
I sinbe in deepe mire where there is ne standing: and (v. 14.) He
prayeth, Deliver me out of the mire, and let me not sinke. Such was
the mire into which Job was cast. And This aggravated Jubs af¬
fliction, God did not only cast mire upon him, but catt him into
the mire, and againe, God did not meerely let him fall into the
mire ot trouble and sicknesse, but he cast him into it. This catt¬
ing notes, first, a violent act, we cast or throw a thing out ot our
hands with force: Secondly, an act of displeasure, when we cast
a thing upon the ground, much more when we cast it into the
dirt and mire, ve doe it with a kind of indignation; what we cast
from us any how is offensive to us, much more doth that offend
us, vhich we cast into the mire. Yea to be cast into the mire
notes two things further.
First, Pollution all over; when mire is cast upon us, it defiles
us, but to be cast into the mire, is a total defilement.
Secondly, U most shame, it is a disg ace full thing to be cast
into the dirt, and tumbled into the mire. Τob was in both noti¬
ons ast into the mire, he was afflicted all over, and he was re¬
vil' both in and with his afflictions. He was double-dirted, He

He hatb cast me into the mire,

body.t: it to the ground. Those words, by casting it, are not exprest in the

They are made and appointed to sit upon the heads of Princes,

Thirdly, Note,
There is no suffering condition so low and sordid, but God some¬

That is, such is my present condition: I who was beautifull as

Sicknesse makes us like dust and ashes, but death makes us dust

Note.
Ie can never be brought so lom by any affliction er discase, but

Who can be louer then dust and ashes; theres little proba¬

Second y, Considering Job in this his low condition praying,
Note,

wonder if it be not presently heard.
As I shewed before that Jonab (Chap. 2. 2.) prayed in the

A hearing without doubt, so he assures himselfe; He Mall heare

Now, as affliction puts us upon crying to God) so crying

body.t: and audible to God, as what we speake; Therefore when Job

thee. Thus Tob cryed to God and was not heard, and so have

But some may say, how can we reconcile this to the tendernes
and mercifulnes of God, whose very nature is goodnes, and who
is most free and ready to doe good? Againe how can we recon¬
cile this to those many promises of God in Scripture concerning

and it shall be opened unto you; how are these promises true, if we
Cas Job here) cry unto God, and he doth not hea e us?
I answer, The Lord makes good his word of promise, and acts
according to his own nature, which is infinitely good, yet this
doth not alwayes appeare so to us; the prayer of faith is alwayes
heard and answered, but the answer and goodnes of God to us
in it, is not alwayes reported and discovered to us. God certain¬
ly heares what we speake, but we many times doe not heare what
he speakes, though he speake peace to us. God alwayes heares
the prayer of faith and answers it, but we doe not alwayes heare
what the answer is. It is said expressly (1 Joh.5.14,15.) And
this is the confidence that mee have in him, that if me ashe any thirg

us whatsoever me aste, me knom that me have the petitions that re
defired of him. “Tis a holy scriptural confidence that God will
hegre us when we pray, and therefore every believer may be con¬
fident that he is heard. God makes some deferrs, though, proper¬
Iy, he makes no delays, much lesse gives any flat denyalls to the
prayer of faith. There is a wide difference between the deferring

14) Thus God alwayes heareth the cry of his people, yet Job

When Job saich, Istand up, what doth this gesture intimate?

Hence note;
True Believers will not only pray earnestly, but perseveringly,

Suppose they get nothing at present, yet they uill not be put

Further, When Jeb saith, I stand up, we may consider him in

It uill be our perfect happines in the next life to have a sight of

body.t: I answer, These are not the words, nor is this the speech of ont

them a token for good that he regards their persons, but they
never accuse God, nor say directly, we pray and God doth
not at all regard. To say so were to charge God foolishly and

To conclude, Some read this last clause without a negation,
I stand up and thou regardest or markest mee; and in the Heb ew

So that we assume the negative out of the former part, The ori¬

slation) to bring upon me all kinds of punishment, or to espy all

sed to afflict me, but pleased with my affliction. As if Tob here

And this affirmative translation complyes best with the words

body.t: Thou art become Cruell to me: mith thy stroug hand

For I know that thou milt bring mee to death, and te

Hombeit, he mill not stretch out his hand to the grave,

but now he complaines higher, or shewes the hight of thaz

Verf.21. Thon art become Cruell to me: withthy strong hand
thon opposest thy selfe against mee.
Thou art become; The Hebrew is, Thou art turned, or Chan¬
ged: there is no change nor turning, not so much as a shadow of
it in God, yet as to us he often appeares changed and turned.
So we understand the Prophet speaking of Gods dealing with
the people of Israel, ( Isa. 63. 10.) They rebelled, and vexed his
holy Spirit, therefore he was turned to be their enemy; that is, He
who had bestowed upon them the highest markes of honour and
friendship, did then declare himselfe in the posture of an enemy.
The unkind returnes which they made for the tokens of his love
constrained him ( as it were) to take up Armes, and turne their
enemy, or ( as it followes there) to fignt against them.
So then, This turning may be Considered with a two-fold re¬
spect.
First, With respect to the nature of God; Thus God turneth
not, He ever is what he was, and he ever will be what he is.
Secondly, With respect to the actings of God; Thus in his
actions or workings he changes from what he was, and becomes
what he hath not been. In this sence we are to understand Job
here, when he speakes this extreame hard word of God, Thou

0202.head: Chap. 30. An Expasition upon the Books ef JOR. Verf.21.

body.t: art become Cruell; As if he had sayd, Lord, the Coppie of thy car¬
riage and countenance towards me is Changed: thou O God, whe
heretofore hast been tender of me, and even dandledst mee on thy
knees, as a darling, nom dealest harshly with me, frownest upon me,
and seemest even to dast me agairst the stones: Thoucart become
Cruell to mec.
Te be Cruell, is to shew no mercy, or not to be toucht vith
pitie and Compassion uhen we see others in misery. Cruelty de¬
clares it selfe two vayes.
First, In laving a heavy hand of trouble and affliction upon
others, as those Egyptian Taske-Masters did upon the children of
Israel, till they made them groane under their burden.
Secondly, In not helping or in not shewing bowels to those
uhom we see troubled and afflicted, though we our selves have
not layd so much as a little finger upon them. Not only are they
cruel who put others to more grievous sufferings then they ought,
but they-also are cruel, who are incompassionate towards others
in their sufferings. Whatsoever is exclusive of mercy may be
resolved into cruelty; and therefore wee find to be cruel and not
to shew mercy joyned together as synonomous expressions in¬
tending the same thing. (Jer. 6. 23.) They shall lay hold on bon
and speare: they are Cruel, and have no mercy. Mercy and cruelty
are remotest opposites: and they are most cruel, or have nothing
but cruelty in them, who have no mercy. As this is the descrip¬
tion of the Babylonians, who destroyed Jerusalem, so we have a
like description of the destroyers of Babylon, ( Jer. 50.42.) Ba¬
bylon shall be as cruelly handled as ever that handled Sion.
(Pro. 12. 10) A righteous (or good) man is mercifull, but the
tender mercies of the wicked are Cruell; that is, instead of shew¬
ing mercy they are cruel, or that which lookes most like mercy in
them, is, in effect, but cruelty.
Job seemeth to charge God uith cruelty in both these respects.
First because he layd such heavie afflictions upon him, or pressed
him so sore. Secondly, because being in that condition, so af¬
ficted, so pressed, he shewed him no pitie, no compassion, but
appeared as hard as a rock to him, as not at all moved either with
his calamity, or with his Cry's; Istand up, but thou regardest ne
an; Thou art become Cruell to met:

Thus we see how this good mans spirit was transported; and
it may be very much question'd how it could Consist with the

that he oppoled or hated him.
I answer: First, Job spake this, not to accuse God eyther of
unrighteousnesse, or of changeablenesse, but he was carried out
in extravagant language, by the extreamity of his misery and
paine; he conceaved himselse in such a condition as worse could
not be, and to sence God appeared so severe to him, as if he had
been cruel to him, and opposed him with hatred.
Secondly, I answer, Though Job spake thus as being over¬
borne by his present sufferings, yet he cannot altogether be ac¬
quitted of impatience and passionatenes. And he had fayled thus
more then once before ( Chap. 16. 13. Chap. 19. 8, 9,10.) in
all which texts he spared not to Complaine that God had decla¬
red himselfe as an enemy, or had carryed himselfe like an enemy
towards him. We are not to reckon these passages among his
graces, but his faylings, nor doe they shew, what he ought to
have done, but what he did and ought not, or they enforme us,
what apprehensions a good man may have of God, not what
the affections of God are towards good men. Thou art cruel to
me, &c.

mercy of God) eudureth for ever, repeated as many times as

begins, O give thanbs unto the Lord, for he is good, for his merey
endureth for ever. O give thanks to the God of gods, for his mercy
endureth for ever: and ir concludes as it began, O give thanks io
the God of heaven, for his mercy endureth for ever; That is, God
doth never cease to be mercifull, no, not uhen he acteth with
greatest severity: and though in that Psalme no sad acts of God
towards his Israel be instanc’d in; yet the truth is universal, That
the saddest actings of God in the sufferings of his Israsl, put no
interruption to his mercy; His mercy endures for ever. The Lord
beareth a tendernesse of affection to them in their smartest af¬
flictions; even then he is tender beyond the tendernes of a mo¬
ther to her sucking child; (Isa. 49. 15) Can a mother forget
her sucking Child, that shee should not have compassion on the son ef
her mombe? yea they may forget, yet will I not forget thee. I have
graven thee upon the palmes of mine hand, thy malls are continually
before mee. As it he had said, I can no more forget thee then a
man can forget that which is alwayes in his eye, or the memori.
all whereof he dayly carrieth in his hand And if we look a verse
or two before the text alledged, we shalj find a shining evidence
of the truth I am now upon; At the 13th verse the Lord invites

forth into singing O mountaines, for God hath comferted his peeple,
and will have mercy upon his afflicted. This was good newes, but

misgiving thoughts Zion had of God, and what hard conclusi¬
ons shee had made against her selfe, (v. 14.) But Zion sayd,
The Lord hath forsaken me, and my Lord hath forgotten mee, Thus

nor at all can l forget thec, that is, not have a favourable re¬

body.t: membrance of thee. The greatest stormes of divine anger against
Zion, doe not extinguish the slames of divine love to Zion.
There may be changes in the workes of God, but he is in one
mind, or his mind is alwayes the same to his, and that is a mind
to doe them good by all he doth to them.
Secondly, Observe;
The sence of paine and present smart, may make the bost of
Saintt speak uncomely, and bosides their dutie.
It mis not only too much for job to say of God, but more
then a damned soule can truly say of God, Thou art become Cru¬
ell to mee: He that never exceeds justice is never cruel. We have
heard many of the Saints under greatest sufferings, so farre from
saying God is cruel, that they have confessed, God is good, God i¬
mercifull, God is birde; this losse is of God, this stroke is of God,
this paine is of God, this wound is of God, and yet God is mer¬
cifull, yet God is gracious, yet God is good; If Tob, who in this
extreamity makes report of God as Cruell! and cryes out, O
Cruell ! how Cruell! ( If he, I say) when the fit was over had
been asked his opinion of God, what he thought of God, and
what the thoughts of God were towards him; sutely he would
have said, God is gracious, God is good and kinde to mee: he
would have called him redeemer, (as Chap. 19.25. J and not
destroyer. There he could say, I buow tbat my riditmir liveth,
even when he was ready to dye under his hand, ( and Chap. 13.
16.) Hes also svall bo my salvation: these were his thoughts
when he considered the matter, but when he was carried out in
passion through the violence of paine, how Iniemperately did he
speake? wee caunot almayes juage of a mans estate by his acti¬
ons, or by bis spuches. wbile the hiart is right, words may gee
wreng.
Thirdly, Comparing this verse with the former, where he
said, Icry, aud thou hearest not: and here presently adds; Thou

Observe;
