0208.head: Chap.30. An Exposition upan the Book of IOR. Vers.21.

body.t: We are hard put to it, if we finde not an Income of mercy
vhen we cry to God; but if we finde an inundation ot severity,
O how strong is that temptation! It puts a good man hard to it,
if uhen he cryes to God, his troubles doe not decrease, how
much more when his troubles encrease, or when he gets nothing
by prayer but blows, as if prayer did only put God in mind to lay
more load upon him. If when a poore soule asketh bread, he
hath nothing but stones throwne at his head; If when he asketh
fish, God doth (as it were) sting him with scorpions: This is
an unspeakeable temptarion. Wee know prayer is the afflicted
soules first and last, that is, his best refuge, indeed all his refuge;
and when a man doth not finde any reliefe in his last refuge, how
sadly must this sit upon his spirit? thus it was with Job, not only
was he neglected, not heard, not regarded wben he cryed, but
God prest affliction more and more upon him when he cryed.
The appearances of God in angry dispensations when wec are
praying, secking, begging, knocking, wrestling for mercy, are
very burdensome to the best of men, and cut the soule exceeding¬
ly. Misgivings of mind that God is against us, are our greatest
miferies, in a time of misery.
Lastly, Consider againe how thit good man spake, Thou art
Cruell to me, mith thy sirong hand thou opposest me. Job is set up
for a mirrour of patience, and we have heard of the patiente of
tob, vet here we may see the impatience os tob.
Hence note;
They mbo have strongest grace, have not their graces almay:
in the same strength. Their best graces are sometimis nor¬
sted and get a foyle.
That particular grace which is their Crowne, is not alwayes
crowned or conquering : the Crowne of fobs graces was his pa¬
tience, that’s the grace for which he is cryed up in Scripture, yet
he did not alwayes shew forth patience, nor act the patient man.
Abraham was strong in faith, yet he was not alwayes in the same
strength of faith; we finde his feare too hard for his faith in the
case of his wife, therefore he called her sister, and durst not trust
God in owning his relation, Abrabams faith had ebbings and
declinings. He that hath much humility, may sometimes act
proudiy : and he that hatú much felse deniall, may somerme

0209.head: Chap.30. An fxpofition upon the Book of JOR. Verl. 22.

body.t: act selfe-seekingly. A state of grace is sure, but the workings of
grace are variable; The nature of it is unchangeable, but the de¬
grees of it suffer many changes.Tis the happines of Saints that
the grace which they have in Christ, their head, knows no decay,
as also that the grace which is inthemselves shall recover from
its decayes, and triumph after all its foyles. Lobs grace did so at
last, though he yet proceeds in such a language of complaint as
surther discovers the weaknesse of it.
Vers.22. Thou lifiest mee up to the wind; thou causist mee to
ride upon it: thou dissolvest my substance.
The generall sence of this verse is as the former, a bewayling
of his affliction in the most significant metaphors and highest
streines of sorrow.
Thou liftest mec up to the winde.
Mr. Brougbton translates, Thon tabest mee up unto a winde, ana
causest mee to ride upon it : Here we may behold sob upon bis
Chariot, not a triumphing but a mourning Chariot, He rode
upon the wind, and he tells who set him there, Thou (O God)
causest mes to ride upon it. But what was this wind to which Job
was lifted up, and upon which he rode?
First, By this wind, we may most fitly understand his feirce
and strong afflictions; As if he had sayd, Thou (O Gud) bast gi¬
ven my afflictien full force and scope against mee: thou settest mee
before the mind, and liftest met up witb it; I am alwayes weather¬
beaten, never under the lee-shore. When the storme is up we may
avoyd it much and get to shelter, but he that is lifted up to the
winde is expoled to its full force and course. As the winde rai-
seth and carries away stubble or chaffe, or duft, so most probably
Job conceaved himselfe lifted up and carried away, he scarce kneu
whether, or into what condition by strong afflictions, and temp¬
titions.
Secondly, Tuou liftest mes up to the xinde, is conceaved by
others as an expression of his former felicity; As if he had sayd,
Thou diast list mee uponce to the hight of outmard prosperity, and
madest mee ride aloft as upon the wings of the winde, but now thou
aiseloest my substarce, or breakest mec like a bubble. I was once
in the ekies, but now I'am in the dust.

0210.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Booke of JOR. Verl22.

body.t: And some put an aggravation upon this exposition, as if Job
had suspected, that God did lift him up on high, with a purpose
to cast him downe. But that is too bold an imposition upon the
holy Man, unlesse we understand it moderately; That God lifted
him up on purpose to cast him downe, that in his casting downe
he might have advantage both to try fobs grace, and to glorifie
his own power and goodnesse in raising him up againe to a grea¬
ter hight then he had been at. For as God saith of Pharoab
(Ex-d. 9. 16.) In very deed for this cause have I raised thee ap,
for te shew ix thee my power, and that my name may be declared in
all the eartb ( Now (I say) as God raised Pharoab, and hath
doubtlesse in the course of his providence raised many other wic¬
ked men very high, with a designe to manifest his power and his
justice in casting them downe and destroying them) so he hath
raised up many godly men, with a purpose to glorifie his power
and his goodnesse, both in their casting downe and restoring.
And in this sence we may as fafely say, that God lifted him upto
the wind on purpose to cast him downe, as wee may truely say,
that God did cast him downe after he had lifted him up to the
wind of worldly honour, and caused him for many yeares to ride
peaceably upon it.
But I shall a lietle further exemplifie this notion of riding;
which frequently in Scripture notes great felicity, with outward
pompe and dignity. Solomon saith, ( Eceles. 10.7.) I sax ser¬
vants riding on borseback, and Princes malking as servrots upen
the earth; That is, I saw meane men raised to great glory, they
rid, while Princes (or such as once were Princes) xent on foote,
that is, were reduced to a low condition. And as riding signifies
an honourable state, so especially riding upon the Clouds, spon
the windes, upon the heavens, such riding is an argument of
highest dignity; And ’tis often reported of God himselfe, to set
forth his excellency and glory. ( Psal. 18. 20.) He rode npen a
Cherub, and did fly, yea he did fly upin the wings of the winds.
Thus (Psal. 33. 34. 68.32.) Sing unto God yee hingdomes of
the earth: O sing praises to the Lord, Selab. To him that rideth
on the heaven of heavens which mere of old, lo, he dotb sond eut his
voyce, and that a mighty vorce. Ascribe yee strength unto God,
his excellercy is over Israel, aud his strengthis in the Clouds.
So Mtoses in his Song, (Dent. 33-26.) There is none hte urts

0211.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Booke ef IOE. Verf. 22.

body.t: the Godof Jesarun, who rideth upon the heaven in thy helpe, and in
his excellency on the sky. And when the Lord would set forth the
greatest advantement of his people, he expresseth it by riding,
and by riding on the high places, ( Deut. 32. 13. Isa. 58. 14)
Then shalt thou delight thy selfe in the Lord, and he shall cause
thee to ride upin the bigh places of the earth, and feed thte mith the
heritage of Jacob thy father. In both places, this promise of iding
upon the high places of the earth, is an assurance given of the
most full posse ssion of and dominion over the greatest things of
the earth.
So that according to this sacond Interpretation, to ride upon
the minde, denotes Jebs former highnesse and prosperous state,
in which he was mounted triumphantly, and Gallantiy, upon the
Chariot of worldly Greatnesse. The description which he gives
of his honour in the former Chapter, complyes well uith this
notion; whereas now, he found that true, (Psal. 102. 10.) Be¬
cause of thine Indignation, and thy wrath, thou hast lifted mee up,
and cast mee doune. Naturalists report that the Eagle takes the
shell-fifh, and listingit upra great height, lets it fall upon a rocke
to breake it. Thus saith Tob, Thon hast listed mee up to the winde,
& lettest me fall to crush me, as the next words imply, Thou dis¬
solvest my substance. This is a trath, prosperity is a riding, and a
riding, as it were, upon the wings of the winde, and it may well
be called so, because of the urcertainty and many changes of it:
but I doe not conceave that Interpretation proper to this place,
and therefore I rather adhere to the former.
One of the Rabbines hath a conceit by himfelfe, I may call it
a dreame; that Job did but tell his dream, while he spake thus.
As if through the distemper of his sichnes, he in his sleepe, had
phancied himselfe carried away with the winde into the aire, and
riding on the Clouds: but I leave that as a brain-sicke imagina¬
tion, rather then a serious exposition of the text.
Yet further, these words, Thou liftest mee up totbe ninde, and
causest mee to ride upon it, Compar’d with those that follow, th u
dissolvest my substance, seeme to be a comparison drawne from
Clouds and vapours, which are exhaled and lifted up high in the
ayre by the Sun, but are quickly dissolved and blowne away by
the winde. Thus Tob represents his own condition; he was as a
vapour listed un a while, but soone scattered and blowne away.

0212.head: Chap. 30. An Expofition upon the Book of I° B. Verl. 22.

body.t: Hence note;
God useth much liberty in dealing with his sirvants.
Our God ( saith the Prophet, Psal. 115.3.) is in the heavent
and hath done whatsoever he pleased. He walkes by no rule but his
own pleasure, and though that be in it selfe the best, the surest,
and most unerring rule, yet, as to us, it puts it selfe forth, and ap¬
peares, full of changes and alterations. This day the Lord is plea¬
sed to give us matter of re oycing, and the next day of sorrow;
One day he is pleased to fill us, and another day to empty us.
He sends a winde sometimes to raise us up, and anone a vinde
to cast us downe, he tosseth and tumbleth us to and fro,
even as stubble, and as a dry leafe: and who may say to him,
what doest thou? Doe not thinke that this is a dream, as the Rab¬
bine Interprets it, or a Poeticall fiction, when we heare of men
lifted up to and riding on the winds, and then falling downe to
the dissolving of their substance. The Lords wayes with men are
above our reach, and therefore he fetcheth Comparisons to ex¬
presse them, from the winds, and from the Clouds, os whose va¬
rious motions and interchanges, we can give little account uith
all our shill. Thou liftest mee up to the minde, thou causest mee to
ride upon it:
And dissoluist my substanca
The word signifies, to melt, as mettall is melted in the fire;
and by a metaphor’tis applyed to the fayling of courage, which
is a melting of the mind. (1 Sam. 14. 16.) And the waichmen
of Saul in Gibeah ef Berjamin looked, and behold the multitudi
melted away, and they went on beating downe one another; that ie,
their Courage fayled them, or their hearts fainted. The Prophet
saith, (Isa. 64.7.) Wee are Consumed in our Iniquities, or (it is
this word) mee are melted away in our Iniquities, our ftrength
failes, our Comforts faile, our spirts faile, euery thing failes.
This word is used also (to answer the allusion before mentioned)
to note the melting of clouds when they are dissolved into raine,
or drop away in showers. Thus saith Tob, that of mine which
was most substantiall is dissolved and dropt away like a cloud.
It is sayd (Psal. 46.7.) He (that is God) utterid his voyce,
and tbe tarib melied. And againe, ( Amos 9. 5.) The Lerdos

0213.head: Chap. 39. An Exposition upon the Book of Jos. Verf. 22.

body.t: hosti is he that toucheth the Land, aud it suall melt; That is, both
persons and things shall consume away. Thus every mans parti¬
ctular death is called a dissolution, ( 2 Cor. 5.1.) And the end
of the world (which is a kind of general death)is called the disso¬
lution of it, (2 Pet.3.11.) Seting all these things (that is, the hea¬
vens and the earth with all their substance ) shall be dissolved,
what manner of persons ought me to be, &c. All worldly substances
shall one day be dissolved; And Job in his day of trouble could
say to God, Thou dissolvest
my substance.
The word is of a very various and Comprehensive significati-
on. Some translate it, xisdome: thou dissolvest my misdeme, as
importing his affliction was so great that his very understanding
was at a stand, or that be was doted, as we say, and rendred una¬
ble to make use of his reason, as if his meaning were, thou bringest
mee to my mits end. The Psalmist (Psal. 107.27.) describing the
dreadfull dangers and wonderfull deliverances of Marriners, or
Sea men, saith, They reel to and fro, and stagger lihe a drunben
man, and are at their mits end: we put in the Margin, All their
xisdome i-swallomed up; As the men themselves, Ship and all are
ready to be suallowed up, so their uits are many times swallow¬
ed up with feare and amazement, before the Ship is swallowed up
by the waves of the Sea. Thus Jub is conceaved to say, that his
wisdome was sœallowed up, he knew not what to doe, nor how
to carry himselfe: He seemed now brought to a farre worse Con-
dition then he was in (Chap. 6. 13.) when he sayd, Is net my
helpe in mee? and is wisdome driven quite from mee? doe you
thinke I have no reason nor understanding about me ? but here
according to this reading) his uisdome was driven quite from
him, Thou hast dissolved, or melted don xe all my wildome, I am
not able to make use of it; or ( as others read it) Tuou hast dis¬
solved, or seperated mee from wisdeme: The meaning of both is
but one, I know not what to resolve or doe in this case.
Secondly, The words are translated thus; Thy misdome, or
thy appointment hath disselved met. According to this reading we
may conccave Tob speaking thus; In al this hurry of things, nhon
Lam carried uy ana downe. I bηew not bow, nor whether, and am as
ont altosetber consusea, yet thou, O God, actist toward mee in mis¬

0214.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upan the Booke of JOR. Vers.22.

body.t: dome, thy wisdome hath dissolved mee; or thon hast disselved mee
nisely. True, Lord, I am altogether at uncertainties, as one tessed
nith the minde, but it is by a lan from thes, by thy rule or statute
hat it is so. Iam unsettled, but it is setled in heaven that I sould
be so; I am in a very fleeting condition, as a thing hurried er meved
by the minde, but thou hast establisved it by an immoveable decree
that I should be thus; A divine appointment hath dissolved met;
that’s a good sence.
Thirdly, Thus, Thon hast dissolvid uy desree, purpose or appoint¬
ment;that is, thou hast broken my course of life, and put me beside
my intended method; thou hast declared thy selfe unsatisfied
with my way, and hadst not approved what I proposed to dot,
and so upon the matter, hast gratified mine enemies, who have
hard thoughts of mee, and censure mee as an evill doer; I had
decreed in my selfe what to doe, and how to mannage all my
trusts and concernments; But thou hast seene ir good to rescind,
or nullifie what I decreed, and take mee off by these continued
troubles, from all my intendments. Thou dissolvest my decree.
Fourthly, According to our reading;
Thou dissolvest ny sul stance:
Is plainly this; Thou makest my bodyly strengib to melt awiy,
as also the strength of my estate. A mans worldly goods and pos¬
sessions are commonly called his substance: thou hast melted a¬
way my friends, my children, my servants, my cattel, my power,
my honour, my all; I have nothing lest of this world that can
be called substance. My body, which is left, is but the skeleton of
a body, and my life which yet remaines, is but the shadow of a
life; Thon disselvest my substance.
Hence note;
There is nothing so durable, or lasting among all the good tbings
of this life, but God can melt and disselve it quickly.
Though a mans substance be so compact, and well setled, that
it seemes unmoveable, or not to be shaken, yet how soone doth
it move, yea melt under the afflicting hand of God. That uhich
is as hard as Adamant, melis like waxe, before the fire. What the
Prophet spake in reference to the mountaines or pouers of the
earth, which troubled the peace, or hindered the Comforts of

0215.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Bocke ef JOB. Verf.22.

body.t: Sion, (Isa. 64.1.)O that thou vouldest reut the heavens, that
thou mouldest come domne; As if he had sayd, Lord take to heart
the mrongs and indignities mhich thine enemies have put upon thy
people, as also the blasphemies which they have belched out boldly a¬
gainst thy Majesty; Lord dos not held thy hand any longer, but come
domne like a storme of lightning and thunder, filled mitb a holy fury
and just indignation, as if thou didst rent the very heavens for hast
to be among us. O that nom thou mouldest thus shew thy selfe her¬
on earth, and not alnayes confine thy dreadfull power to heaven.
But what would be the effect of such an appearance? The next
words tell us, That the mountaines might slox downe at tby pre¬
sence. These mountaines are not to be understood properly, but
metaphorically, for the great things, or great men of the world,
those things and pouers which are most Compact and Consoli¬
dated by the best skill and policy of man into a mountain, or into
many (in mans Judgement) impregnable mountaines, flow down
like piles of sno v at the presence of God. Most mountaines are
of a hard massie, some of a rocky substance,yet these flow downe
like a streame at the angry presence of God. It is usuall to see
waters flowing downe from mountaines; but, to see a mountaine
flow downe like water, to see rocks melt and dissolve like waxe
is miraculous. Yet saith the Prophet, the very mountaines shall
fow downe at thy presence, that is, thou dissolvest the strength
of the mountaines, of the great men of the world, and they be¬
come like a liquid streame, or (so the Prophet himselfe explaines
it, v. 2.) As when the melting fire burneth, the fire causeth the
waters to boyle, to mabe thy name tnowne to thine adversaries, that
the nations mar tremble at thy presence. If the Lord cau make
mountaines melt like waxe or snow before the Sun or fire, surely
thole things which are most substantiall shall vanish as a shadow,
as a nothing at the word of bis power.
There are but few things so substantiall that they will a¬
bide, and cannot be dissolved: spiritual things, the favour of God,
his grace to us, his grace in us, our Interest in Christ, these can
never be dissolved. Though the mountaines be removed, ( saith
God) yet I will never dissolve the Covenant of my peace, that
shall stand for ever; every thing shall be dissolved, but not that.
( Pro. 8. 21.) Solomon saith, The Lord will make his people to In¬
herit substance, that is, chey shall have that which is worthy of the

0216.head: Chap.30. An Exposition upon the Book ef JOR. Vers.23

body.t: name of substance; there is a substantiality in their Common
mercies, much more in their peculiar and distinguishing mercies.
Worldly men doe not Inherit substance, The best of their sub¬
stance is like a fhadow; but God giveth his people substance.
And hence The old Saints tooke To sully the spoyling ef their goods,
Enswing in themselves that they haa in heaven, a better and an en¬
during substance, (Heb. 10.34.) a substance that would abide
wind and weather, fire and water, the greatest tryalls, and re¬
maine undissolved, yea untoucht. But whether the Lord deale
out judgements to the wicked, or chastisements to his children,
he soone dissolveth all their worldly substance; whatsoever the
world accounts most substantiall, cannot stand before his decree
of dissolntion.
Verf. 23. For Iknom that thou milt bring mee to death, and to
the honse appointed for al living.
For I kτοπ: That is, I am fally perswaded of this thing, sub
had a knouledge of faith, not only that Christ lived ( Chap. 19.
25. I know that my redeemer liveth) but that himselfe should
die. So the Apostle (2 Cor. 5. 1.) I know that when the earthly
Tabernacle of this house shall be dissolved, &c. Paul speaks of thit
knowledge of faith, which is assurance, and as he knew or was
assured that when the earthly house ot his bodily Tabernacle
should be dissolved, he had a building of God, an house not made
with hands, eternal in the heavens; so he knew or was assured
that the earthly tabernacle of his body should be dissolved. And
when Jeb saith, I knom that thou wilt bring mee to death, this notes
not only that which is very sure and certaine in it selfe, but that
which he himselfe was assured of, and that with a kinde of Joy
and delight; he spake of it as of a thing that he took pleasure in,
as if he had sayd, Tu my Comfort to remember, that thou miit
bring mee to death.
I knom that thou nilt bring mee to death.
The Hebrew is, That thou wilt make mee returne; But he had,
not been dead before, how then could he returne to death? To
avoyde this seeming difficulty, some expound thole words, thou
milt make mce to returne, thou wilt make mee come or goe to
deach, For fo in Scripture to returne is as much as to come;

0217.head: Chap.30. An Exposstion upou the Bok of JOR. Verf.23.

body.t: but there is a great Elegancy in it, if wee take it according to the
Hebrew, thou wilt make mee te returne, and understand it thus;
Thou wilt reduce mee back againe unto the earth. For though,
Job when he should dye could not in congruity of speech be sayd
to return to death, or the grave, because he had neither been deãd
nor buryed, yet when he should dye, he might be sayd (not onsy
congruously but very significantly) to returne to the earth, or to
the dust, because he was once (in the first Adam) there and taken
thence before.
Hence note;
Death brings us back to what nee once mere, and siemes ui
what wec are.
So the sentence uas given (Gen. 3. 17.) Dust thou art, and io
dust thou shalt returne. (Eccles. 12. 7.) The dust shall returne to
the earth as it was, and the spirit shall returne to God that gave it;
mans body is dust materially while he lives, and when he dyes his
body goes to itt owne, the dust, and becomes dust formally.
(Psal. 90. 3.) Thou turnest man to destruction; that is, to death,
(Death is the destruction of all men as to their bodyly composi¬
tion and outward enjoyments, in which sence’tis also sayd, (Isa.
57.1.) that the righteous peris mhen they dy; thus Moses saith of
God, Thou turnest man to destruction ) and sayest, returne yce
Children of men. God having turned man to death, presently
saith, returne yee Children of men, that is, goe beck into what you
were, returne to the dust. Some expound that place by an Irony,
Thou turnest man to destruction, or thou sayest to man dye, and
then returne quit thy selfe from death as tell as thou canst;
come back if thou canst, but I rather take it in the former sence,
implying that by death man is Converted into his oune princi¬
ples. Some render Jubs text so: Death mill restore mee ( that is)
to mhat Ionce mas: if wee consider the dominion of death over
man, in reference to the state of Innocency, so it is a tyranny,
for death takes possession of that which was not its own. Man was
at first set up in a possibility not to dye; but if wee Consider
man as fallen, and as under that Law which God gave; Dust thou
art, and to dust thou shalt returne. Thus death doth its duty,
and brings us ( by the appointment of God) back againe to
what wee once were, that is to dust.

0218.head: Chap. 30. An Expefition upon ibe Bouke dIe n. Verl-23.

body.t: I know that thou milt bring mes to death.
There are tuo opinions about the reason of these words.
First, As if Job spake meerly to move God compassionately
to Consider his frailty, that so he might deale more favourably
with him; I kηoη I shall dye spurily, Lord let it please thee that I
may enjoy a little ease while I live. Good men have often put
God in mind of their frailty, that they might the more move him
to pity. The Psalmist seemes to expostulate with God upon this
poynt (Psal 89. 46,47) How long Lord milt thou biae thy selfe,
for ever? shall thy wrath burn lihe fire? remember how short my time
is: Wherefore hast thou made all men in vaine? As if he had sayd,
The longest time that any man hath or can expect to live, is but
short, therefore Lord doe not shorten that vhich is so short.
Surely man lives to litt le purpose (even in vaine) if he live lesse
then that little time which is commonly cut out and appoynted
for his lise. And as that holy man, urged God with the remem¬
brance of mans short life, that he might prevaile with him not to
shorten it, so David assures us that the remembrance of it mo¬
veth him to compassionate us init, (Psal.103. 13,14) Like as
a father pitieth his children, so the Lord pitieth tbem that feare him;
For he knoweth our frame, he remembreth that me are dust. To
this effect Job is supposed praying. Lord remember I am but dust,
I kηοw I shall die ere long, O spare mee a little, let mee bave fairt
quarter that small while, while I am in this world.
Buc, Secondly, I rather conceive the reason to be, because he
did even despaire of recovery, he saw himselfe so beset with in¬
firmities, so wounded and weakned by his sicknesses and soares,
that he looked upon himselfe, not only as a man sub ect to death,
but as a dead man. Ibuow tbou milt brirg mee to death, I see that's
thy purpose by the way in which thou handlest mee: hee doth
not speake thus as to the generall state of mankinde; for every
man may say to God, I know thou vilt bring mee to death; but
having the symptomes of death upon him, he had the sentence
of death in him, and even saw himselfe upon the borders of the
grave; As if he had sayd, Thert's no escaping death fer a man
ihat is in sach a plighi, or brought so lom as Iam at thùs time.
Hence note;

0219.head: Chap. 30. A Exposition upon the Booke of JOR. Verf. 23.

body.t: First, when mee are under griat sicknesse and meaknesse of bo¬
dy, it is very proper for us to looke upon our selves as
brought to the very gate and valley of the shadom of
death, and dropping into the grave. When mee are very
sicke ’tu good to have a persmasion that me shall dye.
It is our duty to thinke we must dye ere long, and may dye
quickly when we are in health, and strength, when wee feele not
the lest ach in our bones, nor distemper in our bodies, (Tue fl mer
and best perfections of nature art no supersedeas, no stop te present
deatb) but when a man is nothing but soares, and sicknesses, but
paines and paroxismes, what hath he else to thinke of, or what
else should he thinke of, but his dissolution and his grave? When
a man feeles the impressions of death upon him, and sees visions
of death before him, what should he either meditate or speake ot
but of dying, or of his preparations for death? What should he
doe but labour to set all even both God-ward and world-ward,
to see that all is right between God to whom he is going, and his
own soule; as also betueen himselfe and the world, which he is
leaving, or from which he is going. Wee should not put the
evill day farre from us in a good day, but when the evill day hath
over-taken us, then to be talking of life, and hopes of recovering,
is not only unsutable and incongruous, but very unsafe and dan¬
gerous. Some are hardly persuaded they shall dye, though the
tokens of death appeare upon them: and some visiters of the
sicke, when they see the picture of death in the sicke mans face,
will yet feed him with hopes of life: it is good to comfort our
friends in sicknesse with the thoughts of eternal life, but to flat¬
ter them with hopes of this life may prove deadly. How shall
they ever dye with comfort, who are troubled to heare death
spoken of! Wee find Job in that condition talking freely of his
grave, I kηow (saith he) that thou wilt bring mee to death: I look
upon this as a sicknesse unto death, and that now I am upon my
death bed.
Secondly, Comparing this with the event;
Observe;
A godly man may be much mistaken about the purposes ef God
to him in outward ihings, and especiahy about tbe date of bis
oune life.

0220.head: Chap.30. An Expofition upon the Book of JOB. Vers, 22.

body.t: I know ( saith Jub) that thou milt bring mee to death: but fob
was miftaken. Though Saints cannot be mistaken in their assu¬
rances about spirituall and eternal things, yet they may be decei¬
ved in their assurances about temporal things. We may think our
selves sure of outward mercies, and misse them, wee may have an
assurance that death will be the Conclusion of our present af¬
flictions, and yet mis-reckon our selves, as Job did, who had a
very flourishing time of life for many yeares after he gave him¬
selfe for dead. A man may have the sentence of death in him¬
selfe, as the Apostle speakes, (2 Cor. 1 9.) when God (asto
that time) hath given out no such sentence. And therefore wee
ought not to conclude peremptorily in this poynt; For though
the premises of Gods dealings with us, seeme to tell us that death
must be our suddaine conclusion, yet the time is a secret, and faith
in the infinite pouer and goodnesse of God may give us some
hope of restoring when’tis worst with us, we not having recea¬
ved any revelation from God forbidding such a bope. “Tis wis¬
dome to be alwayes ready for death, but’tis more then comes to
our share peremptorily to determine the period of our lives.
As many come short of their reckonings about life, so the recko¬
nings of some are too short. Wee ought every day to number
our dayes spiritually, but no man can number eyther his oune or
any other mans dayes arithmetically, not because they are more
then a man can ( for a child may ) know how to number them,
but because the number of them ( whether few or many, much
lesse how many or how few] is not knowne to any man.
Further, Job seemes to be thus conclusive abont the conclusion
of his life, (I Raow that thou witt bring mee to death) with a kind
of sieet content.
Thirdiy, Hence note;
A godly man can speake very familiarly and Comfortablyef his
death.
Though sob spake complainingly of his sufferings and paines,
yet when he spake of his death, he spake rejoycingly, as one re¬
freshed with good newes. I know that thou milt bring Mee to
death, that’s the thing I expect, and that pleaseth mee. O wel¬
come death! welcome grave; A godly man can please himselfe
with these thooghts, not only as death is an end of all his sor¬

0221.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Bok of JOR. Verl. 23.

body.t: roues, but as ’tis the beginning of his endlesse Joyes.
Lastiy, When he saith, I knom that thou wilt bring mee to
death; Observe;
Death is at the dispese and Command ef God.
Hee doth not say, my disease or sicknesse will bring mee to
death, but, thon wilt bring mee to death; or thou vilt bring mee
to death by the hand of these sicknesses. It is good for us to see
our death as well as our life in the hand of God: death cannot
come of it selfe till’tis sent, or tillit is Commanded ard Com¬
mission'd; unlesse God bring us to the grave, all the sicknesses
in the world cannot doe it; unlesse God say, dye, ail the pouers
in the world cannot kill. I knom that thou vist bring met to
death;
and to the house appointed for all living.
The words are a description of the grave: Jub calls it a heuse,
and a house appointed, and a house appointed fer all living. And
though he saith not by whom this house was appointed for so
great an entertainment, yet doubtlesse he meanes God himselfe
was the appointer, he built this lightsome world as a house for
man to live in, and he hath appointed the darke Grave as a house
for all living; that is, he hath appointed the living when they dre
ro rest and take up their lodging in that house. Thus as men
build houses for themselves to live in; so God hath appeinted a
house for all living men when they dye.
In the Leviticail Law, we read of the Tabernacle ef the Congre¬
gatien, or the Tabernacle of atpointment, because thither all the
people of Israel were appointed to come, and there to congregate
upon severall occasions of solemne worship. Here we have the
house of appointment, or the house of the Congregation, that is, the
house where all men must congregate, and meet together. And
when Jab calls it a house appointed, it hath a double reserence;
First, to place; Secondly, to time. The grave is the place ap¬
pointed of God where the living shall be layd; and it is appoin¬
ted of God when they shall be layd there. It is a house ap¬
pointed
for all living.
That's a great house fure which hath roome enough for the

0222.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Books ef I02. Versa3,

body.t: reception of all living. Usually every living man hath a house
by himselfe; but here is a house for all living. While the living
are in the world, they take up a great deale of roome, but death
puts us neere together, and crouds the men who tooke up the
greatest breadth above ground, into a narrow compasse under
ground, the Grave; That’s the house for
All living.
Some extend all living, to all things that live; Thus the beafis
of the earth, and fowles of the ayre, may be numbred among the
living, but Job is speaking of men only; and so The all living,
are all men living; Adam called his wives name Eve, becanse shee
was The mother of all living. (Gen. 3.20.)As Eve was the mo¬
ther, so the grave is the house of all living. The grave is spoken
of, as if it were but one house, all that have lived are gone to it,
and all the living are going to it; it is the generall Rendevouz,
or meeting-place, of mankinde, all who live in this world, when
they dye and goe out of the world, goe to the grave; That's
their last resort.
Hence note;
First, All that live must die, and all that die are bound for tue
grave; that’s their next stage.
Mankind is as under an appointment for death, so for the grave;
we no sooner begin to live then we begin to dye, and (as" is pro¬
verbially said) me sup death in our first spronful of broath I am sure
we did in the first or neere the first morsel that ever was esten.
When sin came into the world (and that came by eating ) death
came in with it; we may justly take up a complaint againft, or a
lamentation over sin. We may cry out, O sin, sin, sin, Thou hast
(meritoriousty) made all the funeralls that ever mere in the morld.
We had never knowne what it meanes to depart out of this life,
if we by sin had not first departed from the living God. What
Havocke hath sin made in the world? What heapes upon heapes
hath it layd? It was once sayd of the goodly buildings in Rome,
The fins of Germany, ( meaning the money got by the Popes fac¬
tors for sin-pardons granted the Germaus) have built these.
And when we see those goodly buildings The Bodyes of men
min'd and cast to the Ground, yea into the ground, ue may sase.

0223.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Boke ef JOR. Verf.23.

body.t: ly say, The sins of men have unbuilt or pul’d downe their bo¬
dyes. Death is the wages ef fin, ( Rom, 6. 23.) And Master sin
payeth all his servants, with this black and bad money, death.
The Psalmist purs this into a negative Question, ( Psal. 89.
48.) W'hat man is he that liveth and shall not see death? Shall he
deliver his soule from the hand ef the greve? Selah. His meaning
is, no man can avoyde the sight of death, or escape the grave.
And therefore the Holy Ghost doth not leave this assertion
bare, but closeth it with that word of Marhe, that emphaticall
signall word, Selah, to seale and assure the truth of it, or to com¬
mand our utmost attention to it. This is a Selah of meditation,
andit layeth a kind of arrest upon our spirits, not to passe from
the text, till we have seriously and feelingly considered these
words, what man is he that liveth, and shall not see deatt? And
Iest any man should presume he might not, The Psalmist expres¬
seth man not by that common word Adam, which tells him that
his original is from the earth, and so naturally weake and very
britle ware, Nor doth he expresse man by that word Enos,
which implyeth his accidentall or rather providential infirmi¬
ties, sicknesses and sorrowes; But hè calls him Geber, which
represents man in his best state of strength, riches, honour and
worldly grearnesse; as if he had sayd, What rich, what Great,
what mighty man is there that liveth, and shall not see death.
David indeed speakes of some, ( Psal. 49.7, 8, 9,10.) That
trust in their nealth, and boast themselves in the multitude of their
riches, rich men can doe great things, but here is a thing that
they cannot doe: none of them can by any means redetm his Bro¬
ther, nor give to God a ransome for him. From what cannot a rich
man redeeme his brother? it is true of spirituall redemption,
yes that is furthest out of the rich mans reach, money will noz
doe it. (1 Pet. 1.18.) We are not redeemed rith corruptit le things,
such as silver, and gold, but mith the precious blood of the Son of
God; but the Psalmist speakes of a lower redemption, to which
all the riches of man cannot reach, none of them can by any meanes
redeem his brother, or give to God a ransome for him; the redempti¬
on of their soule ( that is, of their person from the grave) is preci¬
ous, and it ceaseth for evere And that he speakes of their redemp¬
tion from the grave, is more clearly expressed at the 1Ith verse,
that he should still live for ever, and not see corruptien. Jesus Christ

0224.head: Chap.30. An Exposition upen tb́t Bor εf IoR. Versizs

body.t: did not so redeem us that we should live for ever, and not see
corroption; It was the priviledge of Jesus Christ the redeemer
not to see corruption; but Jesus Christ, hath not redeemed us
that we shall not see corruption; he hath redeemed us that we
shall live for ever in heaven, but he hath not redeemed us from
corruption, that we should live for ever on earth, or not see cor¬
ruption in the grave; For (asit is sayd at the roth verse of the
Pfalme) We see that mise men dye, likemise the foole, and the brui¬
tish person peristi, and leave their wealth to otkers; As if he had said,
Neither the one nor the other fort of men, could make this use
or improvement of their wealth, to deliver themfelves from go¬
ing to me grave for if they could, they would have layd all out
upon that purchase, but they could not doe it, therefore they
leave their wealth to others. Doubrless they would have given out
all chey were worth, to redeem themselves from the grave; what
would not rich men give to doe this, ch y would leave nothing to
children or Executors, could they but bribe off death with all
their riches. There is no title can be given to man which sets him
further from death, then to cal him God And this high title God
himselfe ( not a flatterer) hath cloathed some men with, (Psal.
82.6,7.) I sayd ye are gods, (but with the same breath he addes)
ree shall dye like men.
And as riches and honour cannot fhelter from death, so nei¬
ther can knowledge nor wisdome: Solomon who was the richest
treasury of wisdome ( of a meere man) that ever lived, did not
only dye himselfe, but sayd (Eccl.2.16.) Hom dyeth the nise man
and the feole? Yea, which is more then that ( unlesse Solomon as
elsewhere, so there by his wise man meant a holy man) wee may
adde, How dyeth the Godly man as the miched? How dyeth the just
man as the unjust? For though there be the utmost unlikenesse
between the godly and the wicked, both in the manner of their
life, and in the consequents of their death, yet in this they are
both alike, they both dye; Holinesse it selfe, as man is constitu¬
ted in this world, cannot shelter from death.
As the reigne of sin ( which was toucht before) brings in the
reigne of death; so where soever sin hath but a being, death will
have a footing. And therefore though just or godly men live not
in sin, yea are dead to sin, yet because sin lives in them, they also
mast dye. Yea hence it came to passe chat Jesus Christ d́yed, even

0225.head: Chap.30. An Exposition upon the Book of JOB. Verl.23.

body.t: because, though he had no sin in him, yet our sins were layd up¬
on him; And if sin where it was only imputed or charged,
brought death, as in the case of Christ himfelfe, then how much
more where it is inherent and acted, as it is in the best of Godly
men. This is a common truth, and generally acknowledg’d, that
all must dye, but ’tis not common for men to live in, much lesse to
live up to the knouledge of this truth, that they must dye.
But some may say, this is not a generall truth; that all must
dye, nor is this an indispencible appointment, That the grave is
the house appointed for all living; Some have lived and not dyed,
and some shall live and not dye, nor ever goe to the grave.
First, There are some, that have lived who never dyed, but
have gone to God, by a leape over the grave, or have escaped the
grave in their way to Glory (Gen. 5. 24.) And Encch malked
with God, and he was not, for God tooke him; this is a difficult
Scripture, but the Apostle ( Heb. 11.5.) gives a full and an un¬
erring Comment upon it, By faith Enoch mas trauslated, that he
should not see death, and he mas not found, because God had transla¬
ted him; for before his translation, he had this restimony that he
pleased God. Encchwas translated, he did not see death; there's one
that never vent to the house of the grave. As God had translated
him before out of a sinfull into a holy state, so Enoch was such
a proficient in grace, that God transsited him fiom grace to glo¬
ry, without so much as looking into the grave. How then is the
grave the house appointed for all living? And doe ve not read
that Eliah made the same escape? was not he taken up to heaven
in a fiery Chariot, (2 Kings 2.23.) there’s another who went
not to that house: how then was it appointed for all living?
And as I have instanced in two that have lived, and went not to
the grave, so the Scripture speakes of many who shall live here¬
after, and never goe to the grave Behold ( saith the Apostle,
1Cor. 15. 51.) Ishew you a mystery, me shall not all sleepe, (that
is, we shall not all dye, that, by sleepe he meanes death, the whole
discourse of that Chapter makes it evident) what then shall be¬
come of us? That’s answer'd in the next word; But ne shall all
be changed, in a moment, in the twinckling ef anere, at the last
trumpet, for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead spall be raised in¬
corryptible, and ve shall be changed. And agnine, (1 Thes.A. 17.)
Then me xhich are alive, and remaine, suallbe canght up tegetber,

0226.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Booke of JOR. Veri.23»

body.t: vith them in the Clouds, to meet the Lord in the aire,-and so shall
me ever be with the Lord. When Christ cometh to Judgement,
the living Saints on earth shall not dye, nor descend into the
grave, but shall present ly ascend or be caught up into the Clouds.
Therefore the grave is not the house of all living.
I Answer.
First, Those few exceptions doe not at all infirme the truth
of the generall rule, but rather confirme it this is the rule, that
all must dye, because none escape, but upon some speciall ex¬
ception. And though none of the Saints on earth who shall be
found alive at the generall resurrection of the dead shall dye, yet
they shall have somewhat which is equivalent to death, they
shall be changed, and death, at the 14th Chapter of this Booke
(v. 14.) is called a change. Tbis change is the putting off our
mortality, that change will be the putting on of immortality;
The one is a change by being uncloathed the other is a change by
being cloathed upon, as the Apostle distinguisheth them, (2 Cur.
3.4.) And because the day of the resurrection when all living
believers shall be changed and not dye, is a secret reserved in the
bosome of God, wee who live can have no assurance of any
change but of that by death, and therefore we have reason to be¬
lieve that God nill bring us to death, or to the house appointed for
all living.
Hence observe;
First, ive dye by appointment, the time us appointed mhen ve
must dye, and a place is appointed for us when me ars
dead.
Death is naturall, but we dye by a Law; we dye by appoint¬
ment. Some say of malefactors who are put to death for crimes
committed against the Law, They are slaine by the Lam; And we
may say of every man, He is slaine by a Lax, (Heb. 9. 27.)
It is appointed for men once to dye, and the grave is the house ap¬
pointed for all living. The living are appointed for that house,
and that house for them; death came in by mans act, but death
proceeds by an act of God; man let death in by breaking a com¬
mandement; and now death assaults and breaks in upon man by
a commandement. God threatned man with death in casc ot sin;
and he hath appointed men to dye, because they have sinned.

0227.head: Chap. 30. Au Exposition upon the Bocke of IOE. Verf23.

body.t: And secing the grave is the house appointed for all living,
Then by way of Corallary,
First, Wee should prepare for our going to that house;
That house is quickly made ready for us, let us make ready for
that house. Doe it, First, by setting your houses in order, (2 Kings
20.1.) Secondly, by setting your hearts in order; How misera¬
ble are they, uho when they are so siche that they cannot live, are yet
so unprepared that they dare not dye. Whatsoever goodly or bean¬
tiful houses we have now, we must short ly have a little dark cold
under ground house, called the Grave be not strangers in your
thoughts to that house, to which, we who should be strangers
and are but pilgrims in this world are travelling every day. And
how stately, ho w proud, how high foever men have been in this
world, they must stoope to and enter into that low built dark,
and silent house; It is the heuse appointea for all living.
Secondly, Seeing it is so, when God calls us to take up our
lodging there, let us quietly and chearefully obey bis call. The
Appointments of God must be obeyed. Christ was obedient un¬
to death, even the death of the crosse, (Phil.2.8.) And he with
a holy anger at any naturall (though unsinfull ) reluctance,
sayd, The cup which my father hath given me, shall Inot drinke?
(Tobn 18.11.) And what cup was that? It was the cup of death,
a bitter eup, about which he made that earnest prayer, (Mat.26.
39.) O my father, if it be vessible, let this cup passe from me; yet
that was not a more ea nest, then it was an humble and submit¬
ting prayer, therefore he adds, (v. 42.) O my father, if this cup
may not passe from me except I drinte it, thy mill be d ns. We may
pray against death, but then we must pray as Christ d d, laying
our prayer at the foote of God. That which makes our lives
sweet as well as holy, is, that we live having our wills drawne
forth in continued acts of obedience to the will of God: and that
which makes death, the bitter cup of death lueet to us, and us
holy in dying is, that we dve in obedience to the uill and ap¬
pointment of Godi The Apostle moves all men to a steddines
(not a sencelessenesse) of spirit under affliction upon this ground,
(IThe-3.3.) That no man be movedby thest afflectiors, for you your
selves knom, that ne are appointed thereunto. I may also caution all
men, against all unquiet motions at the approach of death, for
we know that we are appointed thereunto. We know, That, first.

0228.head: Chap. 30. An Expofition upon the Book ef J0 B. Verf.24.

body.t: the kind; secondly, the time of our death are appointed. Let this
be an argument to keepe off undue trouble of spirit when we
are summon'd to the grave.
This also fhould prevaile with us to make a quiet surrender of
our dearest relations when God calls for them. Death medles
not with thy friend without commission; There is no striving
uith the decrees of heaven; if we doe, we sin and increase our
sorrow by it. To be without naturall affection, is to be below a
heathon; To be over-borne by naturall affection, is to be below
a Christian. The divine appointment teacheth us moderation.
Thirdly, This also flowes from the same Generall truth,
God tabes notice, n'hat becomes of us mhen me are dead, as well
as when we are alive.
God hath appointed a house for us when wve dye; And his
providence watcheth over us there; he hath appointed us our
houses here in this world, and he hath appointed us our house
when we goe out of the world: His care followeth us to the
grave. We doe not dye by hap, or at a venture, nor are we
buried by hap, or at a venture; our house is appointed, and
that’s matter of comfort; God knowes where to fetch eve¬
ry mans bones, where to have every mans dust, he knows
the houses, the duellings of the dead distinctly, and though ma¬
ny thousands be thrust and throng’d into one house, into one
grave, yet God knoweth how to distinguish every mans dust,
and will in the day of the resurrection give him his oun againe.
Jobs faith was raised to this pitch of confidence, ( Chap.19 26,
27.) Though after my skin wormes destroy this body, ret in my flesb
shall I sec God, whom I shall see for my selfe, and mine eyes suall
behold, and net another (or not a stranger) though my reines be
consumed mithin me, er in my bosome. There Job spake his assu¬
rance of a personall resurrection, as here of his personall death.
I knon Thou wilt bring met to death, and to the house appointed for
all living. But how then? or what thoughts had Job further of
his condition, when housed in the grave? He tells us that in the
next verse.

Hombeit, he mill not stretch ont his hand to the Grave; As if he

But what meanes he, by stretching out the hand to the grave?
Ianswer; As The hand of man notes the power of man, so
doth the hand of God his pouer; and to stretch out the hand,
may have a twofold significancy, both according to Scripture
language, and common usage.
First, To stretch out the hand, signifies to hel pe, succour, and
deliver. Wee ordinarily desire a man to lend us his hand, when
we desire his helpe, and when we have a mind to helpe another,
we use to put forth or stretch out our hand to him. When Peter
began to sinke, and cryed, saying, Lord save me, immediately Tesus
stretched ferth his hand, and caught him, (Math. 14. 31.) The
Apostles (-Acts 4. 30.) pray, That the Lord by stretching forté
his hand to heale, and by doing wonders by the name of Jesus
Christ, would confirme them with boldnes in preaching the Go¬
spel. To stretch out the hand to God, is an imploring of suc¬
cour and salvation from him, ( Psal. 88. 9. Psal. 143.6.) And
when the Lord would Thew how ready he is to save and succour
us, he saith, All the day long I have stre ched out my bands unto a
disobedient and gaine-saying pecple, (Rom. 10 21.)
Secondly, Tostretch forth the hand, is to put forth power
to hurt and smite. Thus in the booke of Exodus, ( Chap.3.20.)
the Lord threatens, I uill stretch out my hand, and smite Egypi
with all my wonders. And still when Moses brought those won¬
derfull plagues upon Egypt, he is sayd to stretch out his hand up¬
on it. In this tenour the Prophets often expresse the dreadfull
dispensations of God, in the first appearances of them, as alfo in
their continuance, (Isa. 9. 12, 13.) Notmithstanding all this,

0230.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Booke ef J02. Verf-24.

body.t: his anger is not turned amay, but his hand is stretched out still;
For what? to afflict, yea, to destroy, and cut off his own people.
Thus man puts forth or layeth his hand spon man, as it seemes

37.22.) Lay no hand upon him,’tis the word in this text, stretch

Thus we see, That to stretch out the hand, is taken in Scripture

times stretch our his hand to helpe and deliver, as also to hurt

The word which we render grave, signifieth an heape, becaule

The Latine word notes swelling, because the grave swells upward

79. 1.) where the holy Prophet breakes out into this passio¬
nate complaint, O God the beathen are come into thine inheri¬
tance, thy holy Temple have they de filed: Thes have laid Jexusalem
on heapes; which some understand thus; they have made Jerusa¬

and murdered, that ferusalem was ( as it were) but one grave.
It is sayd of the Children of Israel, (Numb. 21. 11.) where seve¬

signifies Passengers, or Strangers, or as some conceave and read
it, the Hibrewes; As if that word did not denote (as most ex¬

That is, though they who are ready to dye and be carried to

But though we have attained the meaning of the single

Weeping is the effect of sorrouing, or veeping is the lan¬

Jobs was no dry sorrow, his compassionate bouels melted and

The word poore, hath been opened in other passages of this

We may call these naturally poore, as we may call others natu¬

strates the reallity of the other, or is a further testimony of it.
Did not I meepe for him that was in trouble? Was not my soule
grieved for the poore?
Hence observe;
It is a duty to compassionate others in their afflictions.
To weepe for those that are in hard dayes, to be grieved for
those that are pinch't and pin’d with poverty, is a duty to which
we are called under a threefold Confideration.
First, As men, being of the selfe same nature, mould and mat¬
ter with them that are troubled or poore, even nature invites to
sympathize with those that are of the same common nature.
A Heathensayd, 'Tis inhumane not to grieve at humant calami¬
ties; A beast will make a discovery of somewhat like this to¬
wards other beasts, how much more should man towards
mao!
Secondly, Wee are to compassionate those that are poore
or in trouble not only as being in the same generall nature, but
as therefore being our selves subject to the same speciall troubles
whereuith others are troubled, and to the same sorrows where¬
with any other are made sorrowfull. The Apostle gives us this
Argument, (Heb. 13.1, 2,3.) Let brotherly leve continue; be
not forget full to entertaine strangers, for thereby some have enter¬
tained Angels unamares. And at the third verle, Remember them
that are in bonds, as bound witb them, and them which suffer adver¬
sity, as being your selves also in the body; that is, alive in the body,
and so obnoxious to the like sufferings. W’hat hath fallen upon
any man in the body, may fall upon another whilest he is in the
body; as all men have one common nature, so in that common
nature they may quickly meete with the same common afflicti¬
ons. As the Apostle comforts and encourageth the Corinthians

of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he mas rich, yet for your sates
he became poore, that yee thorom his poverty might be rich: He cid
not only pity us in our poverty, but tooke a course to make us
rich, and to set us up in a good and plentifull estate againe.
And he was filled to succour us in our sufferings by a sence of his
oune sufferings. ( Heb. 2. 18.) For in that he himselfe hath suf¬
fered, being tempted, hee is able to succour them that are tempted.
lesus Christ hath tranfferred all our sufferings to himselfe, and
to giveth us helpe in our wants, through a sence of what him¬
selfe once wanted and suffered. This the Apostle had assigned as
the reason why he submitted to a luffering condition, (v. 17.)
Nherefore in all things it beboved him tobe made lihe unto his bre¬
thren, that he might be ꝗ mercifull high Priest in things pertain¬
ing to God, to make reconhiliation for the sinnes of the peeple. Jesus

0252.head: Chap.30. An Expofition upon the Bok of IOB. Verf. 25.

body.t: Christ was mercifull before he tooke our nature, (God is infi¬
nitely mercifull, and Christ as the Son or second person in the
Trinity, thought no robbery to be equall with God, and there¬
fore must needs be infinitely mercifull before hee tooke our
nature) but hee was not mercifull by way of Compassion,
or as having a symphathy with us, or a sence of our sor¬
rowes, and sufferings upon him, from his owne experience, as he
was God; As such purely he could not be sencible of our sor¬
rows in that way. And for this cause ( among many other cau¬
ses) he became man, that so he might be sencible of them, and
that having taken our sorrowes upon himselfe, he might give us
a ready reliefe and helpe out of them. This is compleate Chari¬
ty, when our compassions are active for the reliefe of those that
are in misery. I grant if we compare heart-compassion and hand¬
reliefe together, the former is in it selfe more excellent then the
latter for he that gives reliefe, offers somewhat out of himselfe,
but he that bestowes compassion upon another, gives him some¬
what of himselfe, or from within himselfe, he gives him his heart
and good will, which is better then any cternall gift; yet if any
man shall thinke he hath done enough, (it being in his power to
doe more) for an afflicted friend or brother, when he hath pi¬
tied him and bestowed a parcel of good words only upon him,
let him know he hath done nothing at all for him. Compassion u
better then the fruits of it, but compassion mithout fruit is not good.
He that gives a cup of cold water onty, (where need is) in com¬
passion, shall not loose his reuard, but compassion alone (uhere
cold water is needed, and we have it to give) shall have no re¬
ward.
Lastly, Ifit be a duty to weepe for those that are in hard
dayes, and to be grieved for the poore. Then
First, How short are they of their duty, that reloyce not on¬
ly in, but at the sorrowes of others, and who are glad of their
griefe. The wickednes of such was sheued (v. 9.
Secondly, How short are they of this duty, who in hard daves
upon others, in stead of pitying and weeping for them, upbraid
them with their troubles, and cast their afflictions in their teeth.
Such unnaturall and cruel men, have also been branded from
other passages of this Booke and Chapter.
Thirdly, How farre are they departed from this duty, who

0253.head: Chap. 30. An Exposicion upon the Bok of JO B. Vert.25.

body.t: instead of œeeping with those that weepe, doe their best to ren¬
der theit condition worse, to impoverish the very poore, and so
instead of drying up and wiping off the teares of those that
weep, they make them weep more or afresh How deservedly are
they abhorr'd both of God and good men, who adde affliction
to the afflicted, and put Gall and Wormewood into their cup,
whose soules are in bitternes.
Secondly, The circumstance of time is considerable, when
7ob was thus filled with pity and compassion; was it not inthe
hight and flourish of his worldly wealth? was it not when he
was at ease in his house, and had enough ? was it not when he was
not in hard dayes? when trouble and poverty were farre from
him ? even then he wept for him that was in trouble, and his
soule was grieved for the poore.
Hence observe;
A godly man layeth the troubles and mants of others to heart,
mhen he himselfe is freest and furthest from trouble.
Job being in such prosperity, as he describes in the 29th Chap¬
ter had no cause to weepe for any of his owne concernments.
The Candle of the Lord did shine upon his head, and the rocks
powred him out rivers of oyle yet then he was powring out
teares for the poore. Thus Nehemiah a godly man was the
Kings Cup-bearer, and had ( though a captive ) not only liberty
but the favour of the Prince; yet when he heard of the afflicti¬
ons of his brethren that were in perusalem, he could not then
rejoyce in his personal enjoyments, but wept and looked so sad¬
Iy, that coming to doe his office, the King tooke notice of it and
asked, Art thou sicbe? The affliction of his brethren was his sick¬
nesse, and all the trouble that lay upon him, was the report of
their trouble. When worldly men are at ease, they little thinke
and care as little who is in paine; when they are warme, they
thinke no body is a cold, and when they are full-fed, they scarce
believe that any are hungry. When Dauid wanting bread sent
messengers to Nabal, who made a feast at that time like a King,
he would not take notice of his straits, nor send him so much as a
loafe of bresd. O how many are there, who if they can but get
into an earth!y Paradife, never trouble themselves with those
that are in a wildernes of trouble; sick and poore, and wanting

0254.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Booke ef JOR. Versizó

body.t: persons, are as fatre from their hearts, as sicknes, poverty and
want are from their houses. Fem feele that which others feele,
till they feele it themselves. Tob felt no trouble himselfe, but he
felt the troubles of many others.
Take this Corallary from the whole.
The life ef man in this world is trouble and sorrom.
Wee are either dayly pressed uith our oun safferings, or we
ought to be with the sufferings of others. Most times wee are
pressed with burdens of our owne, and if at any time we are not,
yet there are burdens enow upon our friends and relations at
home, or upon the people and Churches of God abroad to presse
us. Wee may wel conclude from these premises, as old Jacob did,
Few and evill are the dayes of our pilgrimage; For as they who
have had most dayes have lived but a little while, so they who
have had the best dayes have lived but uith little ease, or (as we
say ) in a kind of little ease. What with our oune sorrowes, what
with the sorrowes of others, what have we else but sorrow?
Tob having thus shewed in what frame his heart was towards
those whom he saw afflicted with any evill, proceeds to shew
how himselfe was disappointed of that good which he expe¬
cted.
Verf. 26. w'ben I looked for good, then evill came unto mee.
The word rendred, loohed for, notes hope, which is an inward
looke, or the looke of the mind. The soule hath its eye as well
as the body; There is an eye of faith in the soule, looking upon
the truth of the promise, and there is an eye of hope in the soule,
looking for the good of the promise. And untill we looke to the
promise, believing the truth of it, we can never looke to the pro¬
mise hoping for the good ofit. Thus David resolved ( Psal. 121.
1.)I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from nhence cometh my
helpe, my helpe cometh from the Lord, &c. What eyes did David
lift up to the hills? Surely those of holy faith and hope; And so
did fob, when he sayd here in the text, I loohed
for good.
What good ? There is a threefold good; First, Naturall,
health and strength, Secondly, Civill, peace and plenty; Third.

0255.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Boke ef Io s. Verf. 26.

body.t: ly, Morall or spirituall good, the Grace and comforts of the Spi¬
rit, here in this place Job intends the two former lorts of good,
uith the latter branch of the third; As if he had said, I expected
the continuance of my health and strength of my peace and plen
ry, as also of the joyes and comforts of the holy Ghost But when
I looked for good, or that these good things should abide with
mee.
Then evil came.
Evill is of two sorts; First, of sinne; Secordiy, of suffer¬
ings; the latter is meant here, evill came, that is, trouble came,
effliction came; evill of as many sorts came as the good was, for
the continuance whereof I looked. Evill came upon mee ( as we
say) thicke and threefold, it came upon mee like an armed man,
I could not withstand, much lesse overcome it. Wben I loohed for
good, then, even in the midst, in the hight and heate of my ex¬
pect ations, evill came.
And nhen I waited for light.
The second part of the verse, is in sence the same with the
former; light here is the same in generall with good there ( as of¬
ten elsewhere in Scripture) I maited for light. What then?
Then came darknesse.
As light is the same with good, so darbnes is the same with
evill, and here ( as often elsewbere in Scripture) Darknesse is put
for all sorts of evill. The words are plaine, and need no labour
of exposition. I mhall only note some things from them.
Firft, In Gencrall.
Good men are ofien deceaved of, and misse their expectarion
in thio werld, especially about the things of the world.
A godly man hath a twofold expectation; First, about tbe
things ot the world to come; Secondly, about the things of this
world; A godly mans expect ation shall not be lost in reference
to the things of the world to come, but he may loote many of
his expect ations as to tue things of this world. How often are
we deceaved in our expect ations from men, and then most when
we expect most from them. Aten are a lie, (Pfal. 62. 9.) ac
KK

0256.head: Chap.30. An Expofitien upon the Bok ef JOB. Vers.26.

body.t: active lie, they deceave others, and a passive lie, they are decea¬
ved by others. And they who are most actively a lie, are most
usually and most deservedly a passive lie, or fed uith lyes. We
may loole for this and that at the hand of man, and meete vith
neither. (Isa. 20.S.) They shall be afraid and ashamed of E¬
thispia their expectation, and f Egypt their glery; that is, They
uho expected much helpe, and gloried or boasted of the helpe,
which they should have from Ethiopia and Egypt (as the Jewes
and others did ) looked so long for it that they were ashamed to
looke any longer, and at last uent withoutit; as is expressed in
the words follouing, (v. o.) And the inhabitant of this Isle shall
say in that day, behold, such it our expectatisn mhither mee flie for
helpe to be delivered ( that is, tve see what is become of these E¬
thipians and Egyptians, who undertooke to protect us ] frem¬
the King ef Asyria, (they we see ceuld not protect themselves
from tie sorces of Asyria) and how shall we escape? That is, we
cannot escape by their meanes, vee fly to Ethioria and Egypt for
helpe and deliverance from the King of Asyria, but their helpe
is vaine, they could not helpe themselves. The helpe of man is
often vaine, when he gives us the best helpe which he hath pro¬
mised but some are so vaine, that though they promise us helpe,
they vill not give it. (Zech. 9. 5.) Asphelon-shall sce it and
feare: Geza also shall see it aud be very sorron full: and Ekren for
her expectation shall be ashamed, and the King shall perish from Ga¬
za, and Asphelen shall not be inhabited. There is nothing more
common then disappointments from men. And as men usually
fayle & disappoint our expectation, so God also doth sometimes.
God never fayles his owne promises, but he may fayle our ex¬
pectations, yet ’tis then only, when wee expect without, beside,
or, beyond the promise. ( Jer 8. 15.) Nee loohed for peace, but
no good came, and for a time of heaith, and behold trouble. The
fexes had great hopes that God would give them prosperous
and happy times, But while they looked that God should keepe
promises, they tooke no care to keepe Commandements, ( their
own confession cleares that, (v. 14.) Our God hath given us
n'ater ef gall to drinke, because xe bave sinned against the Lord.)
Thus to hope for the good of the promise, is to hope beside yea
against the truth of the promise. That other Prophet assignes the
same reason oftheir disappointment, (Isa. 59. 5.) Thertfore is

0257.head: Chap.30. An Exposition upon the Bok of IOR. Verf. 26

body.t: judgement farre from us, neither doth justice overtake us, mes vaite
for light, but beh ld ubscurity, fer bri-htnesse, but me malke in dark¬
nesse. And why was all this? The answer is plaine, (v. 12,13.)
For our transgressions are multiplyed besore thre, aud eur sins mit¬
nesse against us, &c. And as for a punishment of sin, as also for the
exercise of patience and tryall of grace, God fiustrates the pre¬
sent expectation of his own people, so much more will he for the
former reason disappoint wicked men of theirs; They shall look
for light, but it vill be darknes for ever. (Pre.10.28. )The hope of
the rightecus sball be gladnes, ( that is, the utmost issue of it shall
be gladnes) bnt the expectatien of the miched shall pirish. The
wicked expect the perishing of the righteous, but that ex¬
pectation of the wicked shall perish, because the righteous shall
never perish. The things which the wicked chiefely hope for,
are perishing things, and that hope often perisheth, But if they
hope for the things which perish not, that hope alwayes perish¬
eth, for they themselves shall perish for ever. This Selomon as¬
serts fully (Chap. 11.7) When a micked man dyeth, his expecta¬
tion shall perish, axd the hepe of the unjust man perisheth. Hope or
expectation is usually long liv’d, and though the hope of wicked
men be blind and sickly, yet it often holds out or lives as long as
they live. But when the wicked dye, they and their hope, they
and their expectation dye and expire together. I grant the
hope of a just man endeth when he dyeth, yet it doth not dye,
but is perfected in fruition, as Solomon more then intimates at
the z3d verse of the same Chapter, The defire of the righieous
is enly good. It is a Maxime in Philosophy, All things desire good;
And in that sence the desire of all men, as it is desire, is onsy of
that which is good. But as the righteous only desire to doe that
which is good, so in strict sence, they only desire to have that
which is good. The desire of the righteous as righteous, is orly
good, and alwayes good; for as he desires God above all, fo
he desires God in all, in whom is all good, and nothing tut
good. Thus the defire of the rigbteeus (and therefore their
hope, for we can hope for nothing but what ve desire) u only
good. But ( as it followeth in the same verse ) The xpictation
the micged is wrath; that is, he expects the accomplisnment of
his urath, or when his expectation is accomplished, it is in urath,
and proves wrath to him. Wee cannot fay, that a wiched man

0258.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Booke of JOB. Verf.26.

body.t: doth properly and explicitly expect wrath, he hath great pre¬
sumpeiens of mercy, but he sha l have wrath in the roome of that
mercy which he presumptuously expected; he looked for many
good dayes here, and for the favour of God hercafter, but he
teldame finds the former, (and when he doth they are evill to
hin ) but he shall not at all find the latter. What good le hath,
he hath it in this world, and ’tis of this world, he hath none of
another kinde, none beyond this world. When the rich man in
hell desired but a drop of water to coole his tongue, he was an¬
fwver'd uith, Son remember thou hast had thy good things, there
are no more to be had for thee.
Againe, Both good and bad may faile in their expectations,
but with a vast d ff rence, the wicked looke and receive not, be¬
cause they looke not in faith, their expectation is but a fancy,
they heve no ground to looke for good, and therefore they looke
for good and receave none. All true good comes out of a pro¬
mise They who have nothing to doe with the promise, (as the
wicked having no faith, have not, though I grant the promise,
(I meane the abíolute promise) may have to doe with them;
Now, I say, the wicked being in the sence opened, without the
promite ) have no ground to expect or hope for the good of the
promise. But as for the Godly, though they presently receave
not what they looke for, yet looking in faith they shall at last,
one time or other receave it. ( Psal. 9. 18.) The needy shall not
almayes be forgotten: The expectation of the poore (that is, of the
godly poore) shall not perish for ever.
Further, sinners disappoint God of his expect ation, and there¬
fore no marvaile if God disappoint them of theirs. ( Isa. 5. 4.)
Woat could have been done more to my vineyard that I have not
done ta it, ( faith the Lord,) Wherefore when I loohed that it
souuld bring forth grapes, brought it forth xilde grapes, ard I look¬
for Tudgement, and behold eppression, for righte-usnesse, and be¬
hold a ery. God hath his expectation upon man, and man, sin¬
full man deceaves God of his expectation : He lookes for righte¬
ousnesse, for reformation, for the fruits of repentance, of faith
and love, but finds none; How justly then doth God let sinners
looke for peace, and not finde it, for mercy and finde none! yea
the best of his people are deservedly shortned in their expecta¬
sions upon this ground, Who is there among them that hath not

0259.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Bocke of JO2. Vers.26.

body.t: failed the expect ation of God? where is that care to please God,
that feare of offending him, ahat circumspect walking, that re¬
deeming of time, mhat deniall of our selves, that zeale for him,
which upon the account of his free grace in Christ, and our hope
throuph Christ, he might hope, yea challenge from us: and if
we make God looke so often for that which hee receives not,
shall we thinke it strange if we receave not that for which ve
looke?
Yet doubtlesse, this uas not sobs case; we doe not find that
he had disappointed thie expectation of God in any thing. (hu¬
mane fraylety only excepted) And as God gave him a high te¬
stimony in this poynt, so also did his owne conscience; And
therefore uhen he saith, I loeked for good, we have reason to con¬
clude that he had a good ground to looke for it, yet he mist is,
when I loobed fer good, then evill came.
Hence observe, Secondly.
A goaly man considering and examining his own heart and l fe,
may find no speciall reason there uby Gud efflicts bim, er
causeth evill to come apon himo.
God taketh away good, and senes evill upon us for one of
those two reasons; eyther
First, When we grow wanton and vaine, or play the wan¬
tons, and feed our vanity with the good things of Ged, uhen
wee let goe the bridle of moderation, and serve our bell es ra¬
ther then the Lord Jesus in the use of our worldly comforts,
then’tis time for God, and usually God takes that time to take
them from us, aud give us ashes for bread, or mingle our drinke
with weeping Thus Christ denourcech A moe to them that laugh
now, ( Labe 6 25.) They are not threatned with a woe meerely
for laughing, To doe so is not only lawfull, but innocently na¬
turall and proper to man as man. But Christ thunders a woe a¬
gainst (as Solomon calls it, Eccl. 2. 2. ) mad or immoderate
laughter and rejoycing in the use of the creature, aster such
laughing comes crying, woe and sorrow.
Secondly, Evill comes usually instead of the good wee looke
for, when our hearts are hardned and our bowels shut up against
all pity and compassion towards those who are under the present
sufferings of evill. This brought cvill upon Terusalem when shee

0260.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Book of JO E. Verf.26.

body.t: looked for good ( Ezek. 16. 49.) Pride, fullnes of bread, and a¬
b undance of Idlenesse mas in ber, neither did shce strengthen the
hand of the poore and needy. But it was not thus with holy fob;
he did not drowne himselfe in carnal pleasures, he did not steepe
his spirit in earthly enjoyments, Nor did Tob looke upon
himselfe as unconcern’d in the troubles, and straits of the distres¬
sed and necessitous. Jobs heart was not fill’d with his riches and
possessions, but with pity and compassion to the poore. Now
though tob was a man of this admirable temper, both as to his
owne aboundance, and the wants of others, both as to the good
which himselfe once had, and as to the evills which others endu¬
red, yet when he looked for good, evill came, and he was not
only disappointed of his hopes, but afflicted greatly. Some have
met with sufferings, which ( though as sinners they have deser¬
ved, yet) they have not procured by theit sinnes. God afflicts
none of his people but for holy ends, but he affl cts many of
them without any respect to their unholines.
Thirdly, Consider the word, when, which referrs to the cir¬
cumstance of time, wherein evill befell Tob; when I looked for
coed, then evill came. This when, may have a double reference.
First, to the time of his prosperitie, and so to his looking for
good, was the continuance or prolongation of it. Now com¬
pare the scope of this verse, and this season wherein sob looked
for good, with the former verse, Did not I mecpe with him that
was in trouble; and
We may observe;
They that are pitifull and charitable to others in their sor¬
romes, may mith a hopefull probabilitie looke fer the continua¬
tion of their owne comforts.
Our condoling with and succouring those who are in trouble,
is a faire argument that we shall keepe our peace.
Secondly, when, may referre to the time of his affliction;
And that, both as he looked for pity in and deliverance out of
his affliction, or the renewing of his prosperity, wben I louked fer
good, that is, when I in my afflicted state, waited lor good, for pi¬
cy from men, and for the repaire of those sad breaches, which
were made upon me by the hand of God, then evill came, and I
was more wrapt up in or entangled with trouble then before.

0261.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Book of IOB. Vert. 26.

body.t: Hence note;
Hee that hath helped others out ef their afflictious, may preba¬
bly looke for pity in and helpe out of his affliction.
Christ gives that gencrall rule ( Luke 6. 38.) with tbe same
measure that yee mete mithall, it shall be measured to you againe.
That rule hath the force both of a promise and of a threatning
in it. And as it respects the quantity, that you shall have as much
or more measured to you then you measure; so it respects the
kind and qualicy of that which is measured more. For if we
measure evill to others, we must looke that evill shall be mea¬
sured to us againe: and if we measure out good to others, we
may warrantably looke that good shall be measured out to us
againe; Jeb thought he should have the good of compassion
measured out freely to him in his affliction, he having measured
it out abouudantly to others in theirs. And that the hearts of
men would never have been hardned into stones in the day of his
calamity, when as his heart had melted into terres at the cala¬
mity of others. That of David gives much assurance of this,
(Psal.41.1, 2,3.) Blessed is the man that considereth the poore,
the Lord vill deliver him ( not the poore only, but him also that
wisely considereth the poore) in the time of trouble; ibe Lerd
mill preserve him, and keepe him alive, and he shall be blessed upon
the earth; and thou milt not deliver him to the mill of bis enemies.
The Lord will strengthen him upon the bed of languisbing: theu
vilt mabe all his bed in his sichnesse. To consider the poore, is
both to pity and helpe them. And he that is pitifull to the poore,
shall according to this Scriprure be delivered out of trouble, or
preserved from trouble, both which are high acts of mercy.
And therefore fob seems to wonder at it, that evill should come,
when he had this and so many other probable grounds, upon
which he might looke for good.
Hence take two Corolaries.
First, we are apt to thinke strange of our afflictions, mhen me
see ne reason for them¬.
If wee cannot charge our selves with sin, wee conclude, wee
mhall not suffer.
Secondly, Note.

0262.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Bocke ef JOR. Vers.27.

body.t: They who have been mest ex ect in their malkings, sould yet
looke and prepare for changes.
Grace gives us a good title, the best title to earthly things,
but it doth not assure the possession of them. They who are dead
to worldly enjoyments, may yet see them dye. And how com¬
passionate soever any man hath been to the poore, pained and
afflicted, yet himtelfe may become poore, and pained, and af¬
flicted; as fob shewes us further by his owne experience and ex¬
ample in the next verse.
Vers. 27. Ay bowels boyled and rested not; the dayes of af¬
flictin prevented mee.
From this verse to the end of the Chapter, Job reckons up se¬
verall sad effacts of his afflictions and sorrowes.
My bowels boyled, or, were hot.
As I was full of sorrows without, so l was inwardly inflamed as
it were with sorrow, His bowels were as a seething or boyling
pot upon the fire. The Bowels signifie in Scripture First, the most
feeling compassions of the mind : Put on ( saith the Apostle,
Col. 3. 12.) as the elect of God, bowels of mercy; that is, be yee
very mercifull. Secondly, The Bowels signifie the most secret
