workings and cogitations of the mind. (Pro. 20. 27.) The spi¬
rit of man is the caudle of the Lord, searching all the inmard parts
Cor Bowels) of the bellz; that is, those thoughts, contrivements,
and conceptions which lye closest or most out of sight in the
mind of man. And hence the boyling ef the bowels, imports in¬
ward trouble, or troubled thoughts, eyther uith seare or griefe
or both. Thus ’tis sayd of Daniel ( Dan. 4. 10.) He vas asto¬
nished for one heurt, and his thoughis troubled him; and so of
Belshazzer when he saw the hand writing upon the wall ( Dan.5.
6. ) his countenance was changed, and his thrughts troubled him;
that is, his breast or bowels were full of boyling tumustuatirg
thoughts. Many Scriptures set out the inward Agony of the
mind by fire and boyling. A man ing eat perplexity, is as if he
were in a fire, or a fire in him; care is a fire, feare is a fire, and
so is sorrow, My bonels boyled ( saith Jeb) As the Lords anger
is like a burning fire, ( Lam. 2. 3.) Hee hatb cut fin his fierce

0263.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Booke ef JO R. Verf.27.

body.t: Anger all the horne of Israel, he hath drawn back his rght hand
from before the enemy, and he burned against Jacob like a flaming
fire which devoureth round about. Now as the Lords anger, which
causeth him to bring trouble upon a people or a person is like
fire so is that sorrow with which man is affected in the day ofthe
Lords anger. Thus spake jeremie (Lam. 1. 20.) Behold O Lord,
for I am in distresse, my bowels are troubled, my heart is turnea
mithin mee. The heart or bowels are the seate of the pessions;
And when passion is so strong that it turnes the heart, and so
hot that’tis layd to make the bowels boyle, Then passion is at the
highest, Ay bomels boyled
and rested not.
The Hebrew is, Were not silent, paine makes a noyse, paine
speaks lowd. (Isa. 16.11.) My bomels shall sound like an harpe
for Moab. And when wee are freed from paine a sweete silence
followeth. (Psal. 107. 29.) Hee maketh the storme a calme, so
that the waves thereof are still (or the waves thereof are silent)
what a roaring noyse is there in a proper storme at Sea? and is
there not a roaring noyse in the metaphoricall stormes of trou¬
ble? or if we take the words rested not, in their ordinary sence,
then they note the uncessantnesse of his sorrow; That resteth,
which ceaseth or giveth over working; as it is sayd (Exod. 20.
11.) In six dayes the Lord made heaven and earth, the Sea and all
that in them is, and rested the seventh day; Thus Jobs boueli bor¬
led and rested not, that is, his sorrow ceased not, he had no ( luci¬
da intervalla) comfortable lightsome intermissions of or vacati¬
ons from his paines and griefes, He had not fever fies, but a con¬
tinuall burning fever; New fewel was dayly, yea hourely ad¬
ded to feed the fire and keepe his bouels boy ling; My bowels
(saith he) boyled and rested not.
The dayes of affliction prevented mec.
He bad sayd a little before (v. 16. ) The dayes of affliction
have taken hold upon mee; here he saith, they have prevented mee,
that is, they came suddenly upon mee, or unlook d for. Some
reade, they met mee, so the word is rendred in that charge against
the Moabites and Ammonites ( Deut. 23. 3, 4.) Even to their
tenth generation sall ihey not enter into the Congregation of ibe
LI

0264.head: Chap.30. An Exposition upon the Booz ef JOB. Verf.27.

body.t: Lord for ever, because they met you not with bread and with xater
in the way mhen yet came cut of Egypt, &c. Now whether we read
tobs text, The dayes of affliction met mee, or prevented mee, the
sence is the same, Implying, that those dayes of affl ction came
somewhat una wares, or when he locked not for them, or when
he was looking, as he sayd in the former verse for other for better
dayes. There are tœo sorts of mecting, First, looked for, Second¬
Iy, unlooked for, oftentimes a friend meets us whom ve thought
not of, and so may an enemy; The latter meeting is meant here.
Such meetings are uncomfortable preventings.
Some conceave Job (ayd, The dayes of tvill prevented him, be¬
cause he met with those evills in the best of his Age, which usu¬
ally come not till the latter end, or close of a mans age. There
are some evills and affl ctions which are so usuall in old age
that they are even naturall or congeniall toit; of these Solomon
speakes and cautions young men, ( Eccl. 12.1.) Remember now
thy Creater in the dayes of thy yeuth, mhile tht evill dayes come not,
nor the yeares dram nigh, when thou shalt say Ihave no pleasure in
them. Let any man but live, and he shall out-live his bodily
strength and pleasures. What can we expect to meet with in old
age but paine and forrow ? When, as Solemon there Allegoriz th
the Sun, and the light, and the Moone, and the Starres are dark¬
ned, and the clouds returne efter tbe raine in the day when the kte¬
pers ef the house shall tremble, and the strong men fhall bom them¬
selves, &c. That is, when the powers of nature shall inevitably
suffer an universal decay; What can any man (I say ) expect
then but paine and forrow ? But when a man is in the best of his
dayes, he looks for good dayes, and the continuance of his body¬
ly ftrength. Therefore Job being broken not only in his estate but
in his strengch, being not only impoverished but pained and dis¬
eased, in the best of his dayes, he might well say, The dayes of
affliction have prevented mee.
Againe, Some read this in connection uith the former verse,
as if what he saith here, were an effect of what he said there, Be¬
cause nhen I looked for good, evill came to me, and mhen I hoped
for light darknes came upon mee, therefore my bomells boyled xithin
mee, so that they could not rest. Taking the text in this depen¬
dance,
Oblerve;

0265.head: Chap.30. An Exposition upan the Book of IOR. Verf.27.

body.t: It is exceeding painfull and afflictive to misse our expectatiens,
or not to receave the good mhich me hope and vaite for.
When we looke for evill, and expect the coming of trouble,
'tis burdensome & grievous enough when it comes; But to meet
vith evill when we waite for good, doubles the weight of evill.
To be crossed in our expectations, makes our crosse heavy and
our bowels boyle.
Then how vill the bowells of wicked men boyle in forrow,
for ever when they shall be quite frustrated of their hopes and
loose all their expectations? such are often full of hopes, and
bigge with the expectation of good thinge, not only in this life
but in the next, They hope their soules shall gue to heaven when
their bodyes goe to the grave, they looke for light, even the
light of glory afrer the darknesse of death, but darknesse shall be
their portion, and they shail goe to the generation of their fathers,
where they shall never set light. In the 7th of Mathew (v. 24.)
we find wicked men looking for, yea laying claime to glory;
They xnocke at heaven gate, as if they had much acquaintance
there, yet all they shall heare from Christ is, I never knew you,
depart from mee ye that worke iniquitie. O what boyling of bow¬
ells will these men feele in the fire that never goeth out, When
holy job found iuch a boyling of his bowels in a fire that quickly
went out? My bomels boyled,
the dayes of affliction prevented mee.
Hence note, First.
The boliest and best of men, are apt to thinke afflictions further
eff from them then they are.
We usually say, Bad newes comes before it is loobed fer. Every
godly man thirks he may fall into affliction; But though hee
hath a sence of this upon him, that afflictions may come; yet he
thinks them further off then they are, or that they will not come
so soone as they doe. The Prophet speaking of voluptuous sen¬
sualists sayth ( Amos 6. 3.) They put the evill day farre from
them. And as these put it farre from themselves, so the false Pro¬
phets assured others, that it was not only farre from them, but
should neyer over-take them, ( Jer. 14. 15.) Therefere tkus
saiththe Lord concerning the Prophets that prophesie in my name,

0266.head: Chap.30. An Expalition upon the Booke of JOR. Verl.27.

body.t: and I sent them not, yes they say sword and famine shall not be in
this Land, by sword and famine shall these Prophets be consumed.
And againe, (Jer. 5. 12.) Toey nave belyed the Lord, and said
it is not hee, neitber shall evill come upon us, ntither shall wee see
sword nor famine. (Now as evill men put the evill day farre from
themselves, and false Prophets put is farther from them, so godly
men seldome thinke that the evill day is so neere as indeed it is.
Yea they may have a secret hope that the evill day will not come
at all, but that they shall dye in their nest, as lob once said,But as
God prevents us often uith his mercies & loving kindnesses, Da¬
vid hoped he would; The God of my mercy shall prevent mee,
( Psal. 59. 10. ) and he prayed what he would, (Psal 79 8.)
O remember not against us our former iniquities, let thy tender
mercies speedily prevent us; for nee are brought very lom. And as
God sometimes doth it, beyond both our hopes and prayers.
(Psal. 21. 3.) For thou preventest him with the blessings of good¬
nesse thou sertest a Crowne of pure gold upen his head. Now (I lay)
as God hath preventing mercies, he sends in mercy, or such a spe¬
ciall mercy, before wee looke for it; so it is as true, that God
hath preventing ludgements, and that hee sends in afflictions be¬
tore they are looked for; sad troubles, sad sicknesses, sad break¬
ings, sad losses, sad miscarriages of servants and children come
unlooked for upon many of the servants of God. David expe¬
rienced this allo, (Psal. 18.5.) The sorrowes of hell compassed
mee about, the snares of death prevented mee; That is, deadly
snares, such snares as endangered my life surprised me, when I
had no thought of any such mischiefe.
Lastly, Note.
Unexpected afflictions, afflist us most.
As evill shall most certainly come upon those sinners uho ex¬
pect it not. ( Amos 9. 10.) All the sinners of my people shall dy
by the sword, mhich say, the evill shall net evertabe, nor prevent us.
So it will be most terrible to them when it comes. As to misse
the good that wee looke for ( which was observed before) so to
meete with any evill that wee looked not for, cuts to the quicke.
lob looked for good, but it came not, He looked not for such
troubles, and they came. The dares of evill prevented him. As
vee may looke for good, so evill should not be unloohed fo¬¬

0267.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Beoke of IOR. Vers. 27.

body.t: If the coming of trouble be looked for, it uill not trouble us so
much when it comes. We may possibly prevent or hide our
selves from expected evills, but to be sure we may be the better
armed for them. N’hereas they who doe not foresee them at all,
feele them most. What perill, what poverty, what crosse what
sicknesse, what losse is there that we may not looke for? Are
not all these incident to our nature as we are men? Are they
not deserved by us as we are sinners? yea as ue are Saints, wee
may looke for tryalls; and if as Saints we looke not for them,
we hardly know what it is to be a Saint. “Tis our wisdome to
way-lay troubles in our thoughts, and personate the worst
outward estate sometimes, while we enjoy the best. They are
not only uise men, but the best and choysest Saints, who use
their good dayes and things, as if they might every day change
to worse, yea to the worst. To looke for evill fearefully is be¬
low faith. tut to looke for it preparingly, is a very spirituall ex¬
ercise of faith. To be upon the racke of expectation, is to ante¬
date our sorrowes; but to be upon thoughts of them, and so to
converse with them, that ( as the Apostle saith ) the fiery tryall
may not be strange to us, this as it is our duty, though tryalls
never come, so it will be a great support to us when they come.
It is sinfull œhen wee are behind-hand in meditating what wee
may suffer, as well as when wee are behind-hand in considering
what wee ought to doe. They undergoe tryalls with most pati¬
ence, uho are ofrenest minding a day of Tryall. And usually
they have unlooked for comforts, who are graciously looking
for their Crosse. And chough it be good to be full of holy
faith, that our mercies shall be continued, yet it is as good to be
full of a holy feare that our mercies may be changed. Happy are
they mhs are at once believing for good dayes, and preparing for
them; yea happy also are they who are at once believing about evill
dayes, and preparing for them. This was the frame and posture
of Righteous Noahs spirit, ( Heb. 11.7.) Who by faith, being
marned of Ged of things not seene as yet, moved with feare preta¬
red an Arke to the saving of his house, by the which he condemned
the world. The old world would neither believe nor feare the
coming of the Flood, and so were drowned and swallowed up¬
in it, The dayes of Affiction at once prevented and destroyed

0268.head: Chap. 30. An Expofition upon the Book of JO B. Verf.27.

body.t: them; Noah did both believe and seare the coming of the
Flood, and so escaped it; while his faith assured him the
Flood would come, his feare provoked him to provide an
Arke (as God had appointed) to save himselfe and his in when
it came. To be prevented by mercy, is the sweetest and purest
way of receaving mercy, and to be prevented by affliction is the
sorest way of enduring affliction.
This latter age of the world, or (as I may callit) Dreggs of
Time, hath much need of this awakning consideration; seeing
Christ himselfe hath foretold us that the same Spirit of slumber
and carnal security which possessed the old world ( as wee com¬
monly call it) shall also possesse the world when ’tis indeed
growne old, ( Lube 17.26, 27, 28, 29.) As it was in the dayes
of Noe, so shall it be in the dayes of the Son of man, (that is, in all the
dayes wherein Christ reveales himselfe in any eminent way of
judgement against the world, and especially in the lost judgement
day) they did eate, they dranke, they married wives, they were gi¬
ven in marriage, (that is, they did all these things as if they had
nothing else to doe, and nothing at all to feare, though Noab had
thunder'd the approaching deluge in their ears) untill the day that
Noah enterd into the Arke: and the flood came and destroyed them
ab. The dayes of Affliction by water did not more prevent and
surprise that old world, then the day of Afflidtion by fire shall
prevent this. That day shall come when (as the Apostle Peter
speakes, 2 Ep: 3. 2,3.) sceffers shall come, malking aster their
omne lusts, and saying, where us the promise of his ceming? Will
not that day of affliction prevent these men ? Let all prepare for
it, the most will be prevented by it.

0269.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Bok of IOR. Vert,

body.t: I ment mourning mithout the Sun: I stood up, and
I cryed in the Congregation.
I am a brother to dragons, and a companion to
owles.
May shin is blache upon mee, and my bones are burnt
mith heat.
My harp also is turned to mourning, and my organ
into the voyce of them that weepe.
PHese foure verses continue and conclude Jobs complaint, or
I lamenting discourse about his grievous sufferings.
I went mourning.
Iob confesseth himselfe a stranger and a traveller in this world,
as all his fathers were, and his travel was a sad one, I ( saith he)
meut mourning.
The word which wee render mourning, signifies, black or
blacknes, hence some translate, I went in blache, or in blacke¬
Garments. Blacknes is the mourners colour, and garments Of
black are the mourners livery; wee render clearely to his sence,
I ment mourning. The Church ( Cant. I. 5.) saith, I am like
the tents of Kedar. The Kedarens lived in tents, and theirs were
black tents, they lived in open fields, under the scorching Sun;
so that when the Church sayd, Iam like the tents of Kedar, her
meaning was plainly this, I am black; And when Job saith, I ment
mourning; wee may understand him both of inward sorrow, or
sorrow of the heart, in wbich sence Dauid professed ( Psal. 38.
6.) I goe mourning all the day long; and expostulates (Psal. 42.
9.) Why goe I mourning because of the oppression ef the enemy: as
also of sorrow exp essed outwardly, either in speech, gesture, or
habit; As wee commonly say, Such a man goeth in or weareth
mourning.
Hence note;
As the best of our life hath sorrow mixt mithit; so much of
our life is nothing else but serrow.

0270.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Booke of JOB. Vers.28.

body.t: Christ himselfe, nas a man of sorron, and acquainted vith
griefe, (Isa. 53. 2, 3.) He was not only a sorrowfuil man, but a
man of forrov, while he vas paying the debt of our sin, and pur¬
chasing joy for sinners. Therefore wee who are not only sinfull
men, but (in a fort ) men of sin, must not thinke much, if wee,
who also ( through grace) are his members, doe in this agrec
uith our head; if wee are men of sorrow, as hee was, if wee are
acquainted dayly with griefe, as he was, if wee goe mourning as
he did, ue have no reason to be offended at it. Our dayes, at
best, are few and evill, as J'acob sayd; and at worst, our dayes
are but many evills; And should it not make us long for that
life uherein wee shall sorrow no more, nor know what it is to
goe mourning any more? When our Garments shall be alwayes
white, as to innocency, they shall be so allo as to joy, and wee
shall not be blackt with sorrow, when wee are fully washt from
the blacknes of sin. I ment meurning
without the Sunne.
The Sun is expressed by three words in the Hebrew, whereof
the first signifies to be a servant or publicke minister of God to
the world; A second signifies D ynesse, because the Sunne by
heate causeth drynesse; A third (that of the text) signifies
heate, which doth not only dry, but warme and comfort.
Some read the words thus; I went mourning out of the Sun;
so Mc. Broughton, I walked blaet out of the San. As if he had
sayd, I tooke no pleasure to malke in the Sun; I had so much griefe
a upon my heart, so much darknesse mithin, that the outmard light
mas little or nothing to mee; mhen the Sunne shined, it did net
shine to mee; te mee the Sunne was as a cleud, or but a shadow, yea
I avoyded the Sunve, and sought solitary places nhere to mourne in
private, and meepe out my sorrens by my selfe alene; I went mourn¬
ing out of the Sunne.
Hence observe;
Those creatures mhich are most pleasant in tbemselves, give us
no content in great sorrones and afflictions.
To a soule in bitternes every thing is bitter except Christ;
and to a darkned soule no Sun shines bright, but the Sun of righ¬
teousnesse, Solomon saith (Eccles. 11.7.) Truln lighe us snett,

0271.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Bocke ef JOB. Vers.28.

body.t: and a pleasant thing it is, for the eyes to lehold the Sunne; yet a
man in sorrow, especially a man of sorrow, cares not for the
light of the Sunne, he drawes the curtaine, and vill make all
darke, till the day-starre ariseth in his heart and gives him light.
The things that are most sueet and contentfull to nature, have
no sueetnesse, give no content, or are out of date, to a man dis¬
consolate, till God saith unto him, Be of good cheare, be com¬
forted. Neerest natural Relations, wife, children, friends, are
dead to a disconsolate soule; Greatest worldly possessions ho¬
nours and riches, houses and lands, thousands of gold and silver,
are savourlesse to a distressed soule, hee goes mourning out of
all these things, or mournes in the midst of them. The Scripture
saith, (Pro. 11. 4.) Riches profits not in the day of mrath, but
righteousnesse delivereth from death. Riches are no advantage,
no shelter at all to wicked men, when the wrath of God breaks
out upon them, and they are no better then poverty to a godly
man, when the favour of God is hidden from him. Wee cannot
comfort any man in an evill day, by telling him of his baggs of
gold and silver, of his lands and houses, he goes mourning when
such comforters have done and spoken their best.
Secondly, These words, (as we translate) I ment mourning
mithout the Sunne, may signifie no more but this; I nas in
such a mourning condition as had no comfort at all in it. Some are
in mourning, and yet have some Sun- beames when they mourne,
that is they have some comfort, some joy in their sorrows, some
light ariseth to them in their dark esse but saith Job, I ment
mourning mitheut the Sunne, I had nothing to comfort mee;
no light, o refreshing rayes to keepe up my spirit, I went mourn¬
ing, and no Sun to comfort me. The sorrow of some men hath
nothing but forrowr with it. As there may be an estate so com¬
fortable that it hath nothing but comfort, or’ris a comfortable
estate quire through. ( Pro. 10.22) The blessiag f the Lord
mabete rich, and he addeth no sorrow mith it. Many make them¬
selves rich in such a way, as addeth much sorrow to their riches,
yea (us the Apostle speakes of such rich men, 1 Tim 6.10) They
pierce themselves through with many sorrows. Ill gotten riches in
stead ot making their owners hearts merry, make their conscien¬
ces axe, ard give them many a stitch in their sides: But uhen the
blessing of God upon honest endeavours makes a man rich, hec

0272.head: Chap.30. Au Exposition upen the Book ef JOB. Verf.28.

body.t: eates the labour of his hands uith jov, and knous not what for¬
row (in that poynt) meaneth, His estate is comfortable, and
so is his life; Such a man hath pure comfort. Now (I lay ) as
there may be a condition so comfor able, that it hath no sorrow
with it; So there may be a condition so sorrowsull, that it hath
no joy with it, so darxe that it hath no Sunne with it. Mony
poore soules goe mourning without the Sunne, and krow not
for a long time what comfort meanech. Christ the Sun of Rgh¬
teousnes can shine npon us, and give us light inour greatest out¬
ward darknesse; but ostentimes he doth nor, and then such a
soule cryes out, I goe mourning without the Sunne; I cannot
fiad Christ, I have no communion with, no communications of
lignt or love from Christ, that’s a sed condition in deed. And sech
was theirs who are spoken of (Isa. 50. 10 ) who though they
feared the Lord, and obeyed the voyce of his servant, yet malked
in darknisse, and saw no light.
Thirdly, I went mourning without the Sunne; may be ex¬
pounded thus, I was scorcued blache, but it was not mith the
Sunne. As if he had sayd, Oty blacknisse, or my mourning
hue was not from the heate of the Sunne. That did not disco¬
lour mee, I was not offended at all by that, nor much by any
outward cause; my blacknesse was caused by inwa d sorrou,
Bodyly blacknesse is usually from che Sunne, but many (in fobs
case) are blacke without the Sunne. As the Seripture speakes al¬
so both in another case and in that: They are drunten but not
mith wine, ( Isa. 29. 9.) that is, they are drunke with sin, while
they drinke iniquity lixe water, and take their full cupes of it.
Some are drunken with pride and selfe-confidence, others are
drunken with griefe and trouble, as the same Prophec hath it,
( Chap. 51. 21.) Heare nom this thon afflicted and drungen, but
not nith mine; With what then? with affliction. So we may
answer from that i7th verse, of that Chapter; Awake, amake,
stand up O Jerusalem, nhich hast drunko at the haud of the Lord
the cup of his fury; thou hast arunben the dretgs of the cup of
trembling, and mrung them out. Now as these were drunken and
not with wine, so Job uent in black or mourning but not with
the Sunne He was not San-buent, but sorrow burnt. As that
godly serrow, mhich morbes repentance unto salvation net tobe re¬
pented of, is followed with many blessed effects upon the sonle

0273.head: Chap.30. An Ewposirion upan the Book ef JOR. Verl. 28,

body.t: which are exactly enumerated by the Apostle, (2 Cor. 7. 11.)
and as the sorrow of the morld (that is, sorrow either meerely a¬
bout world̂ly matters, or in a worldly manner) is folloued uith
that dreadfull blacke effect, Death, as the same Apostle saith at
the roth verse of that Chapter; The sorrow ef the morld morbetís
death. So that sorrow which a godly man often meets œith both
in and from the world, may be followed with very grievous and
visible effects upon him. The Church before sposen of, (Cant.
1.5.) having sayd, I am like the tents of Kedar, that is, (as hath
been expounded) I am blacke, presentiy (v. 6.) telle us the
cause of her blacknesse; Lock not upon mee (that is, either with a
despising or despairing eye) because I am black, because the Sun
hath looked upon mee. What Sun ? The Sun of persecution and
trouble from the malicious world hath looked upon mee. Perse¬
cution springs not out of the dust, but is darted from above (as
the providence of God permits) like the beames of the Sun.
The Church was blacke with the fiery beames of that Sun. The
visage of the Church in her captivity and famine mas blacker theu
a coale, or ( as ue put in the Margin) darher then blachnes; And
the Prophet either considering that or some other grievous af¬
fliction of the Church, saith of himselfe, (Jer. 8. 27. ) For the
hurt of the daughter of my pesple, am Ihurt, Iam blache: astouish¬
ment hath taken hold on mee. Job was in a famine, comparatively
to his former plenty, and he was in a reall famine and deep con¬
sumption of all his former comforts; He had a Sun of perse¬
cution looking upon him also, hee was persecuted both by the
Devill and by evill men, yea his good friends (thoughnot in¬
tentionally ) had a hand init too. And as he had alr thete out¬
ward troubles, which grieved him not a little, so he had inward
trouble, which grieved him much more, and paired him at the
very heart; He endured both the hiding of Gods face or favour
from him and the appearings of his angry frownes; The angry
appearances of God, or the arrows of bis appearing anger were
shot into hie spirit. And O how blacke did thele hot imprefsions
make him! He might say with truth enough, accordig to the
tendency of this incerpretation, I went mourving, or élacbe, mitb¬
out the Sunne. I had so many extraordinary Sunnes casting their
scorching beames upon me both visibly and invisibly, thet l nesd
not ascribe the cause of my-pityfull blacknes to the ordinary
There
Sun.

0274.head: Chap.30. An Expasition upon the Booke of JOR. Veri.28.

body.t: There is yet another reading of those words, which I shall
but touch and passe away.
The Greeke and vulgar Latine trarslations, say not as wee,
I ment mourning mithout the Sun, but I ment mourning mi hout
fury or anger; a word in the Hebreur of neere sound to that
which signifies the Sun, signifies alfo anger or fury. And as to
the matter it selfe, wee know blacknesse procceds from heate,
Negrots or Blackmores are borne iu hot clumates; and as black¬
nes proceeds from heate, so heate causeth choler or anger. This,
or that before mentioned might be the ground of tht diversity
in the translation, which though I approve not, vet the sence
is good, and wee may make a profitable use of it Jib and such as
he, the truly godly, goe mourning mithout furr, er mit hout wrath.
A godle man doth not rage when God affl cts him, he is not
fill'd with anger because full of sorrow, hee is not like a vild
Bull when God puts him into his net, but abides patiently and
quietly under the hand of God, hee entertaines his afflictions
kindly, as the Lord sayd bis people should or ought, ( Lev.26.
41.) If then their uncircumcised heart be humbled, and thocy then
accept of the punishment of their iniquitie, then mill I remember my
Covenant mith Jacob. The Lord lookes wee should accept our
Chastisement, not excepragainst it much lesse be in a fume or
rage, in a storme of passion, or in a fret, when his hand is henviest
onus. Nothing is more unseemely then when we are ffl cted
to be discontented. Man naturally cannot beare blowes, but lifts
up his thoughts furiousle agaiest him that smites him But know
"tis dangerous to mingle anger uith our sorrow, or to be trou¬
bled in our selves when God is pleased zo send us trouble This is
a good sence, but I doe not iesist upon it, the other reading be¬
ing more cleare to the text. I ment mourning mithout the Sun,
Istood up and cryed in the Congregation.
Jobs troubles put him into various postures, of which he could
give no good account. He could neicher sit, nor lie, nor stand in
quiet. When he stood up suddain fits and pangs came upon him.
He stood up and cryed The word cry hath been opened before
more then once Here? bs c-ying implyes two things.
First, The dist esse of his spirit, and the extreame sorrow of
his heart. A man in distresse cryes out for one of these three rea¬

0275.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Booke ef JOR. Verf.28

body.t: sons, cither, first, because he is afraid, or secondly, because he is
pained, or thirdly, because he would be helped and comforted.
fob cryed, and he cryed vehemently, upon the latter two, if not
upon all these three reasons.
Hence note;
Tocry out in paine, is not inconsistent witb patience.
q à was a man of patience, yet he cryed out; as he cryed out
before in prayer, so here for paine, and succour in his paine.
The patience ot Jesus Christ had a perfect worke (as the Apostle
(James 1.4. ) advi eth and exhorteth ours shou'd) et when he
was in the extremity of his sufferings, hee cryed out; Even He
sayth the Scripture, (Heb. 5 7. ) in the dayes of his flish ffe red up
prayers and supplications, mito strong cryes and teares, unto him¬
that was able to save bim from death, and nas heard ix that hee
feared. The Evangelist Mathem tells us hee doubled his cry,
Chap. 26.46.) About the ninth houre Jesus cryed mith a loud
vyce, saying, bli, Eli, Lamasabachtbani, that is to say, my God,
my God, why hast thou forsaken mee. And at the soth verse. Te¬
sus mhen hee had cryed agains mith a loud voyce yeelded up the
Ghost Here was cry upon cry, when Jefus Christ had cryed, hec
cryed againe and gave up the ghost; Then he gave his bitterest
cry, his bearing groane, when like a woman in Travaile to bring
forth that blessed Berth life for us, he gave up his owne. It is
not unbecoming a man of strongest courage, y ea of strongest
faith to cry out in great extremities; Christ did it who had the
strongest courage and the fullnesse of grace. To cry out mur-
mu ingly, is not only uncomely but sinfull, but to cry out hum-
bly and sensibly dishonours no man. A good man in great paine
sayd, I groane, but I doe not grumble. Nature at best, even when
clorthed with Grace, being pincht and pained will bemoane it
felfe. Tub stood up and cryed, and that not in secret, but as it fol¬
loweth,
In the Congregation.
It may be questioned what Congregation did he cry in? May
wee not suppose fob a prisoner in his house, shut up in his Cham¬
ber by sicknes? How then did he cry in the Congregation?
I answer, though Tob went not to the Congregation, yet 'tis

0276.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Book of JO B. Verf.28.

body.t: probable that a Congregation came to him;' Tis sure, many came
to him, some to counsell him, and some to see him, some to
comfort him, and some to wonder at him; for he was a spectacle
ts the world, to Angels, and to men. Now ( saith f b) in the very
Congregation, when there was a great company, a throng of visi¬
tants round about mee, I cryed; his forrow was so great that he
could not bite it in, nor conceale it, no not from the Congrega¬
tion; extremity of paine will vent it selfe, ’cuill out, let who will
be present, though a whole Congregation be present. Thus
the good man sets forth his forrow in all the circumstances
of it.
I shall passe from this verse when I have only minded the rea¬
der that some expound it in connexion uith the 25h, where pob
professeth his compassionate feeling of the miseries, forrowes and
sufferings of others; Did not I meepe for him that was in trouble?
Was not my soule grieved for the poore? As if he had sayd, Ihad
so great a sence and fellon-feeling of other mens afflictions, that I
ment mourning without the Sun; nothing could comfort mee mhile
my friends mere forremfull: I thought the Sun did not shine upon
mte while they mere in darknesse, and not only so, but I coula not
containe or content my selfe, till I had presented their case to the
mhole Congregation, that I might move othert to pitie them and
pray for them as well as my selfe. That’s a truth, but I rather keepe
to the former rendring, and take the words as importing the
publication of his owne sorrowes, not of the sorrowes of others
in the Congregation. And if wee would know what the speciall
forme of his cry in the Congregation was; some conceave it
drawne up and expressed in the next verse.
Vers.29. I am a brother to dragons, and a companion to omles.
As if Job had thus bemoaned himselse before all Beholders;
Alas, alas, I am no more (I sce) reckon'd or esteemed among men
as a man; nor doe I fiud my selse fit for the society of men, but of
beasts and birds rather, and those the mest unmanly ameng beests
and birdi, Dragons ard Omles, nhose fashion or custome of life
seemet more agrecable to my present temper and condition, then that
ofia man. I am a brother te Dragons &c.
Dragons are forted among the beasts of the earth, Oules a¬
mong the fowles of the ayre. But how was fob a brother to the

0277.head: Chap. 30. An Expesition upou the BooR of JOB. Verl. 29.

body.t: one, or a companion to the other? I answer, when Job saith,
am a brother to Dragons, it notes only thus much, I am much at
least somewhat like them, or I am reduced to such a condition
providentially as they are in naturally. I, by my affliction am
rendred such as they are by their constitution. The word ber¬
ther is often used in Scripture, to note likepesse aud no mere.
Thus Simeon and Levi are called brethron by cheir old dying fa¬
ther Jacob, ( Gen.49. 5.) Wee cannot imagme that hee in¬
tended only to tell us that they were brethren in natute, for so
all his twelve sons were as well as they two; but whenbe fayd,
Simeon and Levi are brethren, his meaning was this they are men
of a like spirit, they are both fierce and bloody, ar leaft thry mer¬
so in one remarkeable action, Instraments of crueliy mert in thei¬
habitations, in their anger they slew a man, &c. Yea it is concea¬
ved that Simeon and Levi were Brethren in a worser murder
though a most blessed one in the effects and fruits ofit) then
that of the Shechemites; For as it is undeniable that the Priests
who were of the tribe of Levi) were the most cruell enemies
that Christ had, and sought his death with greatest earnestnesse;
so (as our late learned Annotators upon the Bible have obser¬
ved) fome say, Judas who betrayed him, was of the tribe of
Simeon. Thus these two tribes were Brethren in bloodshed as
muchras in blood. Svlomon also gives us this notion of a Brother,
(Pro. 18. 1.) Hee also that is strathfull in his worke, is brotber
to him that is a great naster; that is, hee is like him, heis such an
other, a sl athfull man is as bad as a wastfull man; He that folds
up his armes in idlenes, and he that opens his hand in wastfullnes,
resemble each other as to their issue, though they are very diffe¬
rent in their way; for as one of them gets nothing, so the other
spends all he gets or hath, and it is all a case, whether a man gets
nothing, or spends all, for both come to nought. And as one
descants both wittily and truely upon them, they like Brethren
beare the same coarte, The Ragged coate of Beggary, only uith
this difference: The waster runs into Beggery. Buc the sluggard
or he that is sloathfull sits still, till Beggery comes upon him.
Now in the same sence, that the sloathfull man is brother to the
waster, fob was a brother to Dragom, hee looked upon himselse
under that present dispensation, as very like them. I am a bro¬
ther to Dragont.

0278.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Beoke ef JOR. Verl.29.

body.t: The word which wee render Dragon, signifieth also, a wbale,
so we renderit (Chap. 7. 12.) Am I a Seav or a. Whale? So
that, this one word hath two great monsters in the belly of it;
Firtt, The Whale, who is a water-monster as to bignesse, Second¬
Iy, The Dragen, who is a Land monster as to dreadfullnesse.
Here wee take the word for the land monster, I am a brother to
Dragons,
and a companion to Owles.
The sence is one in both, some render, a companion to Ostriches;
The text strictly is te the daughter of the Ostrich, er of the Owle.
And hence some understand it of young oules, which make a
great noyse, when the old ones are gone from them, bur it may
as well be understood of oules in General by a common He¬
braisme, so the Daughter of the Ostrich or Owle, is the Ostrich
or the Oule her selfe. Which manner of speaking was opened
and exemplified by many Scriprure-instances at the Sth verse of
this Chapter.
And though in this verse, the word is rendred by some, Omle,
by others, Ostrich; yet we should rather keep to our translation,
because the Ostrich is expressed by a distinct word at the 39th
Chapter of this Booke, v. 16. And the etymologicall sence of
the word here used is applicable to the Owle rather then to the
Ostrich. For it signifieth to make a horrid schriching noyse;
and to answer one another in it like an Eccho, as Owles use to
doe.
Lastly, When Job saith, Iam a brother to Dragons, and a com¬
panion to Owles, wee may understand it in one of these two
sences.
Firft, Thus; I sit alone as they doe, Dragons are melancho¬
ly creatures, they love solitary places and desa is and darkest re¬
tirements. Hence Ihat of the Church ( Psal. 44 19.) Though
thou hast sore breken us in the place ef Dragons, is rendred by the
Septuagint, In a place un-inhabited er unst to be inhabired. Dra¬
gons dwell where none dwell, as they are dangerous neighbours,
all men avoyd them, and as they delight not in neigl bour-hood,
so they avoyd all men. Nor are owles more sociable then dra¬
gons, They (we krow) sit all day alone, and come abroad on¬
Jy in the night, when all other birds are gone to roost, or are at

0279.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Books ef IOR. Verf.

body.t: rest. And if at any time they appeare in the day, all the birds in
the ayre make a riot against them, and either beate or hoote
them home againe. We read in severall Scriptures, that as soone
es the Lord threatens to make any Citie desolate ard without
inhabitant, presently Dragons and oules are named sor the in¬
habitants of it. ( Isa. 13. 19.) Babylen the glory ef kingdomes,
the beauty of the Chaldees excellency, shall be as when Gd ouer¬
threw Sodome and Gemorrha, it shall never be inhabited, that is, by
men; by whom then? even by dolesull creatures, owles and dra¬
gons, (V.21, 22.) And in a like case the same Prophet saith,
(Chap. 34. 13.) It shall be a habitatien of Dragons, and a court
fer owles. They shall King it and Lord it there. So that when
job saith, I am a brother to Dragons, aud a companion to owles,
his meaning is, I love solitarinesse, and delight to be alone; hee in¬
deed sayd before, I stood up, and cryed in the Congregation, many
came about him, but they, it seemes, were rather a trouble to
him, yea a kinde of terror to him by their unkindnesse. The com¬
pany that came to him used him little better then ordinary birds
doe the oule, some making a wonderment at his misery, and o¬
thers (as he complained about the beginning of this Chapter)
hooting at him in derision. Thus he was a companion to owles.
And befides, 'tis the nature of sorrow to desire solitarinesse:
Looke away from mee, (saith the Prophet, Isa. 22.4.) I will meepe
bitterly, labour not to comfort me, &c. Thus sai th Job, I am a bro¬
ther to Dragens, &c. I would be alone, ( as Dragons and owles
covet to be) in my sorrowes, rather then have the company of
such comforters. The Prophet Jeremiah maketh a like wish (up¬
on the sence of the trouble which hee had among his people
Chap. 9. 2.) O that I had in the wildernes a lodging place of
rayfaring men, that I might leave my people and goe from them,
for they be all Adulterers, and an assembly of treacherous men.
He that desireth a wildernes life, desireth a retired folitary life,
and declares himselfe a brether to Dragons, and a companion to
Oxles.
Secondly, When Job saith, Iam a brother to Dragons, and a
companion to Omles, his meaning may be this, I doe as they;
what's that? Dragons make a mournfull cry, a terrible noyse.
Naturall histories speake much of the dreadfull cryes of the Dra¬
gon, especially uhen he is in battel with the Elephant; and as

0280.head: Chap.30. An Exposition upen the Book ef JOB. Vers.29.

body.t: all naturalists agree, that the Dragon makes a fearesull noyse
and howling, so the Scripture consents with them, (Mich.1.8)
Therefore I mill maile and homle, I mill goe stript and nabed, I mill
mabe a mailing like the Dragons, and mourning like the Owles.
When the Prophet would expresse his deepest sorrowfull sence
of the miseries, which he foresaw falling upon Samaria and jeru¬
salem for their Idolotry, he knew not how to parralel it, but by
that of Dragons and oules, I mill make a wayling libe the Dra¬
gons, &c. For her nound is uncurable; or, shee is grievously sicke
of her mounds, as we put in the Margin. Wee find David com¬
plaining in language neere this, ( Psal. 102.6, 7.) I am like a
Pelican of the wildernes; I am like an omle of the desart; I watch
and am as a sparron alone upon the house-top. And Hezekiahs
thank(giving Song sets forth the forrows of his sicknesse in such
like straines, ( Isa. 38. 14.) Like a Crane or a swallom, so did I
chatter, I did mourne like as a dove, mine eyes faile with looking up¬
ward O Lord, I am eppressed undertake for mec. The dolefuil dit¬
ties and lementing tunes of these birds and foules, The pellican,
the sparrow, the Crane, the swallow, and the dove, beare a cor¬
respondence with this protestation of Jub, I am a brother to Dra¬
gons, and a companion to Owles. They are solitary, so am I, they
chatter and cry and mourne out their sorrowes, so doe l. The
worst of their conditions and lamentations is not worse then
mine; I am their brother and companion in afflict ion.
Lastly, Some expound the Dragons and the omles here spo¬
ken of by Job metaphorically, for those termble cruell and un¬
couth ones that were about him whose carriage uas so inso¬
lent and inhumane, so voyd of compassion, yt a of discretion to¬
wards him, that as David once said. My soule is as among Lions,
so fob might say, mine is among oules and Dragons, that is, a¬
mong men either fierce and Dragonish, or among men inconsi¬
derate and Owlish. In the 19th Chapter Job brings such a
charge against his whole family or Domesticke relations (v. 15.
&c.) Thay that dwell in mint honse, and my maidens count mee
fon a stranger, Iam an Alien in their sight, I called my servant,
and he gave mee no Ansmer; my breath is strange to my mife,
though I entreated fer the childrens sabe of mine oun body, jea young
Children despised mee, all my inward friends abh rred mec.
They from uhom he mighe expect the readiest offices of lore

0281.head: Chap.30. An Expofition upon the Book of Jo ». Verf. 29.

body.t: and duty, seemed to have put off not only their particular and
speciall bonds of duty, but even common modesty, and civillity,
acting rather the part of beasts then of men, of Dragons and
oules rather then of wife, friends or servants. Are tĥere not
many even at this day, after so long a shining forth of Gospel
light and love, who shew no more pity or charity, give no more
comfort or succour to their brethren in the flesti, yea to their
brethren ( by profession ) in the faith, then a Dragon or an
owle will doe ? and may not they who have such friends and
kindred say, (without breach of charity) wee are Brechren to
Dragons and companions to Owles: This interpretation carri¬
eth a faire Tropologicall or morall instruction in it: But the for¬
mer being textuall and proper, I insist rather upon that. I am a
brother to Dragons, and a companion to onles.
Hence note;
First, They that are highest in Grace and Saintspip, may yet
act sometimes, not only belon their grace and Saintship,
but even belom reason and manbood.
Tob was as holy a man as lived; yet he uas sometimes in his
distresse more like a Dragon or an owle then an holy man. He
continued alwayes in the same grace, yet his grace did not al¬
wayes continue the same. He had much, very much cause of
griefe, yet he grieved too much when he made a wayling libe the
Dragons and a mourning like the owles. A godly man may act
below himselfe, even like a beast two vayes. First, in sinning, as
David confessed, (Psal. 73. 21, 22.) So foolish mas Iand ig¬
norant, I was as a beast before thee; Neverthelesse, Iam continu¬
ally mith thee, thou hast holden mee by my right hand. When Da¬
vid envied the prosperitie of the wicked, he censured ir as a beast¬
Iike folly and igporance, and judged himselfe not only unlile a
holy man, but unlike a man that’s rationall. While good men
give any scope to a lust, and doe sinfully, they play the beasts,
and behave themselves more like Dragons or owles then true
believers. Secondly, as good men are sometimes like beasts in
sinning, so also in forrowing. The Apostle would not have be¬
lievers sorrom (for the dead) as others (that is, ac Heathens)
mhich have no hope, much more would he not have thom sorrow
either upon that or any other account like brutes, which have no

0282.head: Chap.30. An Exposition upon the Bocke ef JO2. Veri.29.

body.t: understanding, no knowledge; yet who knowes how farre hee
may be transported by the weight of an affliction, and the pres¬
sure of griefe: Sains doe not alwayes meurne lize Saints, they
sometimes mourne like Dragons or like Owles.
Secondly, Observe;
ute may be called brethren and companions of those whose
manners and actions uec immitate, mhat though mee are not
at all akinne to them, or in cempany with them, yet wee arc
their companions and brethren mhen me do or suffer lihe them.
Wee are lihe te every thing mhich mee imitate, nhether it be
good or bad.
As Christ told fome of the Jewes, the Devil was their father
becaule they walked in his wayes, and resembled him in their
workes; so we may call any one a mans Brother, whose worxes
he resembleth. Solomon gives us this in a full assertion, (Pro.13.
20.) He that malketh xith wise men shall be mise; but a cempani¬
on ef fooles shall be destroy'd. To walke with them is not to take a
turne with them in the fields, or barely to goe in company with
them when and whether they goe; but to walke with the wise,
is to follow their example, and to tread the same pathes of
a isdome which they tread. They who thus walke uith vise men,
attaine to wisdome, and prove vise men themselves. And when
S. lomon adds, A companion of foules shall be destroy’d; his mean¬
ing is not, that every one that is in the company of a foole shall be
destroyed, but he that conformes to them and takes up their
fool sh fasbions; He that is or doth like a foole, is properly a
fooles companion, and only he. In which sence Solamon speaks
againe, (Pre. 28.7.) Who so koepeth the Law is a misc son, but
hec tout is a companion of rioteus men ( that is, he that doth like
riotous men) fhameth his Father; Hee that doth like a D agon
is Brother to a Dragon, and he that doth like an owle, is a com¬
panion of owles. I may adde, He that doth like a dogge, or
a swine, or a foxe, is their Brother and companion. I am (cryed
pob) a Brother of Dragont, and a companion to owles. And hee
gives us some further account why he was so in the words which
follar.

0283.head: Chap. 30. An Expofition upon the Bocke of JOR. Vers. 30.

body.t: Vers. 30. My skin is blache upon mee, and my bones are
burnt xith heate.
The skin is the outward or upper garment of nature; The
beauty and bravery of nature appeares in the skin. What was
become of Jobs beauty and bravery we may easily judge, when
he made this complaint;
Ay skin is blacke.
He had said a little before, I went mourning or blache mith¬
cut the Sun, now saith he, my shin is blacke. But what made
Jobs skin blacke? or what meanes he by the blacknes of his skin
Hee was blacke without the Sun, his skin was not tannd (as we
fay) nor burnt blacke with the outward heate of the ayre. but
with the griefe of his heart, His sorrows boiled up, and chan¬
ged the colour of his skin.
Hence observe.
First, Grcat afflictions and sorrows, quichly fade she beauty ef
the body, and spoyle the fairest face.
Strong (especially if lasting) diseases take off beauty, or give
blacknesse in stead of beauty. (Psal. 39 11.) when thou mith
rebuhes dest cerrect man for iniquitie, thou mabest his beeuty to
consume amay like a mothe, surely every man ie vanity, Srlab¬
The tkin cannot hold its oune against the ill effects of sickresse,
much lesse uhen the rebukes of God upon the soule for iniq ity
are mingled with the sicknes of the body. Then looke after spi¬
rituall beauty, the beauty of the soule, that growes fairer by af¬
fliction, that never fades by sicknesse; nothing but the sin of man
and the anger of God can make that fade. When the fleshy skin
waxeth black with sorrow, that retaines its beauty ard its bright¬
nes. The beauty of grace holds against the coldest ! lasts, and the
most burning heates. Jobs skin was blacke, his spirit uas not.
When Stephen the protomartyr was under tryall for his life, and
neere stoning to death, Ah that sate in the Counfel looking sted¬
fastly on him, saw his face as if it bad been the face of an Angel,
(Acts 6. 15.) Stephens skin waxed fairer as the fury of his
persecuters waxed hotter; God was pleased to print (as it were)
a visible not Guilty npon his face, while his adversaries were ac¬

0284.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Bock of JO B. Vers. 30.

body.t: cusing him of blasphemy as blacke as a coale. And though the
skins and faces of many of the Saints have been persecuted and
afflicted into blacknes, yet their soules and consciences never
could, but under the darkest appearances or covers of trouble
and sorrow they have still retained a reall comelinesse, and under
the blackest skin, a beautifull soule. While David said (Psal 119.
83.) I am become like a bottle in the smoake; (he said also,) Tet do
I not forget thy statutes. David through the force of his afflicti¬
on was like a bottle in the smoake, which if of leather shrinks
and shrivels up, and if of more solid materialls, yet loosethits
beauty and is quickly sooted blacke. But when David uas as a
bottle in the smoake, yet the holy frame of his heart did not
shrinke nor alter; for he adds, Tet doe I net ferget thy precepts;
though my beauty is gone, yet my grace is not; Iam like a bot¬
tle in the smoate, ( that’s true) but I doe not forget thy Statutes,
that’s as true. If outward beauty faile, where there is no inward
beauty, if the skin be blacke, and the conscience blacke too, how
great, how miserably uncomely is that blacknesse? The Prophet
lamenting the famine of the Jewes, saith ( Lam. 4.8.) Their vi¬
sage is blacker then a coale, they are not knowne ix the streets, their
abin cleaveth to their bones, it is xithered, it is become lihe a
sticke. And he presents them making a like lamentation (Chap.5.
10.) Our skin mas blacke like an Oven, because ef the terrible fa¬
mine. Thus sicknes, famine, any kind of deepe affliction makes
sad impressions upon the skin, the beauty of that is soone blowne
off, and to be sure old age will shrivel it up & make it look like a
bottle in the smoake. Therefore, I say againe, looke to the beau¬
ty of the soule which fadeth not, which the teares of sorrow
cannot staine nor death it selfe deface. (1 Pet. 1. 7.) The tryall
of our faith (or our tryed faith ) being much more preci us then if
gold that perisheth, though it be tryed with fire, nill be found unto
praise, and honour, and glory, at the appearing of fesus Christ.
Faith comes purified, not corrupted out of the fire; the body
comes out blacke, but grace comes out white. Job was assured of
this ( Chap. 23. 10.) when he hath tryed mee, I shall come forth
as gold. Yet here he saith, Myshon is blacke,
And my bonet are burnt xith heate.
These words are a further and a fuller desctiption of fobs ca¬

0285.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon thi Book of IO». Verl.30.

body.t: lamity. Ay bones ( saith he) are burnt, that is, my affliction
doth not only afflict my skin, or the outside of my body, but
my very bones; it dries up the marrow and moisture there.
I feele a fire within me, drinking up my spirits, and ready to
burne the very beames and rafters of this house of clay, my bones.
As there is a fire which visibly consumes our houses ( wee have
seene many such sad spectacles) so there are fires which invisi bly
consume our bodyes and our bones. God can as quickly kindle
a fire which shall consume this house of the body which him¬
selfe hath built, as those houses which we have built. Some af¬
flictions are as a fire, which bur nes inward to the bones.
Herce Observe.
Great sorrom wasts and spends not only the beauty, but the
strength of man.
It reacheth to the bones. David spake more then once of this
effect of his sorrowes, especially of his fin-sorrows, or sorreus
orcasion'd by his sin. (Psal. 32.3.) When I kpt silence (not
confessing my sin) my bones waxed old, that is, I had such trou¬
ble in my soule, as even hastned me into old age, or made the
symptomes or tokens ofit to appeare upon me before their time.
Davids boues maxed old, He complaines also as sob that his bones
mere burnt, (Psal. 102 3.) Ay dayes art consamed libe smoake,
my bones are burnt as an hearth, my heart is smitten and mithered
like grasse, so that I forget to eate my bread; by reason of the veyce
ofmy groaning my bones cleave to my skin. How many metaphors
and hyperboles, or excesses of speech hath David brought toge¬
ther in this one context, to shew how exce ssively his heart was
wounded with sorrow for the affliction of Sion: Let sorrou
come from what cause it will, if once it be great and sincere, it
will leave markes enow to tell every man where it is. Solomon
saith, (Pro. 15.13.) A merry heart maketh a chearefull coun¬
tenance, but by sorrew of the heart, the spirit is broben. And againe,
more emphatically and just in pubs phrase (Cuap 17 22.)A
merry heart doth good lihe a medicine, but a breken spirit aryeth the
bones. By a merry heart in both texts S l mon interds the same
thing, but he intends neyther of them of carnall mirth The mer¬
ry heart there meant is a heart merry upontholy grourd-e peci¬
ally upon a sighe, by faich, of our reconciliation to God through

0286.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Booke ef IOR. Verf.31.

body.t: Christ, and of our acceptance in him, This will make the heart
merry to purpose, and such a merry heart, or (as some render)
good conscience is like a medicine indeed, it refresheth the whole
body. Now as such a merry heart is a medicine, so there is a sor¬
rowfull heart, which is as a disease or a consumption to the
whole body; it wasts and withers the flesh, it scorcheth and
spoyleth the complection, it dryes the bones, and brenkes the
spirit. Such were Jobs sorrowes, My bones are burnt. And when
he felt such fires of sorrow kindled in him by his great affliction,
It was time for him to silence his Organ and his Harpe. So he
did.
Vers. 31. Ay harpe is turned into mourning, and my organ
into the vorce of them that weepe.
Job having made this sad narrative of his sorroues, what could
be expected but this sad conclusion. Time was when sob had his
musicke: He was wont (it seemes) touse his harpe and organ,
both to excite and expresse his joy, but he eyther totally disused
them, or used them only to play sad and dolefull tunes, to feed
and strengthen sorrow.
Ay harpe is turned into mourning; or according to the
letter of the Hebrew, my harpe is for mourning.
As if sob had sayd, My harp is now for no other service but fot
forrow, 'cis set or wound up to no tune or lesson but lachryrræ
or lamentation. I mind nothing but my troubles, and they al¬
wayes mind me. The harpe which is an Instrument of mirth,
may by a Metanomie of the adjunct be put for mirth it selse, My
harpe, that is, my mirth is turned into mourning,
And my organ into the voyce ef them that recre.
Mr. Broughton renders; And pleasant seunds be neepers vorce.
We had the Organ at the 21thi Chapter v. 1I, 12. They send
out their little ones libe a floche, and their Children dance, they tabe
the Timbrell and Harpe, and rejoyce at the sound ef the Organ.
The word rendred organ, comes from a roote that signifies to
love, and to love with a kind of excesse, eyther because that In¬
strument of musicke is much loved, or because it stirres up af¬
section, and is an incentive of love.

0287.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Boohe ef JOB. Verf. 31.

body.t: The generall sence of the whole verse is but this; my com¬
forting sounds are changed into a mourning sound; all my joyes
are turned into sorrowes, which he expresseth by laying aside
his harpe and organ, which before were a helpe to his joy, and
hightned his delights.
Hence note;
First, Musiche is an ancient Art.
sob had his musicall Instruments; wee finde their invention
mentioned in the very first Ages of the world, (Gen. 4. 21.)
And his brothers name was Jubal, hee mas the Father of all such
as handle the harpe and organ. The two Instruments spoken of by
Job, were invented by Jubal, hee was the Father (the first inven¬
ter of any Art is called the father of all those (though none of his
children) that professe it after him, in which sence Jubal was
the father) of all such as handle (that is, play skillfully upon)
the harpe and orgax.
Secondly, Note;
As musicke was a very ancient, so lawfull art or invention.
It is no sin to have or use a harpe or an organ. Godliresse dotb
not deprive us of eut mard Comforts. Job a man that feared God
had his musicke. Musicke is not sinfull, unlesse
First, when'cis used wantonly to stirre up or awaken lust; or
Secondly, when’tis used unseasonably, and that
First, in respect of the muchnesse or continuance of it at any
time. When men are all for mirth and musicke; wee must not
make musicke our worke, but our recreation, and use it only às
iauce not as diet.
Secondly, In respect of the special state of the time; as we must
not use it much at any time, so not at al, at sometimes. What those
times are the Prophet tels us expresly (Isa.22. 10,12.) In that day
did the Lord God of hosts, call to meeping, & to mourning, & to bald¬
nes, & to girding mith sachcloath, and behold joy and gladnes, staying
oxen and killing sheepe, eating flesh, and drinking mine. Thele two
great affections of joy and sorrow, are both beautifull in their
seasons, even sorrow is comely in its season, and joyit selfe when
unseasonable, hath not only no beauty, but much danger, becaule
much provocation init. And therefore as the Prophet sete a E

0288.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Bok ef JOB. Verf. 31.

body.t: bold of wonder and astonishment before the mention of fuch joy,
(v. 13.) Behold j y and gladnes: as if he had sayd, What a
strange, uhat an uncouch and uncomely sight is this, that men
should thus eyther perversel y contradict, or grossely mistake the
directions of providerce, That upon the very day wherein that
calls to mourning, &c. they should be found rejoycing; Now
(I say) as the Prophet sets a Behold of wonder before such a joy,
so he follows it with a dreadfull denunciation in the next verse,
(14.) And it was revealed in mine eares by the Lord of hosts, sure¬
Iy this iniquitie sball not be purged frem you, till ye die. That is,
it shall never be purged or pardoned, and if guilt be not par¬
don'd, we are in danger of punistiment every houre. To be do¬
ing with harpe and organ in suffering times, may bring swords and
speares upon us. It is both our duty and our security, to humble
our selves, when God humbles us, And to lay away our Musicke
as soone as ever wee see the Lord taking it away. The Lord by
Moses sayd to the Children of Israel, Put eff thy ornaments, that
I may know what to doc unto thee, (Exod. 33. 5. ) God knowes
well enough, what to doe, and what he vill doe vith us at all
times; his counsels and resolves what to doe, depend not upon
what we doe: yet when there are appearances of displeasure, as
then there were against the Children of Israel for their Idolatry
in making the golden calfe, (I xill come ap into the midst of thee
in a mement, and consume thee; When (I say) the displeasure of
God appeares thus against a people) then he speakes as a man
ugresolved eyther for sparing or for destroying, and seemes wil¬
ling to be determin'd eyther for judgement or for mercy, by
what he findes in us. And bids us put eff our ornaments, that is,
lay downe our pride, and lie naked in the dust, that he may know
what to doe with us; as if he fhould say, I will shew thee mer¬
cy if thou repent, or I will punish thee if thou persist in thy
pride and impenitency, Though I have decreed what to doe with
thee, yet thou shalt find my dealings uith thee sutable to what
thou doest. Therefore in a time of passed provocation, and of
seared affliction, let us as the Apostle adviseth ( James 4. 9.) Be
afflicted, and mourne and meepe, let our laughter be turned to mourn¬
ing, and our joy to heavines, let us humble our selves in the sight of
the Lord, and he shall lift us up. Woe to those who will not be
afflicted when God afflicts them, who when God casts them

0289.head: Chap.30. An Exposition upon the Bok of IOR. Vert. 31.

body.t: downe, yet hold up their heads in mirth and jollitie. The Lord
loves to see us beare our Crosse, but he cannot endure to see us
make sport with it, or make slight or it. If God once perceave
us driving away our sorrow with our harp and organ, or drown
ing it in wine, hee can quickly turne that wine into water, and
drowne the sound of our harpe with mourning, and the pleasant
tunes of our organ with the voyce of weeping. The Jewes found
this made good npon them, They would not sit dowre and
weepe over the sins which they had committed in Jerusalem;
but by the rivers cf Babylen, there they sate downe and wept,
(Psal. 137. 1. ) And what did they then with their harpes?
They hung them up upon Willones in the midst thereof; they had
little mind to their musick in that sorrowfull day; yea when the
Babyloxiaxs who carried them away captives, required of them
a song they answered, Hom shall vet sirg? And they did not
answer, Hon fhall' vee sing a prophane song in a strange Land,
but hon shall nee sing the Lords sorg in a strange Land, or, in the
Land of a stranger. They who will not hang up their harpes and
forbeare their song in their owne Land, when their sins call them
to mourning, may soone be forced to both by the cry of their
misery in a strange Land, yea though their enemies call them to
singing.
Againe, Wee may suppose that Job put away his musick, his
harpe and organ, not only as being unseasonable, but irkesome
and troublesome to him, in that time of his trouble. His harpe
and organ gave a harsh sound, and grated his eare, when he was
in that condition; All musiche is eut of tune to an afflicted soule,
'tis grievous to them that are grieved; outward mirth doth often
increase rather then abate our sorrows. The Scripture is full to
that poynt, (Pro. 25.20) As he that taketh away a garment in
cold weather, and as vineger upon Nitre, so is he that singeth songs
unto an heavie heart. A garment taken away in cold weather,
makes the person colder from whom’tis taken, And vinegar be¬
ing cold and moyst, doth but exasperate and draw out the sharp¬
nesse of Nitre, which is hot and dry; Thus a heavy heart by a
kind of Antiperistasis, is made more heavy by a delighrfull song;
even as ( on the contrary) that hot and fiery vapour u hich is in
a cloud, is more enraged and breakes out into thunder and light¬
ning, when’tis compassed about with and more clolely pent in

0290.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Booke of JOB. Verf.31.

body.t: by coldnes. Though in some lesser cases sorrow is moderated,
yea and removed by musicke, yet great and setled sorrowes are
rather exulcerated and vexed by it. And as this is true of com¬
mon sorrow caused by any outward affliction, soit is more true
and most true of that speciall sorrow and heavinesse of heart,
which is caused by pricks of conscience and the sence of sin, or by
the hidings of Gods face, and the withdrawings of his favour.
How ungratefull and unwelcome is carnal mirth to a wounded
spirit? to a soule thet mournes under the apprehe sions of di¬
vine ditpleasure! Therefore when the Apostle James vrould pre¬
scribe that to Saints which is proper both in sad and comforta¬
ble dispensations, he saith ( Chap. S. 13.) Is any among yeu af¬
flicted, let him pray, ( That’s musick in the eares of God) Is any
man merry? (that is, hath he cause to be merry, and is his heart
uound up and tuned toit?) let him sing Psalmes, or (as the
Greeke hath it, for there ’tis but one word )e let him sing, holy
songs he meanes for the matter, and let him sing in a holy man¬
ner, not to please the flesh, but to quicken and recreate his spi¬
rit. Wee see by this Apostolicall du ection, that as our estate in
this world is full of change, so wee must apply our selves to a
change of Duties. Singing is proper to a prosperous estate, sing.
ing not only to the praise ef God, but singing his praise prayer
is our best remedy, as God to whom ve pray is our best refuge,
in a day of adversity and effliction.
Lastly, Note.
God can quickly spoyle all our musicke and mirth, bee can
change our pleasure into paine, our delights into lamentati¬
ons, eur health into sicknes, our harpe and organ into mourn¬
ing and weeping.
The Prophet gives a large description of such a change ready
to fall uponthat Land, ( Isa. 24 7, 8, 9.) The new mine mourn¬
eth, the vine languisheth, all the merry-hearted doe sigb: the mirth
of tabrets ceaseth, the noyse of them that rejoyce endeth, the jay
of the harpe ceaseth, they shall not drinbe wine mith a song strong
drinke shall be bitter to tóem that drinke it. Wine makes the
heart of man glad; therefore to shew how much the wine¬
drinkers shall mourne, he saith the mine shall mourne. Wee read
a like sad denunciation made by another Prophet in the name

0291.head: Chap. 30. An Exposition upon the Beche ef IOR. Verf. 31.

body.t: of the Lord, (Jer. 7. 34.) Then vill I cause to cease from thoe
Citie of Judah, and from the streets of Jerusalem, the voyce of
mirth, and the voyce of gladnes, the voyce of the bridegroome, and
the voyce of the bride, for the Land shall be defolate. And againe,
(Jer.25.10.) M,reover I will take from them the voyce of mirth,
and the voyce of gladnesse, the voycs of the bridegroome, and the
voyce ef the bride, the sound of the miestones, and the light ef the
candle And if Jerusalem hath felt such changes, shall Babyloz
escape? we are assured shee shall not. ( Revil. 18. 21, 22, 23)
And a mighty Angel toche up a stine, libe a great mil st ne, and
cast it into the Sea, saying, thus mith vi lence shall ihat great City
Babylon be thromne downe, and shall be found no more at all. And
the voyce of harpers and musicians, and ef pipers and trumpeters
shall be heard no more at all in thee, and no Craftsman of mhat soe¬
ver Craft spall be found any more in thee, and the sound of a mil¬
stone shall be heard no more in thee, &c. All this is prophecied of
Babylon, when she shall sing her song, Isit a Queene, and am no
middow, and shall see no sorrew ; That is, All is well, and will be
well with mee, shall be Babylons song. But what faith God,
Reward her even as shte hath rewarded thee, deuble unto her dou¬
ble according to her worhes; in the Cup mhich shet hath filled, fill
to her double. Babylon had harpers and trumpeters, to make her
lovers merry, but they shall be heard no more at all in her.
The voyce of mirth may cease in Jerusalem, shee may have a to¬
tal change of her prosperitie; But the voyce of mirth shall be
heard no more at all in Babylon, her prosperitie shall have a
finall change, Hers shall be perpetuall desolations.
And forasmuch as the Lord hath and doth turne mirth into
mourning, and joy into forrow, let us not reckon upon many
good dayes, much lesse that all our dayes shall be good, that is,
dayes of mirth and musicke, dayes ot peace and joy, harpe and
organ dayes in this world.
The Apostle minds us of a very necessary doctrine (1 Cor. 7.
29.) This I say Brethren, the time is short; and he gives us a ve¬
ry usefull inference from it, in the words immediate ly following,
It remaineth, that both they that have wives be as if they had none,
and they that weepe as though they mept not, and they that rejoyce,
as though they rejoyced not; and ther that buy as though they pos¬
sessed uet, and they that use this morld as not abusing it, for the fa¬

0292.head: Chap.30. An Exposition upon the Book ef JOB. Vers.31

body.t: Time is short in all the notions of it. Take it First for the
whole duration of this world, from the first day of the creation
ro the day of the diffolution of all things, so (compared with
eternity) time is short, all times put together make but a short
time. Secondly, take Time for the whole duration of any one
mans life, so’tis shorter, so short, that ’tis nothing. Thirdly,
take time, for the speciall season eytber of doing or enjoying
good in this life, so’tis shortest of all.
The shortnes of time in all these considerations, but especially
in the last, should keepe our hearts in a great deale of modera.
tion towards the best and sweetest of our worldly enjoyments.
And indeed All these Nots in the Apostles text, before asledged,
are not negations, but Moderations or qualifications of our re¬
spects to carthly contentments. V’ee are as apt to over-doe, or
to doe too much in worldly things, as we are to under-doe, or
to doe too little in heavenly things. Our two great fay lings are,
first, that we doe but make use of those things which wee should
enjoy; secondly, that we enjoy those things which we should
only make use of. O how few are there who have learnt that
holy art of Marriagr, To have wives as if they had nane? How
few are there who have learned that holy trade of Merchandize,
To b y as if they possessed not? How few are there who have lear¬
ned that holy skill and cunning in Musicke and disports, To re¬
joyce as if they rejoyced not? How few have learned that divine
wisdome, which containes all that was sayd before, To use this
world as not abusing it. Now what stronger arguments can be
used to provoke every man to the ftudy and attainement of all
these poynts of spirituall learning, then these two which the
Apostle urgeth; præfixing the former of them before all these
practicall lessons, The Time is short; and closing them all with
the latter, The Fashion of this morld passeth away. As the world
it selfe shall passe away shortly, so the most beautifull and de¬
lightfull scheames or shewes of it are passing auay every mo¬
ment. And as every man at his best estate is altogether vanity,
(Psal. 39. 5.) so is the best worldly estate of all men.
In the 29th Chapter of this Booke, Job appeared as likely as
any man to continue in his prosperity, and now you see through
what a hard Chapter of his adversity I have travailed; The way
of this 3othi Chapter is set with briers and thornes, ’tis full of

Verf. 1. Imade a Covenant with mixe eyes; mby then suould I

The summe of this verse is Jubs care, yea carefulnes to pre¬
serve himselse pure, from all taints of unchastity and uncleane¬
nesse, even to a thought.
In it wee more distinctly consider.
First, The meanes which he used sor this purpose, A Cove¬
nant.
Secondly, The partyes to this Covenant, He and his eyes;
I made a Covenant with mine eyes.
Thirdly, The desired successe or issue of this meanes used

I made a Covenant.
The word (Berith) which we render, a Covenant, comes from
a roote which signifies tuo things ( both which are considerable
in the nature and formalities of a Covenant) First, to choose ex
actiy and judiciously; becausc a Covenant ( as all elective Acts)
is an act of sad and ferious deliberation. All Elections are, or
ought torbe made upon the most rationall turne ard suay of
Judgement, not upon any catch of phancy or hurry of passions.
Secondly, it signifies to eate moderately or soberly, this also re¬
ferrs to the nature and use of a Covenant, which is to draw seve¬
rall partyes into a friendly communion and correspondence one
with another. Hence it hath been accustomed upon the making
of Covenants, for the partyes covenanting to feast temperately
together, Gen. 29.30.
A Covenant strictly takenis more tüen a promire; A Cove¬

For the clearing of this doubt; I answer.
First, The word (Bethulah) here used, may be taken in ge¬
neral lor any or every faire and beautiful woman, whether maide,
wife, or widdow. So we read (Joel 1. 8.) Lament libe a virgin
(or young widdow-woman) girded with sackcloatb for the hus¬
band of her yeuth.
Secondly, Tob speaketh by name only of a maide or virgin,
because such in the flower of youth are most beautifull, and so
most alluring, and therefore if they were as dead to him, surely
much more other women in whom there was lesse provocation
to that folly. If a man will not drinke intemperately of the best
wine, much lesse vill he of that which is base and disperited. He
that doth not lust after the fairest face, is above the temptation
of a deformed or unhandfome peice. Chastity is most assaulted
and hazerded by beaury. This was the reason which some Histo¬
rians give why Alexander the Great would not suffer those most
beautiful Perfian Virgins the Daughters of Darius to be brought
into his presence, lest he who had conquered such mighty Armies
of men, should himselse be conquered by those Captive-women.
So then Job instanceth the preservation of his chastity, u here it
was most difficult to preserve it; And having so farre conquered
all folicitations from maiden-Beauty, that he would not so much
as thinke upon a maide, he might well conclude himselse a con¬
queror ( through grace) over all assaults from women-kind.
Thirdly, Tob might say, why then spould I thinke upon a
maide? d'o shew, that if he made conscience of the lesser sin, then
much more of the Greater. Fornication or the committing of
folly with a maide, ( though it be a very great sin and to her an
irreparable dishonor) eis yet a lesser sin then adultery, which is the
committing of folly with another mans wife. And therefore also

wickednes, that he might give evidence how much he abhorred
the latter.
Fourthly, Job a little after (v. 9, 10.) purgeth himselfe ex¬

and therefore here he speakes only of his freedome from those
other sinfull and defiling thoughts about any fingle or unmar¬

The words thus opened, yeild severall instructions.
First, in that Job having made a covenant with his eyes,

Observe.
To sin against a Covenant is a great aggravation of sin.
The more we are bound or justly bind our selves not to doe a
thing, the more we sin in doing it. A covenant is a bond, a sa¬
cred bond, ’tis not safe to trifle with sacred things. The Lord
threatned to send a sword upon his owne people, that should a¬
venge the quarrel of his Covenant, ( Lev. 26.25.)
Secondiy, fob having made a covenant with his eyes, puts the
question, Why then should I thinbe upon a maide?
Herce note.
It is goed ofien to put questions to and catechise our own soules¬
When David found himselfe almost overset uith griefe, he
falls to questioning the matter (Psal. 42. 5.) Wby art thou cast
domne, O my soule, and mhy art thou disquieted in me? Give me an
account, a reason, O my soule, why it is thus with thee? As we
may stop immoderate griefe, by asking a reason why doe we
grieve thus? So we may stop the inordinate motions and desires
of lust, by asking a reason, why should we doe thus? When temp¬
tation hath prevailed with us to doe evill, repentance will cause us
to aske what have we done? yea to consider what we have done.
And when we are tempted to doe evill, common prudence, much
more speciall grace will cause us to aske what are we doing? or
why should we doe it? Some have sayd, that, man by resting, or
a quiet retirement, growes more wise or improves in wisdome.
"Tis as true, that, man by these kind of motions and traverses of
his soule, growes both wiser and holyer. The reason why so ma¬
ny doe things, which are, at leaft, very questionable, is because
they did not question themselves about the doing of them. Wee
say, (and we say it truely) A foole may put more questions,
then many wise men can answer : But that man is not wise, ror
can he doe wisely, who doth not put many questions to himseife
about the things which he is abour to doe.

0307.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition upon the Book of JO B. Vers.1.

body.t: which will be thy eternall ruine, and render thy case remedi¬
lesse,
There are three steps or degrees of sin, before it comes to the
outuard act.
First, When some fleeting transient thoughts of evill arise
from and are slightly formed up in the phancy, or are occasion'd
by the sight of somewhat from without.
Secondly, When the mind stayeth upon such thoughts, gives
them some entertainment, holds parley with them, and hath a
kind of delight in them.
Thirdly, When we close freely with them, and settle fully
upon them, so that nothing delayes the drawing of them forth
into act, but the want of power or opportunity. When evill
thoughts are wrought up to this hight, then sin is fully formed
and shapen in us, suppose the outward act should never be com¬
mitted. And though an evill thonght confidered abstract ly or
init selfe be lesse sinfull then an outuard evill act, yet every evill
thought is very finfull, and concerning their sinfullnesse I shall
lay dotne these five briefe assertions.
First, The least evill thought, thouph unconsented to is sin¬
full, mortally sinfull, it calls for death as the wages of it. If any
evill thoughts are sinfull & deserve death, these also do, The rea¬
son is, because degrees doe not vary the kind or nature of sin,
and therefore they neither adde nor take away the properties or
effects of it; Greater degrees may add somewhat to the proper¬
ties and effects, that is, they may make them greater, but they
doe not adde them. And so lesser degrees may abate or take
somewhat from the properties and effects of sin, but they cannot
take them away.
Secondly, When evill thoughts are consented to, and deligh¬
ted in, they are more vile and sinfull then any suddaine or un¬
premeditated acts of sin.
Thirdly, Some sins, and those the vilest, are or may be com¬
pleated in the thougbts, such are envy at anothers good, rejoy¬
cing in anothers hurt, discontent with our owne condition,
pride in our owne condition, or in any thing we have or are,
as also, unbeliefe of the word ef God, whether in the History
or Prophecy, whether in the promises or threatnings ofit.
Fourthly, Evill thoughes are so sinfull, chat as they are most

nate counsel or command in the Prophet ( Jer. 4. 14.) O Peru¬

this vile thought of thy heart, if any thing or above any ching

(which sob here did ) hold his heart at a due distance from
cthinking of what is unfit. «There are many things to be done,
that we may not doe evill. Firft, we must be sober in the use ot
the creature; Secondly, we must be diligent in our callings; Sa¬
etan uill quickly find us worke, if we find not our owne; Third¬
Iy, we must meditate much in the Word; Fourthly, we must
ftudy the vanity of the creature; Fifthly, we must be much in
prayer; Sixthly, we must admire the beauty of holynes, the in¬
valuable worth of a pure and chast minde; Seaventhly, we must
live much in the thoughts of our owne death, but especially in
the thoughts of the death of Christ. Now as all these things
should be done, that we may be preserved from doing evill; so,
many things must be avoyded, that the same end may be attain¬
ed, chiefely these foure; First, we must avoyd wanton speeches,
lust comes often in at the eare; Secondly, wanton daunces and
