rity would be idle, and ( as it were) have a perpetuall vacation,
did not the providence of God provide such objects for it to
worke upon. And as God by Moses in the Law told the Jewes,
The poore shall never cease out efthe Land; so Christ tells us in the
Gospel ( Mark 14. 7.) Te have the poore with yeu almayes, and
rhensoever ye mill, ye may doe them good. God hath so ordered it,
that we shall never want opportunity, though we often want
hearts to expresse our charity. And lest any should thinke the
poore (because possibly not of their kindred)un-related to them,
therefore the Lord (in that place of Deuteronomie) calls the poore
man ourbrother, and our poore, Thou spalt open thy hand mide un¬
to thy Brother, to thy paore, and thy needy in the land. which though
it had ( grant) a peculiar respect to that people, who were Gods
peculiar people, and all of Abrahams family, yet it reacheth all
people, who are also to account the poore their Brethren, and
so their poore, even as their neerest relations are theirs. Yea the
Lord calls the poore our owne flesti (Isa. 58.7.) And that thou
hide not thy selfe frem thine onne flesp. As if he had sayd; Doe not
withdraw, and pull backe, doe not disappeare when the poore
man appeares, for he is not only flesh as thou art, but thine owne
desh. And so if thou sufferest the poore to perish, thou sufferest
thy selie, even thine owne flesh (in xinde though not in number)
to perish. That Maxime of the Apostle (Eph. 5. 29.) is founded
in nature; Noman ever hated his omne flesp, but nourispeth and
cherisheth it. Are not they unnaturall, who refuse to nourish and
cherish the poore, whom the Spirit of God calls our owne flest?
And if such declare against themselves (according to this rule)

0456.head: Chap. 31. An Expesition upon the Becke of JOR. Verl. 16

body.t: that they are wanting as to nature or natural principles, how
much more are they wanting to Grace and spirituall principles?
The Apostle John (1 Ep: 3. 17.) Admonisheth Saints to fill up
their profession with the ready ectings of this love, and tells them
the neglect of that duty would prove that they had little lore to
God; Who so hath this worlds go ds, and seeth his brother hath
need, and shutteth up his bsmells of compassion from him, how dwel¬
leth the love of God in him? And as such shew little love to God,
so Solomon assures them they shall find little love from God For
God doth not barely propose this duty, but presseth us with the
consideration of our owne danger if ue neglect it (Pro 21. 13.)
who so stoppeth his eares at the cry of the poore, he also shalt cry him¬
selfe and not be heard. There is nothing worse to be feartd, or
which produceth worse effects to be felt by man, then not to be
heard by God. Therefore as Christ exhorts (Math. 5. 42.)
Give to him that asbeth thee: and frem him that mould berrow ef
thee, turne not tbou axay. And is it not a reproach to Chrislians,
not to give to those who aske, when some heathens have been
much troubled when nothing hath been asked of them? Againe,
Tob speakes of the desire of the poore, and the Hebrtwes have a
word, for a poore man, which in the roote signifies to desire, im.
plying that poore men who have little in poss ssion, are much in
desiring to have more.
Hence note.
Ther mwho are fullof mants, are also full of defirts.
As some who have no uants have many desires;they are never
satisfied how much soever tley are filled. So they who are under
reall and sensible wants, cannot but have many desires, and those
so strong and stirring sometimes, that’tis net ensie to with-hold
them from their desire, strong desires vill hardly take a denyall;
poverty puts on to importunity, yea some under great wants, are
so pressed with desire, that they take finfull wayes to have their
desires fullfilled Agur feared this when heprayed Give me not ps¬
verty, lest I put forth my hand and steale (Pro.30.9) The desires of
many are too strong for their consciences, and then they quickly
breake the bounds of righteousnesse and common honesty rather
thenthey will be with-held from their desire. They that are under
a sence of their want in spiritualis, of chcir want of grace, and of

0457.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Book ef JOR. Verf.16.

body.t: the favour of God, of the enjoyments ot Christ, O uhat desires,
what strong and vehement desires have they ? how will they
breaxe through all impediments to obtaine what they desire?
The poore in spirit have greatest desires and use the greatest en¬
denvours after spirituall things; They see they have but a little,
rand therefore they uill be urging to have more, and when they
have got more, though they are thankfull for ir, yet they will not
sit downe init, nor sayit is enough, because still that which they
get gives them a clearer sight of more to be gotten. Their richest
and fullest attainements in grace, doe but discover their poverty
and emptines, and therefore seing themselves alwayes wanting,
they are alwayes desiring; And surely the Lord wil not with¬
hold these poore from their desires, as Job professed he did not
those uho applyed to him for helpe and supply; If I'have with¬
held the poore from their desire,
Or have caused the eyes of the widdow to faile.
These words are neere in sence uith the former. Mr. Brougti
ton reades, If Ihave consumed the eres ef the widdow. Job did not
with-hold any truely poore from their desire, much lesse did he
with-hold the poore widdow from her desire, he suffered not her
eyes to faile; that is, he did not long deferre to doe that for her
which she desired, nor wèary her with waiting. Some doe not to¬
tally deny, but they are full of delays, and they put off poore sui¬
ters so long, that both purse and patience are quite spent. But
(saith Job) I have not caused the eyes of the widdom to faile by
long delayes, much lesse by denyalls. The passions of the minde
are visible in the eye; sometimes wee see joy sitting there, and
sometimes we see sorrow sitting there, at one time we may see
pleasednesse in the eye, at another time displeasure and anger.
Thus also (as here) we may see hope or expectation in the
eye. The earnest intentive looke of the eye upon any man,
hath ( as it were) this voycein it, I desire your helpe. He that
lookes much upon or to another, lookes for somewhat from him.
The looke of the eye to God hath the force of a prayer in it, yea
this is often put for prayer, because in prayer usually, the eye
is listed up to God (Psal. 121. 1.) Imil lift up mine eyes to the
hills from mhence come:h my helpe. Againe (Psal. 123. 2.) Be¬
hold us the eyes d servants locte unto the hand os ibeir Masterz,

0458.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Book of IO B. Verl. 10

body.t: and as the eyes of a maiden to the hand of her mistresse; so our cyes
maite upon the Lord, our God, untill that he have mercy upon us.
That is, we will waite and pray, or pray waiting for his mercy.
And as the eye waites on God, so in proportion upon man.
When Peter and Jehn came into the Temple (Acts 3.) there sate
a poore lame man asking an almes (v. 2.) And Peter fastening
his cyes upon him, with Pohz, sayd looke on us (v. 4. ) As if he had
sayd, you look upon many others as persons able to relieve your
necessities, but now looke on us, and see what we will doe for
you; And he gave heed unto them, saith the text (v. 5.) cæpect¬
ing to receive something from them; that is, he sastned his eyes up¬
on them, he beheld them as an expectant of reliese. Thus the
widdow ( we may suppose) came to deb and look't pitifully up¬
on him, or gave him an humble look of expect ation, as if she had
sayd, give me your assistance, doe such a thing for me; And when
she did so, he did not cause her eyes to faile, nor did he feed her
with vaine hopes, as they doe who are forward to make promi-
ses, but slow to make performance. Every where in Scripture
the frustrating of expectation, is called the failing of the eye, or
is the cause of it. (Psal. 69. 3.) I am veary of my crying, mI
throat is dryed; mine eyes faile, mhile I waite for my Gid: that is,
God is pleased to put me to such long waiting, and expectation,
that my eyes are even worne with looking, and my heart with
expecting. (Psal. 119. 133.) Mine tyes faile for thy salvation,
and for the mord of thy righteousnesse; that is, for the receiving of
the benefit, blessing, deliverance, or salvation, which that word
of thy righteousnesse hath promised to me, and made me to waite
for. And as God, to try the faith and patience of his people, lets
them waite till their eyes begin to fayle; so men eyther through
unfaithfulness or weakness, oft cause the eyes of those uho uaite
upon them to fayle utterly. ( Lam. 4.17.) As for us, our eyes
as yet failed for our vaine hespe; that is, we lookt for helpe, and
no helpe came, and so our eyes failed in our expectation. But up¬
on vhom did they waite in this total frustration? the next words
tell us, We have matched for a nation that could not save us. The
Hebrew is, in our watching we have watched, or (as that Ele¬
gancy imports) we have earnest ly watched for a nation that could
not save us: that is, for the Egyptians who promised us helpe,
and upon whom we trusted for helpe, but all in vaine. They

0459.head: Cuap. 31. An Exposition upon the Book ef Jo B. Vers. 16

body.t: proved a weake reed, upon uhich while we leaned we were not
supported but wounded. R ghteous Jof dealt not tus with his
expectants and dependants; He did not cause the eyes of the
widdow to faile, he did not let them waite till they were weary,
or tired, or grieved. And this ue may understand him speaking
in a two fold reference.
First, As to delayes of Justice; As if he had sayd, I have not
let them waite long for their right, I have not given chem dilato¬
ry answers ard put offes, hoping to be spurr’d up with gists and
brib’d into expedition.
Secondly, As to delayes of charity: As if he had sayd, I have
not let the widd́ow waite long for my almes, what I g ve her, I
give her speedily.
In both these respects, or for both these helps, poore widdows
waite; And they are constrained to waite long for some mens
charity, and longer for other mens justice; so long for both some¬
times that their eyes faile and their spirits sinke in despaire of ey¬
ther. In neither of these respects did Jeb grieve the widdow. He
neicher wronged her himselfe, neither did be delay to right her
when she was wronged by others:he neither made her poor him¬
selfe, nor did he delay to relieve her poverty. Thus he answersthat
which Eliphaz charged him directly uith ( Chap.22.7,9.) Thou
hast not given mattr to the weary to drinke, and thou hast mith¬
holden bread from the hungry, thou hast sent middons away empty,
and the armes of the fatherlesse have been broken. No, saith fob, I
have many witnesses, and my conscience, which is more then a
thousand witnesses, tells me, that, I have not caused the cyes of the
viddow to faile.
And when he saith so we are to expound it in a better sence
then his words expresse: there is lesse in what he spake, then in
what he did for the widdow; for his meaning is this, I was so far
from making her cyes to faile with waiting, that I made her heart
glad, and sent her away rejoycing, because of her just and specdy
dispatch. Expedition hath cost some very deare; fob did not
only not deny the widdow his justice, or his charity, but dispatch
her quickly; none payd for expedition who appealed to his Tri¬
bunal, nor did the expectation of any perish who applyed to him
for reliefe. If I have caused the eyes ef the xiddow ro faile.
Hence note.

0460.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition upon the Boeke ef JO B. Verf. 16.

body.t: Ive eugbt not erhy to helpe the poure, bat ie belpeibem pudily.
Speedy reliefe, is double reliefe; He that gives at once, gives
tuice. Therefore as Solomon adviseth ( Pro 3. 28.) Say not to
thy neighbour, goe, and come againe, and to morrow I nil give,
when thou hast it by thee. As we must not say, but doe, so ue
should not deferre to doe.“ Tis dangerous to say, we vil! give to
morrow when we know not whether a to morrow shall be piven
us. If we have it now to give, let us give it now, for who knows
whether he shall have any thing to give hereaster. And if delayes
are not denialls of helpe to man, yet they are of obedience to
God; who as he commands us to give, fo to give now. The
poore are ready to starve, & shall we be unready to give what we
have ready by us? The poore may perish to day, and whit good
will your Almes doe them to morrow? As God will not beare
it that we should fay to him we will obey him to morrow, when
he calls for obedience to day (take heed of making the Lords eyes
faile in waiting) so God will not beare it, if we say to the poore
goe and come againe to morrow, he requires it to day, though
the poore doe only entreate it. The Apostles rule is (Rom. 12 8)
He that shemeth mercy mith chearefulnesse. And againe (2 Cur.9.
7.) The Lord loveth a cheartsull giver. Now that which a man
doth chearefully he uill doe it sperdily. And every good thing
the sooner it is done, the better it is done. Nor can that be done
too speedily, which should be done presently. To doe a charity,
or to doe Justice late is next doore to the not doing it at all. As
he that askes faintly bespeakes a denyall, so he that grants slowly,
gives with a kind of denyall; And to be sure so much of the bene¬
ficiallnes of any benefit is taken off from those to whom ’tis gi¬
ven, as also so much of the thankes from those who give it, as de¬
lay is made in the giving of it. As the Lord gives sometimes pre¬
ventingly ( Isa. 65. 24.) Before they call I mill answer, or makes
his grant contemporary, or beare the same date with our requests
(as it follows in the same verte) and whiles they are yet speabing
I mill doe; fo should we in our proportion doe to those who
make suites and requests to us.
How contrary to this rule of giving and doing good to others
are they uho seeme to take a kinde of pleasure to put others to
the paine of expectation; They love to he waited on. And they
there¬

0461.head: Chap. 31. An Expofition upon the Booke ef JOR. Vers.16.

body.t: cherefore hold petitioners upon the racke of expectation, because
they love to be waited upon; we may discover three sorts of
this humour.
First, Some when they know the thing desired is not in their
power to doe, yet they will not say plainly they cannot doe it
(to be speedy in denying what we cannot doe, is a favour as well
as to be speedy in granting what ve can doe, yet I say, some vill
not presently say they cannot doe, what indeed they cannot)
because they have an ambition to be attended upon and much
sought unto.
Secondly, Others who from the first moment that a suite is
made to them, are resolved in their owne breasts or are fully in¬
tended never to doe it, though it be in their power to doe it; yet
they will not say they will not doe it, but hold poore suiters in a
long suspence. It is some courtesie to say we uill not doe, what
we have no minde to doe and are purposed not to doe. But the
poliey of some men is too great for this poynt of charity.
Thirdly, There are others, who are both able and willing,
yea resolved to grant the poore their desire, yet for state they
make the poore stay and the widdows waite till their eyes fay le;
And to doe as much torment suiters with their delayes, as they
benefit them with their reliefe. They that take fuch state in do¬
ing courtesies, loose their reward with God, and their respects
from man. He that stayes long for a favour, hath more then halfe
deserved and payd for it."Tis the priviledge of God to make man
waite his pleasure. Yet he never delayes his people but ’tis in wis¬
dome, yea and in mercy also (Isa. 30. 18.) The Lord is the God
of Judgement, blessed are all they that waite for him. As God doth
no man wrong how long sosver he makes him waite, so how long
scever we waite on him we loose no time, nor will it be at all to
our losse. Waiting upon God in faith and patience turnes alwayes
to a good account, and hath Great reward. But let men take
heed how they take state upon them in making the poorest man
waite for their charity, or any man for their Justice. They will be
found fayling in duty who thus cause the eyes of any, especially
(which Job here professeth he did not) the eyes ef the middom to
fayle.
Secondly, Observe.
w'hen suites are long deferred, and unansmered, suittrs are
The
greatly afficted.

0462.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Book of JOR. Verl. 16.

body.t: The fayling of the eyes is painsull, and implyes a decay in na¬
ture; The eyes fayle through old age, or through much bod yly
weaknesse and want. Tis layd (Per. 14. 6.) The xild Afses aid
stand in the high places, they snuffed up the mird like Dragons,
their eyes did fayle because there was no grasse. Whatsoever makes
the eyes fayle is afflictive; Therefore long delayes must needs be
a great affliction, seeing they make the eyes fayle; yea delayes
doe more then make the eyes fayle, they make the heart fayle
too (Pre. 13.12.) Hope deferred, makes the heart siche but mhen
the desire cometh, it is a tree of life. “Tis the word in the former
part of this verse, mhen the desire cometh; that is, when the thing
desired cometh, it is as a tree of life. A lingring hope is like a
lingring consumption, it weakens the whole man. Hope having
conceaved some probable good approaching, waites for the birth
of it; And we are like a woman in travel till it be brought forth:
long travel in child-bearing makes the mother sicke and faint,
and so doth hope make us, when we travel long in the bringing
of it forth. But as a woman forgets the paine of her travel for
joy tûat a man is borne, so doth he that sees his hope, that is, the
thing hoped for borne. This Solomon expresseth to the life, u hen
he saith, The defire come is a tree of life. As uhen Christ who is
called The desire ef Natiens (Hag. 2. 7.) shall come, he uill be
a tree of life to all true beleevers; so in its degree and measure is
the comirg of any good thing which we desire. The fullfilling of
desire is so great a reliefe that it is a kind of New life to the soule,
and causeth our dead hearts to revive. The hearts of many Godly
men have been made sicke when God hath deferred their hope;
David sayd (Psal. 69. 3.) Mine eyes fayle while I waite for my
God. And againe (Psal. 119 82.) Mine eyes fayle for thy mord;
that is, in waiting to receive that good which thou hast promi¬
sed in thy word. Whether God or man keepe us long at a di¬
stance from our hopes, we quickly meete with griefe of heart and
fayling of eyes. Tocal denying and long delaying are not farre
asunder.
Thirdly, Observe.
The middons case and cause must not be delayed.
If widdows are not speedily relieved, they are doubly grieved.
They are weake, and not able to beare much; They are under
sorrow alrcady. To deferre their hope, is to give them forrow

0463.head: Chap.31. An Expssition apon the Books of IO 2. Vert.17.

body.t: pon sorrow. Shee hath sorrow enough for the losse of her hus¬
band, with whom she had lived comfortably. Now every delay
put upon her puts her in minde of that losse and makes that
wound bleed afresh It was not thus ( saith shee) when I had
a husband, then I had no need to waite. now l waite and cannot
get reliefe in my greatest netde. Mag strares shouid be hushands
to the uiddow, and espouse cheir cause (according to Justice)
with tendernes. God charged the Princes of Israel, with this
speci Il defect of duty (Isa. 1. 23.) They judge net the father¬
lesse, neither doth the widdones cause come unto them; that is, they
relule to receave and heart the widdows cause, they will not ad¬
mit it to come before them, shee cannot bribe it to a hearing,
and therefore it stickes by the way, and comes not to a hearing.
Bet though men will not udge her cause, yet God will ( Psal.
68. 5.) A father of ihe fatherlesse, a Judge of the middoms is God
in bis holy habition. God is so much the widdows Judge that he
is spoken of as if he were a Judge for none but widdows. And men
are so little in judging cheir cause, as if they did not udge the wid¬
dows cause at all. The middows cause ( saith the Prophet) doth
not come before them. How greatly doe they fay le in duty who
cause the eyes of the widdo y to fay le, and who adde sorrow to
their state, uhose state at best is a sorrowfull one. This cruelty Tob
at once denyed and abhorred, while he sayd, If I have caused ihbe
eyes of the widdow to fayle. He proceeds to a further testimony of
his tendernes to the poore in the words which follow.
Verf.17. Or have caten my morsell my selfe alone, and the fa¬
therlesse hath not eaten therecf.
In this verse fob shews both his charity, and his hospitality,
charity may be exercised without doores, but hospitality is exer¬
cised within doores. And that hospitality is best which is also an
Act of charity; Tobs was such, He did not eate his morsel himselfe
alone, chere was hospitality, And his guests were not, or not they
only his rich and wealthy neighbours, but the fatherlesse, And
the fatherlesse hath not eaten thereef, there was his charity.
If I bave eaten my morsel my selfe alone.
A morsel is properly but so much meate as we may put into
the moutk at once; By which diminitive word, a Morsel or a

0464.head: Chap. 31. Au Exposition upon the Rocke of JOR. Verl. 17.

body.t: Mouth-sul, the Scripture usmlly sets forth the ancient enter¬
tainments, which were as frugal as they were hearty. When A¬
braham invited those three men, who indeed were Angels, and
one of them ( whom he called Ay Lord ) The Lord of men and
Angels, he only sayd (Gen. 18 5.) Rest vour selues ander the tree,
and I mill fetch a merseluf brtad and confert yce yaur heart:. A¬
braham was sparing of his vords, but not of his cost; he invited
them io a morsel, but provided them cakes made of three mez¬
sures of fine meale, and a calfe tender and good with butter and
milke; you may read this bill of fare (ver. 6, 7, 8.) Thus Eliah
uhen he had desitred the uiddow. woman to fetch him a little
water (1 King. 17. 10,11.) As fhe mas going to feich it, he cal¬
led to her, and said, bring me I pray thee a morsel ef bread in thine
haud; he did not desire a feast, or a full table, but a morsel.
Thus saith Job. Ihave not caten my morsel my selfe alone; that is,
what ever good cheare I had, I had it for others as wel as my selse
and my family, I had a spare roome and a spare trencher for a
friend at my Table, especially for the poore and fatherlesse; These
were my welcome guests, as it follows.
And the fatherlesse have not eaten mith me.
By the fatherlesse, we are not to understand ftrictly, such as had
lost their parents, but any in want or distresse, as hath been shew¬
ed from the same expression in severall other passages of this
booke. When Tob relieved the hungry bellyes of the poore, he
did not only send them a portion from his Table, but he gave
them a place and a portion at his Table, the poore did not only
eate of his meate but sate at meate with him, he did not disdaine
to have them at his Table.
Herce note.
First, Hospitalitie is a dutie.
As we make provision for our selves and family, so ( if able)
we should make allowance for strangers also. When David heard
that Nabal sheared his sheepe, he sent out ten young men to
greete him in his name, and gave them instructions; Tous spall
yee say to him that liveth in prosperitie, Peace be both to thee, and
peace be to tuy house, and peace be unto all that thou hast, &c. Let the
mang men find favour in thine eyes ( fer me come in a good der)

0465.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Rook ef IOs. Vers.17.

body.t: give I pray thee mhatsoever cometh next to thy hand unto thy ser¬
vants and unto thy son David. Had David been at his mercy he
could not have sent him a fayrer message. Yet this covetous
churle was so farre from sending him a liberall present, that he
could not give him a good word, or a civill answer. But present¬
Iy falls a reviling him (1 Sam. 25. 10) who is David? and mho
is the son of fesse? there be mauy servants nom adayes that breake
amay every man from his Mester. Shall I then take my bread, and
my water, and my flesh, that I have killed for my shearers, and give
it unto men, nhom Iknow not xhence they be? As if he had sayd,
Shall I feed these vaggabonds and beggars? The man was all in his
possessives, my bread, and my mater, and my flest, that I have kil¬
led for my shearers; he had not a morsel to send David, but sent
more then a mouth full of bad words. This mans name was a¬
greeable to his Nature; Nabal mas his name, and folly was mith
him. His folly was, he would send nothing to strangers out of his
house; and theirs is libe his, who have nothing for strangers in
their houses. Abraham stood in his tent doore, and no sooner saw
strangers passing by, but called them in and gave them entertain¬
ment. The Apostle ( Heb. 13. 2.) alluding to that act of Abra¬
hams hospitalitie, gives beleevers this Admonition, Forget not to
entertaine strangers, for so some have entertained Angells una¬
wars. We are commanded ( Rem. 12. 13.) not only to distri¬
bute to the necessity of Saints, but tobe given to hospitalitie. And as
this is charged upon all Beleevers, so especially upon the Mini¬
sters of the Gospel (I Tim. 3. 2.) A Bispop ( besides many o¬
ther Qualifications there enumerated) must be sober, ef good be¬
haviour, given to hospitalitie, apt to teach, not given to wine. And
againe (Tit.1. 5.) He must not be given to filthy lucre, but he must
be a lover of hospitalitie; A lover of Good men, sober. Yet note, as in
these texts the Apostle commends hospitalitie to the Mmnisters of
the Gospel, so he regulates it. They must be given to hospitalitie,
yet sober and of good behaviour; They must be given to hospi¬
talitie, yet not given to uine, nor filthy lucre; They must be gi¬
ven to hospitalitie, yet apt to teach; Their hospitalitie must not
hinder eyther their private studyes or publicke labours. That
hospitalit ie which is inconsistent with sobriety, or unfits for du¬
ty, is uncomely and finfull in any man, much more in a Minister
of the Gospel. Some are given to riotous house-xeeping, but fer

0466.head: Chap.31. An Expofition upon the Book of JOR. Verl. 17.

body.t: are given to true hospitality. The former is the abhorrence of a
meere Civill man, the latter is both the duty and commendation
of a Godly man. Moderate seasting of friends is love, and feed¬
ing of the poore in charity, is an ornament to the Gospel and a
fruit of Grace. As their lin is great who lavish out the creature
in surfeting and drunkennes, or who make provision for the fleshi
to fullfill the lusts of it, so also is theirs who basely spare the
creature and will not make provision eyther for their friends to
nourish love, or for the poore to relieve their nece ssities.
Secondly. Consider who were Tobs guests? mostly the poore
and fatherlesse, and he names them only.
Hence observe.
The hospitalitie of good men us chiefly designid for the belpe of
the necessitous, ths poore and the fatherlesse.
Tis most acceptable to God when we seed the poore, though
it be not unlatofull to invite and feast the rich. Indeed Christ be¬
ing invited to eate bread at the house of a Pharisee, said to him¬
that bade him ( Luk. 14. 12, 13.) When thou mabest a dinner, or
a supper, call not thy friends, nor thy brethren, neither thy kinsmen,
nor thy rich neighbour, lest they also bid thte againe, and a recom¬
pence be made thee. But when thou makest a feast, call the poore,
the maimed, the lame, the blinde. This is Christs rule, and Job¬
practise answered it; the fatherlesse did eate with him. Yet the
Scripture last mentioned is not an absolutely restrictive command
to invite the poore and none else; for we are commanded to use
hospitalitie one to another mithout grudging (1 Pet. A 9.) that is,
to give reciprocall entertainments; He doth not only say us¬
hospitalitie, but use it one to another, or mutually, which cannot be
understood of entertaining the poore only; for they are not able
to invite their inviters. Therefore as when the Lord saith (Hos.6.
6.) I defiered mercy and not sacrifice; he doth not prohibit sacri¬
fice, that is, outward performance of duties, or the performance
of outward duties, but shewes that he is more and rather pleased
with mercy then with sacrifice, or that sacrifice without mercy
doth not please him at all. So when Christ saith call the poore
not the rich to thy table, he doth not forbid the bidding of the
rich, but chargeth us rather to bid the poore, and if we have not
enough for both, then, uhat we have to spare must be for thote

0467.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Bock of I0 B. Verl. 17.

body.t: who have nothing, not for those who have enough already. We
must preferre the doing of charities, before the doing of courte¬
sies. It is recorded by Mr. Fore in the Bokeif Martyrs, con¬
cerning that eminent sereant and witnesse of Jefus Christ Tohn
Hooper Bishop of worcister. That he Rept a Constant Table for
the poore, or his Board of Beggars, vho were dayly served with
whole and wholesome meates, before himselfe sate downe to
dinner. There are Great House keepers ivho are not good Heuse¬
heepers, because their house keeping is for the Great not for the
good, not for the house hold of faith, especially not for the poore
of that house hold. B’essed are those feast makers, who make the
bowells of the hungry to blesse them. Solomens good direction
falls in with this good practice, as some expound it (Eccles.11.
1.) Cast thy bread upon the water, that is, upon the poore, or up¬
on those of uhom thou hast no more expectation to reccive any
thing againe, then thou canst ration:lly expect thy bread againe
when thou hast cast it upon the water, or that thou shouldest
reape a plentifull harvest of that seed uhich thou hast cast upon
the wayes of the Sea, not into the furrows of the earth. The ho¬
Iy Prophet assures us, that this feeding of the poore is more ac¬
ceptable to God then our owne abstaining from food ( Isa. 58.
6,7.) This is the fast that Ihave chosen, that thou deale thy bread to
the hungry, and that thou bring the poore that are cast out totby
house. When thou seist the nabed, that thou cover him, and that ibu
hide not thy selse from tbine owne flish. This is the Lords fast, and
the Lord accounts no fast holy, but when'tis followed with such
a feast; and therefore that custome in the Churches of making a
Collect:on for the poore in the close of a day of fast and solemne
humiliation, is not to be reckoned a formality, but an essentiall
part of that Great and important duty. To comfort and refresta
the bodyes of the afflicted, is as plrasing to God, as the afflicting
of our owne soules. “Tis sad to see the poore neglected at any
time, but especially at that time And’tis as sad to sce how the
practice of most, at all times, runs quite contrary or crosse to the
rule of Christ given us in the Gospel, That saith, Invite xot thy
brethren, nor the rich, but the porre; whereas usually the rich a-e
invited and not the poore. And whereas (in spiritualls ) God
fills the hungry with good things, but sends the rich empry away,
most men ( as to corporalle) fill the rich with their good things,

0468.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upou the Bocke ef IOB. Verf. 17.

body.t: with the fatte and the sweete, but send the poore eyther quite
empty away, or only a little relieved ( to keepe them from star¬
ving) with the refuse of their Table. Which latter practice is al¬
so reproved by the practice of lob in this text.
For, saith he, If I have eaten my morsel my selfe alone, and the
fatherlesse hath not eaten thereef.
Hence note.
A good man xill give the poore such ibings as are geod, to cate,
yea sometimes as good as he eates himselfe: He doth not thinke
it below him, that they suould eate with him, and of mhat he
bimselfe eates.
Iob did not put off the poore with scrapps only (though I doe
not say ’tis sinfull to give broken meate to the poore ) yet 'tis
plaine he did not put off the poore with such poore reliefes, nor
should we. Some thinke any thing they have, the worst they
have, good enough for those who have nothing. But as Christ
saich concerning spirituall bread (Math. 15.26.) It is not meet
to tabe the childrens bread, and te cast it to dogs: So I may say in
reference to materiall bread It is not good to take dogs bread, and
to give it to the children, that is, to give corrupt or unsavory bread
and meate to the poore. The best which we have is but given us,
or indeed lent to us, and therefore what we give to the poore
should be good, especially seeing what is given to the poore, is
lent to the Lord, from whose hand we receave all our riches.
And shall we lend base money, or mouldy bread to the Lord ?
Againe, when we feed the godly poore, we feed Christ himselfe
(Matb. 25. 35 40.) and shall we not feed Christ our Lord and
Master with that which is good? Almes is a sacrifice ( Heb. 13.
16.) Now as the Lord did highly disgust it and tooke it very
ill at the hands of the Jewes, when they offered the blinde, and
lame, and sicke for sacrifices; Is it not evill ( saith the Lord,
Mal. 1.8.) Offer it now unto thy Governour, will he be pleased
mith thee, or accept thy person? Yea he adds (v. 14.) Cursed be
the Deceaver that hath in his flocke a male, and vometh and sacrifi¬
ceth unto the Lord a corrupt thing; for I am a great King, saith the
Lord of hests. Now, I say, as the Lord tooke it ill, when the pro¬
per sacrifices were of corrupt things; so he vill not take it well,
uhen these metaphoricall facrifices are no better. Indeed if ve

0469.head: Chap. 31. An Expofition upon the Beokt ef I0». Vert.17

body.t: have no better, if we have but a cup of cold water only to give
ve giving it to one of those little ones in the Name of a Disci¬
ple) fhall not loole our reward ( Math. 10. 42.) But the de¬
ceaver is cursed who giveth that which is bad, when he hath good
or berter to give. There is (I know) a great fault among some
poore, they will scarce be contented uith any thing but uhat is
fine, and of the best; when they have had good wholesome food
given them, they will throw it behinde the doore, or upon the
dunghill. There is a fault also among some rich men, who give
that to the poore which is fitter for the dung-hill, then for the
body of man.
Lastly, Job speakes not here of any feast he made the poore,
but only of a morfel, I have not eaten my morsel my selfe alone,
yet doubrlesse he had plenty at his Table, and did (as the Lord
doth the rich) even load the poore with his benefits and bene¬
ficences day ly.
Hence note.
A gracieus biart counts that but a little that he harb done and
given.
He saith not I have made the poore a feast, but I have given
them a morsel, nothing makes our charity greater in the eye of
God, then when’tis little in our oune, when we call a feast a
morsel, and a full dinner a bit. Plutarch faich, that the Lacede¬
monians gave not only a charity, but a liberality and a bounty to
the distressed Smyrnians, They sent them a very full supply, yet
gave their Messengers instruction to tell them, that they had on¬
ly spared them a meales meate from themselves, and a foddering
from their cattel. As it was the ingenuity of that heathen people
to put but a smal value upon a great benefit; so also it is the pie¬
ty of Christians to doc so; As they fhould not at all blowa
trumpet, or speake much of what they give; so they should not
thinke it much; As this is the fin of some, they thinke much (as
ve say, that is, they grudge) to give any thing; so the sin of o¬
thers is this, they thinke what they have given to be much. The
lesse we esteeme our good deeds, the more God esteemes them;
the lower our charity is rated in our oune boohe, the higher it is
in Gods booke; we fhall not need to feare our worhes fhall not
be enough̀ rewarded, unlesse ue say much or the mos of them;

0470.head: Chap.31.An Exposition upon the Bok of IOR. Vert, 18.

body.t: if any thing bring them a low reward from God, our over-rating
them will. Jub having thus fhewed the opennes of his heart and
hand and house for the free entertainment of the poore and fa¬
therlesse, gives us an account of the time how long or sin ce wben
he had groune into this neerenes of a gracious and discreete ta¬
miliarity and freedome wih them, in the next words.
Verf. 18. For from my youth be was brougbt ap witb me as xitb
a father, and I have guided her from my motbers
rombe.
There is another reading of these words, which I shall speake
a little to before I open our owne.“Tis that of the vulgar latine,
which translates Jobs text thus.
For from my yeutb compassien did grow up xith me, and I did
bring her up evenfrem my mothers mombe.
These words which we render, as a father, consisting of a par-
ticle of likenes, and Ab signifying a father, some conjoyne into
one word signifying sorrow or griefe of mind, arising ey ther from
our owne troubles and sufferings, or from the sufferings and trou-
bles of others, which we properly call compassion. From my yeuth,
compassion (or trouble of mind for the troubles of others ) dia
grow up with me. The minde of this reading is to shew the con¬
naturallnesse of tobs practise with his spirit; As if he had sayd, I
have not been forced, or unuillingly drawne to this course of
charity; but have been moved to it by an inward principle, and
as naturally, as it is naturall for a hound to hunt his prey, for a
bird to fly in the ayre, or for a stone to fall doune ward to the
earth. I have an intrinsecall tendency to this great duty, and am
led, not driven to it. Not that it was naturall to him, in oppositi-
on to that which is by grace; but it became connaturall to him
by grace. Jot knew that as he had his being from God, so much
more his gracious being. He did not make himselfe in his mothers
wombe, much lesse did he make him else mercisull in his mothers
wombe. That was a speciall worke of God upon him, framing
his heart to such workes from the wombe. He attributes nothinß
to himselfe but all to God; for as he knew he was not made man
in the wombe by his owne power, so he knew he uas much lesse
made a good man fromthe wombe by aoy power of his oune.
This

0471.head: Chap.31. An Expssition upon the Rooks of JOR. Verf.18.

body.t: This translation thus expounded carrieth a pious sence.
But most of the learned Hebricians render the text as we doe,
For from my youth he mas broughi up mith me; be? who was that?
the father-lesse.
And I have gaided her from my mothers mombe; ber? who was
that? the widdow. So that fob gives an account of his charirable
practice, as that which he had not lately taken up, but was long
accustomed to.
For from my youth he mas breaght up mith me.
As if he had said No sooner wat I able to looke or step ixto the
world, but I became a friend to the fatberlesse, and a patron and
protector ef the poore. I quickly or very early tooke notice of their
condition, layd it to heart, and gave them my best assistance. The
word uhich we render, He mas breught up with me ( for these
words are there knit up in one) signifies to grow and wax great,
or to be great. Indeed the poore (as we say in our language of
an inward bosome friend) were Great vith Tob, when he was
Greatest. And he as a Father brought up the poore, when him¬
selfe was young, or before he was a father.
Hence note.
Grace workes betimes in some.
As there is a seed of sin and corruption in all children, so we
may see the fruites of the Spirit in some children.
From my youth, he nas brougbt up mith me.
The Apostle Paul saith of Timotby (1 Tim. 3. 5.) From a
child thou hast knomne the holy Scriptures. His first acquaintance
was an acquaintance with God in his word. How sueete is it to
see vertue blossoming when nature doth? and the puttings forth
of faith contemporary with the first puttings sorth of reason; or
to see those acting spiritually, who have but begun to act ratio¬
nally. The Lord should have our first fruits, yea as the old Law
commanded, our first first fruits; They are blessed who remem¬
ber their Creator in eed in any of their dayes,but’tis our duty to
remember him in the dayes of our youth, and to dedicate our
first first fruites unto him. And though some are afraid to presse
good chings upon their children, lest they should over-burden

0472.head: Chap.31. Au Exposition upon the Booke of JOR. Verl. 18.

body.t: them; yet Solomon a wiser then they, yea the Spirit of God, a
wiser then Solomon gives us better advice (Pro 22. 6.) Train up
a child in the way he should goe, and mhen he is old he will not depart
from it. Though some children have gone out of the way in
which they were trained, and their golden youth hath concluded
in an Iron old age; which possibly gave occasion of that reproa¬
ching Proverb, A young Saint, an old Devil: yet of this we are
sure, that few who continue in the Devils power till they are old,
become Saints. And there is no more reason to stop any from
training up a child in the way that he should goe for feare he
hold not onne to old age, then there is to set a traveller in his
right way in the morning for feare he should misse his way be¬
fore night. Usually they tvho begin wel, end wel, and they who
begin in true grace, shall certainly continue in it, and end in Glo¬
TV. A Heathen sayd, Tis a great matter to accustome any one from A
bis youtb to any thing. And another, That sent mith which a new
Caike is seasoned, and so those principles with which a child is in-
fluenced, holds long. Customt hath a great power whether in
good or evill. Thus they speake in nature; And ’tis most true in
grace; That tincture of true holyness which the soule receives,
though never so early, abides for ever. The Prophet saith
Lam. 3. 27.) It is good for a man to beare the yoke in his pauth;
What yoke? There is a two-fold yoke; First, the yoke ot suffer-
ing; Secondly, the yoke of doing: he there speakes of the yoke
of suffering; but it is as true of the yoke of doing; it is good for a
man to beare that yoke in his youth. Some have never met with a
crosse in their youth, and how doth it trouble them to meete
with it in their oîd age? Many have never done good in their
youth, and how reprobate are they in their old age to every
good worke !
Secondly, observe.
A gracious heart ù full of compassion to those that are in want.
They uho have experienced the compassions of God to them¬
selves ( as every gracious soule hath ) cannot but be moved with
compession to others. Compassion to and upon a right ob ect,
is an eminent act of Grace. We carry a great burthen upon our
selves, when we beare compassion to others. As we partake with
others in the good things they enjoy by rejoycing vith them,

0473.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Bo df JOB. Vers.18.

body.t: so we partake with others in the evills which they suffer by com¬
passionating them. When the Apostle Paul had reckoned up
his sufferings or pessions (2 Cor, 11. 24, &c.) Of the feues five
times received I forty stripes save one, &e. In wearinesse, in pain¬
fulluesse, in watchings eften, in hunger and thirst, in fastings often,
in celd and nakednesse: Having I say, thus spoken of his personall
passions; he prefent ly reports the heavy burdens of compassion
which lay upon him ( 28, 29.) Befides those things which are
nithout ( saith he) that which cometh upon me dayly, the care of
all the Churches; xho is weabe, and I am not meahe! mho is of¬
fended, and I burne net. As if he had sayd, whatsoever the af¬
slictions or infirmities of others are, I have my share with tliem.
And as it is the support and comfort of the whole Church,as also
of every beleever, to remember that Jesus Christ beares their bur¬
then with them, that he suffers with them now, as once he suffe¬
red for them ( we may indeed say of Jesus Christ, that all the
poore and afflicted Saints, that ever were, are, or shall be in the
world, have been brought up with him as a father, and he hath
had compassion of them in measure now(I say) as it is the joy of
all suffering Saints, that they are brought up with Christ as with
a father) so it is a great stay and comfort to suffering Saints, that
their fellow. Brethren are affected with their condition, and take
compassion of them.
Againe, In that Tob saith, From my youth he mas brought up
mith me.
Note.
A gracieus heart perseveres in doing good.
Tob doth not say he did it in his youth only, but from his youth;
Some have great appearances of goodness in their youth, but
goodness doth not grow up with them; yea as they grou their
appearances of goodnes decay, and wither, and come to nothing.
I say, their appearances of goodnes, for ( as was toucht before)
we cannot be too confident of the earlyest appearances of reall
goodnes. As Tob began in his youth, so he continued, and grew
up in this spirit, principle aud practise all his dayes.
Fourthly, In that ?eb saith, He was brought uy mith me as
mith a father from my youth.
Obierve.

0474.head: Chap.31. An Expofition upon the Book of JOB. Vert. 18

body.t: A gracieus heart hath a fatberly respest to the fatherlesse.
He not only doth for them as a friend, but as a father; or he
hath not only a respect to them but a fatherly respect. The heart
and spirit with which we doe a thing, is, more then the thing we
doe, Can you doe good as a father? you may doe good as a
man, but can you doe good as a father? To doe so is most plea.
sing to God our father, who as he doth good, so he doth good
as a father. Thus we resd (Psal 68 5.) A father of the ja¬
therlesse, and a Judge of the middens is God in his holy habitation.
And if God be a father to the fatherlesse, doubtlesse he acts with
the heart and in the spirit of a father toward them; and so should
we. Further as Job was like a father to the Fatherlesse, so he was
a Counseller to the widdow, as he fhewes in the close of this
verse.
And Ihave guided her from my mothers wombe.
That is, the widdow, how did Job guide her ? with his coun-
fell and advice, guides shew the right way, that’s the businesse
of a guide job uas the widdows guide, not to shew her the way
to this or that place, but to shew her the way of this or that bu¬
fienes, and to helpe her out of this or that distresse. When shee
poore creature was intangled, and in a maze, not knowing what
to doe, or uhich way to set a step forward in her affaires, then he
directed her. And ( saith he) I have been a guide to her
frem my mothers xombe.
This is a high or hy perbolicall speech, importing that he had
been both early and constant ly the widdowes guide. As the fa¬
therlesse were brought up with him as with a Father, so he had
been the widdows guide from his mothers wombe.
Hence note.
To give good counsel and instruction to the ignorant, is a xerle
of great mercy, even as great a morke of mercy as te give bread
to the hungry, or cloathing to the naked.
We may doe a distressed widdow as good a turne by opening
our mouthes to her, as by opening our purses to her. Good coun¬
sel is a good; Almes and though the Apostle reproves those who

0475.head: Chap. 31. An Expofition upon the Book ef J0 B. Verf. 18.

body.t: give no Almes but in words ( James 2. 15, 16.) If a brothir er
a sister be nabed, and destitute of daily fosd, and one of yeu sar unto
him, depart in peace, be you warmed and filled: not mithstanding ye
give them not those things mhich are needfull to the Body, what doth
it profit? Bare words will not satisfie hunger, nor will they make
a covering for the naked; yet words may procure bread for the
hungry, and cloathing for the naked; and in many cases we may
relieve the necessities of others uith our tongues as uel as uith
our hands. It is a great mercy in God, to guide man (Psal. 32.
8.) I will instruct thee and teach thee, in the may that thou shalt goe;
I will guide thee mith mine eye. And so the promise runs in the
Prophet (Isa. 58.11.) I mill guide thee continually. Now as it is
a great favour from God to good men, to guide them in their
way (the way of man is not in himselfe, Jer. 10. 23.) so it is a
great favour from man to man, especially to a poore man, most
of all a poore widdow, to guide and direct her in her way, to
shew her what course she must steere and take for the right end¬
ing of any intricate busienes, or for the attainement of her righ¬
teous ends. And if to guide others in civill and outward affaires
and concernments be a great charity, then how great a charity is
it to guide poore soules in spiritualls, and fhew them their way
heaven ward? To give answer to that question, What shall I
doe to be saved? or to those, how may l walke to all wel-plea¬
sing? how may I keepe my conscience in all my wayes uithout
offence touard God and toward man? (To answer these que¬
stions, to give counsel in and resolve these cases is I say) the best
charity in the world, infinitely better ( which yet must not be
neglected) then all worldly charities. Soule-guides are the most
usefull and necessary guides; And doubtlesse Job was wel skill’d
and practised in this sort of guiding as wel as inthe other; for so
Eliphaz doth at once upbraid him, and enforme us (Chap.4.3,4.)
Behold thou bast instructed many, and thou hast strengthned the
meake handi, thy words have upholden him that was falling, and
thou hast strengthned the fecble knees. Job had been every way a
guide, and he had alwayes been the widdows guide; I (saith he)
have guided her from my mothers mombe.
Lastly, Note.
A godly man is not satisfied with doing good once er twice, in a
little matter, or for a little mhile, but he mould doe good in all

0476.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition upon the Bocke ef IOB. Verf. 18.

body.t: matters and almayes (as fob did it) even from his mothers
wombe.
To sin or doe evill once or at any time is too much and too
often, because we ought not to sin or doe evill at all: But as we
cannot doe good too often, so unlesse we doe it often, it will be
tous as if we had not done it at all, because we ought to doe it
alwayes. Some who began late to doe good, have been accepted
and rewarded, but how soone soever we begin to doe it, we shall
neyther be accepted nor rewarded, if we cease or give over doing
it. How much are they mistaken, who if they have done a poore
soule good once, thinke themselves discharged for ever from do¬
ing any more? once in their dayes, they thinke enough for all
their dayes: yea they will repeate and report what they have
done, as an argument why they should doe no more. He did good
from Defigne not from Nature (I meane renewed Nature) who
saith, he hath done enough, and will doe no more, when ’tis in the
power of his hand to doe more. He that is good, will according
to his ability and opportunity, according to time and talent,
doe good once and againe, more and more, often and ever. As
he that sate on the mhite Horse ( Rev. 6. 2.) vent forth conquer¬
ing and to conquer, that is, with a purpose never to leave con¬
quering while there was an enemy to conquer; so A good man
gors forth doing and to doe good, as long as there remaines any
good undone which he can and is called to doe.

0477.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition upon the Bocke ef J0R. Verf.19.

body.t: If Ihave seene any perish for want of Clothing, or
any poore mithout Covering.
Ifhis loynes have not blessed mee, aud if he were
not warmed mith the fleece of my shecpe.
If I have lift up my hand against the fatherlesse,
mhen I saw my helpe in the gate.
OB proceeds in the vindication of his Charity touard the
J poore, his fayling in that poynt of duty having been objected
against him in the 22th Chapter, that he had hardened his heart
and shut up all bowels of compassion to those who were in di¬
stresse; yea that he had not only not supplyed their wants, but
taken what they had from those who wanted (v. 6.) Thou hast
stripped the naked of their cloatbing. And therefore as in the for¬
mer Context, he denyed that he had with-held the poort from their
desire, or had caused the eres ef the middom te faile, so in these words
he affirmes that he had been so farre from stripping the naked of
their cloathing, that he had Clothed and Covered them.
Verf. 19. If Ihave seen any periso for mant ef Clothing.
The eye affects the heart, Jabs eye did so much affect his heart
when he saw the naked, that he could not but put forth his hand
to put a covering upon them: his owne cloathes did not sit easie,
nor keepe him warme, while he saw the poore cold and naked.
The vulgar latine reades the text, If I have despised him that
was ready to perisb for mant of Clothing. As we are apt ( so the
Apostle James tells us, Chap. 2.2,3.) to have respect to a man
with a gold ring, that weares goodly apparrel, or gay cloathing;
so a man in brave and rich apparrel, is apt to despise the poore in
raggs. This version carries a cleare sence, but our owne is clearer
to the letter of the text. If I have seene
any perish for mant of Clothing.
That is, ready to starve and die with cold and nakednes; Job
doth not say, if l'have seene any want gay Cloathes (which are

0478.head: Cuap.31. An Exposttion upon the Book of JOE. Verl, 19.

body.t: often but flaggs of vanity) he did not supply the pride of any,
but the necessities of all. Charity is discreete as wel as pitifull,
and as it is ready to relieve the uants, so it uill not nourish wan¬
tonnes in any. They were perishing persons, not vaine or proud
persons whomfobs charity cloathed. If I (saith he) have seene any
perisb for want of cloathing.
Hence note.
First, Dying is perishing.
Thus the Prophet phrasethit (Isa. 57. 1.) The righteous pirih
and no man layeth it to heart. Deathis not a perishing as to our
future eternal beeing, but as to our present temporall beeing:
Naturall death is our perishing to all worldly comforts; eternal
death is our perishing to all comforts. The worst death and the
worst of death is but the perishing of our comfortable being, not
of our being.
Secondly, Perishing is here supposed the effect of want.
Hence observe.
Nchednesse or want of Clothing, is a killing mant.
The body cannot beare nakednesse long and live: the body
can no more beare the want of Clothing, then it can beare the
want of bread; Cold kills as well as hunger. See in this, the bit¬
ter fruits of sin: it is said (Gen. 2. 25.) The man and his mife
mere both naked, and were not asbamed. There was no matter of
shame in nakednesse, when there was no matter of sin init. And
as man was not ashamed, so he was not acold by reason of his na¬
kednesse, the ayre was not then injurious nor afflictive to his bo¬
dy; whereas now Clothing serves not only to hide shame, but to
keep us from perishing. There are two great uses of clothing; First,
to cover our nakednes; Secondly, to preserve our lives: As death
is an uncloathing, so we dye if we are not Clothed. And here let
mee minde you, in a spirituall sence, of another Clothing, which
if ue want we must indeed perish, and perish for ever; O how
many are there that are ready to perish for uant of that Cloth¬
ing ! what’s that? why, it is Christ, they that are not clothed with
him shall perish eternally, not only in body, but in soule (Rom. 13.
14.) Put ye ontbe Lord Jesus Christ. Clothe your selves uith him;
Christ is our spirituall Clothing: First, in his righteousnesse to

0479.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition upon the Booke of JOE. Vers.19.

body.t: Justifie us; so he is our Clothing to cover our sin-guiltinesse.
Secondly, in his graces to Sanctifie us; so he is our cloathing
not properly to cover, but to cleanse us from our sin-filthinesse
and pollution. (Eph. 4. 24.) Put on the nex man; that is, Christ
in his Graces, or the Graces of Jesus Christ. ( Colos. 3. 12.) Put
on as the elect ef God bowels of mercy, loving kindnesse, humilitie,
&c. Here’s clothing indeed; and remember how much soever
you are clothed, you will perishi for want of Clothing, unlesse
you be clothed with Christ, both to Justifie and to Sanctifie you.
Remember that warning of Christ to the Church of Laodicea
(Rev.3. 18.) I counsel thee to buy of me gold tryed in the fire, that
thou mayest be rich, and white rayment that thou mayest be cloa¬
thed. If I (saith Tob) have seene any perisp for mant of Clothing,
Or any potre without covering.
Consider both in this and the former part of the verse, how
universally fob speakes; he doth not say, if I have seene this or
that man perish for want of Clothing, but, if I have seene any pe¬
risb for mant of Cloathing, or any poore without Covering.
Againe, W’hereas Teb said before, If I have seene any perisp for
mant of Clothing; he saith here, if I'have seene any poore mithout
Covering: though they were not ready to perish for want, yet if
they being poore wanted, or were without a covering, he gave
them where-with-all to cover them. And possibly, this covering
in the latter part of the verse may be extended further then cloa¬
thing in the former part ofit. A house is a covering as wel as a
garment. And the poore many times are naked not only of
cloathes, but of houses, they have not a house, nor a hole in a
house to hide their heads in. We may well suppose sobs charity
so large, that when he saw the poore want any thing needfull for
them, uhether cloathing or housing to cover them, he provided
for them, and did not suffer them to be naked, eyther cloathlesse
or harborlesse; he did not let them lye in the streetes or open
ayre, but gave them convenient shelter from the in ury of the
weather. Christ, who endured more then allafflictions for our
sakes, endured this also in particular; The foxes have holes ( saith
he, Math. 8. 20.) and the birds have nests, but the Son of man
hath not mhereon to lay his head. Christ was poore without this
covering: And so are many poore at this day, who find not a
Tob to give them a covering.

0480.head: Chap.31. Au Expesition upon the Booke of JOR. Vert. 19.

body.t: Further, The roote of the uord here used for a cevering, is
applyed in Scripture to the pardon of fin, (sal.32.1.) Blessed
is the man mhose iniquity is forgiven, and whose sin is covered.
When sin is pardoned ’tis covered, God lees it no more with a
vindictive eye. Exeuses are garments of our oune making to co¬
ver sin; woe unto those whose sins are thus covered. Pardon is a
Garment of Gods providing and making to cover sin with, Bles¬
sed are they whose sins are thus covered. Those poore who are
without a covering for their bodyes, are to be pitied, but with
what teares should we lament those (how rich soevet they are in
this world) who are without a covering for their soules! and so
stand naked in the stormes and under those dreadfull droppings
of the urath of God. But to the scope of the text.
First, In that sob saith not only, If I have seene any perisb,
but, if I have seene any poore mithout covering.
Observe.
wet oughi not enly to belpe the poore against destroying and tit¬
ling mants, but even against pinching and afflicting wants.
What though the poore be not quite flarved with cold and
hunger, yet if they are so pressed with these wants, that their lives
are made altogether uncomfortable, and as it uere a continuall
death, our neglect of them is inexcusable. As God gives the rich
not only enough for their necessities, but for their moderate de¬
light; so the rich should at least give to or provide for the poore
enough to satisfie their necessities, and fit them for the duties of
this life.
Secondly, As to the particular charities here Instanced in.
Note.
To Chath the nabed, to previde covering for the harberlesse,
are speciall remarkable acts ef Charity.
The latter of these acts of charity is reckon'd up among many
acts of righteousnesse (Ez-k. 18. 7.) If a man be just, &c. if he
hath given his bread to the hungry, and hath covered the nated mith
a Garment. We have both put into the description of a true fast
(Isa. 58.7.) Is it not to deale thy bread to the hungry, and that
thou bring the poore that are cast out to thy house; mhen thou setst
the nahed that thou cover him. Jesus Christ will say to the sheepe

0481.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Book ef Io B. Verl.19.

body.t: on his right hand in that Great day, I mas a stranger and ye tooke
me in, I was nabed and ye clothed me: and (v. 43.) he will say to
the gostes on his lest hand, I mas a stranger and ye tooke me not
in, nahed and ye clothed me not. When Dorcas dyed the widdous
shewed the Coats and garments which she had made while she
was with them (Acts 9 39.) What Coats were these? and for
whom? They were Coats for the poore and needy; Shee did
not spend her time and estate in making rich apparel for her selse,
but convenient coates for the poore; And it seemes shee had a
store of them ready made as the needs of the poore appeared.
That good woman was full of charitie, and as charity nill cover
a multitude ef sins (I Pet. 4. 8.) that is, it will not strictly take
notice of, but in silence passe by the faults and faylings of many
when they are against our selves especially (as charity, I say, tbus
covers a multitude of sins, which are the spirituall nakednesse of
others) so it will cover the bodyly nakednes of as many as it can;
and provokes us rather to have but few cloathes our selves, then
that the poore should have none. When the people (Luke3.
10,11.) said to John Baptist, Wbat shall we doe? he answered and
said unto them, Hee that hath tmo coats let him impart to him that
hath none, and he that hath meat dot the libe. How unbecoming is
it that any should have not only food and rayment, but full ta¬
bles and wardropes, variety of meates and many changes of ap¬
parel, and yet see the poore starve and goe naked! yet some let
their old clothes lie by them till they are moth-eaten, while o¬
thers are naked, & suffer time to weare them out rather then the
poore. The Apostle James saith (Chap.5.1, 2.) Goe to now ye rich
men, meepe and homle for the miseries that shal come upon you, your
riches are corrupt, and your garments moth-eaten; you make so
many for your selves, that you cannot weare them out, only the
mothes eate them out, and yet you mabe none for the poore,
nor uill you let the poore have any of them which you have
made, the motbes suall have them first. The same Apostle (Chap.2.
15,16.) she wes us with what cold garments some cloath the na¬
ked, and cover the poore, even with a few good words & wishes,
that’s thinne clothing indeed, and very cheape, yet they who
cloath the poore only with complements, with breath and ayre,
will find it very costly to them, when Christ shall say, I mas nabed
and ye cloathed me net, depart from me. Let them uho will not

0482.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Boak of JOR. Vert. 19

body.t: give the poore any but those cold coverings of words, tremble to
thinke what cold comfort those words will be unto them. They
will pay deare for it at last, who now thinke it good husbandry
to spare their purses, and bestow as little cost as they can, or none
at all (willingly) upon the poore; Iub did cloath or cover them
with good words ( which is more then some bestow upon them,
yea some cover them with bad words, with rebukes and scornes,
with revilings and reproaches, it may be uith blowes, But as Job
did not cover the poore with bad words, so he did not cover them
only with good words) but where he saw any perish for want of
clothing, or the poore without covering, he really or with good
deeds cloathed and covered them.
Thirdly, Job had before spoken of the exercise of his Charity
in feeding the poore, yet that did not satis fie him, he also clothed
and covered them.
Hence observe.
They mho have ability ougbt to abound in all hindes of Cha¬
rity.
He that is truly charitable, doth not only give bread to the
hungry, but clothing to the naked. As wants multiply, so his sup¬
plyes are multiplyed. It is not enough to act Charity of one sort,
or to doe it in one poynt, we must be ready to act it in all. Few
(I grant) have estates like Job, he was a man of great substance,
he had many thousands of sheepe, many hundreds of Oxen, &c.
All cannot equall him, yet all must imitate him, and doe as he did,
though they cannot doe as much as he. The note intends onely,
that every man ought to doe according to his proportion, and not
say, I have done such a good worke to this poore man, therefore
I need do no more, I gave him bread when he was hungry, there¬
fore l need not or at least I am not bound to give him cloathing
for his nakednesse. If we can expresse our charity but once or
one way, that once and one way are accepted. But how often
or how many wayes soever we have expressed it, we are not ac¬
cepted, if we can, but will not expresse it any more. The widdow
(Lube 21. 42.) gave but two mites ( scarse enough to keepe a
man one day from starving, much lesse to provide a man dayly
food and cloathing) yet Christ saith, Shee hath cast in more then
thoy all, and che reason was, because shee had cast in her all. A

0483.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Book of Jo R. Verf.19

body.t: little from those who have little, is looked upon by God as a
great deale; But doe not thinke it enough to doe a little, when
you have ability to doe much; Charge them that be rich ( saith
the Apostle, 1 Tim. 6. 18.) that they doe good, and to shew that
it is not enough for them to doe a litt le Good, he adds, that they
be rich in good worbes, ready to distribute, milling te communicate.
Doe not discharge your felves you that are rich from doing
againe, because you have once done, say not you need not
cloath the naked, because you have fed the hungry; They who
thinbe they have done eneugh, loose the thankes of all they have done.
For as the Apostle (2 Pet. 1. 6, 7.) speakes of adding one grace
to another, to vertue knomledge, and to knowledge patience, and to
patience brotherly kindnesse, and to brotherly kindnesse charitie.
Now (I say) as we are to adde the acts of severall graces, so se¬
verall acts of the same grace together, as you must add to your
vertue charity, so yon must add charity to charity; one way of
charity to another, and one worke of charity to another in the
same way. Charity to men is the Lords worke, both because the
Lord workes it in us, and because the Lord commands us that
worke. Now we must be ( as the Apostle exhorts, 1 Cor. 15.
58.) Stedfast and unmoveable, almayes abounding in the worke ef
the Lord. To doe this worke of the Lord a little, is farre from a¬
bounding in it, and to doe it once or tuice, is as farre from doing
it alwayes. We never abound in any worke of the Lord, if we set
our selves any other bounds in doing it, then the Lord hath set us.
The bounds which the Lord hath set us are only these two, First,
as we have opportunity ( Gal. 6. 10.) Secondly, as we have a¬
bility (2 Cor. 16. 2.) We must alwayes relieve the wants of o¬
thers as we are able, and sometimes (as it was with the Churches
of Macedonia, 2 Cor. 8. 2, 3. ) above what we are able.
Fourthly, Tob doth not say, if I have seene this or that man
perish, or this or that man without covering, but, if I have seene
any perisp, any without covering: As he was exercised in all sorts
of charity, so his charity uss exercised towards all sorts of per¬
sons; As he did not excuse himselfe from clothing the naked, be¬
cause he fed the hungry; so he did not excuse himselfe from feed¬
ing and clothing this poore and naked man, because he had fed
and clothed that or another. "Tis our duty ( so farre as we are
able) not to sce any want, not to see any perish for cold or hun¬

0484.head: Chap. 31. An Expositiou upon the Boske ef IOB. Verf. 20.

body.t: per, both good and bad must be kept alive; we must act the grace
of charity toward them who have not the grace of faith. The
Scripture is plaine, (Gal. 6. 10.) As me have opportunity. Iet us
doe good to all, especially unto them nho are of the houspold f faitb
We must put a difference between men upon whom ue bestox
our charit y, but we must not restraine it from any men, let them
be what they will, they must have reliefe as men; Though they
differ from us in religion, yea though they are irreligious, yet
somewhat must be done for them if they are in vant. Though all
men have not the renewed image of God, yet all men, even the
worst of men, have somewhat of his image. Though all men have
not received Grace, yet all have received the same common na¬
ture. Againe, we must doe to others as we would they should
doe tous. There is no godly man who if he should fall into ex¬
treame distresse, but would be glad to receave helpe and reliefe,
though at the hand of a wicked man, and therefore the Godly
ought to doe good to the wicked in their distresse. Beside, the
hardning of our hearts against them that are wicked, may harden
them in their wickednesse, and bring a scandal upon the professi¬
on of religion. God himselfe hath given us his owne eximple to
doe so (Math. 5. 44, 45.) Doe good to them that hate you, that ye
may be the children of your father in heaven (that is, that you may
evidence and declare your selves to be so) for he maketh his Sun to
rise on the evill and on the good, and sendeth raine on the just and on
the unjust. Holy Job was of this Gospel Spirit, though he lived
long before the hight of Gospel times; he would not see any pe¬
rish for want of cloathing, nor any poore without covering.
Charity is never compleate, nor full handed till we dee all acts ef
Charity, and act charity unto all, in one degree or other; If I have
seene any perisb for mant ef cleathing, &c.
Vers. 20. If his loynes bave not blessed mee, if he mere not war¬
med with the flecce of my shcepe.
To blesse, as mans act, is to wish or pray for a blessing. Man
cannot blesse man but by wishing him well, or praying for a bles¬
sing upon him. “Tis God who blesseth man by bestowing a bles¬
sing upon him; if he doe but pronounce a blessing upon us, we
are certainly blessed. Man sometime blesseth those whom God
abhorreth (Psal. 10. 3.) and often abhorreth those whom God

0485.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition upon the Booke ef JOR. Verf 20,

body.t: blesseth. To blesse unerringly and effectually is only in the power,
or’tis the prerogative of God alone.
But why is it said here, if his laynes have not blessed mee? Are
our loynes the instruments of blessing? I answer,
Ficst, Some take the words figuratively, as if Job had sayd,
If there had been a tongue in the poore mans loynes, had his
loynes been vocall, he would have spoken a blessing with his
loynes We find frequently in Scripture speech ascribed to speech¬
lesse things, to things which have no pouer of speaking. Thus
Christ rebukes the envious importunity of the Pharisees for the
silencing of his Disciples, who cryed Hosannah, blessed be the
King that cometh in the name of the Lord ( Luke 19. 40.) I tell
rou that if these spould hold their peace, the stones mould imme¬
diately cry out.
Secondly, Rather the loynes are here put fynechdochically
for the person, if his loynes have not blessed mee, that is, if the
poore whose loynes l covered have not blessed me. Tis ufuall in
Scripture to put a part for the whole, and a member most con¬
cerned for the man. Here Job represents the poore mans acknow¬
ledgement or thanks, because his loynes were clothed and war¬
med with the fleece of his sheepe.
Thirdly, Which further heightens the sence, when Job saith,
If his loynes have not blessed mee: It may imply the strong, hear¬
ty, and affectionate defires of the poore for a blessing upon Tob;
as if he had sayd, the poore man blessed mee with all his might,
and strength. The strength of a man ( as it is said of Behemath,
tob 40.16.) is in his loynes. And therefore as a man is said to
doe that with his heart which he doth very sincerely, or to doe
that with his soule which he doth very affectionately; So a man
is said to doe that with his loynes wherein hee puts forth his
strength to the utmost. The loynes are the seate of strength;
and hénce among the Latines, a weake man is thus expressed,
man without loynes. And in Scripture to have our loynes
girt, is to doe a thing with readinesse and with all our might
(Luke 12. 35.) so here, if his loynes did not blesse me; as, if he did
not blesse mee feelingly and ftrongly.
Fourthly, (If his loynes have not blessed mie) may signifie, that
Jobς worke of charity in clothing the naked, did it selfe ( as iz
vere) speake for, or bespeahe a bleffing at the hand of Cod for

0486.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Bok d JOR. Verl 20.

body.t: him. As the blood of Abel is sayd to cry to the Lord for a curse
or for vengeance upon his brother Cain ( murder is so foule and
so unnaturall a worke, that though none complaine of it, yet it
will cry out of it selfe) So every act of charity hath a tongue in
it, and cryeth to God for a blessing upon the charitable. The
warmth which we give to the loynes of the naked, and the re¬
freshing which we give to the bowels of the hungry, these very
acts of love and compassion, pray or cry to God for good to us,
though men say nothing of us. This is both a spirituall and an
incouraging sence of the text, If his loynes have not blessed mee.
Hence note. First.
It ù the duty of those nho are relieved, to prar for and nisb a
blessing apon them mho are the Instruments of their reliefe.
Job speakes here not only the practice, but the duty of the
poore, and tells us as much what they ought to doe, as what they
did. From whom soever we receive good, to them we owe ( at
least) thankes, and good wishes. The Gospel teacheth us to pray
for those who despitefully use us and persecute us; how much
more should we pray for those who use us kindly, and provide for
us? The Gospel bids blesse those who curse us, how much more
should ve blesse those who blesse us, or are a blessing to us ? An
unthankfull receiver renders himselfe altogether unworthy of
what he hath already received, much more to receive any more;
our loynes should blesse him that hath covered them, and our
bowells those who have refreshed them. And if so, O how should
our loynes blesse God who hath warmed and refreshed both
loynes and bowells uith so many blessings! how should wee
trumpet forth his praises who loadeth us uith his benefits dayly!
if a poore man ought to blesse his benefactor for any morsel of
bread to stay his hunger, for any cast garment to cover his na¬
kednesse; what should we doe, who receive all our bread, all our
Clothing, all our Comforts, all our graces from the hand of God!
How should we blesse Jesus Christ, who satisfyeth the hunger of
our foules with his owne flesh, who cloathes and warmes our
loynes, with that Golden flecce of his oune everlasting righte¬
ousnesse!
Secondiy, Observe.

0487.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition upon the Booke of JO2. Verf.20.

body.t: If they mho have rectived good by us will not le thanbfull, ibe
very good which ihey have received, mill thanke yea commend
and praise us.
If we doe good, we cannot lose our thanks for it, though no
man thanke us. As the very doing of Good is a reward to it selfe;
so it selfe uill one way or other procure us a reward. Who would
not be alwayes doing good, seeing we are assured that the good
we doe, will doe us more good then those to or for whom we
doe it. If the poore whom we have fed will not blesse us, yet
their hungry bellyes will, if the naked whom we have clothed
doe not blesse us, yet their warmed loynes will blesse us, whether
they will or no. That good which we have done will blesse us.
though they doe not to whom we have done it. Let us not bt
meary in mel-doing ( saith the Apostle, Gal. 6. 9.) for in due sea¬
son ve shall reape if me faint not. Is man ungratefull to us? will he
nor give us so much as a good word, for whom we have done
much good? yet while he carrieth his belly and his loynes about
him, they will blesse us. No sooner is that description of a vertu¬
ous woman and of her vertuous workes concluded, but present ly
followes (Pro. 31. 31.) Give her of the fruit of her hands, and let
her on ne worbes praise her in the gate. Suppose fhe hath no Ora¬
tor to praise her there, yet her workes will praise her; vertuous
actions are the most eloquent Orators. They speake best mho dot
best. And as our good works will praise, commend, and blesse us
when men doe not; so our evill workes or our neglect of good
workes will dispraise and complaine of us when men doe not;
though the poore who aske food and rayment of us and have
been denyed, doe not cry against us, nor vish a curse upon us,
yet their naked loynes and hungry bellyes will. It is said (Hab.2.
11.) concerning houses built by violence and oppression ( many
have raysed their own houses upon the ruine of others) The stone
spall cry oat of the wall, and the beam out of the timber shall an¬
swer it; As if the Prophet had thus expressed it; All the materi¬
alls of the house from side to side, from roome to roome, from
the foundation to the roofe, shall agree in this dolefull song, we
were built by blood, and woe uill be the portion of our builder.
It may be a poore oppressed man knows not how nor where to
complain, yet the stones out of the wall know. Every worke doth

0488.head: Chap. 31. An Expofstion upon the Beoke of JoB. Verl. 20.

body.t: eyther curse or blesse us. The good or evill uhich ve doe, vill
speake good or evill of us. It is an extreame misery if our workes
are evill, though all men speake tell of us. And it is a great mer¬
cy if when no man speakes good of us, our workes are good.
That the loynes of the poore blesse us, may satisfie us when we
misse the blessing of their lips. If ( saith Tob) hùs loynes have not
blessed mee,
If he were not warmed mith the fleece ff my sbeipe.
Wee are not to take the fleece properly, as if Job wrapt a fleece
about the loynes of the poore, But, by his fleece, he meanes gar¬
ments made of his fleece; or cloath to be made up into gar¬
ments.
If be were not xarmid.
Ieb did not only give the poore man somewhat to cover his
nakednesse, or to hide his shame, but he gave him that u hich was
comfortable to him, that which was a defence against the wind
and weather; he mas warmed ( saith he) mith the fluece
of my heepe.
Not mith the fleece uhich I tooke from other mens fheepe.
Job was as honest as he was charitable. He cloathed the nakeq
with his owne fleece. The word here used for a fleece, signifies
any thing, that being cut is ready to grow againe; Tis applyed
in Scripture; First, to the mowne grasse; Secondly, to the shorne
fleece. Grasse is, as it were, the fleece of the earth, and wool is
the grasse of the sheepe. That Prophecy of Christ (Psal.72.6.)
which we translate, He shall come domne lihe raine upon the mewn
grasse; others translate, He shall come duvne lihe raine upon a
fiiece of wool. Yet, I conceive, the former version most proper in
the Psalme, because of the words which follow, and lihe shomers
upon the earth. But in Job the text restraines us to the latter sig¬
nification, A fleece of wool, uhich is the naturall matter of cloa¬
thing; If he mere not marme mith the flecce of my sheepe.
Hence note.
First, wee sould ģive tbe pogre nos only that mhich ù fer bare
necessity, bus ser tbeir cemfert.

0489.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Book ef JoB. Vers.20.

body.t: Jeb did not cloath the poore with sheep-skins when he had
taken the fleece off from them, but he cloathed them with the
flsece. God began the Clothing of man with matter of the lowest
rate ( Gen. 3. 21.) wit h Coats of skins; but God taught sob to
make the poore Coats, not with the skins of the sheepe but with.
the fleece. The people of God are described in their perlecuted
state ( Heb. 11. 37.) Wandering in Sheep-sins and Goat.skins.
Those Worthyes in the faith had much adoe to save their owne
skins, or (as Job speakes) to escape with the skin of their teeth
from the rage of cruel tyrants, and therefore glad of the bare
skins of beasts to cover or disguise their owne. Our charity is a
kind of persecution, if it puts the poor into no better a habit, then
per secution did those blessed Martyrs. I know good clothing may
