be made of skins wel wrought without the fleece; yet febs charity
giving the fleece not the bare skin to the poore for cloathing,
teacheth us to be somewhat liberal when we are charitable, and
to give the needy though not the best yet not the worst for their
reliefe.
Secondly, In that he saith, with the fleece of
my sheepe; note.
wue must be sure that mhat me give to the poore, mhether in food
or rayment, be of our omne.
Job gave them of his owne morfel to eate (v. 17.) and here of
the fleece of his owne fheepe to weare (Pro.3.9) Honour the
Lord with thy substance. We cannot honour the Lord in giving
that, which we have gotten by dishonouring rhe Lord, that is, by
transgressing the Commandement of the Lord. Doe you thinke
you can fulfill the law of love or Charity, by breaking the law of
Juflice or righteousnesse! Nathan speke a Parable of this import
to David, when he would Convince him of and reprove him for
his sin (2 Sam. 12.) He tells him of tuo men in one City, the
one rich and the other poore, &c. and there came a traveller to
the rich man, to whom indeed he gaye,'tis like, free welcome and
entertainment, but at whose cost ? he had store of his own; But
( saith Nathan, v. 4.) he spared to take of his omne flock, and of his
omne herd to dregse for the mayfaring man that was come unto him,
but tecke the poore mans lambe and dressed it for him that was come
to him. He was hospitable at his neighbours charge. David was

0490.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Bock of IO R. Verl. 21.

body.t: so scandal 2’d at this parabolical history, that his anger was great¬
Iy kindled, and presently swore a sentence of death against the
man that had so done. And surely if David uas so offended with
that mant hospitality, God will not be pleased with those mens
charity, who give reliese out of that which they have wrongfully
gotten. To feed the hungry and cloath the naked at other mens
cost, is not to honour God but to mocke him. Tis a great wick¬
ednesse to doe Injustice that we may doe acts of charity: And
when men have deserved the curse of many by griping, then to
hope for the blessing of some by giving. Wee must not be chari¬
table with other mens flecces, nor fleece others ( as we say ) that
wee may be charitable. Shall we furnish our selves by cruelty
to performe workes of pity? and when wee have fleeced others
by harsh, rigid, extorting courses, shall we then hope to make a¬
mends for all, by sending a part of our fleece to the poore? How
unacceptable shall I say, or rather how abominable is this chari¬
ty to God! Take heed of cloathing any by making others naked;
Give not that bread to the poore, which you have unduly gained
though from the rich. What is wrongfully gotten must be resto¬
red; and if we can neyther find those whom we have wronged,
nor their heyres to restore it to, then the poor are their heyres, as
was shewed at the 18th verse of the 2oth Chap.And what (in that
case) you give the poore, must not be given to them as an Almes,
but as their dues; not at all, in a way of charity, but of Justice.
Or not as that which you have a liberty to give, but as that
which you have no liberty to keepe. Looke then that the fleece
which warmes the loynes of the poore man comes from the
backe of your owne sheepe. See how Exact this holy man uas
in all his wayes; he gave all manner of charity, and he gave to
all, and it was pure charity, he gave his owne. To cleare which
yet further, fob having thus protested for his charity to the poore,
protests against all manner of injustice towards the poore.
Vers.21. If Ihave lifted up my hand against the fatherlesse,
xhen I sam my helpe in the gate.
To lift up the hand in Scripture is taken sometimes in a good,
and sometimes in an evill sence; there is a lifting up of the hand
for; and there is a lifting up of the hand against.
More distinctiy, First, in a good sence; To list up the hand is

0491.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon ihe Bok of Jo B. Verl.21.

body.t: a gesture of praying, or of praise; I wil ( saith the Apostle) that
men pray every mhere, lifting up pure hands (1 Tim. 2. 8.) Prayer
in the essence of it is a lifting up of the heart to God, and in sig¬
nification of that’cis accompanied wich the lifting up of the hand
to God. Secondly, to lift up the hand, is a gesture of swearing,
or taking a sacred oath. Thus Abram answered the King of So¬
dom when he offered him the spoyles ( Gen. 14. 22.) I have lif¬
ted up my hand io the most high Ged (that is I have sworne) that
I will not take &c. And thus the Lords lifting up his hand is his
swearing (Ezck. 20.5.) Tous saith the Lord God, in the day when
I chose Israel, and lifted up my hand (or suare, as we put in the
Margin ) unto the seed of the house of Jacob &c. Thirdly, it is a
gesture importing readines, and speciall intention in doing a thing
( Psal. 119.48.) Ay hands (saith David) also will I list upto
thy Commandements; as a man that is willing to doe a thing, and
addresseth himselfe to the doing of it, lifts up his hand; so a God¬
Iy man is described listing up his hand to fulfill and obey the
Commands of God. Fourthly, lifting up of the hand is a gesture
intimating our desire to call or invite another to come to us, or
doe somewhat for us ( Isa. 49. 22.) Thus saith the Lord, behold
I mill lift up my hands to the Gentiles; that is, I will call them
into the fellowship of the Church, and admit them into the
Common wealth of Israel who have all this while been aliens
fromit.
Againe, To lift up the hand is taken in a bad sence; And so it
must be understood here, as that addition necessitatęs it, against
the fatherlesse. Thus to lift up the hand against any’one, notes,
First, a present purpose to hurt or vexe. Secondly, it signifies a
menace or threat; Tis ordinary to shake or lift up the hand at
those uith uhom we are much displeased. Thirdly, it notes actu¬
all rebellion and opposition, or revenge (2 Sam. 20.21.) A
man of mount Ephraim, Sheba by name, the son ef Bichri hath lift
up his hand against the King, even against David: that is, he hath
done wickedly against David, or set himselfe against David, to
rayse sedition and ruine him. We may expound it in any of or in
all these three notions, as used by Job; If I have lift up my hand
against the fatherlesse; that is, if I have done any thing that beares
the signification of an ill intendment, or of a threatning against
the fatherlesse, much more if l have nsed any violence against the

0492.head: Chap. 31. An Expofition upon the Bocke ef JOB. Vers.21.

body.t: fatherlesse, to oppresse him in his right, then &c. Some expound
that of the Prophet (Isa. 58. 9.) If thon take away frem the miast
of thec the putting forth of the finger, and speabing vanity, as a
threatning both by word and gesture, and so in tendency to smit¬
ing with the fist of mickednesse, of wbich the Prophet spaxe at the
fourth verse foregoing. It seemes the Jewes were wont to deale ri¬
goroessy in urging the Law upon their debtors, much more upon
suppose malefactors, even to violence and striking. So they dealt
with Christ (Math. 26. 67.) Then did they spit in his face and
buffeted him, and others smote him mith the palmes of their handi.
Which uncivill usage he doubtlesse receaved eyther by the com¬
mand, or at least by the connivence of those in power; And so’tis
sayd expressely of the High Priest Ananias, that he Commanded
them that stood by Paul to smite him on the moutb (Acts 23. 2.)
Against all these rigorus courses Job protests while he saith, If I
bave lifted up my hand against the fatherlesse: As if he had sayd,
I have neyther threatned, nor have I actually vexed the poore
and fatherlesse, I have neyther given a signe or intimation to o
thers, by lifting up my hand to afflict them, nor have I done it my
selfe. I conceave also we may thus take it in a way of diminution,
as denying the least hurt, or appearance of hurt to the father-
lesse; As if he had sayd, I have been so farre from oppressing
them, or laying my whole weight upon them, that I have not so
much as lifted up my hand against them, or touched them with a
little finger. The Pharisees (as Christ chargeth them in the GO-
fpel) layd heavy burdens upon others, which themselves would
not touch so much as with a little finger; Job was so tender-
hearted and compassionate, that he would not lift up bis hand,
no nor wrongfully lay the weight of his little finger upon the fa¬
therlesse.
Lastly, Because they were wont in Ancient times ( and ’tis a
use in these times) to give their vote by lifting up the hand when
matters came to the question, therefore some interpret these
words; If I have lifted up my hand against the fatherlesse, as a de-
niall that he had given his suffrage or voyce against them Accor-
ding to all these interpretations, especially the two last, Tob re-
pells and denyes that Charge of harshnes and ill dealing with the
poore to the utmost; He had neyther heart nor voyce, neyther
hand nor tongue to doe them wrong, eyther by himselse or by the

0493.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition upon the Books ef JOR. Vers.21.

body.t: agency of others. If I have lift up my hand against the Father¬
lesse,
W'hen I sam my helpe in the gati.
Job puts this as a speciall note of his Integrity; the vulgar La¬
tine renders very significantly, Even nhen I sam my selfe of grea¬
test power in the gate. By the Gate here understand (as osten be¬
fore) the place of Judgement, which according to the manner of
the Jewes, as also of other Nations, was wont to be in the gate
of the Citie: Now, saith Job, I have not oppressed or crushed
the fatherlesse, when sitting in the place of Judicature, I saw all
that were about me ready to assist me, and take part with me in
any matter, if I had but desired it. I had authority enough in my
oun hand to order what I would have done, & I had the strength
of hands enow to execute my orders; none durst oppose or con¬
tradict mee, the Judges themselves would have complyed with
me, had they feene me inclining to such a Judgement : yet though
I had all these advantages on my fide, I have not made use of them
to the wrong of the poorest orphan; If Ihave lifted up my hand
against the fatherlesse; Thus fob seemes to say, Imight have bad
xhat I meuld, if Ihad but lift up my hand I could have done what
I list, and none on earth could binder me, no man durst Complaine?
or if any had, hom would he have mended himselse? tbe Judges were
for mee, I had helpe in the gate; If I had trampled upon my opposers,
and thrust their cause out of the Court, they had been as, to mee, re¬
midilesse, though I bad not been guiltlesse; but Ihave not onty fer¬
borne, but from my very heart abborr'd to doe such unworthy things.
This surely was his sence or to this effect, when he sayd, If I have
lift up my hand against uhe fatherlisse, nhen I saw my hespe in ibe
gate.
Hence note.
First, To dœ any thing mhich hathin it but a sadon of oppres¬
sing the poore is very sinfull.
The putting forth of the finger, the lifting up of the hand, a
signification of our consent to afflict the fatherlesse, is an high
offence, both against God the righteous Judge, and against man,
whose right is overthrowne. The rule is expresse (1 Thes.5.22.)
Abstaine from all appearance of euil.

0494.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon thi Bok of JOE. Verl. 21.

body.t: Secondly, Observe.
To have poner in eur hands to dee mrong, is a great temptation
to doe it.
He that hath ability to opprefse, seldome wants opportunity
to doe it, and ’tis more seldome that he wants a minde to doe it.
Laban told Jacob (Gen. 31. 29.) It is in the pomer cf my hand to
doe thet hurt; He could have crushed Jacob, and, what hinder'd
him? Surely not a principle of love to righteousness, nor a holy
feare of wronging him, but a divine rebuke (as himselfe acknow¬
ledged in the same verse) the God of your fathers spake unto mee
yester-nigbt, saying, take thon heed that thou speake not to Jacob
eyther good or bad. facob also told him as much (v.42.) God hath
seene mine affliction, and the labour of mine hands, and rebuked thee
yester-nigbt. As if he had sayd, unlesse God had stopt and checkt
thy power from doing me a mischiefe, thy owne heart, thy con¬
science had not. Solomon adviseth (Pro. 3. 28.) Say not unto
thy neighbour, goe, and come againe, and to morrow I will give thee,
mben thou hast it by thee; that is, when it is in the power of thy
hand to doe it. As we have all need to be excited to doe good,
though we have power in our hands to doe it; So when many
have power in their hands to doe hurt, they can hardly be dis¬
suaded or kept off from doing it. That ue have a pouer to doe
good, doth scarce tempt or stirre us to doe it: but the very ha¬
ving a pouer to doe evill, tempts us as often as the occasions of it
are presented to us. Nothing hinders some from doing evill, but
the want of worldly power; O what a world of evill would these
doe, if they had power! And the best of men, the greatest lovers
of righteousnesse find worke enough sometimes uith their owne
hearts to keepe cleare from acts of unrighteousnesse when power
and occasion, joyning with their owne Interest, meete together.
Hence note. Thirdly.
It is an argument of much grace, not to dot evill when me have
power and opportunity in our hands to doe it.
That man gives a strong testimony of his owne Integrity, who
hath not a heart to doe that evill which the power in his hand
enables him to doe. It cannot be denyed, but our refusall to doe
any evill which we have humane helpe enough to doe, fhexes the

0495.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition apon thi Booke of JOR. Veri.21.

body.t: prevalency of divine helpe. Then Grace is mighty in us, or as the
Apostle speakes ( Col. 1. 29.) morbetb in us mightily, when we
are weake as to those sinfull workes, for which we have the grea¬
test eyther natural or civill power. Paul could say (2 Cor. 13 8.)
I can dee nothing against the truth, but for the truth. Paul could
have set his wits against the truth, and plaid the Sophister as well
as any other man; but he had no heart to doe any thing against
the truth. This is an infallible argument, not only of the truth
but of the strength of grace (2 John 3. 9.) He that is borne of Gid
cannot sin (why not ?) not because he hath not a naturall power,
not because he hath no civill power, not because he hath no cor¬
tuption suiting sin, not because he hath no temptation provoking
him to sin, not because he alwayes wants opportunity to sin; He
that is born of God, hath most of these advantages to sin always,
and he sometimes hath all of them, so that, none of these are the
proper reasons why he cannot commit sin. The true reason is, be¬
cause his heart is turned and set another way, or because (as that
Scripture expresseth the reason) the seed of God remaineth in him.
When a Godly man hath as much power and opportunity as o¬
thers to sin, yet he doth not sin as others, because the power of
grace not only restrains and supercedes, but changeth and altereth
the pouers of Nature. We should alwayes doc the same things, if
ue were alwayes the same men. We fhould all do alike, if we were
all alike. How glorious is that grace of God in man, which gives
him a power not to sin, how much soever it is in his power to
sin: And still the glory of that grace is the greater in keeping us
from sinning, by how much our power to sin is greater for a
Magistrate who seeth (as Job did ) his helpe in the gate to afflict
the fatherlesse, or subvert any man in his cause, and yet not to
lift up a hand or a finger, not to contribute the least appearance
of his power to doe it, but (as doubtlesse Job also did ) to contri.
bute all his power against it, This is Justice in Triumph.
Further, For as much as Tob saith, that he saw his helpe in the
gate.
Observe.
Men in great power and place cannot want helpe to carry
tboron the mest unjust and oppressive actions, if they doe but
desire it.
When¬

0496.head: Chap. 31. Aa Exposition upon the Becke of JoR. Verl. 21.

body.t: When fezabel the Queene had a minde to murder Naboath,
shee saw her helpe in the gate, shee wanted neyther false wit¬
nesses to accuse him, nor ignorant or unrighteous Judges to con¬
demne him. When Abshalom was resolved to slay his Brother
Amnon, he did but make his minde knoune, and he Fad helpe
enough. How many have been thus encouraged to adventure in
a bad cause; O, say they, we see our helpe in the gate; tis but bri¬
bing such a one, and the match will be quickly made up a present
will winne such a mans heart, and he will winne us tuo or three
more and we have a way to get a fourth, and if we get but a fifth
or a sixth, we shall carry it against all the world; let our cause
be what it will, we see our helpe in the gate. Thus Judgement is
bought and sould uithout respect eyther to honour or to hone¬
sty. There hath been such Corruption in all ages, it were indeed
the glory of our age if no such corruption vere to be found a¬
mong us. But are there not some whose office it is to relieve the
oppressed, who have lent a helping hand to their oppressors?
The fatherlesse rarely find helpe in the gate, but they uho lift up
their hand against the fatherlesse, finde too much helpe there.
How sad is it when they that should helpe the fatherlesse in the
gate, see the fatherlesse trod under-foot in the gate, and give
them no helpe! woe to those who helpe the mighty against the
weake in a wrong cause, or who vill not helpe the weake against
the mighty in a right cause. How shall such stand before the just
God in the gate of the great Judgement, who have overthrowne
the cause of the poore in the gate unjustly, especially consider¬
ing how ost their ears have been beaten with these admonitions,
and in what light they live.
Fifthly, note.
Righieouus Aagistrates will not use ibeir pomer to oppresse otbers,
bow much opportunitie and aduantage soever they have to dee
ii, ibough they see their helpe in the gate.
A righteous Magistrate knowes, that he only can doe that mhich
he can lanfully or rightly do.As the Law gives him no power, so he
is convinced, that he hath no pouer beyond, much lesse against
the Law; and therefore concludes, I can doe no more then
ought to doe; He had rather be accounted weaxe then unjust, and
impotent then oppressive, yea he counts this his ftrength and
Lastiy,
power, not to oppresse, not to be unjuft.

0497.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Bok ef JOB. Vers.21.

body.t: Lastly, In that Job would not lift up his hand against the fa¬
therlesse, when he saw his helpe in the gate.
Note.
Mex in powir soould not satufie ibemfelves xith wbas xill
passe among, or be countenanced by men, but consider mhat ue
right in it selfe, mhat is right in the sight of God, and that they
are in the fight of Ged.
A bad bufinesse may passe very well among men, and we may
have Advocates who uill answer for us, and stop the mouthes of
all gaine sayers; But can they stop the mouth of conscience?
can they blinde the eyes of God, or impose upon him? God is the
Judge of all the earth, and he will at last sit in Judgement upon
all the Judges of the earth; Now, as Moses pleaded with God
about his threatned and intended Judgement upon Sodome (Gen.
18 25.) Shall not the judge of all the earth doe right? Doubt¬
lesse he will, chough all the ludges of the earth should do wrong.
And as he will doe them right, whom the Judges of the earth
have wrong’d, so he will pronounce a righteous Judgement upon
all unrighteous Judges. The Judgement of God will be very
terrible upon those who have done any thing ( and not repented
of it) against the Law; but his Judgement will be most terrible
upon those who have Judged against the Law, and eyther for
feare or favour, for the satisfying of their covetousnes or revenge
have perverted Justice, and overthrowne the righteous cause of
the poore and fatherlesse in the gate. Jehoshaphat sayd to his
Iudges (2 Chron. 19.6.) Take heed what ye doe, for ye Judge not
for man, but for the Lord, that is, ye doe not so much fill my place
who am your King, as Gods place who is King of Kings. How
severely therefore will the Lord proceed with unrighteous Jud¬
ges, sceing, as much as in them lyes, they make or render God
himselfe an unrighteous Judge?
Therefore to shut up this poynt, let men in power dili¬
gently attend the end for which they have receaved their
power, and then they will not eafily goe out of their way
in the exercise of it. Surely what the Apostle asserts concer¬
ning the end of that power which the then Apostles did re¬
ceive, and all the Ministers of the Gospel since, in their ca¬
pacity, have receaved (1 Cor. 13. 8) is true in the Gene¬

0498.head: Chap.31. An Exposition apou the Book of JO R. Verl. 21.

body.t: rall concerning the end or scope of all Magistraticall power,
it is for edification, and not for destruction. Magistrates should
more attend building then pulling doune, and be more in pro¬
tection then punishment. Magistrates are sayd to beare the sword,
not to be swords, and they are sayd io be Shields (Psal. 47. 9.
not to beare Shields; And all to shew that protection and pre¬
servation are more essentiall and intrinsecall to their office then
destruction and punishment are. Protection is the most proper
worke of Magistrates. Indeed destruction is their worke too,
but that is a by-worke, that comes in a way of consequence, as it
doth also in the Ministers worke. The word is the savour of death
as well as the savour of life; but that which is or should be chiefty
aimed at in both these great Ordinances of Magistracy and Mini¬
stry, is Edification and Protection, not destruction: and if at any
time destruction, yet only the destruction of the wicked, and evill
doers, yea only of wickednes and evill deeds. What shall wee say
then eyther of or to those Magistrates, who in the exercise of
their power ayme at destruction rather then at protection, yea at
the destruction of the poore and fatherlesse, rather then of the
proud and mercilesse. Is There any honour in such a victory?
Let all who are invested with a lawfull power, take heed they ose
it lawfully. The worst use power can be put to, is the oppression
of the poore, and the bearing up a bad cause. These were the ab¬
horrence of fobs soule; If I have lift up my hand against the fa¬
tberlesse, mhen I sam my helpe in the gate.

0499.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition upon thi Bock of Jo ». Verf. 22.

body.t: Then let mine arme fall from my shoulder-blade, and
mine arme be brohen from the bone.
For destruction from God mas a terrour to me: and
by reason of his highnesse I could not endure.
N the former verse Job earnestly protested his integrity, yea,
I and his tendernesse touard the poore, and fatherlesse, even
when he had the fairest opportunity to crush, and oppresse them;
when he saw his helpe in the gate.
He now bindes that protestation by a solemne and sacred im¬
precation, calling downe a dreadfull Judgement upon himselse if
it were not so. I have met with matter of this nature more then
once before; Job imprecating vengeance upon his own head, to
assure the truth of uhat he had protested. How, and in what ca¬
ses imprecations may be made, hath there been shewed. And,
therefore I shall not stay upon it here, but only a little open the
matter of this imprecation.
Vers. 22. Then let mine arme fall from my soulder- blade, &c.
The Hebrew is, Let mine arme fall from my shoulder. The word
rendred shoulder-blade, notes all that breadth of the body, from
the neck to both the armes. And ’tis used metaphorically by the
Prophet ( Zeph. 3. 9) to expresse that onenes of heart and spi¬
rit, which shall be among the people of God in the latter dayes;
Then will I turne to the people a pure language, that they may call
upan the Name of the Lerd, to serve him with one consent, or, with
one sboulder (as we put it in the Margin) Which is an allusion ey¬
ther to oxen drawing unitedly and at once in the same yoake, or
to severall men unanimously joyning their strength to beare the
same burden. “Tis translated back, (Psal.21.12.) Therefore shalt
thou make them to turne their backe, or their shoulder; we put in
the Margin, Thou sualt set them as a Butt, when thou shalt make
ready thine arrows upon thy strings, against the face of them; wee
render clearely to the scope of this place in Job, as well as the
ience of the word, The shonlder, or the shoulder-blade; the next
And
clause is of the same sence.

0500.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition upon the Booke ef JOB. Verf.22.

body.t: And let mine arme be broken frou the bone, or, from the chan¬
nell bont.
The word signifieth a reed or a cane, as also a speare, which is
long and slender like a reed, The bone in the arme reaching from
the shoulder to the elbow, or rather to the hand-wrist, resembles
also a cane, both as to the length and hollownes of it, Let mine
arme be broken from the bone.
This imprecation may be considered, eyther with reference to
all that tob spake in the former Context, or more particularly,
to the 21th verse, to which’tis most sutable, hitting the poynt
sully, according to the Law of retaliation; If mine hand ( saith
he ) hath been lifted up against the fatherlesse, then let mine arme
fall from my shoulder-blade; As if he had sayd, let God punish me
in that very member and part, vhich may most evidently poynt
out my sin. Let him even write my sin upon my judgement;
which cannot be done more visibly, then when a man who hath
un uniy litt up his hand against the fatherlesse, feeles his arme fal¬
ling off from his shoulder-blade. Let mine arme fall from my
shoulder blade, &c. Hence ( passing by the doctrine of impreca¬
tions before hand led) we may observe.
First, The losse of an arme or limb of the body, is a grievous l'sse.
God hath so compacted and built up this house of clay, mans
body, he hath put it in-to such an exquisite frame, that if any one
member be wanting, or but out of order, the whole is disabled,
if any one member be lost, it is a losse to the whole body. The
Apostle treating of that spirituall body or corporation, the
Church (1 Cor. 12. 26. ) shewes what a sympethy there is or
ought to be among the members, and that in the suffering of any
one of them, they all suffer, the whole spirituall body suffers in
one member, even as the naturall body doth The eye sees for the
whole body, and the eare heares for the whole body, and the
hand workes for the whole body; and therefore the losse of any
one member is a great losse, because ’tis both the paine and losse
of the whole body. And if so, Then
First, Let us be sensible of their ffliction, who saffer the losse
of a limb or bodyly member.
Secondly, Let those be thankfull who injoy the usc and bene¬

0501.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition upon the Booke ef JOR. Verl.22.

body.t: fit of all their bodyly members; a man that uants the use of his
arme, oh how thankfull would he be, to have it restored againe?
yet while we enjoy the use and service of all our bodyly mem¬
bers, we seldome take notice of the mercy, or are truely thank¬
full for it.
Thirdly, Let us be admonisht, to imploy every part, and mem¬
ber of the body well let us use our hands, our feete, our eyes,
our tongues to the honour of God. That’s the Apostles advice
(1 Cor.6. 20.) Te are bought mith a price, therefore glor fit God in
your body, and in your spirit, mhich are Gods. God hatn a title, a
right to the service of both, not only by creation, because he made
them, but by redẽption, because he hath bought or payd for them.
Let all our bones honour the Lord, as David resolved his should
(Psal. 35. 10.) All my bones shall say, Lord who is libe unto thee?
Those bones which God hath compacted, and joyned together
in that admirable structure of the body, should joyn in his praise,
and all the members of the body shoula be yeelded as instrument:
of riphteousnesse unto God (Rom. 6.13.) Take heed of abusing
so much as a little finger, doe not give up a hayre of your head
to the service of sinne, for it is the Lords; let us take heed of
mis-imploy ing our bodyly members, lest we provoke God to de¬
ny us the comfortable use of them. For,
Secondly, Note.
Ie ù jost, that they who abuse the members of their body, to the
hurt of man, or the dishonour of God, sould lose the use of
them-.
He that lifts up his hand unrighteously, forfeits the use of it,
and God hath sometime taken the forfeiture. Wee take a knife
out of a childs hand, when we see he doth hurt with it; much
more a sword out of a mad-mans hand, who is bent ro doe hurt
with it. Surely as we take artificiall instruments of hurt out of
their hands who abuse them, so God may justly take away the
use of any naturall instrument which ve abufe. Thus the Justice
of God over-tooke Jeroboam (1 Kings 12. 4.) who when he list
up his hand against the Prophet that prophesied against his Ido¬
latrous Altar, presently his hand withered, and he was not
able to draw it in, or to bring it back, till the Prophet prayed for
the restoring ofit. God can quickly wither a hand or an arme

0502.head: Chap.31 An Exposttion upou the Book of JOR. Verl, 23.

body.t: that is stretcht out to doe mischiefe. "Tis a righteous thing for
God to smite an abused eye with blindnesse, to smite an abused
eare with deafenesse, an abused arme with lamenesse, and an abu¬
sed tongue with an inability of speaking. “Tis fit that should be
destroyed which perverts the end for which it was made; and an
equall thing, that God should recall his favours when we fight
against him, or act crosse to our duty with them.
Iob having given us an assurance of his integrity, by impreca¬
ting this penal evill upon himselfe, proceeds to give us a rationall
account of it, or to shew us what it was, that stopt him from act¬
ing that sinfull evill of oppressing the poore, the fatherlesse, and
the widdow.
Vers.23. For destruction from God mas a terrour to me: and
by reason of his highnesse I could not endure.
The word rendred destruction, signifies properly any noy¬
some killing vapour; Such are the wrathfull dispeesations of God
to man: As if he had sayd, I was not afraid of any trouble, or de¬
struction from men, but destruction from God was a terrour to
mee.
The vulgar Latine translates wel to the sence, though wide
from the letter of the text, For I alwayes feared God as the maves
of a raging and tamultuous Sea, ready to over-mhelme me; As if he
had sayd, I saw a Sea of wrath, into which I should plunge my
selfe, by such unrighteous actings. Such visions or appreher sions
of an Angry God, to see him as a raging Sea ready to su allowus
up, or as a consuming fire to devoure us when we sin, ate great ef¬
fects of a lively and working taith. But l fhall not stay upon that
version, because ’tis rather Rhetoricall then literall.
Mr. Broughton renders, The Omnipotents feared noe held me;
that is, it tooke hold of me, and withheld me from oppressing
wayes.
We say, Destruction from God; Some more close to the Gram¬
maticall strict nes of the text: Destruction of God, where the Geni-
tive case notes the fficient cause, not the subject of destruction,
that is, first, such destruction as God uses to send upon oppres-
sors, or secondiy, such deftruction as eminently and evident ly
declares the power of God, and that God is the author of it,
was (saith fob) a vterror ro me, I by faith did apprehend that

0503.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Books of JOR. Verl.23.

body.t: destruction which God in his word threatneth sinners, especially
oppressors with, as if I had already felt it. Destruction from God
mas as a terror te me.
There is a tuo-fold terror; First, that which doth arise from
a meere slavish feare of God as a Judge or avenger; Secondly,
there is a terror, which ariseth from a child like feare, at once
looking upon God as a father, and as a righteous Judge. This
terror was upon sob; He knew that ( though a sonne, though a
Child) if he should take liberty to breake the bonds of duty,
and transg esse the Law of God, he should smart for it; bis fa¬
ther would not be a cockering, or an indulgent father to him,
but he should feele the smart of his rod and feele it the more, by
how much he was the neerer to him. Thus the Lord told his
owne people (Amos3 2.) Teu only have I knoune of all the fa¬
milyes of the earth, therefore I mill punish you for all your iniqui¬
ties. Destruction from God mat a terror to me.
Hence note. First.
God is mighty to destroy, as mell at to save.
There is one Law-giver, ( saith the Apostle, James 4. 12.)
mho is able to save, and to destroy, he can as easily destroy those
who violate as save those who obey his Lawes. There is the same
power of God in both, and God is honoured in the exercise of
both these pouers. That Title by which God is so often ex¬
pressed El shaddai, imports the destroying, as w ell as the preser¬
ving, saving, and nourishing power of God. As God hath de¬
clared himselfe, so we ought to honour him, to owne him, to stu¬
dy him, and to know him, know then, there is destruction from
God, as well as salvation from God. And, as to the Lord our God
belong the issnes (or out.gates) frem death, that is, God hath
choyce of wayes to deliver his servants from the extreamest dan¬
gers of death, So to the Lord our God belong the entrances unto
death; that is, God hath infinite wayes to lead his enemies into
the chambers and snares of death.
Secondly, If we consider who are the objects of this de¬
struction, even they who are guilty of oppression; or in what case
tob feared it, namely, if he had lift up his hand violently or un¬
tigoteously against the fatherlesse.

0504.head: Chap. 31. Ar Exposition upon the Esoke of JOB. Veri. 23.

body.t: Observe.
They uho destroy men unjustli, may justly expect destruction
from God.
God is a God of destruction, but he is destruct ion to the wick¬
ed only, or to unjust destroyers. God is a God of salvation to his
owne people, a believer needs not feare destruction; I ( saith
Christ Joh.10.31.) have given them eternal life, and they shall ne¬
ver perisb. Indeed while a believer acts, unlike a believer, God may
deale with him, as he doth with unbelievers, he may deale uith
him in outward dispensations, as he doth with the world, while
he conformes to the world; but take him under the notion of a
believer, he is not within the compasse of destruction : God is to
him, only a God of salvation. The destruct ion of God is the pro¬
per portion of men-destroyers. The miched are sons of perdition
so Judas was called ( Joh. 17.12.) And so Antichrist is called
(2Tbef. 2.3.) the wicked, I say, are sons of perdition) in a dou¬
ble notion; First, they are sons of perdition actively, they make
it their worke fometimes to destroy others, and the destruction
of others is often the consequent, yea the proper effect of their
worke; Secondly, they are the sons of perdition passively, that is,
they shall certainly be destroyed; and so 'tis expressely prophe¬
cyed concerning the latter of those sons of perdition, (2 Thes.2.
8.) whom the Lord pall consume with the spirit of his mouth, and
destroy mith the brigbtnes of his coming.
Thirdly, Note.
A believer hath, and may have dreadfull apprebensions es the
destroying pomer of God.
As be mabes God his feare (Isa. 8. 13.) in opposition to the
feare of mans destroying power, so it is good for him to feare the
destroying power of God, and often to consider the wrath of
God against sinners, to keep himselfe from sinning against God.
For though a believer obeyeth and keepes off from sin upon
higher, and nobler termes then œrath, yet he makes a good im¬
provement of those termes; trath and destruction from the Al¬
mighty are such a terror to him, that as he will not, so he dares
not fin. As we are delivered by Jesus Christ out of the hands of
all our enemies, that we may serve him in holinesse and righte¬

0505.head: Chap-31. An Exposition upon the Book ef IOB. Verl.23.

body.t: ousnesse without the feare of man, so in the feare of God all our
dayes. All believers are warned to worke out their salvation mith
feare and trembling (Phil. 2. 12.) that is, they should feare and
tremble to doe any thing which doth not (as the Apost le speakes,
Hebi6. 9. ) accompany salvation while they are working it out.
Princes must be just rulirg in the feare of God ( 2 Sam. 23.3.)
The Kings of the earth are called, ( Psal. 2. 10.) To serve him¬
mith feare, and to rejoyce before him mith trembling, to kisse the Son
least he be angry, Destruct ion from the Almighty should be a ter¬
ror to them against doing evill, who by their effice are a terror
to evill-doers.It was the unjust Judge who neyther regarded men
nor feared God ( Luke 18.2.) God delights to see the sonnes
of men honour him in all that he is, he delights to see them ho¬
nour him in his justice, and in his wrath, as well as in his love and
mercy. When Christ saw his Disciples daunted with the feare of
men, ( Luke 12.4, 5) He saith, Be not afraid of them that kill
the body, &c. But I will foremarne you mhom you shall feare,
feare him, mhich after he hath hillid hath pomer to cast into hel, yea,
I say unto you feare him. While he takes them off from the feare
of man, he doth not take them off from all feare, yea he urgeth
them with the feare of God; He would have destruction from
the Almighty a terror to them. And, such is the pronenesse of
man to sin, that he needs all manner of helpe, and the strength of
all sorts of arguments to keepe him from it.
Lastly, We may take this counsel from Tobs profession, when
we are about to doe any thing, let us examine and consider, whe¬
ther God allow it or no; If he dissallow it, let us forbeare and
feare to meddle vith it, though men flatter us or give us liberty,
yea though they assist and give us helpe. The reason why so ma¬
ny breake the rules, both of piety touards God and of honesty
towards man, is because they have layd by or aside, all feare of
destruct ion from the Almighty. Destruction from the Almighiy
xas a terrer to me;
and by reason of bis Highnesse I could not endure.
The roote of the word here rendred Highnes, signifies two
things First, to lift up; Secondly, to beare. Upon which ground
this text is diversly trar slated, Some thus, by reason of his meight
or burden I could not endure; or, I could nos beare his burden. But

0506.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Book of JOB. Vert. 23.

body.t: what was this heavy burden? The wrath of God is a burden,
and the only burden uhich man cannot beare. I, saith Jub (ac¬
cording to this trarslation) was pressed in my spirit with a sence
of the wrath of God. The weight of divine displealure is intole¬
rable, who can beare it? that’s a good sence, and theresore threat¬
ning Prophecyes in Scripture ( which are manifestations of the
wrathfull displeasure of God against menor Nations ) are often
called burdens. Thus we read (Isa. 13 1.) The burden of Baby¬
lon mhich Isaiah the son of Amos did see. And (Isa. 15.1.) The
burden of Muab, Because in the nighi Arif A ab is layd wast.
Once more ( Isa. 17. 1.) The Burdenof Damascus; Fehold Da¬
mascus is taken amay from being a Citie, and it shall be a ruineus
heape. See the like, Chap. 19 1. Chap. 21.1.11. Chap. 22.1.
Chap. 23. 1. All These Prophesies declared heavy Iudgements
ready to fall downe upon the head of Babylon, Moab and Dumas¬
cus, &c. to crush and ruine them, to breake and destroy them.
Thus Tthu spake when he had executed the sentence of God up¬
on jeheram, (2 Kinge 9. 25.) Then said Jehu to Biakar his Cap¬
taine, take up and cast him in the portien of the field ef Naboth the
Jezreelite: for remember, hom that mhen I and thou rede together
after dhab bis father, the Lord layd this burden upon him; that is,
passed this heavy doome upon him. There is one very observable
Scripture (Jer.23.33.) where the people are charged with mock¬
ing the Lords Prophets for their frequent use of this word. The
Burden ef the Lord: And mhen this peeple, er the Prophet ( that is,
false Prophet) or a Priest (that is, a prophane Priest) shall aike
thee, saying, mhat is the burden os the Lord? thou sbalt tben say un¬
to them, mhat burden? I mill even fersake you saith the Lord; mhen
they shall arke, that is, when they shall say in scorne, or scoffing¬
Iy, mioat is the burden of the Lord? we know you have some bur¬
den for us, we use to heare nothing but burdens or threatnings
from you, as if you were borne with the word burden in your
mouthes (So they derided the Prophets, and their threatning
Prophesies, called burdens) what is the burden of the Lord? thou
shalt say unto them, I will even sorsake you saith the Lord. Thst’s
vour burden, and that’s enough to breake your backs for ever.
And to shew how highly the Lord was displeased with their abu¬
sing his Prophets for the frequent use of this word, he tells them
( v. 34.) And as for the Prephet, and the Priest, and the peorle,

0507.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition upon the Book of JO B. Verf. 23.

body.t: that shall say, the burden of the Lord, ( that is, if any one shall say
it with scorne or derision to the Prophet) I uill punis that man,
and his house, I will be a burden to him saith the Lord; Yea the
Lord was so offended with their abuse of this word burden, that
he commanded it should be no more used (as many words which
men have corrupted, are dis-used by men) (v.35.) Thus sball
re say every one to his neighbour, and everyone to hit brother, what
bath the Lord ansmered, and mhat hath the Lord spokent As if he
had sayd, Be sure you use this scorning word no more, but if you
inquire of the Prophet, you shall speake thus, Ihat hath the Lord
ansmered and spoken, (V.36.) and the l'urden of the Lord shall you
mention no more; for every mans mord shall be his burden; for you
have perverted the words of the living God, of the Lord of hoasts our
God. (V.37.) Thus shalt thou say to the Prophet, mhat hath the Lord
ansvered? and mhat hath the Lord spoken? Thus he repeats it a¬
gaine. And whereas notuithstanding this prohibition, the peo¬
ple continued to use this word, The burden of the Lerd; Marke
what the Lord saith at the 38th verse; Because you say this word,
the burden of the Lord, and I have sent unto you, saying, Te sbal
not say the burden of the Lord; theresore behold Ieven I will utter¬
ly forget you, and I will forsake you, and the City that I gave you,
and your fathers, and cast you out of my presence: and I will bring
an everlasting reproach upon yeu, and a perpetuall shame, mhich
shall not be forgotten. I have insisted upon this notable Scripture
only to shew, how famous that word was, The burden of the Lord,
importing a prophesie that carried the signification of the sorest
displeasure of God in it against a provoking people; as also how
that word became infamous when the people abused it, saying in
scorne, The burdenof the Lord; As they also in scorne abused that
most precious word, The Holy One of Israel. For, because the Pro¬
phets were wont to Preface their Sermons, with, Thus saith the ho¬
Iy One ef Ifrael, or somtimes to conclude them, with, The holy One
of Israel hath sayd it; Therefore the prophane ones among that
people sayd in derision (Isa. 5.19.) Let him make speid and ha¬
sten his worke, that me may see it; and let the Counsel of the Hely
One of Israel draw nigh that ve may know it. Thus they in Isaiah
made a jest of that most excellent Name of God, The Holy Qne of
Israel, as these in Jeremie derided those dreadfull Messages of
God by his holy Prophets, called, The Burden of the Lord. But

0508.head: Chap. 31. An Expesition upon the Bocke ef JO R. Veri. 23.

body.t: to returne from this digression, occasion'd by the correspondence
of many Scriptures with this version of pobs text, I could not beare
his meight or burden.
Now from this reading of the words, By reasen of his burden
o beavines I could not endure.
Observe.
Tue wratb of God is very burdensome.
Tis a burden too heavy to be borne; Man cannot beare it;
The Apostatizing Angels could not beare it; yea Jesus Christ
himselse, when he undertook the redemption of fallen man sueat
drops of blood in bearing it. David confessed (Psal. 38. 4.)
Mine iniquities are gont over my head: as an heavy burden, they
are too heavy for me. But what made his iniquities so heavy? doubt¬
lesse it was his apprehension of the vrath of God which his ini¬
quities had deserved, and by their guilt subjected him unto. Car¬
nal men have mountaines of iniquity upon them, yet are not bur¬
dened with them, but make light, yea a sport of them, because
they are not sencible of that wrath which is due to them. Moses
in his prayer (Psal. 90.11. that’s the title of it ) cryeth out, uho
knometh the power ef thine Anger? even according to thy feare, so is
thy wrath. There is a power, and a weight in the anger of the
Lord, which no man ( who apprehends it) is able to endure or
stand under; yea, no man is able fully to apprehend it. As there is
an incomprehensible love of God; even a hight, and brendth, and
length, and depth, which man is not able to comprehend; so is his
anger, so is his wrath incomprehensible. They who apprehend
the least ofit, are pressed with its veight beyond enduring. As
glory which is the full manifestation of God to the soule, in his
love, and goodneffe, and holinesse, is called a meighi, (2 Cor. 4.
17.) what weight? not a burdensome weight, not an oppressing
weight, but an honourable weight, it is called a weight, because
of the greatnes, and excellency of it, and because it makes those
who have it weighty and honorable. Now as there is a blessed
weight, or a weight of blessednes in Glory; so there is a misera¬
ble ueight, a weight of misery in that wrath of God, which is
ready to be poured downe upon the head of sinners. Tis such a
weight of misery as will crush the strongest Giant like a moth.
And unlesse God put forth a power in man to beare him up un¬

0509.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition upon the Booke ef JOR. Vers.23.

body.t: der the power of his anger, it would sinke him to nothing. The
Apostle ( Heb. 10 31. ) gives warning to all, lest they come un¬
der this weight. It is a fearefull thing to fall into the hands of the
tiving God; that is, to fall under the weight of his displeasure.
When David had sayd ( Psal. 32. 4.) Day and nighe thy hand
mas heavr upon me; he presently tells us what sad effects he found
ofit; My moysture ( saich he) is turned into the drought of sum¬
mer. The weight of God. hand is heavy upon his owne people,
in time of affliction, and desertion, when he at once chastens them
aud hides his face from them. But what is that to the hard of
God that shall be upon the wicked for ever?If that anger of God
(which doth but purge and cleanse the Godly be so heavy, O how
eheavy is that anger of God which reprobates and consumes the
ungodiy? When, they falling into the hand of God, the hand of
God falls upon them, it will fall heavy upon them indeed. The
Prophet speakes of the lighting domni of the Arme of God mith the
indignation of his anger, and with the flame of a devouring fire, mith
scattering, and tempest, and hayle-stones (Ila. 30. 30.) Whenthe
power of God ( called by the Prophet his Arme) cloathed with
the indignation (that is, with the very spirits) of his anger, like
a devouring fire, or a scattering tempest shall light downe or rest
upon sinners (in which sence Damascus is called the rest of tbe
burden of the word of the Lord, that is, of his urath declared in that
burdensome word, Zach. 9. 1. When, I say, the wrath of God
fhall chus light downe and rest upon sinners) O how restlesse vill
they be for ever!
But I will not stay any longer upon this version of the Text,
though it be a profitable one, and sutable enough to Tobν scope.
Our rendring is cleare and proper,
By reason of his highnes, I could not endure.
The roote of the word which we translate Highnes, signifies to
elevate, or, lift up; and it imports both highnes of place, and
highnes of power and dignity, locall highnes, and civill highnes.
And therefore Princes are expre ssed by this word, because they
are high, or persons lifted up above the rest of the people; by
reason of bis highness ( of his Princely Highness or Ma esty)
I could not endure.

0510.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon ths Rook ef IO B. Verl. 23.

body.t: The Hebrew is only thus, by reason of his higbness I could not,
leaving us to conceive uhat he could not doe, by reason of the
highness of God; and hence the supplement is variously made to
this, I sould not; and it may be questioned what was it that J b
could not by reason of the Highnes of God? First, some read,
I could not withstand or resist, he would be too hard for me; Se-
condly, Mr. Brougbten reads (which reacheth the same sence) I
could not stand befere his Highnes. A third makes the supplemert
thus, I ceuld not escape, nor get out of bis hand; his highnets is such,
that if I had done wickedly, there had been no avoyding or flee
ing from his revenging hand. We make up the sense with the
word Endure, by reason of his highness I could net endure. And in-
deed as he could not stand nor withstand, nor fly from him, so it
is as true that being under the hand of God he could not endure
his Highnes. The power ard Greatnes, the excellency and High¬
nes of God, dasheth man out of countenance, and confounds
him.
But why could not fob endure the Highnes of God, seeing the
Prophet speakes of those who rejoyce and triumph in it (Ia.13.
3.) Ihave commanded my sanctified ones, I have also called my
Mighty ones for mine anger, even them that rijoyce in my Higt¬
ness.
I answer, The Lord in that place describes those Worthyes to
whom he had lifted up his banner (v. 2.) and whom he had fitted
for that Great setvice of his anger, the over throw of Babylon;
and therefore he termes them sarctified ones ( that iz) men spe¬
cially prepared and set apart for that worke, as wel as miç hiy enes
for his anger, that is, mighty to execute his anger upon Bab lon;
Now they whom God doth call and spirit for any Noble under¬
taking in the execution of his anger against Babylomsh enemies,
have much cause to rejoyce and exult in the Highnes of God, or
that they therein serve the high God. But when any man in stead
of being the instrument, is the object of Gods anger, how can he
then rejoyce in his Highnes? Yea then he must say ( as Jub here
did upon supposition of Gods anger against him) By reason ef hi¬
Higbnes I cannot endure.
Hence observe.
Fird, Highness belongs to God.

0511.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Booke of JOR. Vert.23.

body.t: God is often in Scripture called, The high God, the most high God,
and unto God highness and power properly belong; power and
highness are originally and fundamentally in God all the power
and highness that are in the creature, fl w forth and are derived
from bim. As God is the fountaine of all the Goodnes, so of all
the Greatnes that is in man. There are high ones among men,
but highness is the Lords, yea the High ones are the Lords; He
constitutes them, and he rules them at his pleasure, & for his plea¬
sure. ( Pfal. 135.5.) Our Ged is above all gods. There are gods
many, and Lords many, as the Apostle speakes (1 Cor.8.5) that
is ( as himselfe explaines it) there are many that are called Gods.
All Magistrates are called Gods, and God gives them leave to
weare that title, yea himselse hath put that title upon them, yet
tous tbere is but one Grd, the fatber of whom are all things, and we
6y him. The God of Heaven is infinitely above all the gods of
the earth, Kings and Princes; And what is the Highnes of Idolls,
or dung-hill gods to him, when the gods upon the throne are no¬
thine unto him? Our God is abeve all gods : or, as Solemon ex¬
press.th it (Eccl. S. 8.) He is higher, then the highest. As in na¬
ture there is nothing Greater then the Greatest, so none Higher then
the H.ghest. There is no degree beyond the luperlative. This
maxime holds universally in things of the same kinde; But there
may be somewhat of one kinde Greater then the Greatest and
gher then the Highest of another kirde. There is no man
Higher then the Highest man But God is infinitely Higher then
the Highest of men. Yea as all the wisdome of man is folly to the
wisdome of God, and all the strength of man weakness to the
strength of God; so the Highnes of the Highest men is louness
and basenes to the Highnes of God. This super. fuperlative High¬
ness of God appeares,
First, in the extent of his Iurisdiction. The soveraignty of
God hath no bounds nor limits, it reacheth to all places, and to
all times; men who have great power in some place, have none in
other places: men, who are high at one time, are low at another
time; but the Lords highness and pouer are alike at all times,
and in all places. Thou Lord ( faith the Prophet, Psal. 92. 8.)
art mest High for evermore.
Secondly, This his Highness appeares in the absolutenesse of
his Jurisdiction; he governes by no law but his will, nor actshe

0512.head: Chap. 31. Au Exposition upon the Backe ef Jo R. Verl. 23.

body.t: by any rule but his pleasure. Our God is in the Heavens (laith the
Church in answer to that feared reproach of the Heathen, Psal.
115.4. nhere is nom their Ged?) and hath dene whatsetver he
pleased. And thus much a Heathen Prince, The Highest then on
earth, ascer seven yeares banishment among beasts was convinced
of (Dan. A. 34,35.) And at the end of the dayes, I Nebuchaa¬
nezɇar list up mine eyes unto heaven, and mine understanding re¬
turned unto me, and I blessed the Mest High, and praised and lu¬
norid him that liveth for ever; mhose deminion is an everlasting
dominion, and his kingdome from Generation to generation; And all
the inhabitants of the tarth, are reputed as nothing, and he doth ac¬
cording to his will in the army of heaven, and among tbe ixhabi¬
tants of the earth, and none can stay his hand, or say unto him, what
dest thou? Here’s absolute Highness or Soveraignty: God doth
uhat he will and he cannot be stopt or stayed in wohat he vill
doe: and as none can stay his hand from what he will doe, fo
none can question or call him to an account for uhat he hath
done. And here I might shew the Highnes of God in the abso¬
lute exercise of a sixt fold power; First, in commanding, Se¬
condly, in forbidding; Thirdly, in permitting; Fourthly, in re¬
warding; Fisthly, in punishing, Sixtly, in setting up and pulling
downe, what & whom and how he will. He doth all thele things
(and these are the flowers of his Crowne) according to the plea¬
sure of his owne will, and mho may say unto him, what dest thou?
Take three or foure Inferences or Corallaries from the consi¬
deration of this Highness of God.
First, If God be so High, Then malte bumbly before him, and
keepe your spirits low, that is, lonly. The Prophet proposeth the
peoples Question (Mich. 6. 6.) Wueremith shall I come before tt e
Lord, and bow my selfe before the high God? shall I come before him
mith burnt efferingi, mith calves if a ytare old! mill the Lord be
pleased mith thousands of rams, or with ten thousand rivers of oyle?
Shall I give my fiest borne for my transgression, the fruit ef my body
for the sin ef my soule? As if they had layd, If any of these chings
will pleuse the Lord, the most high God, he shall have them with
all our hearts: yet they would not give Cod their hearts, whch
was the thing he looked for. Thus they hankerd and beate the
bufh, desiering to put the Lord off œith shadowes and cereme¬
aies, wich facrifices and oblations. But still they kept close to

0513.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the BooR ef IOB. Vers.22.

body.t: their sins, and their hearts were farre eff from him. They would
be very prosuse, spare for no cost, muke hi perbolicall offers of
thousands oframs, and ten thousands rivers of oyle, yea if God
would have ( which of all outuard things were most deare and
precious to them) their very children in sacrifice, he shou d have
them, yet in the meane time, that which was the true sacrifice
and onty acceptable to God (Psal.51. 17.) their hearts or them¬
telves (Rem. 12. 1.) in a way of sprrituall obedience, they would
by no meanes offer unto Ged. And therefore to shew the vanit
and hypocrifie of all these fayre and formall flourishes, The Pro¬
phet comes plainely to the matter (v. 8.) He (that is, God)
hath shewed thee O man, what is good; and mhat doth the Lord re¬
quire ef tb́ee, but to doe justly, and to loue mercy, and to malke hum¬
bly mith thy God? As if he had say d, Away with these flattering
pretensions; you doe but shufle and trifle vith God in all these
things; you need not make so many queryes about what will
please God, He hath spoken his mind clearely, Dot just ly, and shem
mercy, there's the all of second Table duties; malke humbly mith
thy God, there's the fumme of first Table duties. Surely, to walke
humbly & with a lowly mind besore the high God, is the best of,
yea all sacrifices; a submitting spirit is most sutable in all our ap¬
proaches to the supreame power. The High God expects our
spirits should comply with what he will have us doe, and with
whatsoever himselfe is pleasrd to doe with us. There’s nothing in
man so answerable to the bighness of God as submission. The
Apostle James comprehends the whole of our duty in two things,
whereof the first is submission, the second is resistance ( Pames 4.
7.) Reßist the Devill, submit to G d. This posture of mans spirit is
intended in that of his body ( Lam. 3. 28.) He sitteth alone, and
brepeth silence, bicause he hath borne it apon him; that is, he who
is under the yoke of God, ( He had sayd a little before, it is geod
for a man to beare the ycke in his you: b) ought to be quiet, he must
not make eyther a slirre or a clamour about the dealings of God
with him. As it is our strength to sit still in dependance upon God
for his helpe ( Isa. 30 7, 15.) so it is our uisdome to sit still in
fubmission to the hand of God. The high God lookes that eve¬
ry high imagination, every thought exalting it selfe uhether a¬
gainst any of his standing lawes and ordinances, or tempory dis¬
pensations and providences, should be brought dovne (2 Cor.10.

0514.head: Chap.31. An Expofition upos tbi Book of Jo ». Verf. 23.

body.t: "Tis all the reason in the world that the will of the high God
should be above our wills, that his will should be uppermost,
who himlelfe is so.
Secondly, The highness of God. should lead us to give him
high services; wee should serve the Lord in loulinesse of mind,
tut not with low minds; our minds and hearts should be exceed¬
dingly lifted up in the service of the high God. That was a very
holy as vel as a Noble resolution of Solomen about the buildirg
of the Temple ( 2 Ceron. 2. 5.) The house mhich I build is great,
for great is eur Ged abeve all g.ds. Solomon would proportion a
house for God, according to the God of the house, he is a great
God ( saith he) and therefore he must have a great houte; he is
a high God (faith the Scripture) therefore he must have high
services, he must be served with a heart lifted up. The heart of
good King ]ehsshaphat was lifted up, or incouraged and strengthe¬
ned in the wayes of the Lord ( 2 Chron. 17. 6.) As he was serving
the high God, so his heart went high in his service. When we
pray, our prayers should be high prayers, or pravers lifted up to
the high God; I lift up my seule to thte sayd David (Plal.25.1)
Such was the desire of King Hezekiah, in his Message to Isaiab
the Prophet, in that day of rebuke and blasphemy (2 Kings 19.4.
Nherefore lift up a prayer for the remnant that is left. Thus allo
the praises of God, should be high praises, (Ptal. 149 6.) Let
the high praises of Ged be in their mouth: yea all our thoughes and
words concerning God should be high (Exod. 15.11.) We
should both say, and thinke, thinke and say, uho is a G d hhe un¬
to thee?
Thirdly, The consideration of the highness of God, should
make all other things low in our eyes. As he that hath low or lit¬
tle thoughts of God, will quickly have high and great thoughts
of himselfe, yea he will thinke every thing Great, so he that hath
great and high thoughts of God, thinks nothing great or high
but God. How little are the greatest dangers, and the greatest
enemies in our eyes, when once God is great there. We shall say
(As Zech. 4. 6.) Nho art thou O Great mountaine before Zerub¬
babel ( that is, the power and strength ofthe high God in Zerub¬
babel ) thou shalt become a plaine: God never makes mountaines
plaines for us, till he hath made mountaines plaines to us, or in
our estimation. The Apostle having a high esteeme of Christ,

0515.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition npou the Book of IO R. Verl. 23.

body.t: Accrunted all things, but duxg, and dross, (Phil. 3. 9 ) (The
reason why any over-rate the things of this world, why they
reckon their gold and silver, better then gold and silver, and
their honours better then honour, is because they under-rate
Christ, they account Christ lesse then Chrift, his blood lower,
then his blood is, and his sufferings of a smaller value, then his
sufferings are. They make Christ lesse then he is, else they would
never make the things of the world greater then they are. What
a nothing is all in our selves to us, and all in others to us, yea all
other both things and persons to us, when we have seene God in
Christ our All, or our Allnes in God túrough Christ ! Did we
converse with God by faith in his highness and greatnes, what
could be high or great in our eyes in comparison of him? Wee
commonly say, Nothing is high or great to a highor great spirit,
how much more may we say, nothing is high or great to a spirit
hightned and greatned in God.
Fourthly, The remembrance of Gods Highness is very com¬
fortable to all that are in a low condition, they having an inte¬
rest in him, or being (tbrough grace) related to him. The High
God sets the poore on high ( Psal. 107. 41.) For as another Scrip¬
ture assures us, Though our God be high, yet he hath regard to the
lowly (Plal. 138.6.) Here is comfort to those that are low and
lowly, who are low in estate, and lowly in spirit, who have the
grace of lowlynes in a condition of lownes; They have a friend
on high, and he being higher then the highest, can rayse those on
high, who are lower ( in their owne fight) then the lowest.
Lastly, If the Lord be most High, then let us make the Lord
our highest end, and exalt him, not only in, but above all our selfe¬
aymes and designes. The best way to set forward or attaine to
our oune ends, is to make God our highest end. While we sin¬
cerely advance the name of God, ue need take no care of our
oune advancement: let God alone with that. But if any man
sets his oune ends above God, let him know, he sets himselse a¬
bove God too, yea he makes himselse his god; which is at once
the hight of sin, of madnes, and of presumption.
Againe, When Job saith, By reason of his bighnesi I could not
endure; Consider Job was a man in high place himselfe, Tob held
the hight of the Hill, others were but inthe valley, in those times
to which these words referre. And yet, saith he, by reasen ef hi¬
Hence
bighness I could not endure.

0516.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition upin the Bosbe ef IOR. Verl. 23.

body.t: Hence note; Secondly.
They that are highest havt reason to tremtle at tue highness
of God.
They who are Cedars for hight, and Oakes for strength, can¬
not endure by reason ofhis Highness, yea the Loré v ho is high
loves to shake the High ones, and to cast them downe. (Isa. 2.
11,12.) The day of the Lord ef h sts soak be upon every onc that is
proud, and lifted up, apon all the Cedars of Lebanon, &c. And at the
I9th verse the Prophes tells us, The high enes snall gre into the
holes of the rocks, and intn the caves of the earth for feare ef the
Lord, end for the glory of his Majesty, mhen he ariseth to shibe ter¬
ribly the earth. As Satan hath a spitefull ambition to be dealing
with those who are most eminent for grace in the Church; This
Christ told Peter ( Luke 22. 31.) Simon, Siman, Behald, Satan
hath defiered to have you, that he may sift you as wheate: So the
Lord hath (ifI may so speake) an holy ambition to be dealing
with those who are most eminent for power in the world; I
meane with those, who as they are high in place, and power, so
high in their owne thoughts. The Lord hath no quarrell uith
those that are high, because they are high, but because they carry
themselves proudly in their highness. (Ex d. 18 11) In the
thirg nherein they dealt proudly, Ged was above them; God did not
oppose them because they were high, but because they were
high minded. The high arme (with a high mind ) shall be Praben
(16 38 15.) And hence that Caution to the high ones of the
earth (Psal. 75. 4, 5.) Lift not up rour hornes on higl, speake not
with a steffe neche: for premotion cometh neither from the Eest, ner
from the mest, nor from the Suth But God is the Juage, he put¬
teth downe one and setteth up another. This consideration, that’tis
the High one in heaven who makrs men high or low on earth,

To every high minded one the Lord will say, as (Jer. 42 16.)

or any metaphoricall Eagle. How often hath Ged pull’d downe

body.t: the throne of Princes,or Princes from their thrones (fer. 13 18.)
Say to the King, and to the Queene, humble your selves, sit downe
for your princi pality sball come domne, even the Croure ef your glo¬
rj. The Lord puts the Question to the highest and the ftrongest
(Extk. 22. 14.) Can thy heart endure, or can thy hand be strong,
in the day that I shall deale mith thee? As if he had sayd, How
strong and high secver thou art, yet mhen Ithe mest high ont hall

inconsiderable, and sprinke to nothing. That’s the ground of the
Apostles objurgation, Doe ve provoke the Lord to jealsusie? are ye
stronger then be? (1 Cor. 10.22.) can you standit out with him
are ye his march? Is a Thistle any match for the Cedar, or a
whelpe for a Lyon? much lesse, infinitely lesse is man for God.
How easily can the Lord thunder downe from his highness, and
from his high places, upon the heads of the tallest Anakims and
mightiest Nimrodt in this lower world! And if they who are
high, cannot endure nor stand before the highness of the Lord,
what shall become of them who are low? As the Apostle Peter
argues in another case (1 Pet. 4. 18) If the righteous scarsely be
saved, where shall the ungodly and the sinner appeare? So I may in
this, If the strong cannot at all stand before him, how shall the
weake and poore? And if the weake and poore ones presume
to sinne, and provoke the Lord, they shall find his highness as
terrible to them, as to the highest, richest, and greatest in the
world.
Thirdly, From that other reading of the words, By reasonof
his Highness I could not escape.
Observe.
As no man is able to beare the mrathof God, so no man is able to
flet or get away from it.
And how sad is it when a man cannot escape from that, which
he cannot endure! If the displeasure of God were such as we
could avoyd or run from, such as we could get out of the reach
ofit, sinners had somewhat to beare themselves upon: but as ve
are not able to stand in his hand, nor endure his hand, so we can¬
not get out of his hand. Now, as no man, no nor the Devil with
all his powers of darknesse is able to plucke a believer out of the
nrotedting and faving hand of God ( Tob. 10. 29.) fo no manye

0518.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Bok of IOB. Vert. 23.

body.t: able to deliver himselfe, nor can he be rescued by any other, out
of the punishing and revenging hand of God. And as there is no
getting out of his hand, so no keeping out of it; we can neyther
flee nor hide our selves from him who is every where. “Tis grie
vous, when a man falls into the hand of his conscience, because he
can neither flee, nor hide himselfe from his conscience, every man
carrieth that about him, wheresoever he goeth. This (I say)
makes a mans case unspeakeably miserable, when he salls into the
hands of his own conscience. And is it not much more sad, when
a man falls into the hands of God, who can be infinitely more
terrible to us then our consciences, and who only makes our con¬
sciences at any time a terror tous ? Remember sinners, you can
no more ( no nor so much) get out of the hand, or cleare from
the hand or presence of God, then you can from the hand or pre¬
sence of your oune consciences. Whether soever you goe, God is
with you, whether you will or no. Whether shall ne got frem his
presence? if mre ascend up into heaven, he is there; and if me make
our bed in hel, he is there, &c. ( Psal. 139. 8.) And where soever
we are ( suppose we could be in heaven, yet ) if an angry consci¬
ence and an angry God be withus, we make our bed in hel, or
our bed is a Hel to us. How can creatures cemfort those to whom
God is a terror? Woe ro sinners, who provoke that God, whose
presence they can neyther abide nor avoyd.
Thus sob hath given an account both of his integrity (in those
particulars opened) and likeuise of the reason why lie kept his
integrity. Destructien from God mas a terror to him, ard by rez¬
son of his highness he could uot endure. As fub would not sin against
God because he loved him, so he durst not sin against Ged, be¬
cause he feared him.
He now proceeds to give a further account of himselfe, by
shewing that as he had not gotten riches by unrighteousnesse, so
he had used and dispensed them righteously; tor suppose a man
hath not pulled his riches out of the mouthes and bellyes of the
poore, nor hath wronged any man by open violence, or secret
f aud, to advantage his owne estate, yet he may be an unrighte¬
ous Steward, or a covetous retainer of his estate: his heart may
goe out sinfully upon that which came in without sin; Against
this job protests in the next words.
JOB 31.
