body.t: If Ihave made gold my hope, or have said to the
fine gold, Thou art my confidence;
If Trejoyced because my mealth was great, and be¬
cause mine hand had gotten much.
Y the former context Job cleared himselfe (which aspersion
L had been cast upon him by his friends more then once) from
any unlawful or oppressiog wayes of gaine, He had not lift np his
hand against the fatherlesse, though he san his helpe in the gate.
In this 24th and 25th verse, he cleares Aimselfe from any undue
frame of spirit in reference to what he had gotten lawfully, or
was lawfully possessed of Nou, he that can professe before God
and men, that he hath not used any undue meanes to get riches,
sand that his heart is not in any undue frame towards riches duely
gotten, This man is a man of men, A man after the heart of God.
And this Job doth, in the words before us, three wayes.
First, He professeth that he had not made worldly things,
no not the best of them (Gold ] his hope.
Secondly, He professeth that he had not made the best of
Gold, (fine Gold) bis confidence. The finest Gold was not the ob¬
ject of his trust.
Thirdly, He professeth he had not made the aboundance of
Goll his joy, nor the muchnes of it the matter of his rejoycing;
If I rejoyced because my wealth mas great, and because my hand had
getien much, &c. Thus Teb disclaimeth joy, hope, and confidence
in the creature, therefore as his hand was cleane in the getting of
it, so his heart was cleare in the using ofit.
Vers. 24. If Ihave made gold my hope, &c.
That's the first thing. He doth not say, if I bave haped for geld,
But if Ihave made gold my hope. Gold is the choysest of earthly
things, tis that refined earth which most men hope for, and very
many covet after. And here gold is put (by a Synecdoche of the
part for the whole) for all earthly things. So that, when Tob saith,
A I bave made gold my hope, his meaningis, If I have made any

0520.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition upou the Beoke of JoR. Vert. 24.

body.t: good thing on earth my hope? One of the Greeke transliters ren
ders, Il Lhave made g ld my safety, my securitie, or the cause why
I was not effraid. As if he had sayd, I did net put feare away from
me because I had xuch gold, or morlaly gonds about-me. I did not
thinbe my selse safe or cut of the reach of danger, because I was rich.
The Septuagint have an elegant ar d'a vecy significant rendring,
though not so clearely complying with the original text as ours;
If Ihave made geld my wife, or, if I have marrud gold. Suc'] is
the spirit of a worldly man touards worldiy things, chat he dotli
not only love them, but is in love with them. As a man doth not
only love her whom he would marry ( lo he doth any friend
but he is in love with her and is restless till he injoyeth her. Yea
I may say, worldly men are married to worldly things, not only
as to a wife (who should be in sub ection to her husband ) but as
ro their husband to whom they are subject. They may justly be
called, wives to riches, and riches their husband, nho are at the
vill and command ef riches. Worldly men are so, more then the
wife is or ought to be at the will and command of her hueband.
But I shall not stay upon that translation, which though it depart
not from the scope of the text, yet from the words it doth. And
therefore I fhall follow our owne which is cleare to both.
If I have made gold my hope.
The word rendred hope or expectation, signifies also the reines
or bowells. One of rhe Rabbins gives this reason ofit, because
the bowells or reines are the seat of the affections, from which as
our feares so our hopes are formed. ( Psal. 7. 9.) The righteous
God trieth the hearts and reines, that is, the whole inner man of
every man, his thoughts and desires, his hopes and aymes. David
beggs of God to make this discovery of him. in the same words
(Psal. 26. 2.) E xamine me O Lord, and prove me, try my reines,
and my heart; As if he had sayd, Lord I am willing to be tryed
to the urmost, and that the bent and inward motions of my soule
may appeare to (from which I know they are not, cannot be hid)
thine all seing eye. Nor is there any thing which lyes more close
and secret in the bosome of man then his hope doth, And looke
what any man earnestly hopes for, his mind is often turning to,
if not alwayes fixed upon. IfI (laith Job ) have made Gold my
hope; that is, if my minde hath been uponit, or in the longing
expectation ofit.

0521.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Book ef JOB. Verl.24.

body.t: Hope is an affiction of the mind put forthor acted upon good, fu¬
ture and pessible. The ob ect of hope ( according te this definiti¬
on) is Good under a two fold notion Hope lookes to that which
is good; no man ever did or can hope sor that which is evill in it
selfe, and to him, if it appeared so to him, though many have ho¬
ped for that which indeed is so, and hath proved so to them in
the event. And as the object of hope is some good thing; so it is
good, First, as fuzure and to come; for that which a man hath
in his possession, or doth already injoy, he cannot hope for: in¬
joyment suallows up hope, or rather perfects it. Secondly, the
object of hope is some possi le good, or such a good as we have
grounds to attaine. Impossibles are rather the object of despaire
then of hope. But though this be the nature of hope strictly ta¬
ken, that it respects only good future or attained and possible or
attainable: yet Gold already attained and possessed is as much
the object of hope in the sence of this text, as that which is only
attainable and unpossess’d. And as men hope to get Gold, so they
make the Gold which they have gotten their hope.
There is a great difference between hoping for gold, and ma¬
king gold our hope. Wee may hope for gold or any of the good
things of this life, but we must not make gold or any thing of this
life our hope.
To make gold eyther gotten or to be gotten our hope, imply¬
eth these foure things.
First, An high estimation of it, as that which can doe great
things for us, or stand us in stead beyond any other thing, to make
us happy.
Secondly, A longing desire after it; There is alwayes so much
desire of that we hope for, that the thing hoped for is sometime
expressed by desire (Pro.13.12.) Hope deferred maketh the heart
ficke, but mhen the desire ( that is, the thing hoped for) cometh, it
is a tree of life.
Thirdly, Utmost earnest endeavours to obtaine it that which
a man makes his hope he will make his worke, and never ceaset h
working, eyther till he hath attained it, or is convinced that there
is no possibility of attaining it.
Fourthly, To make gold our hope, implyeth much trouble
and anxiety of minde, when once ue see our endeavours ineffe¬
cuall and unsuccessefull about the attaining of it. If hope defer¬

0522.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon thi Book of JOR. Verf. 24

body.t: red (as Solomon speakes in the Scripture last named) maketh the
heart sicke, surely then when hope dyes, or (as Zophar speakes,
Chap. 11. 20.) is as the giving up of the Ghost, the heart must
nceds dye too.
Now, when sob saith, If Ihave made Gold my hepe, &c. He
utterly disclaimes, as any such estimationof it, that it could doe
great things for him, or make him a happy man, so that he had
any longing desire after it, or that he used any extreame earnest¬
nes of endeavours to attaine it, or that he was vext and troubled
in minde when by his moderate endeavours he could not attaine
it. Job understood wel enough the worth and use of Gold, he
wel knew how many advantages it brings, yea how potenr it is in
the affaires of States and Kingdomes as wel as beneficiall to pri¬
vate familyes; yet he knew he should have made more of it, then
it is worth, or can be worthy of, if he had made it his hope, and
therefore he professeth; If I'have made gold my bope, &c.
Hence observe.
First, The naturall man makes gold or carthly things bis scupe
and hope.
He would live to grow rich, and lade himselfe with thick clay.
What this godly man professeth he did not, that a naturall man
doth, and ’tis his nature to doe it. He that is ef the earth is earth¬
Iy, and speaketh of the earth ( Joh. 3. 31.) For out of the aboun¬
dance of the heart the mouth speaketh. The words of a man are the
image of nis thoughts, that the thoughts of Naturall men are
earthly, or smel of the earth, we learne from another Scripture
(Psal. 49 11.) Their inmard thought is that their houses shall
continue for ever, and their duelling places to all generations, &c.
And what are their houses but heapes of earth, and the best fur¬
niture of them, Gold and silver but refined earth. The Apostle
(1 Tim. 6. 9.) gives the same character of the naturall man; be
mill be rich; That's his resolve, and the bent of his spirit, that
he lives to and lives for. What he hath is little or nothing to
him, unlesse he hath more; and that more satis fieth him no more
when he hath it, then the little did which he had before. Belie vers
have another bent, we, saith the Apostle (2 Cor. A. 18.) loche not
at the things mhich are seene, but at the things nhich are not seene,
that is, not at naturalls and temporalls, but at spiritualls and eter¬
nalls, these, not those are our ayme or the macke ( so the vord

0523.head: Chap. 31. An Expofition upon the Book of JO B. Vers. 24

body.t: signifies ) at which we shoote and level all our de sirer and endea¬
vours. But worldly men (who are the opposites to me in the
text) they looke at the things which are seene, and they looke
chiefly at them; as for the things that are not seene, they know
not what to make of them. Godiy men have their eye upon in¬
visibles, they expect not their happiness in this world, but in that
which is to come (ICor. 15 19.) If in tou life culy me bave hope in
Christ, met are of all men mest miserable. How miserable then are
they who make the things of this life their hope! who looke for
nothing but what the eye of tence or carnal reason may looke
upon! how many are there, uho if they may have gold and sil¬
ver enough, houses and lands enough, then they thinke they shall
have enough. Though indeed when they have as much as they
at present desire, the mouth of desire is not stopt, nor doc their
hearts say, it is enough.
Secondly, note.
To make gold our hope is exceeding fiefull.
As every man who hath in him a reall hope of glory, purifieth
himselse from sinfull acts and desires (1 foh. 3. 3.) so he purifi¬
eth himselfe from this hope. The hope uhich we have of hea¬
venly things is pure and it purifieth us; but the hope of earthly
things is usually impure, and to make earthly things our hope
cannot but be impure, therefore we have great need to purifie our
felves from all such hopes. (God only is to he made ourchope,
and to make him so is both our duty and our interest. Hope is a
part of that honour and worship which is proper to God; and
'tis worship required in the first Commandement; hope in God
is naturall worship, thar worship which the bare discoveries of
God, tiough he had never made a law about it calls for. The
knowledge of the excel ency and All-sufficiency of God com¬
mands us to hope in him. And to shew how much God should
be hoped for and hoped in, yea and made our hope, the Seripture
more then once calls him our hope ( Jer. 14.8) O the hopeuf
Afratl, the Saviour thereif in time of trouble. And as God is phe
hope of Ifrael, taken collectively for all the people of God, so be
is the hope of every Israelite indeed. Upon this ground the Pro¬
phet makes that deprecation (Jer. 17. 17.) Be not thou a terrour
ante me, theu art my tipe in the day efevill. And cheresore Da¬

0524.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition upon the Bocke ef J9». Verf 24.

body.t: vid inhibits his soule all other hopes but God (Psal.62.5.) Ay
soule maite thou only upon God, for my expectation is from him¬
As if he had sayd, O mr soule, I give thee thus counsel, yea this
charge, I lay this holy command upon thee, doe not waite apen any
creature (as making that thy hope) let thy expectation be frem¬
God alone. He urgeth the same restriction by way of assertion in
the next verse; He only is my rocke and my salvation. As this
Scripture shewes the entirenesse of a Saints hope in God; so that
other is like unto it (Psal. 73. 25.) Whem have Iin heaven but
thet? aud there is none upon earth that I desire besides thee. As if
he had sayd, I neyther know of nor depend upon the helpe ot any
but God alone; and what he denyes as to persons he denpeth al¬
so as to things, to all things on this side God. Hope is the anchor
of the soule, but this anchor must not be cast as the Mariner cast¬
eth his, who that his ship may be stayed in a storme casts his
anchor downward to take hold in the earth: We must cast the
tanchor of hope upwards and fasten it in heaven. So the Apostle
directs (Heb.6. 19.) which hope me have as an anchor of the soule,
hoth sure and stedfast, and mhich entreth into that witbin the vaile,
mhither ths fore-runner is for us entred, even Jesus, &c. Our hope
must enter into heaven and fix there. The best of the earth is not
ground good enough, nor sure enough for our anchor hold.
Whatsoever we make our hope, we make our God, and is there
any thing on earth good enough to be our God? Aoses com¬
plaines to God bitterly of the people of I/racl (Exod. 32.31.)
Oh this people have sinned a great sin, and have made them gods of
gold. They indeed formally made a Golden calfe and worship¬
ped it ; this act of ldolatry was their sin, and their smart; In fo
much that it was a saying among the jemes when ever they were
pressed with any grievous affliction; This is somemhat ef the Gol¬
den calfe. That which was their sin grossely, is in a more spiritu¬
ally sinfull way the sin of thousands every day, They make geds of
gold, or a god of gold. This is done as often as any man makes gold
his hope; and this the worldly man doth dayly, or all his dayes.
Yea so far as any godly man is carryed out inordinately after
Gold, he in some degree makes Gold his hope, and in the same
degree his God. It is sinfull to hope for gold immoderately, but
to make gold our hope in the least degree is abominable. And
XXX

0525.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition upon the Beoke ef JOR. Vers.24.

body.t: they who make it their hope, will quickly make it their confi¬
dence, which is a further hight of this sin, renounced expressely
by job in the next words.
or have said to the fine gold, Thou art my confidence.
But is gold to be spoken with or spoken to?It seemes the heart
hath a tongue, it speakes to Gold. As the foole hath said in hus
beart there is no God (Psal. 14. 1.) So in his heart he saith, gold
is his god, while he saith in his heart it is his confidence. Most
worldly men say this in their heart only ( there are but few so
wicked as openly to professe with their mouthes that gold is their
confidence) Yea many who professe highly that God is their
confidence, will be found upon search to make gold their confi¬
dence.
If I (saith fob ) have sayd ( with heart or tongue) to the fine
gold, &c. As gold is the finest metall, so there is some gold more
fine then other gold. Some gold is nothing but gold, it hath not
the least drosse or alloy in it. Gold is usually minted out with an
Alloy. Tob had no confidence in fine, none in the finest gold.
The Septuagint render, If I have trusted in the precious stone.
As if in the former part of the verse he had disclaimed his hope
in gold, and here in gemmes. But it is better to keepe to our tran¬
flation. The word signifying gold of the highest price; from this
word we have that title of some of the Psalmes, Michtam, a gol¬
den Psalme. If I bave sayd to the fine gold, Thou art
my confidence.
Confidence is the highest act of faith; what we confide in we
settle upon. Confidence is the fullest rest of the soule. An act of
recumbence gives some rest to the soule, but confidence is the se¬
curest rest of the soule. So much the word here implyes, even such
a confidence as leaves not so much as a jealous thought in the
mind. Thus David confesseth (Psal.30.6.) In my presperitie I sayd
I shall never be moved, Lord by thy favour thou hast made my moun¬
taine to stand strong. The rich man was risen up to this confidence
while he sayd ( Luke 12. 19.) Soule thou hast much goods layd up
for many yeares, take thine ease, cat, drinke, and be merry. Then
me have made gold or the things of the world our confidence,

0526.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon tbs Book of JO2. Vert, 24.

body.t: when we find an acquiescence flowing from our recumbence up¬
on them. What is faith but a going out of selfe and a resting up¬
on Christ ? and what is assurance but the soules rest in Christ?
The heart of a carnall man sits downe and rests upon worldly
things, as a godly man sits downe upon and rests in Christ.
Againe, While Tob professeth he had not sayd to the fine gold,
Thou art my confidence, He is brought in personating the counter.
part of a carnall covetous man, entertaining discourse or talking
to his Gold. He no sooner enters his Closet and openeth his
Chest, but he falls into a Colloquie with his gold. As a tnan meet¬
ing a deare ancient acquaintance, presently salutes him, with O my
friend Iam glad to see you! So saith he to his gold, to his fine gold;
O my friend, my love, my joy, my hope, my confidence, I am glad to
see you safe, you mill stand by me mhen all friends fayle you will not
see me want, nor suffer me to be wrong’d, as long as you last, and that
I mist may be for ever. Tea he speakes to his gold not onl, with a
Lind of blandement and adulation, as his choycest friend, but xith a
bind of Adoration as his chiefest good. We commonly say, A penny
in our purse is hetter then a friend at Court. But lome are apt to
thinke the Gold in their purse better to them then the God of
Heaven. Doubtlesse that man doth so, who sayth ( which Tob
did not) to the fine gold, Thou art my confidence.
Hence observe.
First, Man is apt to grom in confidence upon the account of
worldly aboundance.
Thus the Scripture every where deciphers the spirit of world¬
Iy men ( Psal. 49. 6.) They trust in their wealth, and boast i hem¬
selves in the multitude of their riches. Here we have the rich man
trusting and boasting, surely that is very confident trusting, œhich
issues it selfe into boasting. That man is ascended to the highest
step ot faith in God, who makes his boast of God; such faith have
they in fine Gold, who boast in it. David having fhewed the
wicked man, by the righteous judgement of God, rooted out of
the land of the living; shewes us in the next verse the righreous
man at once fearing and laughing at this sight, as also poynting
at him, saying, (Psal. 52.7.) Lot this is the man that made net
God his strength, The words are a divine but cutting sarcasme.
The Original is Geber, which signisieth a strong valiant man;

0527.head: Chap.31. An Exposition mpon the Bocke of JOR. Vers.24.

body.t: As we say in Enghsh, Loe, This is the brave and Gallant man, you
wot of. But who was this for a man? He was one ( saith he) that
trusted in the abundance of his riches. O tis hard to abound in
riches, and not to trust in them. Hence that caution (Psal. 62.
10.) If riches increase, set not your heart upon them. Now what
is the setting of the heart upon riches, but our rejoyeing and
trusting in them. And because the heart of man is so easily per¬
sivaded into this sinfull trust upon riches, therefore the Apostle
is urgent with Timothy to perswade all rich men, not only meere
worldly rich men, but godly rich men against it; yea he urgeth
Timothy to persurade rich men against two sins, which are worse
then all the poverty in the world, yet the usuall attendants of ri¬
ches, Pride and Confidence (1 Tim 6. 17.) Charge them that are
rico in this morld, that they be not higheminded. As chastitie or the
purity both of mind and body is endangered among the pleasures
and delights of the world: so is humilitie among the wealth and
riches of the world. Therefore charge them that are rich, and
charge chem home uith this thing, that They be not high. minded.
How apt are men to be lifted up with the things of this lower
world !Riches at once sinke the mind down-ward in cevetous
cares, and lift it upuard in proud conceits. A litt le of the world
will make some men great in their own eyes, and others despica¬
ble in their eyes; They will not looke upon or speake to a poore
man, scarsely to any man that is not as rich as themselves; They
carry it as if they were men of another world, or made of ano¬
ther mould, if they have got but a step in world ly things beyond
their neighbours. Yea some, who are counted the only wise men,
pride themselves ( like that foolish bird) while they looke upon
their paynted feathers, and thinke they are of more worth, because
they are worth more then their brethren. Many ( saith Mr. Cal¬
vin) who boast now a dayes of riches, are as if a man should
thinke himselfe greatly preferred, when he is but mounted upon
the blade of an onion, and when they have only got upon a mole¬
hil, they beare themselves as if they were carryed in the Chariot
of the Sunne. To see a man rich in purse and poore in spirit is a
great wonder. Now because men are thus endangered to pride by
riches, Therefore (saith the Apostle) Charge them that are rich
in this world, that they be not highminded. And charge them se¬
condiy, That they trust not in uncertaine riches, but in the livirg

0528.head: Chap. 31. Ax Expofition upon the Boohe of JOB. Vers. 24.

body.t: God. There's the rich mans temptation. Riches are a temptation
two wayes especially; First, they tempt men to doe unrigbteous
things, or to goe unrighteous wayes for the gerting ot them,
Secondly, they tempt to vaine confidence as soone av they are
gotten. Let me give you chree briet demonstrations, ro sheu that
there is an extreame tendency in riches to worke up the heart to
a confidence in them.
First, Riches, gold and silver have a strength in them; This
tends and invites to a confidence in them; And though the
strength of riches is greater in epinion then in reality, yet it can¬
not be denyed, but there is a great deale of strength in riches.
Pro. 10.15.) The rich mans mealth is bis strong Citie, the de¬
structim of the ponre is their poverty. The rich man secureth
himselfe against all assaults, and doubts not but he shall encure
the hardest and longest siedge in this wel fortified and uel Gar¬
rison'd Citie, and therefore like a man gotten into a strong Hold
or Citie, he is apt to scorne and bid defyance to all his enemies.
to all wants and dangers. Whereas the poore mans poverty is his
destruction; that is, he being poore ly es open like a Citie without
walls and Gates to every approaching and invading evill. Nowif
riches be, especially if men judge them to be their strength and
fortification, their safety and protection, no marvaile if they put
confidence in them.
Secondly, As they have a strength in them, so an answerable¬
nes to, yea a command upon all outward good things. Solomon
faith ( Eccl. 10. 19.) Money a-swereth all things. There is ( as
some conceave) an elegant Prosepopeia in the words; supposing
speech in all things, or all things speaking and calling aloud to
money, and money speaking, yea giving a satisfactory answer to
all things that speahe toit: nor can it be denyed but that money
(in some sence) gives anstver to all things. First, ordinarily and
honestly it answereth all our bodyly wants, and obtaineth all bo¬
dyly supplyes. A man may have any such thing for money, that
will buy what ever is needfull for or contentfull to this present
life. Secondly, Money will procure asfistance or the helpe of any
mans labour and paines, of any mans art or skill. Thirdly, Mo¬
ney will buy our peace and pacifie the wrath of man. Taceb sayd
(Gen. 32. 20.) I will pacifie him mitb the present that goeth be¬
fore. Atd so Solomon tellsus, (Pro.a 1. 14.) A gist in secret pa¬

0529.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Book of JoB. Verl.24.

body.t: cifieth anger, and a reward in the bosome, strong mrath. The p-ssi¬
ons of men are charm’d with gold and silver. And there are few
so angry with the person of a man, as to be angry with his gift;
especially if it be given (as the text saith) in secret, and tell no
tales. If you can put a reward closely into the bosome, it will be
too strong for strong wrath ard drive it out of the bosome. Mo¬
ney makes all friends againe. Not a word more with many, when
once that hath spoken and done its errand. Fourthly, if men vill
use their gold and silver dishonestly they can breake the Golden
bars of Justice and righteousnesse ( Pro. 17. 23.) A miched man
taketh a gift out of the bosome to pervert the wayes of Judgement.
Gold and silver pervert many things, especially matters of right,
and osten obtaine a covering for the greatest acts of unrighteous¬
nesse. Money hath a great power with those who are in power.
Those powers which we ought to be subject to, are too subject
themselves to the power of it. Fifthly, A golden key will open
any prison doore, and cast the watch man into a deepe sleepe.
Gold will break open gates of iron, as wel as silence the Orators
tongue, and blind the Judges eye; it will bin'd the strong mans
hands, and blunt the edge of the sword; it makes warre, and
makes peace; what almost can it not doe with corrupt minds?
Is it then any wonder that a meere naturall man should say to the
fine gold, Thou art my confidence?
Thirdly, Gold is the worldly mans Idol god. The Apostle
(Eph. 5. 5. Col. 3. 5) calls Covetousnesse Idolatry, and the co¬
vetous man an Idolater, therefore Gold must needs be his Idol,
and riches his deity. As among the Heathens, so among some
Christians, in name, money hath devotions payd it as to a god¬
desse. And if there be this vickednesse and madnes in the hearts
of men to esteeme riches as their god, no marvaile if they put
their trust in them. “Tis naturall for every man to trust in that,
which he accounts his god, whatsoever it is; Though but a leeke
or an onyon, the old Eyptians would confide in it; Though but
a dunghil god, or a devill god, though a new god, a god but of
yesterday, as Moses speakes ( Deut 32. 17.) yet degenerate Is¬
raelites will sacrifice to him. Therefore let me adde these three
words of advice.
First, When God gives you riches, gold and silver, suspect
uhat your hearts may doe with them. It is good to feare almayes,

0530.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Book of JOR. Vert.24.

body.t: especially, nhen ne have mhat me most desire. To be jealous over
our owne soules is one of the best meanes of safety.
Secondly, When you have gold in your hand, pray that it
may not get into your heart, but be kept under your feete, as the
Church is described (Rev.12.1.) having the Moone ( that is, all
worldly things) there. How much soever you have of the world
it cannot hurt you while you keep it under your feete, but if the
least ofit get up into your hearts it will undoe you.
Thirdly, Pray for a right judgement above riches. Wee sel¬
dome erre in our affections, till we erre in understanding; and we
cannot but over-love that which we over value. They only trust
in God, who truely know him (Psal.9. 10.) and they who true¬
ly know what Gold is, will never eyther make it their trust or
trust in it.
Againe, Why doth fob disclaime this confidence? Surely, be¬
cause such confidence is as vaine as it is finfull.
Hence note.
It is a very vanity to put confidence in riches, in Gold or fins
Geld.
For, first, riches cannot make us eyther better or uiser. Solo¬
mon saith indeed ( Pre. 14. 24.) The crowne of the wise is their
riches. But riches never crowned any man with wisdome, riches
are a crowne to the wise, because they as Kings rule over them
and command them; They command them at their pleasure, and
use them for their honour. Wisdome makes riches a crowne;
but riches cannot make a man wise. Wisdome guides a godly man
to the true use and improvement of riches, and so they adorne
him and make him very usefull. But ( as it followes in that text
of the Proverbs) the foolispness of fooles is folly, that is, let a foole
have never so much riches, he will discover his folly and shew
himselfe by so much the more foolish, by how much the richer he
is. Riches in the hand of a foole are out ( as we say) a Fooles¬
Bable, with which he makes himselfe a little sport: or they are
there, like a fword in the hand of a Mad-man, by which he doth
both himselfe and others hurt. Wisdome is good mith an inheri¬
tance (Ecck: 7. 11.) that is, an inheritance enables a wise man to
doe good, and to shew that he is good; But an inheritance is bad
with folly, that is, it doth but enable a foolisti man to doe mif¬

0531.head: Chap.31. An Exposition apon the Book ef IO B. Verf. 24

body.t: chiefe, and publish his owne folly; which though it had not been
lesse had he been poore, yet it had been lesse knowne and seene.
Secondly, As they cannot make us better, so they cannot make
our lives more comfortable to us. This is the ground of Christs
warning ( Luke 12. 15.) Take hecd and beware of cevetousnesse;
for mans life ( that is, the comfort ofit) consisteth not in the abun¬
dance of the things mhich he possesseth. Yea Solomon (Eccl: S. 13.)
shewes, that a rich mans life is so farre from being more comfor¬
table to him, because he is rich, that indeed it is more trouble¬
some; There is a sore evill mbich I'have seene under the Sunne,
namely, riches kept by the omners thereof to their hurt. And (v:17.)
All his dayes also he eateth in darknesse. In what kind of dark¬
nesse? Though he hath Sunne light at his dinner, and Taper. light
at his supper, yet he eateth in darknesse, that is, he hath no com¬
fort nor contentment in what he eateth. How vaine is it to put
confidence in that, which when we have it most, and have it fast,
leaves us comfortlesse.
Thirdly, They cannot, by their oune strength deliver us from
any evill, and they are not at all available to deliver us from that
greatest penal eviil the wrath of God (Pro: 11. 4.) Riches a¬
vaile not in the day of mrarb. They can doe no good touards the
securing us from divine vengeance; Only, Righteousnesse delivi¬
reth from death. And as they cannot at all deliver from the wrath
of God (Ezek: 7. 19) lo they cannot alwayes deliver from the
wrath of man; So some expound that place (Isa. 13. 12.) I mill
make a man more precious then fine Gold, even a man then the gol¬
den medge of Ophir; That is, such shall be the fury and fiercenesse
of those that shall destroy Babylon, that they will not take any
ransome, nor be moved with any offer of the finest Gold to spare
the life of a Babylonian. Further, riches cannot deliver from the
paines of the body, much lesse from the pangs of conscience;
therefore put no confidence in them.
Fourthly, Why should we desire riches, or at all trust in them,
seing they cannot at all satitfie our desires (Eccl:5. 10.) He that
loveth silver shall not be satuefied mith silver, nor he that loveth a¬
bundance mith increase: this is also vanity. The mind of manis so
large and wide, that all this world cannot fill it;nor doth it beare
any due proportion to it. Heaven cannot satisfie the foule uith¬
out Cod, much lesse can this earth, yea, riches, gold and silver

0532.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition upon the Booke ef IOB. Vers. 24.

body.t: are so far from satisfying desire, that they are but fewel to en¬
crease the flame of it. And as they encrease desire, so they take
away or rob us of our rest (v: 12.) The sleepe of a labouring man
is smeet, mhether he eat litle or much; but the abundance of the rich
mill not suffer him te sleepe: That is, he hath such abundance of
cares about his abundance of riches, that he cannot be quiet night
nor day.
And as they are a trouble to the body in hindring sleepe; so
(which is infinitely worse ) they are a snare to the soule, and cast
that into a dead sleepe. How often doe they intangle the spirits,
and weaken the graces of good men? How often doe they streng¬
then their lusts, and furnish their corruptions? They hinder many
from believing and receiving the Gospel ( Luke 14. 16, 17, 18.)
They choake the word in others who seeme to have received the
Gospel (Math: 13. 22.) How often doe riches lead to neglect
of duty, yea to a denyall of God? Hence that good man begg’d
(Prev: 30. 9. ) Give me net riches, lest I be full and dexy thee,
and say, who is the Lord? Julian the Apostate, spoyled the Chri¬
stians, in those times, of their outward estates, and then sayd in
scorne, That he did it to make them more expedite or ready for the
kingdome of hraven, as their Master had taught them. Woe to
scorners, yet there is a serious truth in that Atheisticall fcorne;
We are made the more readie for heaven, by how much we are
the lesse cumbred with earthly things. Lastly, as riches clogge
many in the wayes of God, so they cause some totally to forsake
and Apostatize from that profession which they once made of
them. Thus Paul complained ( 2 Tim. A. 10.) Demas hath for¬
saben me, having loved this present werld. Well therefore might
the Apostle conclude (I Tim. 6. 10.) The love of moncy is the
roote of all evill, mhich mhile some have coueted after, they have er¬
red from the faith, and pierced themselves through mith many sor¬
romes. Adde to all this, that amazing sentence of Christ (Math.
19.23,24.) Then sayd Jesus to his Disciples, verily I say unto
you, that a rich man suall hardly enter inte the hingdome os heaven;
And againe I say unto you, it is easier for a camel to goe through
the eye of a needle, then for a rich man to enter into the kingdome of
God. This saying astonished the Disciples, and therefore Christ
gives a twofold mollifying interpretation of it, first, in the zoth
verse ofthe same Chapter; with men this is impossible, but xitb
y y

0533.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Booke ef JOR. Vers.24.

body.t: God all things are pessible. Secondly (Marke 10 24.) How bard
is it for ttem that trust in riches to enter into the kingdome of God.
So then, ’cis not the possessing or having of riches which renders
the rich mans case so difficult, but trusting in them, ’tis hard for
any rich man, but ’tis impossible for a rich man trusting in riches
to enter into the kingdome of God:and I may say from Scripture
grounds, ’tis impossible for any man who hath riches not to trust
in them, but by the grace and power of God. Judge then how
strong Job was in the grace of God, who could say, that he had
never sayd to the fine Gold, Thou art my Corfidence. Nor doth Tob
disclaime confidence in gold only because it is a vanity to confide
in it, but also because ’tis base, exceeding base to confide in it.
Hence note.
Confidence in Gold embaseth the mind of man, er nothing makes
the soule so drossie as confidence in fine Gold.
Yea, as confidence in Gold abaseth the mind of man, so it aba¬
seth (in mans thoughts) God himselfe. God is litle or nothing to
them, who have an over-great esteeme of Gold. They have low
and poore thoughts of God, who have high thoughts of riches;
yea they thinke the All-sufficiency of God too litle for them,
who looke upon any creature as sufficient for them.
Againe, He that makes gold his confidence, is confident if he
have gold enough he shall doe well enough without God. He
sça se believes that he hath any need of or dependance upon
God, when once he sees himselfe above dependance upon man.
How great a wickednes is it for a man to rob the living God of
that which is his greatest honour, and give it to a livelesse crea¬
ture. As hope, so confidence much more, is proper to God. God
will doe nothing for us, unlesse we make him our confidence.
And the creature will be nothing tous, if we make it our confi¬
dence.
From the whole matter take these two inferences.
First, Of how excellent a spirit are they, who while (lile Jeb)
they have the creame of the creature, and all the contentments
of the world courting them dayly, the rocke powring them out
rivers os oyle, &c. Yet keepe the world at a due distance, and ne¬
ver make the best ofit the least of their hope, nor the All ot it
any of their confidence? how cleane doe such keope their hearts

0534.head: Chap.31. An Exposinion upon th Book of IOE. Vert, 25.

body.t: from the pollution of the world, how pure, how entire to
God!
Secondly, This administers support to the Godly poore, for
as they want many comforts which the rich enjoy, so they are
freed from many temptations wbich annoy the rich. Riches are
a mercy (they are so with the blessing and grace of God) yet
they are a dangercus mercy. And though povertie be a trouble
and a burden, yet it is a safe trouble, and ( comparatively to ri¬
ches) a light burden. I doe not intend pinching poverty, or their
poverty who are in a necessitous condition, but theirs u’ho are in
a meane condition. Gold is good, yet both an inferior good and
an uncertain good; riches make cloggs for the soule in its courle
to heaven, but they make themselves wings and fly as an Eagle to
heaven. Gold is good, but’cis a deceitfull good; riches promise
much, but performe litle; and while they pay our debts, they doe
not pay their owne; Gold is good, but ’tis so to us only when we
use it wel; Grace is so good, that it makes us use it wel; Gold is
such a good as makes most who have it, use it ill, and enjoy it
worse: As fob plainly intimates in the words which follow
For as in these words Job hath renounced all hope in gold, and
confidence in the finest gold, so in the next (which is the common
sin of those who enjoy much gold ) he proceeds to renounce all
inordinate joy or rejoycinginit.
Vers. 25. If I rejoyced because my wealth mas grtat, and be¬
cause my hand had gotten much.
This argues the frame of Jobs spirit yet more spirituall, and
more refined from the drosse of earthlines. Possibly a man may
not make Gold his hope, nor say to the fine gold, thou art my
confidence, whose heart is over affected uith his wealth, and
flusht uith secret rejoycings that his hand hath gotten much;
But, saith Job, I did not so much as rejnce because my mealth mas
great, Mr. Bronghton translates, If I Toyed that my nealth grem.
Wealth, in some mens hands especially, is a grouing thing, it
groues like a plant, it shoots forth buds and blossomes from day
to day, like a tree planted in a fruitfull soyle, and by the waters
side. Job was a growing man in wealth as wel as in Grace, but
this larter growth, not the former, was the matter and occafion
efhis joy.
Egjycirg

0535.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition upon the Bocke of JOE. Verf.25.

body.t: Rejoycing is the opening or dilatation of the heart upon the
receiving of some present good. (That which causeth joy must be
good, and a good thing present; for if it be absent how good so¬
ever it is, it only causeth hope, or ifit cause joy it is because our
hope is so strong and lively, thatit gives a kind of present fruiti¬
on or enjoyment. As sorrow straightens and shutts up the heart,
so joy unlocketh and enlargeth it. If I rejoyced because
my wealth was great:
The word which wee translite mealth, signifies properly,
strength, or, power; and so by a metonymie of the effect, riches
and wealth, because much of a mans strength, of his civill strength
consists in wealth or riches; A wealthy rich man is a powerfull
man; wealth doth great matters in the spheare of this world;
therefore the Scriptures Elegantly expresse riches and strength
by the same word. Tis also rendred Substance ( Mich: A. 13.)
We usually call a wealthy man a substantiall man, or a man of
substance. If I rejoyced because my mealth
was great.
Ieis not so much the thing as the degree of it that causeth re¬
joycing, if a man have but a litle of that which is good, or no
more then will just serve his turne, he doth not rejoyce much,
yea he scarse rejoyceth at all; but when the good which he en¬
joyeth is great, his joy is great. Wealth put alone notes a great
quantitie of worldly goods, much more Great wealth. When
there is much good in the hand, then usually there is much joy in
the heart. Therefore saith Job, If I rejoyced because my wealth
mas great; though I had the greatest occasion and temptation to
rejoyce in vealth, yet I did not; l was possessed of no small mat¬
ters, I was not among the middle sort of rich men, but with the
highest, yet I rejoyced not in my riches.
For the clearing of this protestation against rejoycing in
wealth, it may be demanded; Is it not lanfull to rejoyce in the
gond things of this life? especially in the abundance of the good
things of this life? and doth not lob speake more of himselfe then
is proper to man, or was ever found in a mortall man ? is it possi¬
ble that a man (who enjoyes the use of his reason) should have
vealth, and great wealth, and yet be insencible ofit? or not to
be affected with it?

0536.head: Chap. 31. Au Exposition upon the Becke of JOB. Verl. 25.

body.t: I ansuer, Job doth not pretest against all manner, nor against
all degrees of Joy: for
First, "Tis naturall to man rorejoyce in that which is good,
in any kinde of good; as it is naturall to man (as man) to desire
that which is good; so it is naturall to man ( as man) to re¬
joyce in that which is good. Joyes run to the same length with de¬
fires.
Secondly, We finde that God himselse requires rejoycing,
not only in spirituall, but even in outuard good things. When
the Lord commanded the Children of Israel to bring their sacri¬
fices and holy offerings to the place which he should chuse to put
his name there, even unto his habitation, he there required them
not only to rejoyce in his service and in their soule mercies, but
in their riches and bodyly mercies ( Deut. 12 5, 6,7.) There ye
fhall eat before the Lord your God, and you shall rejoyce in all that
you put yeur hand unto, yon and your houshold, mherein the Lord thy
God hath blessed thee. The things which they put their hands unto,
were their worldly labours and bufinesses, the Lords blessingup¬
on those labours gave them an encrease of worldly wealth; This
blessing they must receave and use with rejoycing.
Thirdly, Joy in outward good things, is a part of that praise
and thankfullnes (and so of that worship) uhich is due and must
be pay'd unto God. He reckons himselfe dishonoured and neg¬
lected, if we receave so much as a morsell of bread with a soure
face, or with a sullen spirit; vea he would haue us chearfull, and
rejoyce in the least outward comforts, which he bestowes upon
us. Now if it be a part of our duty to reioyce in the smallest por¬
tion of temporal mercies, why doth sob so earnestly disclaime re¬
joycing in the greatest? or wherein doth the sinfullnes of rejoy¬
cing in wealth, in great wealth confist?
I answer, rejoycing in woridly wealth, great or little, is not
good.
First, When we so rejoyce in it, as that we sit downe, acqui¬
esse and rest init; All resting joy in the creature is a moving or
going away from God. Such was the joy of the rich man (Luke
12.19.) who when his grounds brought forth plentifully, and he
had prepared great barnes to bestow his fruits and goods in, sayd
to his soule, Thou hast much goods laid up for many yeares, tabe
tbine ease, eat, drinhe and be merry; sit downe here, thou art wel,

0537.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Book ef IOB. Vers.25.

body.t: thou art in a warme place, in a good house; when our soules rest
in corporall enjoyments, this is sin¬
Secondly, “Tis sinfull to rejoyce in wealth, in the greatest
wealth, boasting of it, as a piece (at least) of our happines and
glory. Thus tis reported of Haman (Esth:5.11, 12.) who, when
he came home from Court, called his friends, and Zeresh his mife,
and told them of the glory ef his riches, and the multitude of his chil¬
dren, and of all the things wherein the King had promoted him, and
hom he had advanced him above the Princes and servants of the
King. Haman said moreover, yea Ester the Queene aid let no man
come in with the King into the banquet that she had prepared, bat
my selfe, and to morrem am I invited unto ber also by the King.
Such rejoycing as this eyther in wealth or honour with men, is
one of the surest signes of a heart estranged from the things and
wayes of God. They know not what favour with or by Christ
meanes, who can thus glory in the favours or cry up themselves
the Favourites of the greatest carthly Princes.
Thirdly, “Tis sinfull to rejoyce in wealth as our good, riches
are called our goods, and they are good things, but take heed of
making them your good, as they did, and there were many of them
(Plal.4. 6.) who sayd, who will shew us any gœd? what was that
good which they would so faine be shewed ? It mas Corne, and
wine, and eyle; therefore David saith ( at the zth verse) Thou
hast put Joy into my heart more then in the time when their Corze
and wine encreased. Though corne and wine were good things,
yet holy David would not call them his good, though gold and
silver are your goods, yet woe to them who say they are their
good. We must make nothing our good but God, and the things
of God; there is a holy skill in a believer, he can critically distin¬
guish bet ween his goods and his Good.
Fourthly, So to rejoyce in wealth or in riches, as to forget,
yea or to abite our rejoycing in God, All such rejoycing is not
only vaine but abominable. The greatest joy which a godiy man
takes in his greatest wealth, doth not lessen but highten and en¬
crease his joy in God. The best advantage which he makes of
what God gives him of this world, is to rayse up his soule in the
praises of God David takes notice (Psal. 10.3, 4.) that when
the wicked boasteth of his hearts defire ( and what is the desire of
his heart? Surely his riches; for as it followeth in the same verse.

0538.head: Chap.31. An Exposttion upon the Bock of JOR. Verl. 25.

body.t: he blesseth the coveteus mbom God abhorreth, when l say, he boast¬
eth of his hearts desire) God is not in all his thoughts, that is, God
is not at all in his thoughis. He rejoyceth so much upon a world¬
ly account, that he hath no joy left sor God, or he quite forget¬
teth and leaves God out in his rejoycings. The people of Israel
had a severe caution given them (Deut. 6. 10, 11, 12.) And it
shall be mhen the Lord thy God shas have brougbt thee into the Land
which he smare unto thy fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Ja¬
cob, to give thee great and goidly Cities mhich thou buildedst not,
and houses full ef all good things, nhich thou filledst not, and xells
dig ged mhich thou diggedst net, Vineyards and Olive trees mhich
thou plantedst not; when theu hast eaten and art full, then bemare
that thou forget not the Lord mhich brought thee ferth out of the
land of Egypt, from the house of bondage, As if the Lord had sayd
by Moses, Let not contentment and delight in the good things
which I shall give you to eate, eat out your thoughts of and de¬
lights in me, who am the giver of all these good things. Here's
thy danger & thy snare, lest when thou art come to great wealth,
thou shouldest forget the great God who made thee vealthy.
Fisthly, “Tis much more sinfull to rejoyce in wealth, in great
wealth, when we so rejoyce in it, as not only to forget God, but
to rebell and kicke against him. And indeed as to remember God
and obey him is the same thing in Scripture sence; So they who
forget God are very neere rebellion against him. ( Deut. 32.15.)
Jeshurun maxed fat and Ricked; thou art waxen fat, thou art
gromne thiche, thou art covered mith fatnes; Then he forsocke God
mhich made him, and lighily estecmed the rocke of his salvation;
they provohed him to jealousie with strange gods, &c. Jesburun sig¬
nifies righteousnesse or uprightness. A Tirle most sutable to the
duty of I/rael, who ought to be an upright and righteous people.
But they proved ( when wealthy ) like fatted oxen (to them also
the word in sound is applicaole, and some conceave that Moses
useth it on purpose to give them a close reproofe, I say when Is¬
rael grew wealthy uhich was their fatnes, then like fatted oxen)
they kicked against God who had fed them; that is, they rebel¬
led against the Commands and wayes of God, they refused the
rule of cuty for his worship, and made them new gods; thus
they reioyced in their owne greatnets with neglect of the great¬
ness of God.

0539.head: Chap. 31. An Expositiou upou the Book of JOB. Vers.25.

body.t: Sixthly, So to rejoyce in wealth as by our wealth to make
provision for our lusts, or (as it were) to let out our wealth to
the use of any lust is very sinfull; All such rejoycing the Apostle
forbids (Rim. 13.ult.) Make no provision for the flest, to fullfill the
lusts thereof. Godly men provide for their necessities, wicked men
Iay up and lay out for their lusts.
Seventhly and lastly, any such rejoycing in wealth as doth but
abate the edge, and allay the sweetnes of our Joy in God is sin¬
full; and that’s it which Tob here disclaimes; he did not so re¬
joyce in his worldly wealth as to lessen his heavenly joy. His joy
in riches was a poore joy compared with his joy in God; His joy
in God was above and eonquered all his other joyes.The Church
(Psal. 137.6.) preferr'd Jerusalem before her chiefe foy. The
Godly Jewes in captivity could have rejoyced, and did in the re¬
storing of their civil liberties and priviled ges; but they made fe¬
rusalem their chiefest joy; And why was Jerusalem their chiefe
joy? Surely by Jerusalem they intended their spirituall liberties
and priviledges; the chiefest of which was their freer and fuller
enjoyment of God in his holy Ordinances and appoyntments for
publicke worship. Now when Tob saith, I rejoyced not because my
mealth mas great; it is as if he had sayd, My greatest Joy in world¬
Iy things was not so much as my least Joy in spirituall things, or the
highest of my carthly joy mas lower then the lowest of my heavenly
joyes. Yea his greatest joy in his great wealch uas in that respect
so litle, that he could safely professe he did not at all rejoyce init.
Tob was doubtlesse very thankfull for, and sencible enough of the
favour of God in bestowing such great wealth upon him, yet the
sence which he had of the favour of God in bestowing grace and
salvation, yea and himselfe upon him, did even swallow the re¬
membrance of, and so the joy which he tooke in all other fa¬
vours. If Irejoyced because my mealih mas great.
Hence observe.
First, Man ù api enoughte rejoyce in worlaly vealib.
Were it not so,it had not not been worth the while for Job to
have protested that he did not. Wee have a naturall bent to re¬
joyce in what is pleasing to nature, therefore in riches, which sur¬
nish nature with all varieties of pleasures and contentments; yea
sinfull nature is best pleased with those things which are worst,

0540.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition upon the Booke ef JOB. Vers.25.

body.t: and to rejoyce in that uhich should be the object of our hatred,
and will be (if consented to) the matter of our forrow, sinfull
sordid sensuall pleasures. O how ready are our hearts to open at
the first knocke of worldly delights of any kinde! Indeed the
world is neer of kin to man, even to a great part of the best men;
the comforts of it fit us well, and we can tast and relish them sa¬
vourly; and therefore it is no marvell that our Joyes run out af¬
ter them till grace puts a stop upon them and mortifies them, or
turnes them into another channel.
Secondly, For as much as Job doth not protest against all joy
(as hath been explain'd) but against Immoderate exc. ssive and
Irregular Joy.
Obferve.
Secondiy, That our Toy about tartbly thiugs doth usualy ex¬
ceed and goe out ef Compesse.
Wee are quickly more taken with the world then ’tis worth;
and as we are apt to rejoyce in what we ought not (missing our
object) so (missing our measure) to re joyce in œhat we may, more
then we ought. The world is too narrow for our passions; wee
soone over-sorrow che vorst thirgs which the world can inflict,
and we as soone over-joy the best things which the world can af¬
foard. Christ perceived the heart, of his Disciples transported
too farre in rejoycing at their conquests over evill spirits. For
having called, commission'd, and sent out his twelve Apostles to
subdue & bring in the Jewish Nation to the acknow ledgment of
and faith in bim, at the óth Chapter of the Gospel of Luhe; He at
the first verse of the tenth Chaprer prepared and sent out a band
of seventy Auxiliaries to profecute and advance the same blessed
designe. And to shew that the ueapons of their warfare were
not carnal, but mighry through God, these returning, report the
successe of their expedition, and shew Christ the trophyes of their
victory (v. 17.) Lord even the Devills are subject to us through
thy Name. Yea ( saith Christ) I know it to be so, yours is no
vaine boast, I my selfe can beare you witnes, the effects of your
ministry have been very great in mine eye ( v. 18) I bebeld Sa¬
tan libe lightuing fall from heaven. And because they had manna¬
ged their Commission so well, Christ enlargeth it at the Iorh
verse; Behold Igive yon pomer te tread on Serpents and Scorpierse,

0541.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition upon the Booke of JO». Vers25.—

body.t: and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing suall by any meanes
hurt rou. Now Christ (who knowes the measure and temper of
every spirit ) fore-seing that his Disciples might be over-joyed
with the thought of those past and these promised victoryes and
conquests (which were indeed greater then all the Casars and
Pompeys in the world ever attained unto, he, I say, fore-seing
this ) gave them an allay, by counsel and caution ( v. 20.) Not¬
mitbstanding in this rejoyce not, that the spirits are subject unto you,
but rather rejoyce in this, that yeur names are mritten in heaven.
Where he at once corrects or checks the suspected excesses of
their joy, for victoryes gained over evill spirits, and directs them
to rejoyce in that wherein there could be no excesse, their hopes
of & interest in eternal glory. Now if good men are apt to exceed
in their rejoycings about some priviledges which are of a spiritu¬
all nature (such is that gift of power over evill spirits) surely then
carnal men cannot stop their joyes from exceeding, and godly
men are very prone to exceed in rejoycing about earthly things.
How seldome is it that we rejoyce in spirituall things? wee can
hardly bring our hearts to any due hight or heate of holy joy,
And O how over. soone doe our hearts over-act their joy in tem¬
porall things! When we rejoyce in God, we rejoyce as it we did
not, we rejoyce but faintly, narrowly, sorrily; yea while we are
in the flesh we can never rejoyce enough in spirituall things, only
this is our comfort, that in heaven we shall re joyce in God, and
in God alone, and as we can never rejoyce too much in him, so
then we shall rejoyce enough in him; our joy shall then be full,
and we shall rejoyce our fill in God.
Thirdly, In that Job disclaimes all inordinate rejoycing in his
great wealth,
Observe.
To rejoyce much in the best or greaust of morlaly thingr is
greatly sinfull.
The least of our affections is enough for the greatest good
which this world yeelds. Nor is any thing of this world to have
any thing of our affections, but in a subserviency and subordina¬
tion unto God. The Apostle gives us excellent eounsel for the
moderating of our joyes about, and the drawing off our desires
from creature enjoymente (2 Cor. 7. 30, 31.) The time ù sert

0542.head: Chap. 31. As Exposition upon the Book of IOR. Verl, 25.

body.t: brethren, it remaineth therefore, that they who rejoyce be as if thoy
rejeyced not. So to doe a thing as if we did it not, is to doe it so
litle that we can scarse discerne whether it be done at all or no.
The Apostle doth not totally forbid that joy, but regulates it;
he would have us rejoyce in the good things of this life, yet so,
as it may appeare we are dead to them. And if wee consider
weatth, the greatest worldly weslth in its utmost worth, we have
reason enough to be so. For,
First, as to its matter and extraction 'tis of the earth; Second¬
Iy as to its acquisition and attainment, tis troublesome to get it;
Thirdly, when we have gotten it, new troubles and cares are be¬
gotten by it; Fourthly, the utmost use and enjoyment of it is but
for the short time of this life, and why should we rejoyce much
in that at any time, which we can enjoy but a litle time. Fifthly,
joy in wealth produceth many dangerous effects, unlesse it be wel
tempered and corrected through grace. For,
First, it steales the heart away from better things; while we
feed too heartily upon earthly things, and drinke large draughts
at the cisterne of the creature, we litle minde ( if we doe not for¬
sake) the fountaine of living waters ( Ter. 2. 13) much friend¬
ship and familiarity wich the world, breeds an estrangement be¬
tween God and the soule, the more we converse with creatures,
the lesse fellowship we have with Christ: and then he is jealous
ofus, that ue have found out other lovers, and are growne wan¬
ton with our wealth. This is spirituall Adultery, and a going a
whoring from God The Apostle James calls it so expressely
(Chap. 4.3, 4.) Te asbe and receave not, bicause ye ashe amisse,
that ye may consume it upon your lusts. Te Adulterers and Aaul¬
teresses know ye not &c. The Adulterer cares not for his wise, and
the Adulteresse is estranged from her oune husband, she regards
not his company, And thus when the heart is taken with the
beauty and glitter of the world, it is estranged from God.
Secondly, Such Joy in great uealth blomes up the heart with
vaine ostentation and swells it with pride, nothing keepes the
cheart so low as Joy in the highest things; and Joy in low things,
or in things below, sets the heart on high. Here's a strange con¬
trariety of effects; low things make the heart proudly high;
and high things make the heart graciously low.
Thirdly, Inordinate worldiy joy make, the heart like the
world,

0543.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition apon the Booke of JOE. Verl.25.

body.t: world, foule and uncleane. The world is corrupt, and it corruprs
those who lust after it (2 Pet. 1. 4.) They who re oyce much
in the world lust aster it, and such cannot escape the eorruption
that is in the morld through lust.
Fourtbly, Joy over-acted upon the world deads the heart to
all spirituall actings and quencheth the Spirit. The fire of world¬
Iy joyis as water cast upon the holy Spirit, and upon our graces;
O how deadly cold is the heart of a man to heavenly thines
when once he is heated with rejoycings about the things of the
earth!
Fifthly, Immoderate Joy about earthly things alwayes con¬
cludes in dissatisfaction, often in vexation; The world at best is
not good enough, and at most is not bigge enough to fill or satis¬
fie the minde of man; And still the greater our expect ations are
from the world, (they who rejoyce much in it, expect most from
it, now I say, the greater our expectations are) the greater are
our disappoyntments; Nothing vexeth more then disappoynt¬
ment: and they are most vexed with disappovntments about the
world, who have rejoyced most in it. So that we must say of world¬
ly Joy as Solomon doth (Pro. 14 13.) Even in such laughter the
heart is sorromfull, or if not, yet the end of that mirth ì heavi¬
nesse.
But some may say, how then shall we order our Joy? I uill
answer this querie, First, with respect to those who have more
then wealth to re’oyce in, Secondly, to those who have nothing
but wealth to rejoyce in.
To those who have more then wealth to rejoyce in, that is, to
godly men tvho are begotten againe unto a liv ly hope by the resur¬
rection of Christ frem the dead, to an inheritance incorruptible and
undefiled, to all such I say, let your joy about corporall and tem¬
porall things lead you to rejovce in those things which are spiri¬
tuall and eternall. Take occasion from your great wealth (if
your lot be there) to re’ovce in better and greater things then
wealch. The best improvement of the creature is, to make it a
staire or a ladder to ascend up to God by. And to get a sence of
better things then the earth hath any, is the best use we can make
of the good, of the best things we find on earth. Therefore as
Christ said to those whom he perceaved over- fearing he evills of
this lise, I nil suen you mhom you suas seare, seare bim, who nben

0544.head: Chap. 31. Au Exposition upon the Beoke of JOR. Verl. 25.

body.t: hee hath kild the body, can cast both soule and body into bell; So I
may say to those who find their hearts over-joy’d about the
good things of this life, I will shew you in whom and in what to
rejoyce; rejoyce in him, and in that which can advance both bo¬
dy and soule to heaven.
First, Rejoyce in God thorough Jesus Christ. we saith Paul
(Phil. 3. 9.) are the Circumcision mhich worship God in the spirit,
and rejyce in Christ Jesus and have no confidence in the flesp.
Secondly, Rejoyce in the meanes of knowing and enjoying
God by Jesus Christ. I was glad (faith David, Plal. 122. 1,2.)
mhen they sayd unto mee, let ns goe imotte heuse of the Lerd; Our
fette shall stand uithin thy gater O Jerusalem. In the house of God
the solemne worship of God was celebrated, there he manifested
himselfe to his people, and there they enjoyed his speciall pre¬
sence.» I'his made Davids heart more glad then all the wealth of
his kingdome. The Arbe of I/rael was therefore called and e¬
steemed the glory of I/rael by that good dy ing woman (I Sam.
4.21.) because it was, Furst, a type of the person of Christ; Se¬
condly, a pleoge of his presence with them, thirdly, a meanes of
enjoying him. And lurely what was the glory of Ifrael, was or
ought to have been the principall matter of their joy.
Thirdly, Re oyce in the grace of God, and in the fruits of his
Spirit. One dram yea a graine of grace, gives more cause of re¬
joycing then ten thousand talents, yea then ten thousand moun¬
taines of gold. What are the fruits of the carth to the fruits of
the Spirit? let the beholding and gathering up of those fruits
cause oy in you like the toy of harvest.
Fourthly, Re joyce in the favour and loving kindnesse of God,
That is better then life ( Psal. 63. 3.) how much more then the
good things of this life? When many spake of Corne and wine,
David tooke occasion to speake of the light of Gods Counte¬
nance, and to rejorce in it. Those beames of lighe which shine
from the pleased face of God upon the soule, will cause joyes
there unspeakeable and glorious.
Fifthly Rejoyce in the testimony of a good Conscience, that's
a continuall feast; and more pleasant then musicke at a banquet
of wine (2 Cor. 1. 12.) This is our rejycing, the Testimony of our
Conscience, that in simplicity and godly sinceritie mee have had eur
Conversatien in tue morld. To get and keepe a good Conscience,

0545.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Book ef IOB. Vers.25.

body.t: is more to be rejoyced in, then the getting and keeping the grea¬
test portions of this world. While a Conscience well informed
speakes us faire, we may sing for joy, though all men reproach
and rayle upon us.
Sixthly, Rejoyce in the hope of the glory of God! ( Rom.5.
2.) that hope is better then all your possessions; that goodnesse
which God hath wroughe for us is much to be rejoyced in, much
more that which he hath layd́ up for us.
Seventhly, Rejoyce that your names are mritten in heavin!
Luke 10. 20) That’s better then to have your names written
among the rich, or with the Honorable of the eartb.
Eighthly, Re joyce even in the Crosse of Christ, or in his
sufferings for you. Paul rejoyced so much in that, that he uith
highest indignation or disdaine, forbad the least motion of any
other Joy. ( Gal. 6. 14.) God forbid that I fould gl ry. save in
the Crosse of our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom (or mbereby) the morld
is crucified unto mee and I unto the world. The sorrows and suffer¬
ings of Christ for our sins, should at once wound our hearts wich
sorrou that we have sinned, and affect our hearts with joy, that
through his stripes we are healed of our sin-wounds.
Ninthly, Reloyce, as in the Crosse of Christ for you, so in
your crosse for Christ. How honorable is it to re joyce in suffer¬
ing for Christ, and in our conformity to Christ by suffering. Suf¬
fering for Christ is not every ones priviledge, ’tis given but to
some (Phil. 1. 29) And though suffering even for Christ be
grievous to the flesh, yet as Christ himselfe exhorts (Math. 5.12.)
we have reason to rejoyce and be exceeding glad, for great is our
remard in heaven. So those blessed ones did ( Heb. 10. 34.) who
tooke joyfully the sporling of their goods, knoming in themselves that
they had in heaven a better and an enduring substance. Many re¬
joyce at the encreasing of their goods and livelyhoods, but can
you re joyce in the spoyling ofyour goods and livelyhoods, yea
of your lives for (hrist? that’s joy worthy of a Christian.
Secondly, As for those who have nothing but wealth to re¬
joyce in, meere worldly men, who as they have a great portion in
the things of this life, so they have their whole portion in this life;
I may say to such, cease re’oycing that your wealth is great;
mourne rather for vour misery is great. Goe home and weepe
over your gold and silver, as the Apostle Tamer speakes (Chap.5·

0546.head: Chap.31. An Expofition upoa the Book of JOB. Verl. 25.

body.t: 1,2,3.) Goe to now yee rish men, meep and howle for the misery that
suall come upon you, your riches are corrupt, &c. You that have not
a God, nor a Christ, nor the pardon of sin to rejoyce in, how
can you rejoyce in riches which are corrupt, in gold and silver
which are cankered? The markes of divine displeasure are visible
upon all these en oyments, and will you rejoyce in them ? Nay
rather as the same Apostle counfels you (James A. 9.) Be af¬
flicted and neepe and mourn for your laughier shall be turned in¬
to mourning, and your joy into heavinesse. Tis better to turne your
mirth into mourning, then to have it turned into mourning. They
who turne their mirth into mourning, may finde comfort after it;
But they shall know nothing but mourning, u hose mirth is tur¬
ned into mourning. How sad is it for any to rejoyce for a day,
who are in a condition which tends to mourning for eternity?
Wealth which causeth such joy is perishing, and must shortly be
parted with; but sin unrepented of and unpardoned, which will
certainly produce sorrow, abides upon the soule for ever, and
therefore their sorrow must. That’s the meening of Christ
(Lube 6. 25.) Woe to you that laugh now, for ye sball mourue and
meepe; that is, you wbo laugh in the use or possession of outward
things, and have nothing esse, no grace, no Interest in Christ, no
favour wich God to rejoyce in, shall weepe at last and mourne
everlastingly. Sorron of heart, mithout change of heart, is the por¬
tion of sinners fer ever.
If Irejoyced because my nealth mas great.
Comparing this protestation of tob with that due Composure
of his spirit before spoken of ( Chap. 1.21.) when all was lost,
see there how he tooke it? Naled came I out ef my mother¬
momb, and naked shall I returne; the Lord giveth, and the Lord
taketh away, blessed be the name of the Lord.
Hence note.
They who die not rejoyce much in the possession of worlaly things,
mill xot grieve much at the losse ef them¬:
The reason why sob had such an admirable spirit of moderati¬
on in his sorrow about worldly things, was because he had such
an admirable spirit of moderatiõ about his joy in worldly things;
he never rejoyced much in having them, therefore he never sor¬

0547.head: Chap.31. An Expofition upon ths Bock of IOB. Vers.25.

body.t: rowed much in loosing them. The Apost le puts these two toge¬
ther (1 Cor. 7. 30.) Rejoyce as if yee reiyced not, and weep as if
yte wept not; As if he had sayd; if when these thingt of the world
are taken from you, you would not be oppressed with forrow,
but weep as if you wept not; then, while you hold them rejoyce
as if you rejoyced not. Sorrow will break their backs, yea their
hearts, who see that taken from them, with which themselves
vere over-much taken. We are alwayes afflicted with the pas¬
sion of forrow in parting with any thing, preportionably to our
passion of joy in holding it. If Irejoyced because my mealih mas
gecat,
And because my band had gotten much.
This close of the verse is very remarkable, some rejoyce not so
much in uealth because they have it as because they have got it,
or because cis of their oune fetching in, They more value a les¬
ser estate attain'd by their own Industry, policy, and contrivances,
then a greater de cended to them by inheritance from their An¬
cestors. What is of our oune gaining, is naturally more pleasing
to us then what is of other mens giving. Wee often heare rich
men acknowledging, they had no great matter to begin with,
but this they glory in, their hand hath gotten much. Such will
say of that or’tother rich man, his father was borne before him,
that is, he hath his estate by descent, his hand hath gotten litle.
And therefore it argues a further spirituallnesse in this holy man;
that as he rejoyced not in wealth conveyed to him by his fore¬
fathers, so not in his owne greatest acquirements of wealth, that’s
the scope of these words; If Irejo, ced
because my hand had getten much.
The hand is the great Instrument of action; yet wee need not
understand it, that Job got his estate by hand labour, hee was a
Magistrate, a man of great power and place, but that is sayd to
be gotten by the hand, which is any way gotten by our diligence.
All that we get may come under this title, gotten by the hand.
Thus Solomon speakes ( Eccl: 9. 10.) Whatsoever thy hand find¬
eth to doe, dot it mith all thy migbt. Head.-worke or wit-worke, is
hand-worke in Solomons sence as wel as any other worke. Moses
(Levit 25. 47.) puts the morke of the hand for all kind of worke.
The Hebrew of fobs text is, Because my hand hath found much.

0548.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Bosbe ef JO s. Vers.25.

body.t: So (Psal. 21. 8. Isa. 10.10.) If I rej-yced because my hand had
found or goiten
much.
The word notes a masse or weight of wealth. The Septuagint
translate, If I put my hand to the getting ef innumerable wealth;
As if the meaning were, that he bounded his desires in getting
wealth. Some put their hands yea their hearts to the gatherirg
of innumerable riches; they would be rich without all bounds.
They never thinke they have enough, and therefore they wou d
be alwayes getting more; As the Prophet saith (Hab. 2. 6.) How
long? So we may say, Hom much? No man knowes. The Scho
liast saith, Job did not put his hand to innumerables, because he set a
Iimit to his desres in getting riches; and mhatsoever was beyona
that, he distributed it to the poore. This is a good sence, but I ra-
ther kcepe to that of our owne reading, which doth not make
these words a new protestation, but a highting of that in the for¬
mer part ot the verse. As if he had sayd, Thouph Inot only hgd
much riches, but made my selfe rich, yet I did not rejoyce in it.
Hence note.
First, Much diligence and activitie in any hind, puts us in a
prebable may for the getting ef much.
As sloathfulluesse tends to the loosing of all, so d’ligence to the
getting of much; The diligent hand mabeth rich, that is, there
is a great advantage in diligence toward the attainement of
riches.
Secondly, In that s'b disclaimes his rejoycing in riches as got
by his own hand; He indeed used diligence in getting riches, but
he would not take notice of them as gotten by him.
Hence note.
I is sinfull to ascribe our gaines to car own getting.
They vho doe so, put themselves in the place of God, as if they
were aple to give an Issue to their own Endeavours, and make
them successefull. Whereas (Psal. 127. 1, 2,3.) Except the
Lord build the house they labour in vaine that build it; Except the
Lord beepe the Citie the watcheman maketh in vaine. It is vaine
for you te rise up early, to sit ap late, to eate the bread ef sorrews.

0549.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition upon the Becke ef JOR. Vers.25

body.t: There is a vanitie, that is, a successlessnesse in all that we put our
heads or hearts or hands unto, till God breathes a blessing upon
us. We build in vaine, and watch in vaine, and labour in vaine,
if God with hold or uith-draw his blessing. I (laith Solomon,
Eccl: 911.) returned and sam under the Sun, that the race is not
to the frrift, nor the battel to the strong, neither yet bread to the mise,
nor riches to men of understanding, nor favour to men of sbill, bat
time and shance hapneth to them all; that is, they are under the
over-ruling and all disposing hand of God; W’hich gives such il¬
sues to mens undertakings as himselfe pleases, not such as they
purpose and intend, so that they seeme to fall out rather casually
then answerabiy to those meanes, which have been us'd and man¬
nag’d with the greatest probability in order to their attainement.
Therefore let no man glory in man, how swist, how strong, how
vise. how understanding, how skillsull soever, for no man is able
to assure the effect of what he engageth in or goeth about. He
that thinkes he can doe any one thing effectually, assumes his pri¬
viledge who alone doth all thinge.
Thirdly, Observe.
Carnall or naturall men ascribe their mealth to their omn get¬
ting mere then to the blessing ef God.
When a godly man hath got much in the world, and hath been
very industrious in getting it, when the issue of his la bours riseth
not only up to, but exceedes his expectation; he saith ( as Peter
uhen he had heal’d the Creple) why stand yee locking upon mee,
as if Iby my omn power had got this wealth. When others admire
his successe, he puts it back, with a why doe yee take notice of
mee, as if my wit, my policy, my cunning, my industry, my hand
had done this. I know some are forward enough to ascribe that
to the blessing of God, which they have more reason to charge
upon their own sin, and indirect dealing, upon their injustice and
unrighteousnesse; take heed of fathering such riches upon the
blessing of God. Many are rich by common providence; God
lets them prosper in their sin as a punishment of their sin. Only
they who thrive by righteousnesse may say of their wealth as Ja¬
ccb of his Children, This is that mealth mhich God hath graciousty
given us. Now as some are rich by the grace and favour of God;
lo none are rich but by the leave of God. There are many witty,

0550.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the BoR of IOB. Vert. 25.

body.t: politick and painfull men that could never get riches by their ut¬
