hatb been secretly Enticed, or tempted mith the faire beautie ef toe
Sun and Moone; if I have been seduced with a vaine or easie Cre¬
dulity, to put the Sunne or Moone in the place of God, and tO
give them reverence, this were a grosse iniquity. As children are
enticed with a nut, or an apple, vith a bable or a toy, so are su¬
perstitious persons. What are Idols but toyes and bables, fitter
by farre for children to play with, then for men to worship; nor
are any children (upon a true account) so childish and toyish
as the most aged and serious Idolaters; And indeed the more se¬
rious any are at it, the more childish they are at it. Job protests
against all such levity, If my heart hath been Enticed, if I have
been taken with the goodly appearances, with the shining and
glittering outside of these excellent Creatures, Sun and Moone,
then &c. Is my heart hath been Enticed
in sicret.
The heart of man, even of every man is a secret, 'tis a peculiar
Dddd

0573.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Booke ef JOP. Verf.27.

body.t: to God alone, and theresore it might seeme enough to have said,
If my heart hath been Enticed, but Job adds, If my heart hath been
Enticed in secret, that is, if my heart hath been enticed to worship
the Sun or Moone secretly. God is to be worshipped not only
publiquely but secretly. So the words stand in oppofition to open
or profes't Idolatry. There is a two fold secrecy of worship,
whether true or false.
First, When it is acted wholly in the heart; as there is adul¬
tery in the heart, and theft in the heart, so there is Idolatry in the
heart, which never appeares out wardly at all; that’s one way of
secret worship, when we worship in the heart only.
Secondly, Worship performed by an outward voyce or ge¬
sture, may yet be in secret too, that is, out of the sight and view
of others, in a private place or Closet; as Christ saith ( Math. 6.
6.) Wuen thou prayest enter into thy Closet, and when thou hast shut
thy doore, pray to thy father nhich is in secret, &c. There is a se¬
cretnesse of place as well as of spirit in worship, God seeth secret
heart worship (which we may give him every where) and he se¬
eth secret-place-worship which the eye of man seeth not. The
Lord Calls Extkiel (Chap:8.7.8.) to behold the Idolatry of that
people committed in this kinde of secrecy, they were not only
Idolaters in the secret of their hearts Cor hearty Idolaters) but
in secret places. And he brought me to the docre of the Court, and
xhen I lonked beheld a deore in the wall; Then said he unto me, Sou
of man, dig nom in the vall, and mhen I had digged, behold a doore
(they were immur’d, they were shut up) and he sayd unto me, got£
in, and bebold the miched abiminations that they det here; So I went
in and san &c. Then said he umto me (V. 12.) Son of mau, hast
thou seen mhat the Ancientt of the house ef Israel doe in the darke?
Every man in the Chambers of his Imagery, for they say, the Lord
seeth ns not. When Job saith, If my heart hath been secretly euti¬
ced; we may take it both wayes, If I have been enticed to Idola¬
trous secret heart. worship, or secret place worship, where there
was none to see mee, &c.
Hence observe; First.
Idolatry begins at the heart.
As Christ saith (Math. 15.19.) Out of the heart proceed evil
thoughis, murtbari, Adulieries, blasphemies (which are highest

0574.head: Chap.31. Au Exposition upon the Bok of Ies. Verl. 27.

body.t: dishonours put upon the true God) so I may say Idolatryes
(which are honours put upon false Gods) proceed out of the
heart also. Thus the Law spake to the Jewes ( Deut. 11. 16)
Tahe heed to your selves, that your heart be not deceaved, and ye
turne aside, and serve other gods, and morship them. Though the
occasions ot sin may be from without, or before us, yet the
source and originall of it is in the heart. When the Prophet Isaiah
had at large described the folly and madnesse of Idolaters in the
44th Chapter, from the oth verse inclusively to the zoth verse, he
concludes He feedeth of ashes, a deceaved heart hath turned him¬
afide, that he cannot deliver his soule, nor say, is there not a lie in my
right hand? Idols give a great provocation to the eye, as was
shewed before, but they can doe us no hurt till the heart be
catcht and infected by them.
Secondly, Observe.
Man is not forced, but coz ened, enticed, and flattered into sin¬
full, especially into Idolatrous wayes.
The Apostle James saith (Chap. 1. 14.) Let no max say when
he is tempted I am tempted of God, for every man is tempted mhen he
is drawne away of his omne lust, and enticed. “Tis lust in the heart
which draws away both eye and knee and hand to joyne wit h the
temptation. A godly man is not forced but perswaded and enti¬
ced tothat which is good ( so wee expresse it in the Margin of
Gen. 9. 27.) God shall perswade Japheth to duell in the tents of
Shem; hee shall not thrust him in by force, nor compell him by
Club-law ( as wee say) but his heart being toucht, as it were,
with that blessed Loadstone of divine love, shall freely receave
the faith of the Gospel, and follow Christ. Thus a wicked man
is not driven (though the Devil would be a Driver, and they must
needs run, whom the devill drives) but drawne to sin by the pre¬
vailing enticements of that lust which dwelleth in his heart, and
hath got the hand of him.
Thirdly, In that he saith, If my heart bath been secretly en¬
ticed,
Oblerve.
The most secret acti ef sin are both obvious to and odius in tbe
sight of God.
He feeth in fecret, and cannot but hate ( such is his holiness)
the
D dd d 2

0575.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Booke of JOR. Verf.2y)

body.t: the sin which he seeth; though evill be done out of the Eye of
all the world, yet it is naked and manifest in his sight, with whom
ve have to doe. The closest-heart sin is as cleare to God as that
which is written in the forehead, and ’tis as hatefull alwayes,
sometimes more; For though open sins as to the danger of In¬
fecting others are worse then secret sins, yet if wee consider the
spirit of the sinner, secret sins are the worst. How greatly doe
they provoke God who while they sin against him, would also
impose uçon him, so those Idolaters in secret hoped they should
Ezek. 8. 12.) when they sayd, God shall not see it, hee hath for¬
saben the earth: if wee can but keepe our selves from the eye of
man ( sayd they) ue need not feare the eye of God, we can easily
put a blind upon him. As he that hides his sin by not confessing
it, to he that thinks it hidden while he is committing it, shall not
prosper. A good deed the more secret it is, the better it is in the
sight of God; And an evill deed the more secret it is, the worse
it is in the sight of God.
Fourthly, In that Tob adds in the next verse ( supposing his
sin were secret) it mire an Iniquity to be punisped.
Note.
Secret fins shall not gue unpunisped.
A humane Judge can punish no sin but what is proved by wit¬
ness. Heart-iniquities fall not under any humane sentence. But
heart.fins the most hidden sins shall not escape a divine sentence.
As the most secret good workes done by man to man, and the
most secret holy worship of God, shall receave a reward from
God (Math. 6. 46.) When thou doest alms, let not thy left hand
Rnotp mhat thy right hand doth; that thine almes may be in secret:
And thy father mhich seeth in secret, himselse shall remard thet
epenly. And mhen thou prayest enter into tby Closet and sput thy
dosre, &c. and thy father that seeth in secret, he-shall reward thee
openly. Now, I say, as good, so evill workers in secret shall be re¬
warded (each in their kind) openly by God who seeth in secret.
Fifthly, Obferve.
The heart is specially to be loobed to in worship.
As we are not accepted by God in true worship, though we
draw neere to him with our lips, if our hearts are farre from him;

0576.head: Chap. 31. Aa Exposition upon the Beoke of IOB. Verl. 27.

body.t: Isa. 29.13. ( many give ourward worship to God, but there’s
no heart in it) so they are abominable in the sight of God who
draw neere to Idols with their hearts in false worship, though
their lips and knees be farre from them. I grant, God will not
beare it if we give so much as corporall reverence to Idols (as
Naaman the Assyrian seemed to desire a dispensation to doe in
the house of Rimmon, 2 Kings 5. 18.) though we professe to re¬
serve our hearts to him, But he will lesse beare it if we give our
hearts to Idols, though we refraine all corporall reverence. Out¬
ward acts alone or without the heart in false worship are abomi¬
nable in the sight of God, yet inward acts though alone or
without the body ly, are much more abominable. When we wor¬
ship God in secret places, and in the secret of our heart, we give
him the truest acknowledgement of his God head. God is most
honoured by Congregational or publick worship, but he is most
pleased with private worship, with private family worship, and
private Closet worship, yet with none of these without heart¬
worship which is the most private worship of all. When we at
once approve and powre out our hearts in secret, this is pure
worship indeed. And though we act no Idolatrous worship o¬
penly, yet if our heart be in it, his soule abhorres us. Outuard
false worship dishonours God most, but inuard false worship
displeaseth him most. Job was carefull to uorship God with his
heart both secretly and openly; and he was as carefull not to give
any secret, or heart-worship to Idolls, as he was to avoyd their
open worship; If my heart hath been secretly Enticed
And my mouth hath kissed my hand.
In these words Job denies the giving of any outward worship
to the Sunne and Moone; As if he had sayd, I have been so farre
from giving them my beart, that I'have not so much as givem them
my hand, or as some explaine it, with reference to the former part
ofthe verse, I never had any inuard heart motion, or it was ne¬
ver so much as in my thoughts to performe any outuard act of
adoration to the Sun and Moone. More particularly;
There is a three-fold Interpretation of this Clause, Mr. Brougl¬
ton renders the whole verse in connexion with the former, If I
admired the Sun when it sbined; and the Moene malking precious;
Tuat my beart mas closely dectaved; xo, my hand kissed my meuté,

0577.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Book ef JoB. Verf.27.

body.t: He gives his sence in this short glosse upon it, I stopred all Idola¬
trous speech of Star-worship: for mbich Babel bred confusion. As
if he had sayd, I have not so much as entertained dispute or chan¬
ged a word about false worship. One of the Rabbins taketh the
text in the same sence, as if Job had closed up his mouth with his
hand against all such discourses.
Secondly, Others following our translation give the sence thus;
If my hand hath bissed my mouth, that is, if l' have been urapped up
or amus’d in a silent wonder when I beheld the Sun and Moone.
The putting of the hand to the mouth hath been used as an Em¬
bleme of silence; and some silence is a kind of reverence or wor¬
ship. According to this interpretation, Job seemes to say, I have
not been struck silent with any admiration of the shining Sun or
of the Moone walking in brightness.
Thirdly, rather, as our reading imports, the words are a deni¬
all of any outward act of Idolatrous worship; and so the phrase
is used both in Scripture, and among ancient Authors. There is a
two-fold kissing; First, in way of salutation among friends and
familiars, Secondly, in a way of homage & submission, or at least
in a way of honour and respect towards superiors (Gen.41 40.)
Pharaoh saith tofoseph, Thou shalt be over my house, and according
to thy word shall all my people be ruled, or (as we put in the Margin)
be armed or kisse; that is, they shall submit to thy order and com¬
mands. Such was the kisse which Samuel gave Saul when he had
anoynted him King (1 Sam. 10.1.) Then Samuel took a viall of
oyle, and pomred it upon his head, and bissed him, and said, is it not
because the Lord hath anoynted thee to be Captaine over his Inheri¬
tance? As if he had sayd, I, by the Lords appoyntment, have an¬
noynted thee King, and in token of my subjection to thee as my
Soveraigne Lord, I have kissed thee. So (Pro. 24. 26.) Every
man spall kisse his lips that giveth a right ansuer; that is, every
man shall love, honour, and respect him. And to fhew that kis¬
sing implyeth subjection to Kings and Princes, the Kings and
Princes of the earth are commanded to bisse the Son ( Psal.2.7.)
with what kisse? not only vith a kisse of love and affection, but
with a kisse of homage and sub’ection; the Kings of the Earth
to whom all doe homage, even they must doe homage to Christ
the King of Kings. This kissing of the Son is opposed to the
breaking of his bands, and casting away his Cords from them in

0578.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Book of JOR. Verl. 27.

body.t: the beginning of the Psalme: and as this kissing doth note ho¬
mage, reverence, and respect in generall; so especially it notes
the reverence or worship given to Idols (1 Kings 19. 18) when
the Prophet Eliah Complained that there vere no pure wor-
shippers left, the Lord ansuered, Tet I have lest mee seven thou-
sand in Israel, all the hnees mhich have not borred unto Baal, and
every mouth mhich hatb not Rissed him. Baal as I shewed upon the
former verse was the Sun. So ( Hes: 13. 2.) And now they sin
more and more, and have made them molten Images of their silver,
and Idolls according te their omne understanding, ad of it the morbe
of the Crafismen: they say of them let the men that sacrifice Esse
the Calves ( that is, worship them ) in Dan and in Bethet.
Besides these Scripture evidences; severall of the Ancient
both Fathers and Historians make mention of this worship-ge-
sture. That is most remarkable which Minutius Fœlix reports
of Cæcilius, who locking upon the Image of Serapis ( signifying
the Sun) according to the use of the superstitious vulgar, he put
his hand to his lips and kissed it. And Tertullian directing his
speech to the Heathen, tells them, Most of vou, out of a devoti-
on to the heavenly bodyes, use at the rising ot the Sun to greece
it with a kisse. And because they were not able to reach the Sud
and Moone in the firmament, therefore they used to list up their
hands to them, and then put them to their mouthes in token
of Adoration, or that they receaved their breath and life from
them; and sometimes they did not kisse their hand at all, but only
drawing their lips into the forme of a kisse bowed themtelves.
But when they adored artificiall Idols or Images of any matter
made with hands, then they used to kisse the Image it selfe if it
stood within reach. Cicero in one of his Orations tells us how
The Brazen Statue of Hercules was had in so much vencration a-
mong the Agigentines a people inhabiting a Citie so called in Sici-
ly, that the opening of its mouth and chin, were much morne by
their frequent hissing of it when tbey came io morfbip. From all
these testimonies it appeares that the old heathen nations were
wont eyther to kisse the Idol it selse which they Adored, or as a
symbol and token of adoration to kisse their hands and make a¬
beysance towards it. And doubtlesse Tob had eyther seen or been
informed of the like custome in those elder times, aud therefore
by way of denyall sayd, If my month hath Rissed my hand.

0579.head: Chap.31. An Expositiou upon the Bock of JIOB. Vers. 27.

body.t: Hence note; First.
Outmard adoration of any Creature is finfull.
We may give reverence to men, but we must not adore them,
how great soever, how much lesse may wee adore sencelesse
things, whether naturall or artificiall. As wee must not give them
our hearts, so not our hands, not our mouthes. God requires the
heart especially in worship; but he must have our bodyes also.
When the Apostle calls to the worship of God, he expresseth it
by the body ( Rom. 12.1.) I beseech you brethren by the mercies
of God, present your bodyes a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable
unto God, mhich is your reasonable service, or (as some render it)
your fervice according to the word. As if he had sayd, If you
would worship according to the word, present your bodyes,
that is, your whole man, soule and body to God. Now where the
body only is exprest as the subject of worship, it implyes at least
that it must not be lest out in holy worship, nor allowed to any
false or Idolatrous worship. There is a generation who say they
serve God with their spirits, and then what though they be at
Idolatrous worship with their hodyes, and bow their knees to
Baal? what though their hand kisse their mouth, or they doe a¬
ny out ward act according to the custome of the place where they
are? so their hearts be with God; but God will have the hand as
well as the heart, hee will have the body as well as the soule de¬
dicated to him. As a prophane wretch once said, Ihave sworne
mith my tongue, bat I have reserved my heart uxsirorne. So some
goe to false worship with their bodyes, and say they will keepe
their heart to God. Let such remember that of the Apostle
(1 Cor. 6. 20.) Tee are bought mith a price, therefere glerifie God
in your body and in your spirit which are Godi. God is to be glo¬
rified in all our wayes, especially in his worship, with all that
which he hath redeemed or bought. Take heed of giving so much
as a kisse or a bow to Idolls. Many of the persecuting Heathens
in the primitive Church were satisfied if a Christian would but
take a litle frankincense and throw it upon their Altar; yet the
faithsul! professors of those times chose rather to die then to doe
any thing, though never so litle, which might carry the least sig¬
nification so much as by a meere externall act of complyance
with them.

0580.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition upon the Bocke ef Jo e. Vert. 28

body.t: Secondly, Note.
Superstitisn is very Ceremonisus.
Superstitious worfhip is a kind of Antick worship what bow¬
ings, what cringeings are used at it? how ridiculous are many at
it, while they weu d be thought most z alous? He that reades
the Popish ritualls might thinke they intended rather to ceurt it
and complement it with God, then humble themselves besore
him Or that they came to his worship rather to shew themselves
mannerly, then to be made more holy. The simplicity of the
Gospel, and the worship of God in spirit, knoues none of these
fashions, And the best acceptance which such uill find with God
vill be signified to them in that chiding Qyestion; Who requi¬
red thele things at your hands?
Vers. 28. This also were an iniquitie to be punisped by the
Iudge: for I sould have denied the God that is above.
In opening the 2oth verse, we have seene both the pronenesse
of mans nature to the sin of Idolatry, and the nature of Idolatry;
And in openirg the 27th verse, we have seene the manner how I¬
dolatry workes, both internally inticing the heart, and external.
ly by kissing the hand, or by outuard adoration, and prostration
ofthe body: In this verse job proceeds to fet forth the hainous
sinfullnes of ldolatry.
Verf.28. Thus also were an iniquitie to be punisbed by ihe
Judge, or, This is an iniquitie for the Judge.
There are three readings of these words.
First, Some conceave them only importing the sinfullnes of
this sinfull practice. So the Chaldee Parapurase, and so the Vul-
gar Latine: This is a grande or the greatesainiquitie. The Sep-
tuagint give the same sence, translating; And this verily is in mi
opinion the greatest sin: All these speake nothing at all of the pe-
nalnesse of the sin, or as it is a sin to be punished by the ludge,
but all three agree with one consent that Idolatry is a grievous
sinne.
A second reading also saith nothing of this sin, as a motter to
be punished by the Judge, but saith only, This is a Judged sin;as if
the meaning of fob were, This sin of Idolatry is in the Tudgemint
E ce e

0581.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition upen ths Becke ef JOR. Veri28

body.t: of many. if not of the mest, a very great wichednesse.
Thirdly, The Originall is translited strictly to the letter;
This is an iniquitie for the Judge; that is, as we supply the text,
This it an iniquitie to be punished by the Judge. Mr. Broughton
falls in with this reading; So this had been a sin to be judged, that
is such a sin at the Judge ought to take notice of, and to punish.
From these three readings of the text,I shall give you these three
notes or observations, and intend but to touch upon the two for¬
mer; my stay uill be upon the latter.
From the first, which makes these words signifie nothirg else,
but an apgravation of the sinsulnesse of ldolatry.
Observe.
Idlatry is a griat, a hainous, a grand iniquitie.
And it is so because it strikes so directly at God; As old Eli
sayd to his sons (I Sam: 2. 25.) If one man sin against anotber,
the Judge shall judge bim (the Hebrewis, The Gods shall judge
him, that is, The Magistrates shall judge him, who in Seripture
are called Gods) but if a man sin against the Lord, who suall en¬
treat for him? There is no sin which man commits against man,
but God is concerned in it, and wronged by it. But some sins are
committed immediately against God, and fly directly in his face,
among which Idolatry is a chiese one. Noy if a man sin against
the Lord, that is, presumptuoussy and knowingly, wbo shall entreat
fer him? that is, what man can mediate a reconciliation or make
upthe breach between man and the offended Majesty of God?
None but Christ can heale this breach; And to shew how excee¬
dingly God is offended and prophaned by Idolatry, yhe Scripture
calla it a provocation of the eyes of bis Glory (Isa. 3. 8.) which that
it referres to their Idol-worship is cleare from the zoth verse of
the second Chapter. There are many provoking sins, but we may
place ldolatry in the head of them. God cannot abide to behold
that sin, it is even a paine to the eyes of his glery, or to his most
glorious eyes. Can a husband endure to see his wife goe into the
embraces of a stranger? Idolatry is a going awhoring from God,
and an unchast follouing of other lovers. God is of purer eyes then
to behold auy iniquitie ( Hab. 1. 13.) There is no sin that hee
takes any pleasure in, least of all in Idolatry. How can hee with
patience behold that impurity wherein he sceth his owne glory

0582.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Bok o IO E. Vert, 28

body.t: darkned, his love slighted, and his name so immediately abu sed?
The Scripture calls it also an abominatien, which refers to the bur¬
densomeness of any thing to the stomacke; As Idolatry is a mott
unpleasant spectacle to the eye of God, sol’tis loathlome tobis
stomacke, he cannot beare it; His owne people the Jewes turned
his stomacke (as I may say) when they turned to it, and he spew¬
ed them out of his mouth for it. Idolatry is that Gall and urorm¬
mood, sçoken ot ( Deur: 29 18.) which how offensive they are
to the tast or palate every one knowes. Thus Idolatry is evtry
way offensive, it is a paine to the eyes of God, a burden to his
stomack, bitternets to his palate, all which are spoken in a figure
to set forth the greatnesse of this sin; and the Lords great dis¬
pleasure against it.
Besides, to shew how great this sin is, the greatest fins are in
Scripture but shadowed by, likened or compared to Idolatry;
wee cannot put a worser title upon any sin then to call it Idola¬
try; as if the sinfullnes of Idolatry were the measure of all other
sins; and as any sin comes neerer to that, so much the more sin¬
full it were (I Sam: 15. 23.) when Samuel reproved Saul tor
his halfe obedience ( which was indeed a non obedience, yca a
Rebellion ) in executing his Commission against the Amalekites,
he saith at the 23d verse; For rebellion is as the sin of mitch craft,
and stubbornnesse is as iniquitie and Idolatry. Saul did not pro¬
perly commit that sin of Idolatry, when he fayled in the executi¬
on of the command of God against the Amalekites, vet to sheur
the hainousnesse of that sin, Samuel told him, his Stubb rnisse
rat as iniquitie and Idolatry. As all those fins which are against
our neighbour, are summ’d up in that one sin of blood or mur¬
der (lsa: 1.15. Ezek 9 9) because that is the height of all the
evill that a man commits against, or can infl ct upon his neigh¬
bour; so that all impieties against God, are included in Idolatry.
And we find these two mentioned in one verse, as the heads to
which all the sins of jerusalem were reducible (Eztk. 22.2 3,4)
Nom thou son ef man, wilt thou judge, milt thou judge the blœedy
Citie: Tea tbou shult shew her all her abeminations; Then say ihou
tbus saith the Lord God, The City sheddeth blocd in the micst of it,
that her time may come, and maketh idols against her selfe to difile
her selfe. Thou art beceme guilty in thy blood that thou hast shed,
and hast di filed thy selse in thine Idils xtich thou hest made. Thus
Ido¬
E e e c 2

0583.head: Chap.31. An Expesition apon tbe Books of JOR. Verf.28.

body.t: Idolatry is macch with murder, being indeed a payre of match.
lesse sins; The one fighting in chiefe against God, the other a¬
gainst man.
From the second reading; Note.
Idolatry or creature worship is a practice mhich in all timez
hath been judged sinfull and miched :’tis a judged iniquitie.
In the worst ot times some have appeared against it. Gideon
uas called Jerub-baal ( Judg. 6. 32. ) because he cast downe the
Idolatrous Altar of Baal. In all times some lerub baals have ri¬
sen up and both pleaded and acted against Idol-worship. It were
easie both from Scripture as also from the history of the Church
to give an account that as in every age ldolatry hath found pa¬
trons and advocates, so opposers and impleaders, who have ac¬
eused, arraigned and judged it for one of the foulest abominati¬
ons: but to engage so farre in that way, would be out of mine.
From the third reading, Observe.
Idolatry is a sin, not only great in it selse, and which hath been
great in the account and judgement of Godly men in all ages,
But a sin which falls under the cognizance, and so under the
sentence of the fudge; this also mere an iniquitie to be punished
by the Judge.
I grant that those words, to be puuished br, are not expressed in
the Hebrew text, wbich is concise, according to the Idiom of that
language; and so gives it only thus; This also is an iniquitie for
the Judge. David spake in such a briefe ( Psal. 120.7) I am¬
peace, or I peace, that is, I am for peace, I am a lover and liker of
peace. So here, This also is an iniquitie for the Judge; that is,
Cas we render ) an iniquitie tobe punished by the Judge. This sup¬
plement or glosse is no corrupting of the text, ( as it hath been
over-boldly charged) but a faire exposition ofit.
Yet here a question ariseth about the Judge that is to punish

God the Judge of all men will judge and punish ldolaters. There
is no Question but ldolatry is a sin uhich God will judge, bar

body.t: whether it be a truth taken exclusively as to all other Judges, that
is a Question. God will punish Idolaters, and he will punish them

First, Job seemes to put it as a specialtie upon this sin ef Ido¬
latry beyond many other fins, that it is a sin to be punished by

cluding all otherJudges, then there is no more said of this sinthen
of any other. For God will judge all the sins of all men all the

ment, mith everz secret thing, mhether it be good, or mhetber it be e¬
vill; and as a Jusge he will punish the sins of all those u ho goe

punishment of that Judge; let the sin be what it will, let it be the

God will judge and punish that man for it eternally. So thut, I

petent with or common to any other sin whatsoever. Yet fob in

able by God, which yet neyther can nor ought to be punished by

on to take notice of.
Further, secondly, there are some sins punishable by man, of

(Heb. 13. 4.) Marriage is honourable among all, and the bed un¬
defiled, but mhoremongers and adulterers God nill Judge. And it

gainst that sort of sinners. Yet though God is spoken of in that
Scripture as the only Judge of whoremongers and Adulterers,

Thirdly. I conceave, fob gives a distinction of sins in this Chap¬
ter, uhereof some are purished by God alone, and others l'oth

body.t: by God and man; and so much the word Also at the heginning
of the verse seemeth to intimate, This also mere an in quitie to be

ges. Job passing from this sin to severall others, from all which

dolatry, This also is an iniquitie to be punished by the Judge. I have

I know some make the connection with the verse immediately

vetous, yet no man Enoues the heart, which is che proper seate

body.t: of covetousnesse. And if it were infallibly knoune that a man
were covetous, y et the civill Magistrate cannot punish any man

But there is no necessitie at all that those coupling or connect¬

tie to be punished by the Judge. And if wee peruse all the for¬

tioned (v. 39.) which, I suppose, will appeareupon examina¬

Por these reasons and considerations, I cannot incline to their
opinion, who restraine the Text, to God alone as Judge; though
no doubt God will most eminent ly judge this iniquitie of Idola¬

this;
It is the Magistrates dutie to punist Idolatry.
It is an iniquity to be punished by the Judge. As the great
Iudge in heaven will certainly doe it, so earthly Judges may and
ought to doe it. There are not a few (I know) who urge it as the
Magistrates duty to punish almost upon every dissent in religion,
and to drire men by his sword to an orthodoxnesse in opinion;
or that the Magistrate must draw his suord upon every one who
doth not comply with that which is publickly ouned for truth:
They would have all men who dissent from what is so held forth

body.t: tauglit not only as Gideon did the men ot Succotk, (Juëg S 16.)
mith the bryers and thornes of the wildernisse, but uith bonds and
imprisonment, with fines and confiscations, yea in some cases pu¬
nished with death. Such a spirit hath appeared even in chis age,
as was in Paul, when Saul (Act. 9. 1. ) breathing ouc threat¬
nings and slaughters against all who helieve not as they believe,
or who dissent from their opinion and pract ce, so mahing roome
or cutting a way for what they call religon into the heatts and

I ke an universall or wild toleration, for every one to doc and
speake, act and vent what they please in matters of religion, or
in the worship of God; so I doe as much dislike their universall
non-toleration, who say, the Magistrate must by force and power

renet, or what is generally owned within his dominion or Jurisdi¬
dtion.
And therefore I conceave that the matter ly eth between these
tuo extreames; and to give my owne sence upon the occasion
offered in this text, I shall take a litle Libertie beyond my ordina¬
ry way of exposition, to shew two things.
First, In reference unto all men, what they ought to doe in
case of difference from their brethren in opinion about the things
of God.
Secondly, What the Magistrate is to doe in that case.
First, For Brethren, I say, indifferency of spirit in matters
of saith and worfhip, as if it matter'd not, or were not worth
the while to stand uponit, what opinions, and perswasions men
are of, or what way of religion they are in, this, I say, is hatefull
to God, and should be the abomination of every good man Eve¬
ry man ought to pray and labour sor a spirit of disce ning about
and of zeale for the truths and holy appoyntments of God,
Secondly, The meanes which the Scripture holds out to all
for the reducing of erroneous persons, is to persuade and argue

(v.3.) Contend tarnest ly for the faith mhich mas once delivered
to the Saints; hec would have every one contend and contend
with all the weapons of this holy warre, which the authority of

strations, and divine reasonirgs, o consute and repell errors, and
Thirdly,
stop the mouth of Gaine- sayers.

0588.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Boobe ef JO B. Vert. 28.

body.t: Thirdly, The more pernicious any false doctrine or practice
in religion is, the more earnestly it ought to be contended against.
Thus farre every error in opinion and sinfull practice in worship,
should be judged by all men.
Further, as to the Magistrate, I shall lay downe these foure
Conclusions.
First, All those evill opinions, and heresies, which tend in
their owne nature to the disturbance of the civill peace and good
government of mankind, ought ro be suppressed by the Magi¬
strate, and the owners of them to be punished by all luch meanes
as are suteable to the conservation of the publick safety.
Secondly, All such opinions and erroneous doctrines as are
accompanied with any notorious sins in practice, (which sins are
also actually practiced by the followers and abetters of those o¬
pinions, like that of the Nicolaitans of old, or the Ranters among
us) tending to or teaching uncleanenes, and opening a doore for
lust and removing the ancient Land-markes of good and evill,
and so letting in a flood of wickedness. These, doubtlesse, the Ma¬
gistrate ought to take notice of, and to suppresse.
Thirdly, All professed Atheisme and open blasphemy against
God, ought to be punished by the Magistrate; I doe not say that
every opinion which hath blasphemy in it by deduction or re¬
mote consequences, but that which is bare-faced and professed
blasphemy against God, the Magistrate ought to punish. The rea¬
son is, because such cannot say that the Magistrate punisheth them
for their conscience, seeing they cannot so much as pretend con¬
science for what they say or hold; conscience being that po ver
of the soule, which hath immediate communion or converse vith
God and therefore suppoleth God to be, and to be such a one
as he hath ( according to their apprehension of him, though not
alwayes according to the truth of his beeing) revealed himselfe
to be :and therefore they who deny God to be, or blaspheme
him in his beeing, can never pretend any thing of conscience for
it. Conscience is a tendernesse to offend God, now for a man to
blaspheme God, and to professe atheisticall principles, this takes
away all colour of conscience in tendernes to offend God; and
how can he complaine that he suffers for his conscience, who
hath no conscience to suffer for?
Fourthly, That Idolatry u to be punisoed by the Magistrate,
Ffff

body.t: I need not goe any further for a proofe then the Text, though I
doe not restraine all punishable Idolatry to that particular way
mentioned in the text, the worshipping of the Sunne. Moone, and
Starres; but I say any !dolatry of that rank, and rate, is to be
punish d by the Judge. To cleare my meaning in this we may
distinguish of Idolatry.
First, There is Idolatry improperly so called; which is the
inordinate going forth of the soule to any creature, in love, in de¬
fire, in delight, in trust or confidence; this kind of ldolatry was
spoken of at the 24th verse; If I have made Gold my bope, or havs
said to the fine Gold, Thou art my corfidence. Thus the Apostle
(Eph: 5.5.) calleth a covetous man an Idolater. Now uhen I
soy ldolatry is a sin to be punished by the Judge, I doe not meane
this kind of Idolatry, which is so called in a metaphoricall sence,
though the fullnes of that si be in it in a spirituall way, yet that's
not the ldolatry here intended.
Secondly, There is Idolatry properly so called, and that is
two-fold.
Fist, The worshipping the true God by false meanes, or in a
wrong way, which is strictly the Idolatry of the second Com¬
mandement; Thou shalt net make to thy seife any graven Image,
&c. that is, thou shalt not worship God in a way of thy oune
devising: Though thou pretendest to worship the true God, yet
if thouuse meanes of thy owne to helpe on thy devotion, thou
art an Idolater. What the Magistrate may doe as to the punishi¬
ing of this sort of Idolatry, I shall not medle with it, seing it be¬
longeth not to this text.
Secondly, Proper Idolatry is the setting up, and worshipping
of a false God; This is, strictly, Idolatry against the first Com¬
mandement; And This is not only a worshipping of the creator
by the creature, but a worshipping of the creature for the crea¬
tor. Of this the Apostle speakes (Rom. 1. 25.) Mbo change the
truth of Gid into a lye, and morship and serve the creaturt more then
the creator, who is blessed for evermore. Some are of opinion that
there was never any Idolatry (especially not among the profes¬
sing people of God) but of the first fort, Ard that all their Idols,
even Baal and Afptaroth were only false meanes of worshipping̨
the true God; Yet I doubt not but there is an Idolatry spoken of
in Scripture, and used in the world, which is the setting up of the

0590.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon th Boct of Jo2. Vert.28.

body.t: creature for God; and of this Idolatry the text and poynt I am
upon is chiefely intended; If I beheld the Sunne mhen is shined,
or tut Moone walbing in brighintsse, &c. that is, if I have fallen
downe to these creatures, and given them adoration, then &c.
To cleareit a litle further, wee may distinguish of this Idolatry.
First, In its internall acts, when the heart is enticed.
Secondly, In its externall acts; when as fob saith, tbe mouth
kisseth the hand; that is, when by outward practices and prostra¬
tions towards the creature a man declares his worship ofit, or
that he attribute a divine pouer thereunto. Of the former ldo¬
latry, that of the heart, the Magistrate can have no proofe, and
therefore cannot punish it. But when Idolatry holdetb up its
head avowedly, then the Magistrate may and ought to take no¬
tice of it, and punish it. That the Magistrate did punish such Ido¬
latry among the Jewes is without controversie, the Law is ex¬
presse for it (Deur: 13. 6,7, 8, 9, &c. to the sixteenth verse)
when any man sayd, Come let us goe serve otber Geds, he mas to be
stoned mith stones till he dyed. And that the Magistrate may punisti
fuch kind of Idolatry at this day, besides the authoritie of this
text. Wee may argue thus;
Sach evill acts committed by man as are contrary to the light ef
nature, or mhich a man guided only by the light ef nature might
spun and avoyd, tbe Magistrate may punisb, er they are punisbable
by the Magistrate;
But this hind of Idolatry we art speaking of, is an evill act agairst
the light ef nature;
Thertfere the Magistrate may punisp it. The major or fist pro¬
position is agreed by all, whatsotver is against the light of na¬
ture the Magistrate may punish; the light of nature is the spheare
of the Magistrates activity. And for the minor or second propo¬
sition, that sucb Idolatry is gairst the light of nature, is proved at
large (Rome 1. 19 20.21,22.) where tne Apostles drift or scope
is to shew that the old Gentiles sinned against the light of nature
when they committed that grosse Idolatry, For ( saith he) that
which may be buou ne ef God, is manifest in or tothem, (who are
meerly in nature) for God hath suered it unto them; how hath
God shewed it unto them ? not by the light of Scripture, nor by
the light of che Spirit, or divine revelation, but by the frame or
fabrick of the worlu, as it followeth plainely in that place; For
EFfF 2

body.t: the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly
seene, being understood by the things nhich are made, even his eter¬
nal power. & God- head, so that they are xithout excuse. The reason
uhy such ldolaters were without excuse, was because the very
light of nature mighe teach them, that there is an eternall pouer
and God. bead, who made the world, or that the world was made
by some eternall power, It could not make it selfe; And therefore
they must needs be inexcusable who worshipped the things that
are made in the place of their maker. Seeing then, this kind of
Idolatry is a sin against the light of nature, and the Magistrate
hath power to punish sins against the light of nature, it follows
that where such Idolatry breakes forth, and proofe is made of it,
the Magistrate may punish it. This also is an iniquitie to be puni¬
sued by the Judge. The ground why it is so is also assigned by pob
in the next words.
For I should have denied the God that is abeve.
As if he had sayd, If any require an account of my opinion,
why I assert, that Idolatry is an iniquity to be punished by the
Judge, my answer is this, Idolatry is a God-denying sin. And I in
adoring the Sun and Moone as Gods, suould have denied the God
that is above.
The word rendred to denie, is taken first metaphorically for any
kind of deceaving our expectation. Thus the Prophet speakes
Hab. 3. 17.) Though the labour of the Olive shall faile, or ly,
that is, yeeld no oyle, and when the harvest comes short of hope,
the latines say, the har vest lyes, that is, it deceaves the hope of the
husbandman.
Secondly, Taken properly it notes a direct deniall of what is
asked (Gen. 18. 15.) Then Sarah denied, saring, I did not
laugh.
Thirdly, It signifies tobe-lye, which is to report a matter o¬
therwise of another then it is (Per. 5. 1I, 12-) They have belied
the Lord, and said, it is not he, neither shall evill come upon us, nee
spall not see sword, nor famine.
Fourthly, It notes the yeelding of feigned or false subjection
(Psal. 18.44.) Thine enemies should have submitted theuselves
(or lyed) to thee; that is (as we put in the Margin) yeelded
feigned submifsion, 80 (Plal. 66. 3. D/al. 81. 15.) The pro¬

0592.head: Chap. 31. Au Expesition upon the Beke of Jo R. Vert, 28.

body.t: vidences of God doe sometimes so over-power the enemies of his
people, that they are compelled to pretend subm sũon, thougn
their hearts be farre from it. There is much of this kinde of lying
in Idolatry, a pretending of sobiection, and lubmission to God,
when indeed there is nothing in the heart but stubbornnes and
rebellion against him.
I should have denied the God that is abeve.
What it is to denie God, may further appeare by its contrary,
confessing ( John 1. 24. 20.) He confessed and deried not but con¬
fessed; confession is opposed to deniall. There is a tuo fold con¬
fession; Firft, a confe ssion of repentance; Secondly, of praise.
(Gen.49. 8.) Judah thy Brethren shall confesse or praise thee, that
is, they shall make confession of thee to thy praise, they shall not
be ashimed of thee, but acknowledge thee, and readily give them.
selves up to be governed by thee. Our confession of God stands
in direct opposition to the deniall of him, And it is a confession
of praise, and honour, which we give to God; lo Christ speaketh
of himselfe (Math: 10. 32, 33.) Whosoever shall confesse me be¬
fore men, him mill I confesse also befere my father which is in hea¬
ven; But mhosoever shall deny me before men, him xill I also denit
before my father which is in heaven. And againe ( Marke 8. 38.)
uhosoever tberefore shall be ashamed of me, and of my words in tbis
adulterous and sinfull generation; of him also shall tbe Son of man be£
ashamed mhen he cometh in the glory of his father, mith tbe holy An¬
gells. From these Scriptures compared together, we see first, that,
not to confesse Christ is to deny him, & that to deny Christ is to
be ashamed of him, as if he were not worth the owning. When
Job saith, I should have denied the God that is above, we may under¬
stand him in every sence of deniall. Some ldolatro is a flat deni¬
all of God, and all Idolatry is but a feigned subjection to or a
flattering of God, a belying of God and a shamefull disowning of
him. Yet I conceave, the deniall here intended is specially a flat
and plaine deniall of him, Ishould haue denied the God that is a¬
bove.
Hence oblerve.
First, To deny God is a hainous wickednesse.
Tis all sin bound up in one. God is denied many wayes; Fust,

0593.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Boor ef JOB. Verf.28.

body.t: in regard of his beeing, or that he is. This is the grossest deniall
of him; Secondly, in reference to the manner of his beeing, or
that he is such as he hath indeed declared himselse to be. Thus
God is denied when we forme up such notions of him in our
braine as are unbecoming his glorious Mnjesty. When we have
apprehensions of God unsutable to his holynes, his mercy, his ju¬
Rtice, and his power, wee deny the God whois, and set up a God
who is not.
Againe, there is a two fold denying of God First, in words
expressely and openly; Secondsy, in practice, closely and con¬
si quentially. The Apost le gives us the ground of this distinction
(Tit: 1. 16.) Ther confisse that they knom God, but in works they
deny him. There may be at once a professing of God, and a de¬
niall of him. Many a mans practice speakes aloud that there is no
God, when he makes a sayre confession and profession of him
with his tongue.
This pract call denyall of God may be run into five wayes.
First, To live in a professed course of sin, is a denying ot God;
For, first, such deny their obligation to obey God, or the abso¬
lute dominion of God to command them, Secondly, they deny,
much more, any willingnes ( which is our duty) to be subject to
the will of God Thirdly, they deny the Justice and goodnesse of
that Law under which they are, and by which they oughr to
walke. An obstinate sinner beares his testimony boldly against
God in all that he is, and in all that he hath spoken.
Secondly, They may be sayd to deny God in their practice,
who doe not, Farst, hope for the reward of obedience promised;
nor Secondly, feare che punishment of disobedience threatned.
If any man shall say in bis heart, what dothit profit, or what
good shall I get by walking holyly and humbly with God ? and
what hurt shall I get if I take libertie to walke unholyly, and
proudly against Ged? This is not only a denying, but a desying
of God, who is a remarder ef them that diligently secke him¬
Heb. 11. 6) and will take vengeance of all them that villfully
and resolved ly disobey bim. They ( saith the Prophet, Zeph. 1.
12.) are men set led on their lees (that is, hardned in sin) that say
in their heart, the Lord mill net doe good, ntither vill he doe evill;
that is, he vill neither reward nor punish. It matters not whethet
ve doe good or evill, for he uill dot neyther to us.

0594.head: Chap.31. An Expofition upon the Book of IOB. Vert. 28.

body.t: Thirdly, They thât sware falsely deny God eminent ly, chough
they doe it never so covertly. Such eyther suppose that God
doth not know they fuare falsely, or that God will not punish
nor be a sœift wirner (as he hath sayd he will, Math:3 5.) agairst
fasse smearert.
Fourthly, Not to love God is to deny him, for he that doth
not love God, doth not acknowledge him to be gnod, and so de¬
nieth him tobe. We love that which we judge to be good, there¬
fore they who doe not love God, deny his goodnes, and so (up¬
on the matter) his very beeing; seing God can no more cease
to be good, then he can cease to be.
Fisthiy, ( which is the speciall way of denying God intended
in this text) The worship of a false or Idol God, is a deniall of
the true, of the living God. And the Idolater may wel be sayd
to deny God with a lye; because he that doth not acknouledge
and reverence God but the creature goeth against the dictates os
his own mind; seing man by nature may not only see God in the
creature, but distinguish him from the creature.
At best, Idolaters deny God by attributing that honour to
creatures which God never gave them, nor alloweth us to give
to any but himselfe. The noblest creatures in the uorld, the holy
Angels in heaven, are but our fellow. servants. When Tobn would
needs fall downe before the Angel, and wor ship him, he sayd, Se¬
thou doc it not. I am thy fellom servant: and as the highest crea¬
tures are our fellow servants, so all other creatures are our ser¬
vants; God made the whole host of heaven, and all things here
below to serve man, as hath been sheued before: therefore to
worship them, though we should say we doe not terminate our
worship in them, but offer our worship by them, yet that is a de-
nying of God. Idolaters put a worship upon God instead of wor¬
shipping him; Will-worship is the worfhip of our owne will, not
the worship of God, who vill be worshipped only as himselse
willeth.
But as for those who not only worship God by the creature,
but the creature for or as God, they deny God most grossely,
for though they deny not that God is, yet they deny what God
is; They eyther deny that God is but one, or that he is such a
one as he hath manifested himselfe to be, both in his word and
works. Indeed to set up another God, or to say, there are many

0595.head: Chap. 31. An Expofition npon tés Book of I0B. Verf. 28,

body.t: gods, is to say, there is no Cod. Polytbeisme ir Arbeisme. And
therefore the A postle concludes of Idolaters ( Rom: 1. 15.) They
change the truth ef God into a lie; that is, into an Idol. Idolls are a
lie, eyther first, because they promise, or pretend what they are
I not in truth; or second ly, because they are a plaine deniall of the
true God. IfI (saith Pob) had Adored the Sunne, I shou'd have
deñied the God that is above, yea though I should notuithstand¬
ing that, acknowledge him to be above all gods; and that my
humbling or bowing my selfe to the creature, was not to abate
but rather to exalt my worship of him, that being only (as I mighe
pretend) a help to my devotion. For he that boweth before or to
a creature in worship, whether he saith he doth it only as a
meanes to draw up his heart to God, or as a signe of the presence
of God, or as to a Mediator between God and him, (in the for¬
mer sence Papists worship Images, and in the latter Saints and
Angels, he I say, that doth any of these) will be found a denier
of God, how much sotver he boasteth of the worship of the one
true God, and denieth that he worshippeth the creature as God.
I suould have denied the God
that is abeve,
Job useth that word above significantly, having spoken of the
Sunne and Mooce before, which are above us, or on bigh, he
add́s, If I had morshipped Sunne, and Meone, I had denied the God
that is above, not only above the earth, bur above the Sunne
and Moone, and all the host of heaven. The Sun is below in com¬
parison of the God above; this God who is above all in power,
and above all in place, above all in glory, above all in d'gnitie.
should I have denied.
Hence note.
Ged is abeve by à more eminent and special presence.
God is neither above nor below as circumscribed in any place,
God is both above and below as filling all places; Cod is not
more above then he is below as to his reall presence, but God is
more above then he is below as to the manifestation of his pre¬
sence. In this sence tob speakes of God as above; and we find
throughout the Scripture, that all prayers, and speeches, directed
to God, are directed to him as above. As letters sent to a Prince,

0596.head: Chap. 31. An Expositiou upon tbe Boobe ef JoO B. Verf. 28.

body.t: are directed to him at his Court, which is the place of his usuall
residence, and where he most declares his pouer and greatnesse;
so all the prayers, speeches, addresses made to God in Scripture,
are made to bim as above, or in heaven. Christ givingus thnt
patterne of prayer (Math: 6.) directs us to God above, Say our
father mhich art in heaven; Christ knew that, God our father is as
much on earth as in heaven, in regard of his essentiall and reall
presence, yet he bids us pray, Our father mbich art in heaven, not
our sather which art on earth. And uhen Christ himselfe prared
to his father, ( Juh. 17.1.) He lift up his eyes to heaven, and said,
Father glorifie thy Sonne. (Heaven is the babitation q Gods beli¬
nesse, and ef his glory; And therefore they who in thele times de¬
cry such speeches as these, and will let us know they know no¬
thing of heaven or hell, neyther what they are, nor where they
are, let fuch know ic is enough for us to know, what the Scripture
saith, that heaven is abve, and heil belom; and why should not
we speake as the Scripture speakes, let above and below be what
they will. Therefore when ve speake to God, let us remember
that he is above, and let us get our hearts up to him, let us (as
the Church speals in her low and delolate condition, Lam. 3.41.)
List up eur hearts and our hands unte God in the heavens How un¬
comely as wel as sinfull were it, if while we pray to the God that
is above, our hearts should be groveling here below.

0597.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition upon the Bocke ef J0B. Verl.29.

body.t: If Irejoyced at the destruction of him that hated
me, or list up uy selfe when evil found him:
(Neither have I suffered my mouth to sin, by wisbing
a ourse to bis soule.)
N this context Job still afffrmes the clearenes of his oune In¬
I tegcity, and in speciall, his clearenes from any boyling defire
of revenge upon his sorest and most professed Adversaries, which
he proves,
First, Because he had not expressed, no nor been affi cted with
that passion of joy at the downfall of his adversary, or in the
day of his sorrow. Thus he speakes in the former part of the z9th
verse.
If Irejoyced at the destruction ef him that hated me; that is,
I Cid not rejoyce at his destruction.
Secondly, He proves it by his avoydance of such actions, as
testifie a spirit of revenge, and those are two.
First, He had not used any proud gesture, or insulting beha¬
viour toward his Enemy, uhen suppressed and brought under¬
foote. This he intends inthe latter part of the 2 oth verse, where
he saith, or list up my selse mhen evill found him.
Secondly, He professeth that he did not vent any spite¬
full words, or evill wishes against his person, ( v. 30.) Nei¬
ther have I srffered my mouth to sin by misping a curse to his
soule.
Yet further, Job proves his innocence as to this sin of revenge,
by shewing his aostinence from and forbearance of all those act¬
ings, whether secret or open, though greatly provokt and pres¬
sed thereunto; though he wanted not those about him, who
were continually blouing the coales, and urging him to right
himselfe to the utmost upon those who had wronged him, yet he
was not moved. This I conceive to be the sence of the 31th verse,
If the men ef ay tabernacle said not, Oh that me had of his flesp!
ne cannet be satisfied. Of which hereafter.
Thus yon have the sum ard aime of these two verses, I shall

0598.head: Chap.31. Au Exposition upon the Book of I° 2. Verl, 29.

body.t: now proceed to the particular explication of them.
Verf. 29. If I rejoyced at the destruction ef him that hated mee.
Joy is a passion of the minde, arising from the apprehension
of some present or neere approaching good. Holy fob (it seemes)
never looked upon the evill which befell his enemy, as a good to
himselfe, and so it was not to him a matter or occasion of joy.
If I rejyced.
The word notes a very Fresh ard active Joy, such as appeares
in menupon the liberal drinking of uine ( Psal. 104.15.) wine
maketh glad the heart ef man; that is, it makes him heartily glad.
And to some, the teares, yea the blood of their Enemies tast as
sweetly, goe doune as pleasantly, and are as refreshing as a Cep
of the most delicious and richest wine: It purs (as it were) a new
life into them, to see their enemies in the snares of death. Job was
of another spirit; If Irejoyced (saith he) as one refreshit with
wine, when I saw the blood of mine enemies; If I tooke content
in their sorrowes, or comfort in their groanes, Then let my sor¬
rowes be multiplyed. If Ire joyced
at the destruction of him that hated met.
The word which we render destruction, notes utter ruine, or
ruine without remedy, such a ruine as is not capable of reliefe;
or as the Lord threatens Babylon by the Prophet (Isa. 47.9.
Judgement in its perfection of it; that is, a compleate and irreco¬
verable overthrow. The beasome of destruction ( spoken of Isa.14.
23.) fweepes all away at once, even the most precious Jewels and
richest treasure of sinners are but as dirt and rubbish before it.
Its such a cleane riddance, that ( as another Prophet, Nab: 1. 9.
expresseth it) Afflictien shall net rise up the second time. Some
destructions leave some worke for a second, yea for a third de¬
struction; but there may be a destruction which leaves nothing
to be destroyed, not a stone upon a stone, as Christ prophecyed of
the destruction of Jerusalem. When Tob saw his enemy thus de¬
stroyed, and those that hated him broken with a breach that
could not be healed, and which utterly disabled them for ever to
doe him a mischiese, or revenge themselves upon him, Tet he re¬

0599.head: Chap.31. An Expesition apon ibe Booke of JO R. Verl.29,

body.t: joyced not at it. If I rejyced at the distra ction of him
that hated mee.
The roote of the word rendred to hate, signifies both to hate
and to neglect, yea to contemne; and thole whom we hate,
ve aluayes neglect, and often contemne too. So the word
is used Gen 26.27. as also 2 Sam: 13 22. And Absalom spake ux¬
ta his brother Amnox neither good nor bad ( that is, he sl ghted and
contemned him) for Absal m hated Amnon because he had ferced
his sister Tamar. As he spake nothing at all to him ábout that
matter, the abuse of his sister, so doubtlesse he grew more reser¬
ved then formerly towards him in all other matters, because he
hated him. jobs haters were also his deriders and despisers, as
was shewed at the first, ninth and tenth verses of the former
Chapter. If I'have rejoyced at the destruction of him that hated
mec.
To cleare hoy much Tob sayd, uhen he sayd, the men at whose
ruine he did not rejoyce, were such as hated him, let us consider
what he did not say of them.
First, He did not say, If Ihave rejoyced at the destruction of
him that mas not my friend, or benefactor; and yet not to doe ano¬
ther good when we have power and opportunity in our hands,
is a degree of hatred; he that withholds a favour from him who
needs it, is a negative Enemy.
Secondly, He did not say, If I rej yced at the destructim of him
that never mrong d me, nor did me harme: And yet there are many
who doe so, yea who rejoyce at the destruction of those who ey¬
ther have, or would have done them geod.
Thirdly, He did not say, If I rejoyced at the destruction of him
that hatb taken distast, and displeasure at me; not a few are ready
to doe so upon every light occasion, yea though we, may be un¬
der the present displeasure of a man as well as of God, who yet
really loves us.
But fob saith plainely ( and what could he say more to prove
the truth or highten the degrees of his charity) If I rejoyced at the
destraction of him that hated me, even mith a deadly hatred; If I
rejoyced at the destruction of my worst enemy, my inward ene¬
my, my hearty enemy, whose spirit was steept in bitternes, in the
guil and wormmood of implacable malice against me, who as he

0600.head: Chap. 31. Au Expositis upon the Beoks of Jo ». Verf. 29.

body.t: hath often sought to destroy me, so he would have re orced to
purpole, and clapt his hands for joy at my destruction. Such as
this, was the character of the man that hated Job, of the man at
whose destruction he did not rejoyce.
Thus we see of what temper Job was. Job lived in darhe times,
in times farre remote from the fullnesse of Gospel light, yet how
full was his heart of Gospel love. He lived long before Christ in
the world, yet how like was his love to the lovs of Christ? who
not only did good to, but dyed for those that hated bim. Jol¬
charity might wel become, yea it was such as is rar ely found a¬
mong those who live in the clearest Gospel light. Certainly hee
fatre exceeded the light and learning of the Jewish Rabbines and
understood the meaning of the Law of love in those times better
then the Pharisces did in Christs time. What greater cvidence of
love ( except that of Christ himselfe, who, as was sayd before,
dyed for those that hated him ) could be given then this, not to
rejoyce at the death or destruction of him that hated him?
Yet, Some possibly may object; Had it not been a greater e¬
vidence of love, if Job had done good to him that hated him, then
only not to Rejyce at the destruction of him that hated him? Is it
not more charitie to doe good to an enemy, then not to rej yce
at the evill which he suffers?
Some have sayd, The reason why Job sayd not, he did good to
or loved his enemies, or those that hated him, was because the
Iaw of loving an enemy was not in force in his time, and so he
was not obliged to such a duty. For proose of which opinion
they alledge that of Christ in his Sermon upon the Mount
(Math: 5.43.) Te have heard that it hathbeen said ef ela, Thou
shilt love thy neighbour, and hate thine eremy. Which they Inter¬
pret as if this were the rule given by God for those elder times,
Theu shilt love thy neighbour, and hate thine entmy Whereas
when Christ saith, Ii hath bien sayd, he doth not meane, that
this was the rule given out by God to them of old, but this vas
the Glosse given by man: God said in the Law, Thou sbalt love
thy neigbbour; but he never said, Tóou spalt hate thine enemy;
that was the exposition or comment which the Pharisees made
upon the text, and it was indeed a grosse corruption of it. As if
that Commandement, Tuou shalt lsve thy reighbour, implyed,
Thas suali hate téine enemy: I'hus they interpreted the Lau ty

0601.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Book ef JOB. Verf.29.

body.t: the rule of Contraries; As if because we must love our neighbour,
therefore we might hate our enemies; and possibly they were
mifled to that Interpretation, by those charges which the chil¬
dren of Israel receaved, to roote out the old Inhabitants of the
Land of Cauaan, the Jebusites, the Peresites, &c. M’hence they
drew downe this false conclusion, as if they might hate all sorts of
Enemies, even private personall enemies. But though the Law of
Loving our Enemies be, in speciall, a Gospel Law both published
and practised by Christ in a more cleare and excellent way then
ever before; yet the Law of loving an enemy (as to the matter
and substance of it) was from the beginning, as will appeare fur¬
ther in the prosecution of this point, therefore that was not
the Reason.
The true reason why job did not expresse the Integrity of his
fpirit in this matter, by saying, he did good to his enemies, but by
saying, he did not rejoyce at tbeir destruction, was, Because not to
rejoyce at the destruction of an enemy, doth shew a very greaz
degree os love and goodnes to them, yea in some cases it is all that
love which we are to shew, and all the good we are bound to doe
to an enemy; For though we are to love Enemies, yet we must
not give out all our love to them. There is a love of pitie, and
thert is a love of delight; A love of Complacencie, and a love of
Compassion. The love which we are to give out to enemies, is a love
of pitie and compassion, not a love of Complacencie and delight;
For no man is bound to take his enemy into his bosome, and to
give him an opportunit y to ruine him, nor is any man bound so
to doe good to his enemy, as to enable him to doe him hurt. So
that, Not to rejoyce at the destruction of an enemy, may carrie
the full sence of the Law, commanding us to love our enemies.
Againe, I answer, That, often through the shews and fhadows
of pretended love and doing good to an enemy, the heart of man
is deceaved. For while he saith he loves his enemy, he doth only
fay so. And whereas some thinke they love an enemy, because
they doe not actually attempt to revenge themselves upon him,
or to take auay his life; this also may fall short of any the least
degree of love to him: but not to rejoyce at the destruction of an
enemy, is a convincing argument of love to him & signifies much
more then meerly to abstaine from hurting or destroying him. So
that, both the fincerity and the strength ofour love to anenemy

0602.head: Chap.31. An Expositioh upon tbe Rαok o I0R. Vert, 29

body.t: is most discernable in our not rejoycing at his fall. Thus one of
the Ancients determines this question; The presperity ( saith he y
er the fast of an enemy, is that which puts us indeed to tbe rryall &f
eur lave. The prosperitie of an enemy tryeth us whether we can
beare it and not be suprized with envy; his fall tryeth us, ibether
we can see it, or heare of it, and not be surprized with joy. And
doub:les, He that is troubled at his enemies prosperitie, will also
rejoyce at his calamitie. So that the greatest tryall of true Go-
spel love to an enemy, lieth in the mortification of all such Joyes.
And how hard it is not to rejoyce at the hurt of an enemy, or of
one that hates us, no man knows but he that hath been hated and
hurt by an enemy. A man may for ever forbeare to hurt his ene¬
my, or to lay violent hands on him, and yet he may heartily wisti
his destruction by the hand of others. And he that rejoyceth at
the hurt of another, may rather be judged to want pouer then
a will to hurt him himselfe; or that he forbears to hurt him that
hated him rather because he was aff aid of hurting and endanger¬
ing himselfe by doing it, then because he had had no mind to doe
it. And therefore Job puts himselfe upon the highest and surest
tryall, whether his heart were right in this thing, while he saith,
If I rej-yced at the destruction of him that hated mee.
Further, Consider how love riseth by severall stepps or de¬
grees.
First, To doe a Friend good is a great act of love; yet it is
nesse to doe him hurt. Is this tuy bindnes to thy friend?
Secondly, Ie is a great act of love to beare wrong done by an
enemy patiently, yet not so great as frecly to forgive him that
wrong.
Thirdly, It is a great act of love, not to hurt an enemy uhen
we have power to doe it; yet it is a greater to doe him good; or
to repayre, in what we may, his honour. When Cæsar command-
ed the Statues of Pompey, which some had pul'd downe, to be set
up againe; Cicero told him, That in restoring the Statues of Pom-
pey he had erected his owne.
Fourthiy, Not to rejoyce at the misery of an enemy, is an act
of perfect charity.
Fisthly, To mourne at the fall of an enemy, is an act of pu
rest pity.

0603.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition upon ths Book of JO2. Vers. 29

body.t: From these severall stepps of love, the question receaves a clea¬
rer answer, why Job doth not expresse his Integrity in this poynt,
by saying he loved or did good to him that hated him but by say¬
ing, he rejoyced not at his destruction.
Here first, If we duly consider what kind of man lob uas (as
appeares both by the testimony which was given him by God
(Chap. 1.1.) ard by that which he gave of himselfe, as in the
presence and feare of God inthe 29th Chapter of this booke)
we may well stand and wonder how he could have an enemy,
or why any man should hate him, Pob, both as a man, and as a
Migistrate, deserved to be ( as a Great Prince was once called)
The delight of manbind. He was to the poore so curteous, so mer¬
cifull to his friends, so just to all, that surely all men had reason to
delight in him, yea to make him their delight, yet he had enemies,
and such as maligned him; If I rejorced at the destruction of him¬
that hated mee.
Hence observe.
Gud men, even tle best of men, they who leve Gad, and art la¬
ved ef God, are often hated, extreamely hated among men.
David, A man aster Gods owne heart, complaines of that
hearty hatred which he found in and from the world (Psal. 69.
4.) They that hate me mithout cause, are moe then the haires ef my
head; Hoy many they are no man can tell, neyther could David
tell how many enemies he had, not only because he had many se¬
cret enemies uhom he knew not, but because his very knowne e¬
nemies were so many, that (according to common language)
they were innumerable.
Enmity is rooted and fixt in the hearts of all naturall men a¬
gainst holy men; And though it be not alwayes seene working,
yet it is alwayes at worke. Thus the Lord told the Serpent, that
is the devill, who had abufed the Serpent to be instrumentall for
the fall of man (Gen. 3. 15.) I mill put enmity betmeen thee and
the moman, bet mien her sred and tby seed; that is, betteen the
Godly and the wicked: The spirituall seed of the Serpent, hates,
and they cannot but hate the spirituall seed of the uoman, ’tis
their nature to doe it, and therefore they must needs doe it. The
fire shall as soone loose its heate, or a stone its weight, as a natu¬
rall man his hatred of those chat are spirituall. God himselfe is

0604.head: Chap. 31. An Expofition upon the Boobe ef JoB. Verf. 29.

body.t: hated by all ungodly men; They are enemits te him in their mind
by wicked worbes ( Col. 1. 21.) and so they are to all those who
beare his image. The Apostle purs these two together (Rem. 1.
30.) Back-biters, haters of God; No wonder if they back bite
men, who hate God. And as Christ hath forewarn'd (Matb.10.
25.) If they have called the Master of the house Becle bub, how
much more shall they call them of his houspold. All true Believers
are of the houshold of Jesus Christ, yea they are his members.
Christ our head was hated by the world, and therefore his mem¬
bers must looke for hatred while they are in the world. This en¬
mity brake forth into act as early as it could; The second man
that ever was borne in the world was hated by him who in nature
was the First borne, Caine hated his Brother, and his hatred con¬
cluded in the murder of his Brother (Gen. 4 5, 8.) The Apostle
John sheweth us of what linage Caine was, while he exhorts to
love (I Epist: 3. 11, 12.) This is the message that ye have heard
from the beginning, that me should leve one anuther. Nst as Caint
who mas of trat miched one and slew his Brother. Caine who hated
and slew bis brother, was not so much Adams son as the Devils
son; and that he was so, is cleare by the rea on which the Apostle
assignes why he slew him, even because his omne morhes nere evist,
and his Brothers righieous. That was all the reason which he had
to hate bim; and no other appearing reason had Job given any
man to hate him, but because he was perfect and urright, a man
that feared God and eschemed evill. As the Flefhi which is in a Be¬
liever hates ( wherefore else doth it lust against and continually
oppose) the Spirit (Gal. 5. 17.) so they who are only flesh,
lust against those who are spirituall, or who (as’tis say d of Isaac
in opposition to Ismatl, who was borne after the fleso) art borne
after the Spirit. For these also are contrary one to the other,
which is the reason given by the Apostle in the other text, why
there is such an endlesse warre betwten flest and Spirit in a Be¬
liever) yea, There is a five-fold contrariety between a Godly
and a wicked man.
First, They are contrary in their nature; unholynes (by reason
of sin)is the nature of a wicked man and holynes (through grace)
is the nature of a godly man; He not only escaptth the corruption
nbich is in the morld throngh lust, but is made a partaker ef the di¬
vine nature (z Pet. I. 4
H h h h

0605.head: Chap. 31. An Expofition upon the Booke ef JOR. Verf.29.

body.t: Secondly, They have a contrary pedegree and originall. Its
said of Cain, hi mas of the miched one, that is, the devil, but Saints
are borne of God, he is their father.
Thirdly, They are contrary in their course; The Godly walke
in the way of Gods Commandements, in the narrow way; the
wicked walke in the way of their own hearts, in the broad way.
Fourth'y, They are contrary not only as to their external¬
courie, but as to their internal motions, their hopes and their
feares, their joyes and their sorrowes ( these are the motions of
the soule) are as contrary as their natures are, or as the foure
windes of heaven are.
Eifchly, and last ly, They are contrary in their ends; taking the
end in a double notion.
Eirst, As end imports our ayme and defigne: A godly mans
chiefe ayme is the glory of God; A wicked man aymes at him¬
selfe chiefely, or at selse advancement in all he doth, God is not in
all his thougbts ( Plal. 10. 4.) that is, not at all in his thoughis,
eyther to mind his word as his rule, or his glory as his end.
Secondly, They are contrary in their end, as end notes the
upshot and conclusion of all. Marke the perfett man (saith Da¬
vid, Psal. 37. 37, 38.) and behold the upright; for the end of that
man is peace. But the transgressors shall be destroyed together, the
end of the micked shall be cut iff; that is, This shall be their end
(and’tis a sad one) they shall be cut off and destroyed. Now
they who differ in all these respects, and are under a contrariety
of nature, of pedegree, of way, of motion, of end, how is it possi¬
ble but there must be enmity and hatred betueen them? The one
is light, the other darknesse, now as the Apostle argues it (2 Cor.
6.14.) What Communion hath light mith darknesse? No more
hath righreousnesse with unrighteousnesse. What agreement hatb
the Temple of God with Idols? No more hath he that beleeveth
uith an Infidel. The wicked are called Serpents, Wolves, Lyons,
these names are not spit out of a rayling mouth, or from a splee¬
nish spirit, they are not the evaporations of an angry man, but
they are dictates of the holy Spirit, and bestowed upon them by
the most wise God, who knowes unerringly how to call every
thing & person by a name, most significative both of their nature
and temper. On the otner hand the Godly are called by the same
Spirit ofGod, Sbeepe, Lambs, Deves. And there is not onty a

0606.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon tbe Book of JOE. Vert. 29

body.t: difference between these, but a contrariety, yea an ant parliy as
to qualities and principles. Now antipathies are not agatost this
or that Individuall only, bur against the whole kind, and especi¬
ally against the most eminent individualls of any kind. And there¬
fore because Tob was a man so eminent and exemplary, both for
piety and for Justice, he was hated the more. Tis the nature of
evill men, te hate those that are good, and’tis their custome the bet¬
ter thty are the more to hate thtmo.
Secondly, Whereas Job saith, If Irejoyced at the destruction
OC him that hated mec.
Observe.
Man is very apt to rejoyce in the hurt, or at the fall of those
that hate himo.
Some Heathens have found the revengefull taking auay of an
enemies lise more sueete to them then their oun lives; and while
Job professeth he did not, doubtlesse he found a great Combat in
himselfe not to doe it; ’tis no easie thing, not to re oyce when
an enemy falls. Desire of revenge eyther upon an apprehension
of wrong receaved, or of hatred expressed by others against us,
doth so deeply possesse the minds of many, that there’s nothing
more d'fficult then to restraine it, how difficult then is it to re¬
move and heale it ? And furely if the best men examine their
hearts honestly and thoroughly, they shall find a great deale of
this old leven ly hidden in them, even while they are professing
against it, and thinke they have purged it out. Who is there that
hath not some secret rejoycings and pleasing motions within,
when he heares of the death or hurt of his enemy? and how ha d¬
Iy can some, who are great Masters at the art of dissimulation, dis¬
semble it? As for the grosser sort of Mankinde they declare this

For answer to this ob ection, we must distinguish, First, of E¬
nemies; Secondly, of Joy.
Enemies are of two sorts; eyther private, or publick, eyther
enemies to a man, or ( as l may say) enemies to mankind, espe¬
cially to a sort of mankind.
Againe, Some are not only publick, but resolved and incor¬

people of God. Now when we affirme, that ’tis sinfull to rejoyce
at the destruction of those that hate us, or of our ene mies, we are
especially to understand it of private and personall enemies, and
not of the enemies of our publick peace, or of Sions prosperitie.
And yet we may exceed in our rejoycings even at their destructi¬
on, we must therefore distinguish, as about enemies, so about
y.
First then, there is a joy meerly at the mischiefe fallen upon
our enemies.
Secondly, There is a joy, because by their fall some good or
benefit redounds to the publick, as namely, Free dome from civill
bondage and bloody persecution for conscience sake, the free pas¬
sage of the Gospel, and the pure administrations of worship. It is
not lawfull to rejoyce at the destruction of the greatest or worst

others, and as their cutting off, curs them off from an opportuni¬

body.t: remember there are none so neere destruction as they who re¬

Upon this ground Solomon prohibits all such joyes ( Pre. 24. 17,

in doing so he falls into sin, which is the worst kind of falling, so
he is in danger of falling into some worser misery then he. God
who righteth us by the fall of an enemy, will also right himselfe
upon us if we displease him by any sinfull rejoycing at his fall.
When the Lord ( as Solomon here saith) turnes away his wrath
from that enemy in whose fall he sees any rejoyce, he will turne

wrath from that enemy in whose fall any rejoyce, doth not fig¬

When thine enemy falleth, thinke thus; I my felfe am eyther like
