them joyned are the instruments of speech, so any of them alone
are expressed to be so in Scripture; Neither have I
soffired ny palaue or mouth te fin.

0618.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upou the Book of JOR. Verl. 30.

body.t: The Hebrewis, Neithor have I given my mouth to sin, that is, I
have not given way to my mouth, nor indulged this liberty to
my tongue; I have not taken off the bridle of a watchfull re-
straint from my lips, nor let my words run at random without
controule. So this forme of speech is used in the oth Chapter of
this Booke (v. 18.) where Job complaining of the pressures, the
continuall pressures that burdened him, sayth, he ( that is, Gad)
mill not suffer me to take my breath, the Hebrew is, be mill not give
me, ( that is, leave) to take my breath. Thus (Gen-20.6.) when
Abrabam by dissembling (at least) that Sarab mas his wife put
her into a danger of being abused by At imelech, who yet be¬
ing rebuked by God in a dreame, could plead, In the integrity of
my beart and innccency of my hands have I done this; yea (saith the
Lord) I knom thou didst this in the integrity of thy heart, for
mithheld thee from sinning against me; therefore suffered I thee not
to tonchher; As if the Lord had sayd, Thou wast ready to have
given way to thy affections, but I uould not; I would not suffer
thee to run into that error. In this manner Moses (Numb: 21.
23.) expresseth that unkind stop which the King of the Amorites
gave the Children of Israel in their march to Canaan, And Sihon
would not suffer Israel to passe through his border; the Hebrew is,
Sihon nould not give Israel ( that is, freedome) to passe through
his border. And thus’tis sayd in that prophecy concerning Christ
(Psal: 16. 10.) Neither vilt thou suffer thy holy one to see cor¬
ruption, or, thou milt not give corruption any power over thy holy
one; corruption ( had it been let alone to take its course) vould
have seised upon the body of Christ, as well as upon the boëy of
any other man, but God did not give corruption leave to doe so,
he would not suffer it to take its course against him. To dy was
enough to satisfie the penalty of the Law; There was no necessi y
that the body of Christ should corrupt to doe it; yea if the body
of Christ had corrupted in the grave, his satisfaction had not ap¬
peared. The same language is used in another Psalme, to signifie
preservation from civill corruption ( Psal. 121 3.) He mill not
suffer tby foote tobe moved; that is, none shall be able to disturbe
thy peace; the text is, He mill not give thy fiote to be moved; As
if he had sayd, many will endeavour to cast thee downe but by tbe
power and providence of God, thou shalt be upheld and main¬
tained firme in thy place or standing. This word is used againe

0619.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon ths Book of JOE. Verf. 30.

body.t: (Ezek. 14. 8.) where the Lord tells his people, that if any of
them coming to a Prophet to enquire of him, should yet set up I¬
dols in his heart, and put the stumbling blocke of his iniquity be¬
fore his face, he would set his face against that man, and make him
a signe aud a proverb; The Hebrewr is, I mill giut my face against
him, that is, I will give leave to my urath and fierce indignation
to proceed in full force against him. The face in Scripture signi¬
fies, as love and favour, so wrath and anger, because there is usu¬
ally a discovery or an image of these passions printed apon and
discernable in the face. Once more, the Prophet Daniel speakes
in this forme ( Chap. 9. 3. ) to shew how he put out all the
powers of his soule wrestling in prayer with God, When I under¬
stood by bookes the number ef the yeares mhereof the mord ot the Lord
came te Jeremiah the Prophet, that he mould accomplish seventy
yearis in the desolations of Jerusalem. Then I set my face unto the
Lord God to seche by prayers and supplications, mith fastirg and
sack- cloth and ashes. The text is, Igave my face, that is, I gave my
selfe wholy up to these duties of prayer and fasting. I put no re¬
straint no stop nor checke at all upon my spirit, but let it goe
forth with all its mighi, striving and working with God for the
accomplistment of that gracious promise to and prophecy con¬
cerning his captivated people.
Thus we see the force and usage of the word throughout the
Scriptures of the old Testament; and in this sence we are to un¬
derstand Jobs profession here, neither have I suffered (er given)
my mouth to fin; As if he had sayd, my mouth was forward and
ready enough, if it might have had leave, or if I would have gi¬
ven it liberty to have wished ill to my enemy, but I did not suffer
my mouth to run into that sin:
I grant it is a harder matter not to suffer the heart to sin, then
not to suffer the mouth to sin, and therefore when fob had sayd
in the former verse, that he had put a stop upon his heart, he did
more then say (which he saith here) that he had put a stop upon
his tongue; the motions of the seule are lesse in our pomer then those
ef the bodyly members; yet to shew that he was compleate in this
point of love even towards his enemies, lob expresseth it by both.
It is usuall in Scripture to speake of that first which is hardest to
be done, or not to be done, and then of that which is easiest;
making the latter a signe of the former, or making the latter

0620.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Bok ef IO ». Verf.30.

body.t: which is casiest more credible, when we have overcome that
which is more difficult. When Job had once assured us, that bis
heart did not run over in rejoycing, we may easily beleeve, that
his mouth did not breake out in evill speaking; Nither have I
suffered my mouth to sin.
First, In that he saith he did not suffer or give way to any
passion, or distemper of his spirit to vent it selfe at his tongue.
Observe.
The corraptiens of a good man may prisse bim, and presse bim
sore, botb to doe and speake sinfully.
tob was hard put to it, when he saith, be did not suffer his mouth
to sin: he had much adoe to locke up his lips. Meses was a very
holy and a meeke man, the meekest man on the face of the earth,
yet corruption was so stirred in him, that once it prevailed over
him, and foyled him sorely; he could not hold his tongue, but
(being vext and angry) spabe unadvisedly with his lips (Pfal.106.
33.) The power of innate corruption is chiefely seene in two
things.
Firft, In the opposition that it makes against our doing of
good, This the Apostle treats of at large (Rom.7.18 23.) uheu
I mould dee good evill is present mith me: mhen to will is present,
how to performe I knom net; why not? what hindred ? his cor¬
ruptions stood up in opposition and rebelled against the goed he
was about to doe, as he confefsed at the 23d verse: I see another
lam is my members warring agairst the law of my mind, and bring¬
ing me inte captivity to the law ( that is, the power) ef sin, mhich
is in my membert. His corruptions brought such an army against
him, that (as ’tis sayd Gal: 5. 17. upon the same corsideration of
the lustings of the flesh against the Spirit) he could not doe the
thing that he would. Lust would alwayes stopus wholy and it usu¬
ally clogs us extreamly when we are addressing our selves to any
holy duty. And therefore we are exhorted (Heb:12.1.) as te lay
aside every neight (of worldly encumbrance) so, the sin mhich doth
so tasily beset ui (any special indwelling corruption) ihat so me may
run uith patience the race that is set before us; as a man that hath a
burthen at his backe,or a long garment dangling about his heeles
is unfit to run a race, so are they for the spirituall race who are en¬
tangled with the love of the worid, or with any sinfull complian¬
ces.
KKKK

0621.head: Chap. 31. An Expofition upon the Book ef JOR. Verf.30

body.t: Secondly, Naturall corruption bestirres it selfe, and shews its
power by provoking and pressingus, by gording and moving us
to that which is evill. Of this the Apostle Tames speakes (Chap.I.
14.) Let no man say when he is tempted, Iam tempted of God;
for God cannot be tempted mith evill, neither tempteth hee any man;
that is, he doth not tempt any man to the evill of sin; God doth
not provoke nor blow up any mans lusts or passions, his pride or
covetousnesse. He tempts many by putting them to the harder
exercises and services of Grace; but he tempts no man by drax¬
ing out or stirring up his corruptions. How then is man tempted?
The Apoftle ansuers in the next words; But every man is temt¬
ted, mhen he is drawne away with bis oune lust aud inticed. “Tis
lust which intiseth, and by entisement drawes man to sin. U sually
the devill sets lust a-worke, and lust sets man a-worke, yet lust
doth osten set man a worke, though the devill ftand by and doe
nothing. Our lusts, that is, our lustfull and deceitfull hearts are
a fountaine of sin, tis no easie matter to resist, and’tis extreame¬
ly hard to conquer the motions of them. Thus the power of lust
is great, both in opposing us when we would doe good, and in
provoking us to doe evill. Tobς mouth would faine have been
speaking unduly, but he did not suffer it.
Secondly, Observe.
Atist men, that I say not all men, saffer themselves to run in¬
to, more tuilli or sins, both by speech and practise, then tuey are
necessitated unto, or, they commit many sins mhich they miģus
avoyd.
As some doe even envite temptations and provoke their lusts
to activenes, so there are none so active as they ought and might
to resist temptations, and repell their lustfull provocations.
Though a man in his naturall state hath no power to doe that
which is properly and spiritually good, y et man even in a naturall
state hath a power to stop himselfe in somewhat that is evill; a
naturall man may put some checke upon his lusts and corruptions,
he may bridle and binde them more then he doth. And as tliere
is no naturall man that gives himselfe such a stop as he might a¬
gainst sin; so there are very few (if any) godly men who doe it.
They that have grace, rarely improve their grace to the urmost
in hindering and checking the torrent of their corrupt affections.

0622.head: Chap.31. An Exposuiou upon the Book of Jo». Vert. 30

body.t: As naturall men are led captive by the devill at his uill, so the
best of men fayle in setting their renewed uill resolutely against
the devill. The Apostle doth more then imply the deficiency of
beleevers, both in resisting lustfull motions from within, and sa¬
tanicall solicitations from without, while he saith (Rom. 6.12,13.)
Let not fin therefore reigne in yeur mortall bodyis, that je fould
obey it in the lustr thereof. Neither yeeld ye your members as instre¬
ments of unrighteousnesse unto sin; but yield your selves unto God,
As if he had sayd, Your corruptions will move, and Sat an uill so¬
licit you, they will be calling upon you to give up the members of
your bodyes,and the powers of your soule as instruments or wea¬
pons of unrighteousnesse, but I exhort you to turne a deafe eare
to them, and hearken only to the call of God, who commands
you to yield your selves unto him, as they that are alive from tbe
dead, and your members as instruments of righteousnesse unto God;
that is, make it appeare that you have received a new spirituall
life, by your yielding to God, and by your not yielding to the
devil!: doe not give up any of your members at his summons,
let not any lust have your tongue, or hand, or eye, or foote. As
Moses would not yield Pharoab a hoofe to stay behind from the
service of God, so let not us yield a hayre of our head to be an
instrument of unrighteousnesse unto sin, how strongly soever Sa¬
tan or lust move for it; And to be sure they will not be wanting
in moving. Let a man (which is the particular case of the text
be wronged, or at least thinke he is, presently he heares the devill
who is a revengefull Spirit, or his owne spirit of revenge calling
for his understanding to plot some way of revenge, for his heart
to wish it, for his tongue to threaten it, or for his hand to act and
execute it. In all such cases, wee should peremptorily deny to
yield so much as a litle finger to such a service. And he that doth
so, is indeed ( through grace) a Master of himselfe, and a Con¬
queror over Satan. But we may lement that there are so few of
these Conquerors and Masters of themselves, so few uatchfull
keepers of these instruments, of these weapons of unrighteousnes;
most quickly and easily yield them up and let them out, to the
service eyther of this spirit of revenge, or of some other evill spi¬
rit. Where are the men that can say (as Job here did ) in truth,
we have not suffered our mouth to sin when we have been temp¬
ted to speahe sinfusly, we have not suffered our eye to sin, when

0623.head: Chap.31. An Expesition mpon the Bocke of IOR. Verf.30.

body.t: we have been tempted to looke wantonly, we have not suffered
our hand to sin, when we have been tempted to act unrighteous¬
Iy. A truely godly man can say, that he suffers when he sins,
that is, he is rather passive then active in sinning, being hurryed
and violently over-borne by temptation, but this will be the
charge and condemnation ot the world, that they have suffered
themselves to sin. Peter rebuked Ananias (Act. 5. 3.) because
he had yielded up his tongue, an instrument unto sin, why hath
Sathan filled thine heart, to lie to the holy Ghost, and to heepe bache
part of the price of the laxd? Why didst thou yield up thy tongue
at the command of thy covetous, or thy unbelieving heart ? why
hath Sathan filled thy heart? Thou mightest have denyed Satan
when he tempted thee to deny part of the price. Thus the Lord
may say to most sinners, why hath Satan so prevailed ? why have
you yielded your hearts and consciences as slaves and captives to
him, without ever striking stroake for it? Consider this thing, It
is matter of great glory not to yield our selves at the call or com¬
mand of corruption, and it is not only the sin but the shame of
man, to suffer himselfe to be captivated by the command, or to be
at the becke and disposal ofhis lusts.
To cleare this a litle further, I shall shew by what steps or de¬
grees the Judgement of God acts touards sinners in this thing, as
also by what steps or degrees the lusts of men worke towards the
enslaving of themselves in this most miserable bondage of corrup¬
tion.
First, God in way of punishment suffers men to be overcome
and drawne away by their lusts. Thus the Apostle saith ( Act¬
14. 16.) God suffered all nations (except the Jewish nation) to
malhe in their owne wayes; that is, he did not checke or stop them
in their sinfull wayes and workings, as he did his owne people the
Jewes ( for we are not to understand the Apostle absolutely, but
comparatively) there never was any man, much lesse a Nation of
men in the world, who had not some stop against sin, the stop of
the light of nature at least; but every nation hath not had the
stop of ordinances, the preaching of the word, che motions of the
Soirit, these the Jewes Gods peculiar people had when the old
Gentiles had them not; they were suffered to goe onne in their
owne wayes without the light of the word, or helpe of holy or¬
dinances. Thus it is sayd (Psal. 147. 19, 30.) Ho seneth bus

0624.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition upon the Becke of Jo». Verl. 30.

body.t: Word unto Jacub, his Statutes and bis Judgements unto Israel:
he hath net dealt so mith any Nativn, and as for bis Judgements they
bave not hnownt them. In this sence God suffered all Nations to
walke in their owne wayes; He gave them not his word, his Sta¬
tutes, his Judgements, to shew them his wayes, or to hinder them
in their owne, and this was a sore Judgement.
Secondly, God doth not only suffer nations and persons to
walke in their owne wayes, but sometimes ( uhen his urath is
boyled up to the highest ) he gives up nations and persons to their
owne hearts lust ( Rom: I. 26.) For this cause God gaut them up
unto vile affections: for even their momen did change the naturall
use into that which is against nature; and (v. 28.) God gave them
over to a reprobate minde (or a mind voyd of ludgement) to dot
those things which are not convenient. God did not only leave
them to their lusts, and let them worke wickednes wit hout checke
and controle, but in a Judiciary way he put them into the hand
of their lusts, and (as ’tis sayd in that dreadfull prophetical threat,
(Psal.69.27.) He added iniquity to their iniqui:y; that is, he gave
them full scope in sin, making their latter in quity the punishment
of their former iniquity. The fullfilling of which threat upon the
Jewes, who maliciously persecuted and crucified Christ, is set
doune at large by the Apostle (I Thes:2.15, 16.) nho both
Rilled the Lord Jesus, and their omne Prophets, and have persecuted
us: and they please not God, and are contrary to all men; forbidaing
us to speake to the Gentiles, that they might be saved, to fill up their
sins alway: for the wrath is come upon them to the utmest. The A¬
postle saith not, wrath is come upon them, but (notant er) the mrath
is come upon them to the utmost; that is, The wrath threatned
in the Plalme last cited, Adde iniquity to their iniquity; for thus
the Jewes were given up to the wrathfulnes of their oune spirits
against Christ and the Gospel, to fill up their sins alway, as the
Apost le there speakes. And so God added iniquity to their ini¬
quity, and did not let them come (as it follows in that place of the
Psalme) into his righteousnes; that is, into the righteousnesse of
Christ by faith, but left them as to the pollution of their oune
lusts, so to a Justification by their owne workes ( Rom. I0. 3.)
which was a greater judgement then the other, and the perfect¬
ing of the threatning to the utmost.
Thus ve ses how Godin his secret but most righteous Judge¬

0625.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Bok ef IOR. Verl.3e.

body.t: ment, first suffers men to walke in their owne wayes, and then, se¬
condly, gives them up to their owne hearts lust. Now consider
also how and by what steps the lusts of men worke to the enthral¬
ling of themselves unto sin.
First, Most men suffer themselves to be carried auay by every
temptation; they never checke any sinfull motion, they say not
to their hearts, What are you thinking? nor to their mouthes,
what are you speaking ? nor to their hands, what are you doing
nor to their feete, whether are ye walking? but suffer heart, and
tongue, hand, and foote, to run what course they uill, and the
best of Saints take not such a strict course, eyther with their hearts
or tongues, hands and feete, as they ought.
Secondly, Many doe not only suffer themselves to sin, but
give themselves up to sin. That’s the word which the Psalmist
useth, while he speakes of sinning by word (Psal. 50. 19.) Thou
givest thy tongue to evill, and thy tongue frameth deceit. And that's
the Apostles word (Eph.4.19.) while he speakes of sinfull workt,
whe being past feeling, have given themselves ouer unto lascivious¬
nes, to worhe all uncleanenes with greedines. They who give them¬
selves to sin, doe more then suffer themselves to sin; They as'tis
sayd (Psal.36.4.) Set themselves in a way that is not good, that
is, in an evill way, or in the worst of wayes; yea they (in direct
opposition to that of the Apostle, (Rom. 12.1.) present their bo¬
dyes a dead sacrifice, unholy and abominable unto God, accepta¬
ble to the devill, which is their unreasonable or unwordly ser¬
vice.
Thirdly, There are some who doe more then give, they sell
themselves to doe evill; as ’tis sayd of Ahab (1 Kings 21.20.)
There was none libe Ahab (he was a wicked man by himselfe) xho
sould himselfe to morhe mickednesse in the sight of the Lord, wbem¬
Jezebel his mife stirred up. And so the Lord speakes of those A¬
postatizing Idolatrizinglewes (2 Kings 17. 17.) They caused
their sons and their daughters to passe througb the fire, and used di¬
vination, and inchantments, and sould themselves to doe evill in tht
fight of the Lord, te provehe him to anger. How divinely contrary
was fobs practice to the practice of all these! He did not suffer
himselfe to sin, these not only suffered, but give up & sould them¬
selves to do evill. All men are given to sin by nature, but some do
by a hind of covenant give up themselves unto sin, men are given

0626.head: Chap.31. Au Exροfιιίοκ upον thι Bok of JOR. Verl. 30

body.t: to this or that sin by their temper, thus one is given to anger,
another to wantonnes; this is bad enough, but for any to give
themselves to sin is farre worse, and they uho sell themselves to
doe wickedly, doe worst of all. “Tis the affliction of Saints that
they are sould under sin (Rom. 7. 14.) and ’tis the joy and af¬
fectation of some wicked men to fell themselves unto sin. They
doe ill enough who suffer themselves to doe evill, but they are
extreamely wicked who devote and dedicate themselves to it,
especially they who make a compact with the devill, who make a
Bargaine and sale of themselves to doe it. Blessed and holy is that
man who can say and say truely what ob here did, I have not
suffered my mauih te sin.
Thirdly, Observe.
A godly man watcheth over himselfe, over his mouth especially,
lest sin breake out there.
David gave this counsel to others ( Plal. 34. 13.) Keepe thy
tongue from evill, and thy lips from speabing guile. And he tooke
this courfe and counsel him ( Psal. 39. 1, 2.) I said I nill take
heed to my wayes, that I sin not with my tongue: I mill keepe my
xouth nith a bridle, mbile the micked is before me. I mas dumbe
with silence, I held my peace, even from good, and my sorrow was
stirred. Thus David, religious David (as Job) did not suffer his
mouthte sin. And the Apostle fames tells us (Chap. 1. 26.)
If any man seeme to be religious, and bridleth not his iongue, but de¬
ceiveth hu owne heart, that mans religion is vaine. That, such a
mans religion is vaine, may be understood two wayes. First, that
he hath no religion, nothing but a shew of it, that which hath
nothing but a fhew, shewes it selfe to be nothing. Meere appea¬
rances are nullities. Some who seeme religious, speake so vainely,
that their religion is as vaine as their speech, and we may argue
that the one is nothing, because the other is worse then nothing.
Secondly, Such a mans religion is vaine, because his religion doth
not performe its office, which is, to bridle up his tongue from
sinsull speakings, and all the members of his body from sinfull
actings. That which doth not reach the end to which it was ap¬
pointed and designed is a vaine thing. Surely David vas afrayd
his religion might fallunder this sentence of vanity, when he pray¬
ed so heartily ( Plal, 141. 3.) Set a match (O Lord) before my

0627.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Book of JOB. Verf. 30

body.t: mouth, beepe the doere of my lips. God who is infinirely glorious
will yet condescend to be our doore keeper, to be a doore. keeper
to our hearts, yea to keepe the duore of our lips, he will not dis¬
daine that office when we humNy sue unto him to undertake it.
As a godly man beggs of God to open his mouth for holy uses
(Psal. 51. 15.) Open theu my lips, and my mouth shall shew fortb
thy praise (we cannot open our lips to the prayse of God, unlesse
God come with his key and unlocke them) so he beggs of God
to shut his mouth, and keepe the doore of his lips for him, that
he sin not with his tongue.
Fourthly, “Tis remarkeable that Job did not say I endeavou¬
red that my mouth should not sin, but he saith, Neither have I
suffered my mouth to fin.
Hence observe.
A godly man caresully watching cver himselfe, hupes his
mouth from sinfull speakings.
He doth not only attempt this restraint, but he may attaine it;
This labour shall not be in vaine in the Lord. Yet we are not to
understand the poynt, as if a Godly man might attaine to sucha
corquest over corruption as never to sin at all by word, but as to
this or that temptation he may. Thus Job prevailed over his
heart and tongue not to curse man, his reall enemy as before he
did, not to curse God when he acted towards him in appearance
like an enemy. But saith not the Apostle James ( Chap. 3 8.)
The tongue no man can tame, it is an unruly evill. This some
understand with reference to the torgues of other men, who can
tame his intemperate tongue that boasteth, my tongue is my omne,
who is Lord over me? But we may better understand it of a mans
owne tongue; The tongue is often too hard for the whole man;
no man can tame it; that is, no man can tame it of himselfe; but
a man may obraine power of God to tame it. This unruly evill
may be ruled & brought under good government by the strength
of grace. The tongue is an unruly evill, but not an unconquera¬
ble evill. A godly man may come off with victory, and be more
then a conqueror (through the strength of Christ ) over all those
temptations which would set the tongue afire in evill speaking,
or by evill speaking kindle a fire among others. The tongue is a
fire, and’cis Bellowes also, from both ill tongued persons are just.

0628.head: Chap. 31. An Expositiou upon tbe Boobe ef IOR. Verl. 30.

body.t: Iy called incendiaries, yet this fire may be quench't, and these Bel¬
lowes may be broken and made breath. lesle as to the kindling of
the flames of contention.
Indeed the opposition of most as against other corruptions, so
against this of evill speaking is not to conquest, though they make
some offers to bridle their tongues, and say they will not suffer
their mouth to sin, yet their tongues are their Masters. I will give
you a two-fold reason why the opposition which many make
against this evill of the tongue, or any other evill is not to
victory.
First, Because tis weake and slight; A carnall mant resisting
of evill is like his desiring of good; He desireth good, but attaines
it not, because his desires are weake and cold, there is no strength,
no heate in them: thus also he opposeth evill but cannot prevaile,
because he opposeth it faintly.
Secondly, "Tis not only weake but falle and treacherous; He
is not reall and hearty in it; Tob set himselfe in good eurnest a¬
gainst his tongue, when it was ready to breake out sinfully, and
he did it prevailingly. His was a hearty, and therefore an effe¬
ctuall resistance. While some decry both evill workes and evill
words, they delight in them, and hold secret correspondence with
them. Tob opposed his tongue really, and he had his will of it;
He suffered not bus moutb to fin.
Fifthly, Observe.
Th month, or tongnt of man, is a very great and coumon iestru¬
went of sin.
That's the generall truth of this verse. The tongue is an en¬
gine of more mischiefe both to our selves and others then any o¬
ther member of the body. The Apostle saith ( Rom. 3. 13.) of
naturall men, Their Throat is an open sepulcher. Which similitude
stands in two things; First, because there comes a stench out of
their throats by filthy ill-sented and unsavoury words; Second ly,
because they gape after and devoure the credit and good name of
their neighbours. The tongue of man being rightly used is his
glory. When David saith ( Psal. 37. 8.) Amabe my glorz, hee
calls his tongue to awake. The tongue is mans glory because it
lifteth up the glory of God, and as the tongue of a godly man is
his glory, so che tongues of wiched men are their shame, they

0629.head: Chap. 31. An Expofition upon the Booke ef JOR. Verf.30.

body.t: proclaime their owne sin, and hide it not. We are such as our
words are; Such, I meane, as our words ordinarily are. No good
man can speake much evill, and how litle socver he speakes (being
convinced of it ) he repents of it. And though a bad man may
speake good uords, yet his words (except in sound ) are no bet¬
ter then he is. For while he speakes what he is not, or meanes not,
or believes not, or practises not, though what he speakes be good
in it selfe, and may doe good to others, yet as spoken by him, tis
as bad as he is; He is hypocriticall, and fo are his words. There¬
fore the Apostle James concludes (Chap. 3 2.) If any man of¬
fend not in word he is a perfest man; not only pertect, as perfecti¬
on is opposed to hypocrisie and notes fincerity, but perfect as
perfection is opposed to a lesser degrer of grace, and notes our
growth and progresse in holynes. He is not only a beginner, but
a great proficient in grace who offends not in word. That man
hath a great command of his thoughts, who can command his
tongue; and so declares himselfe a perfect man. And when the
Apostle saith, If any man effend not in werd, he intimates that there

Solomon saith (Pro. 18. 21.) Death and life are in the power of the

whether they are bound for death or for life, for heaven or hell.
That's the meaning of Christ (Matb. 12. 37) By thy mords thou
halt be justified, and by thy words thou shali be condemned, we are
not justified in a strict sence, eyther by our words or workes;
nothing but the righteousnesse of Christ receaved and applyed by
faith can doe that; yet according to the usage of the tongue the
sentence of condemnation and justification uill be pronounced in

have spoken: and as others have heard them spesking, so they
chall heare Christ speaking.
Againe, As we usually fall into tongue sins, so ue easily fall
into them. For, first, there is a speedy passage between the heart
and tongue, the heart is quickly at the tongues end; evill thoughts
ure foone formedup into evill mords, Secondiy, fpecch is a natu¬

body.t: rall and humane act flouing from the light and lise of reason,
there is no labour, no study for it; words are at hand presently,

Tis a griefe to the Spirit of God to heare bad words come out of

"Tis not only pleasant but profitable. Many a mans tongue brings

or they trade off their wares with lyes Solomon (Pro. 21. 6.)

fro, of them that secke death. Where he shewes, First, that therés
much gaining by lying; when a man is buying and selling, when
he is driving a bargaine, how apt is he to make an ill use of his

hurts muche, for Thirdly, they who speake lyes see ke death. But

rectly, but many seeke death consequentially; they seeke death,

ing is the way to death, even to eternall death. Thus the getting
of treasure by a lying tongue, is a vanity tossed to and fro, ef them¬
that seche death; that is, the wealth and treasure which they get

selves or their heires. In this sence also that of the Apostle (Jam:
3.6. Jis a truth: The tongue le a fire (it sets that on fire which is
got by sinfull words) and the tongue is a world of iniquitie ( that

course of nature, and (would you know whence the tongue takes

body.t: faculcies of soule and body, by which nature moves and makes its
course; so it selfe is set on fire by him who hath disordered the

To co-clude this poynt, and so to passe to the latter part of the

First, AIl Idle or workelesse words, that is, words which worke

37.) All such word: (I say) are sinfull. Those are evill words which
doe no good as wel as those which doe hurt. Eliphaz sait h to Tob
(Chap. 15. 3.) Should a xise man reason mith unpr fitable talke?
or mith speeches wheremith he can doe ne good? While we speake

Many are troubled at those words by œhich they have done hurt
to, or infect ed others, but few are troubled for those words by
which they have done no good, or not edified others.
Secondly, Uusea sonable words are offensive words. (Eccl.3.7.)
Thert is a time to keepe silence, and a time to speake. A word fitly
( that is opportunely) spoken, u lihe apples of gold in pictures of

Thirdly, As the mouth sins by unseasonable words, so speci¬
ally by unseasoned words ( Col. 4. 6.) Let your speech be almayes
mith grace, seasoned mith salt. Words are seasoned with a two-fold

rer. Those must needs be unseasoned words that have neyther

ment the ungracious words which proceed from the mouths of

Fourthiy, Harsh, uncharitabie and Cenforious words, are ths

body.t: sins of the mouth. Christ will come to judge the ungodly for the
hard speeches which they have spoken against him ( Jude v. 15.)

Fifthly, Hasty inconsiderate words, spoken to men, but esp:¬
cially to God, are sins of the mouth; hence Solomons cautioz

ther; we should confider our words before ue utter them, and

Sixthly, Obscene wanton words are very sinsull; These the

Let your tongues be employed in the praises of God, not in poy¬
soning one another;filthy words are poyson taken in at the eare,
and they defile and infect the heart,
Seventhly, Boasting proud words are sinfull. They that suel

selves; It is best both to thinke and speake of our felves, below

Eighthly, Detracting lessening words concerning others are
sinfull; as proud men make more of themselves then they are,
so they usually diminish the worth of others. It is immodesty to

Ninthly, Flattering words are sins of the mouth, these are
directly contrary to the former, the detractor takes away from

tering words in all men are sinfull; so those and theirs especially

ceeding sinfull, and no lesse dangerous. Faithfull are the πoundi
of a friend ( saith Solomon, Pro. 27. 6.) but the tisses of an enemy

body.t: are dectitful. The wounding friend is a just reprover; The kis¬

Tenthly, Slandering and reproaching words, which cast dirt

Eleventhly, Prophane and blaspheming words, when any

Tuelfthly, Provokirg quarrelling words, such as stirre up

To all these we may adde, scoffing, and jeering words; grie¬
ving, cutting, and vexing words; spitefull and malicious words,

be named, are sins of the mouth, then consider how great an in¬
strument of sin the mouth is, and remember you will have some¬
uhat to doe, to doe ( as this good man did) not to suffer your

Iob having affirmed, that he did not suffer his mouth to sin,

fin,
by misbing a carse to hù sonle.
That is, to the soule of my most professed and wretched enemy.

The word which we render to miso, signifieth, First, to demand

body.t: also out of their deselatt places. Thirdly, as here in the text, it is

And he said unto his mother, the eleven hundred shekelli of filver

body.t: he chould have brought mischiefe enough upon the children of

with it. That man is miserable enough who is under a curse; and
therefore whatsoever misery j br enemies attempted to bring up¬
on him, he never wished this misery, a curse upon them.
Further, Job doth not say, I did not wisb a curse upon his estate,
or upon his children and family; he doth not say, I did not œish
a curse upon his labours and undertakings, nor doth he say, I did
not wish a eurse upon his body, But he saith, I did mish a curse
upon his soule.
What the soule is, hath been sheued at the 15th verse of the
former Chapter, and the severall significations of the word in
Scripture was shewed at the 16th verse of the same Chapter,
Here we may take it,
First, Strict ly, in opposition to the body: now as to wish a
curse is to wish the greatest evill, so to wifh a curse upon the soule
is to wish the greatest curse A man may beare a curse any where
better and eafier then upon his soule. Better have a curse upon
our estate, or name, upon the children of our bodyes, or upon our
owne bodyes, then upon our soules. There the curse goes deepest,
and lyeth heavyest.“Tis sayd of Joseth when a captive and a pri¬
soner (Psal. 105. 18.) His feete they hurt mith fetters, he was

are exceedingiy hightned in urath and resolutions ofrevenge,i¬

0636.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition upon the Boohe ef JOB. Verf. 30.

body.t: uill not serve their turne, nor satisfie the passion of their vindi¬
ctive spirits to wish a curse upon the bodyes of their enemies,

provoked one who had offended him to blaspheme God, and

damne them litle knowing or not at all believing what the dam¬
nation eyther of soule or body is. In this first sence of the word,
Job surely, was at furthest distance from wishing a curse upon the

Secondly, We may take soule for the life; neither se did Job

nemy to death, nor beg of God to cut off the threed of his life.
The Lord sayd to Selomon (I Kings 3. 11.) Because thou hast

thinke Rands in our way, and them wrapt up even in the darknes

Thirdly, I conceive we may take the word soule here in the
largest sence, as it signifies the whole man; I have not mished a

Hence note.
First, The beart and mouth of man are naturally bent to wiso
and bespeabe evill tocthers.
The Apostle puts this among the other the bad qualities of all
those who are under sin, that is, all persons unregenerate ( who

ally done us hurt ? Every man naturally desires that uherein he

body.t: beare to wish it; They who can doe no hurt to others can wisti
it, and ufually they who can doe least wish it most, and what
their hands cannot reach to, they strive to reach and effect with
their tonpues. Salvian found this cursed Spirit, the Spirit of cur¬
sing, much up in his dayes; Curses (saith he ) are the first instru¬
ments ef anger, aud that mhich me sannet doe because ve are
veake, me uish may be done, because me are enraged. To pray for
good to others, or to blesse them, is one of the most proper

them, is one of the most proper workes of unrenewed nature.
Secondly, Observe.
To curse or wis ill to another, though an enemy, is very finfall.
Cursing is one of the worst uses or services the tongue of man
can be put to, as blessing is one of the best. He that wisheth a
a curse upon another, puts God to the doirg of that, which cy¬
ther, first, he is not able to doe, or secondly, is afraid to doe, or
thirdly, is ashamed to doe: now what a wickednesse is it for man
to desire God to doe that for him, which as himselfe cannot, so
he is eyther afraid or ashamed to doe. Christ in his Sermon up¬
on the Mount (Math: 5. 44.) commands us to love our entmies,
and to blesse those that curse us. And the Apostle saith (Rom 12.
14.) Blisse them that persecute you, blesse and curse not. The Law
of Gospel love doth not rest in Negatives. Tis much to refraine
from evill actings towards an enemy, ’cis more to refraine from
uishing him evill, or cursing him, but ’tis most of all to blesse him.
And wheras some may wonder why the Apostle should say, Blesse
and curse not, and not rather curse not but blesse; for a man that
abstaines from cursing may not yet proceed to blesse, but it would
be a strange thing if when a man hath blessed his enemy he should
then proceed to turse him. I answer, when the Apostle saith,
Blesse and curse not, I conceave his meaning may be only this,
that we should cary it alike, First, ro all persecuters, and not blesse
some and curse others, or Secondly, that we should cary it alike
at all times; and not by any extremity which they use tous, turne
our selves from blessing to cursing.
But some may say, Is it altogether unlawfull to curse an ene¬
my, or to wist him evill, have we not many examples of dread¬
sull curses in Scripture; David powres doune a whole shower

0638.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upou the Bock of 1° 2. Verl. 30

body.t: of them upon the heads of the Jewes, whom he foreshewed cruci¬

snare before them, and that mhich should have been for their velfare

upon them, and let thy wrathfull anger take hold of them. These

they may not see, and bon domne their backe elway. We read also,
that when a Captaine was sent up with his fifty to apprehend E¬
liab (2 Kings 1. 10, 11.) He prayed, axd sayd, IfIbe a man of
God, tben let fire come domne from heaven, and consume tbee and thy
fifty; and thert came donne fire from heaven and consumed him¬
and bis fifiy. And when chiléren mocked Elisba his successor, and
sayd, Goe up thou bald head, goe up thou bald-bead; he turned back
and lookt upon them, and cursed them in the name of the Lerd, and
presently there came forth tmo shee beares out of the mood and tare
forty and tuo children of them ( 2 Kirgs 2. 24) Doth not Paul
curse false teachers ( Gal. 5. 12.) I mould they vere even cut ff
that trouble you. And we have an irrecoverable curse pronounced
by the same Apostle upon all false hearted professors (ICer:16.
22.) If any man love not the Lord Jesus Corist, let him be Anathe¬
ma Maranatha; that is, let him be accursed till the Lord come,
let him be everlastingly accursed, then surely it is not lawfull to
curse.
I answer; First, That place in the Plalme is rather a prophecie
then an imprecation, or’tis a propheticall imprecation, fore tel¬
ling from God what evill should fall upon the Jewes, not a
wishi from himselfe that evill should fall upon them. The Spirit
of God fore-seing how the obstinate unbeleeving Jewes would
be hardned against, and act their malice to the utmost upon
Christ when he should come in the flesh, stirred up and directed
the Spirit of David to declare this heavy doome against them.
Secondly, The Prophets and holy men, mentioned in Scrip¬
ture, who cursed others, may be considered eytber as private per¬
sons, and as to their personal concerrments, and in that capacity
they used all meeknesse of speech, and cursed none; or they may
be considered as publick persons, imployed in Gods worke, or
called
M m m m 2

0639.head: Chap.31. An Expesition upon the Boske ef JOR. Verf.30.

body.t: called to make knowne his mind to the sons of men; and in that
capacity as they were not to feare any man, so not to spare any
man; They being charged at their own perill to tell others what
perill they were in. And therefore they boldly declared the curse
of God ( not their owne ) against thole who deser ved it.
Thirely, I answer; these curses proceeded not from a spirit
of revenge, or from any impulse of wrath in the Prophets them¬
selves, but were spoken, First, to terrifie the wicked, and leave
monitory examples of the righteous judgements of God before
the eyes of all men. Secondly, to confirme and encourage the
faithfull, by letting them see how suddainely and how easily, e¬
ven with a word of his mouth, God could destroy their strongest
enemies, yea that they are already blasted by, and withering un¬
der a curse. Thirdly, those curses were denounced in a heat of
zeale, for the glory of God, and the good of the Church, they
had not the least heat of private revenge in them.When the Pro¬
phets and Apostles breathed out curses, like the fumes and flames
of hell it selfe, against sinners, their minds were calme, serene, and
heavenly. Last ly, chose curses were pronounced (not as carnal
men curse one another in a storme of passion, but) by vertue of
their office and commission. As the civil Magistrate gives sen¬
tence of death upon a malefactor, who disturbes the publicke
peace, and offers violence to the life of his fellow citizens; so did
the Prophets and holy men of God, pronounce the sentence of
some fearefull curse upon the knowne and incorrigible enemies of
God, and of his people.
So then those Scripture examples before mentioned, are no
warrant or ground at all for any to belch out Curses against the
soule state, life, or person of another upon personal respects.

The word here translated, to be sati, fud, signifies also to smiare,

Me ( said the men of Jobs Tabernacle) cannet be satirfied.
That is, nothing uill stay our hunger but the flesh, nothing uill

without that
mee cannot be satisfied.
The word signifies any kind of filling, whether to satisfaction,

Thus in all ages men of power have had tempters neere them,

Secordly, Consider Tob was farre from any such hunger or

The men of sobs Tabernacle were so farre from patiente at

Thirdly, No doubt fob was hard put toit to refraine his pas¬

body.t: ednesse; but his wife was the temptresse, and bid him make the

a mife. Let fervants remember they cannot in any thing more dis¬
serve, nor disoblidge their Masters, then by serving their ill hu¬
mours and passions, when commanded by them; How wicked
then are those servants uho nourish their ill humours, and adde
fewel to that fire which they should labour to quench? Wee can¬
not doe any man a worse office, nor shew him more reall dis¬
affection, then by abetting him in evill, and oyling his wheeles
by counsel or encouragement, when we see him in any sinful mo¬
tion. Such counsel hath osten proved fatal, and such encourage¬
ments doe but hasten, yea precipitate men into ruine. The Apo¬
stles rule is ( Heb. 10. 24 ) Let us provoke one another te love and
to goed morkes. The best need a spurre to doe uel; He is the truest
friend and the most faithfull servant, who is fullest of these holy
provocations; He loves his friend to purpose, who provokes
him to love; and that servant workes for his Master to purposes
who provokes him to good workes. But to provoke to wrath,
to revenge, or to any evill worke, is to officiate for the devill, or
to doe the devils worke, whose proper worke it is ro provoke us
to evill, and to obstruct us in all good workes. And ’tis hard to
determine who serves the devills turne, and promotes his interest
most, he that hinders and cooles the spirit of another that is about
to doe good, or he that thrusts him forward and furnisheth him
with assistance to doe evill.
Fourthly, Note.
Not to doe, or to forbeare the doing of that evill to mhich xe are
provoked, and greatly proveted, is an argument of much
strength of grace, or of a great measure of goodnes.
It had been well if fob had not taken revenge upon his enemies.
when friends ( perceaving his Spirit bent that way ) had advised

from doing any intended evill. David (1 Sam. 25.) was much

body.t: resolved to revenge himselfe upon Nabal, his heart uas fiered
with fury enough to consume him and all that he had, his fury

the land of I/rael, Erch. 38.18. His fury, I say) was come up in
his face; yet how meekly did he submit, how soone uas he taken
off by the dissuasion of Abigail a discreet woman, who gave him
advice and Councell to the contrary ? Blessed be the Lord God of
Ifrae! ( saith he ) mhich sent thee this day to meete me, and blessed
be thy advice, and blessed be thou, mhich hast hept mee this day from
coming to sped blood, and from avenging my selfe mith mine omne
band. This (I say) was a great act of grace; but it is a farre
higher act of grace to forbeare revenge when vee are provoked
and councelled to it : when it shall be whispered in out eare;
will jou endure this? mill you beare this? nill you be such a focle?
mill you stand lihe a stocé or a stone ? Surely for a man to be as dease
as a ftock to such whisperers as these, is grace in the height of it.
As it shewes much strength of grace when we are strongly set up¬
on by the temptations of Satan, to resist and forbeare, so when
we are set upon by friends, by servants, or relations; who in such
cases are as the Devills right hand, to assist us in doing mischitfe.
Againe, as ( on the other side ) not to doe that good which wee
are advised, and councelled, yea provoked to, by friends and re¬
lations, who are ( which is one of the best offices of a friend ) like
goads in our sides to put us on in the wayes of holinesse, (as, this
I say) argues much strength and prevalency of corruption; so it
is an evidence that grace prevailes mightily in the soule uhen be¬

rocke, and are as the deafe Adder that stops her eare against the

have the best eares who cannot heare, and the best hearts who

Fifthly, Observe:

body.t: that fob did so, that hee reproved his servants here, as he did his

body.t: It uill not satisfie a godly man to have corruption a litle re¬

If I covered my transgressions as Adam: by hideing

OB having spoken much in many particulars for the vindica¬

had my failtings as mel as other men, for I also am a son of Adam;

If I have covered my transgressions.

body.t: The original word signifieth properly to cover with a garment?
or vaile, with any thing, which gives shadow or is a meanes of
concealment. Yet some distinguish the native signification of this
word from another in the Hebrew tongue somewhat neere it in
the letter; that signifying to cover as houses or tents cover us
(& from thence the word Succoth signifying tents or booths, is de-
rived) weP cover us by being over us, or we being in them, where¬
as this word signifies to cover as cloaths or garments cover us,
by being put upon us, or by our putting them on.But not to stay
upon that strictnesse of the word in its proper sence; here we are
to understand it metaphorically, and so’tis applyed two wayes in
Scripture; First, to that gracious act of God in pardoning our
transgressions; Secondly, to that ungracious act of man in deny¬
ing or excusing his transgressions. Tis anact of greatest grace in
God to cover our transgressions by a pardon. He never shews
himselfe more as God, then when he thus hides the sin of man.
And’tis an act most opposite to grace, for man to cover his sin by
denying or excusingit; man never shews himselfe more a man,
a sinfull man, then when he covers his sin. That act of divine
pardoning Grace David expresseth in the language of Jebs text
(Psal. 32. 1.) Blessed ì the man mhose transgression is forgiven,
and mhese sin is covered. By whom covered?̀ not by himselse but
by God. That which is called the forgivenes of sin in the former
part of the verse, is called covering of it in the latter part. Solo¬
mon speakes the same thing of God, though he useth another
word (Pro.25. 2.) It is the glory of God to conceale (or cover)
a thing; he meanes a sinfull thing, or that which is worse then no¬
thing, sin. To cleare this a litle further, we read in Scripture of a
foure-fold covering of sin for good.
First, There is a covering of sin, by mercy or free love; that
indeed is the fountaine from whence this transcended favour, the
forgivenes of sin floweth tous. I,even I am he ( saith the Lord,
Isa.43.25.) that blotteth out thy transgressions for my name sake,
and vill not remember thy sins. That is, the rise and first moving
cause of this is in my selfe, it proceeds out of my owne bosome.
There is no moving cause antecedent to the love of God, why
sinners are pardoned, though there be a first or chiefe working
cause of the pardoning or covering of our sins; And that is the
next way of covering sin.

though he stop the proceedings of justice, he looseth nothing by
it abecause as sin is covered by his owne mercy, so by the merito¬
rious obedience of Christ, œhich gives full satisfaction to all the
demands of justice. The mercy seat or propitiatory (which was
an illustrious type of Christ ) covered the Arke in uhich the Law
was kept (Ex-d. 25. 10, 17.) This mercy seat was of the same
Iength and breadth with the Arke. And Muses was commanded
to puc the mercy seat upon the Arke, implying that all our trans¬
gressions of the law of God, are covered by the righteousnesse
of Jesus Christ, who is both our propstiatory (Rem. 3. 25. ) and
our propitiation (I Joh. 2.2.) that is, who by the sacrifice of
himselfe hath made our atonement or agreement with God,
which was figured by the propitiatory or mercy seat, covering all
those transgressions which we were any way chargeable with by
the Law.
Thirdly, Sins are covered as by the mercy of God, and the
righteousnesse of Christ, so by the charity of man. Thus any god¬
Iy man may and ought to cover the sin of his brother (I Pit. 4.
8.) Above all thingi have perfect charity among your selves: for
charity shall cover the multitude of sinnes. True charity hath a gar¬
ment long and large enough to cover many, yea a multitude of
fins. Charity cannot cover our own sins as to the jastification of
our persons before God, 'tis a garment too thin and too narrow
for that purpose, nor was it ever cut out & appoynted by God to
such a use; but charity should and may cover the sins of others,
as to the preservation of their credit among men, and the main¬
taining of our peace and correspondence vith them. “Tis dange¬
rous as wel as unwarrantable to cover the sinnes of others by
flattery ( such a covering of sin is not only an encouragement to
sin, but may prove the utter undoing of the sinner) but to cover
a sin by charity, that is, while we are admonishing or wisely re¬
proving our brother our selves, to conceale it from others, or not
to publish and blaze it abroad to his shame, or the provocation
of passion in him, is a great piece of Christian duty, and may be
a mesnes of recovering him from the power and practice of his
fin. Thus Solomen faith (Pro. 10. 12.) Harred ßirretb ap ftrése,

body.t: but love covereth all sins; That is, the love of man to man pre¬
vents wrath by covering sin for the sinners good, not to cloake
and harden him in his sin, but to winne him out of it; or love co¬
vereth, that is, pardonetb all the sins of others so farre as they
concerne any injury done to us; thus Christ teacheth us to for¬
give those that trespasse against us (Math: 6.12, 15.) yea love
causeth others to forgive us the wrongs which we have done
them; whereas hatred (that is, any expression of hatred eyther by
words or actions) doth but stirre up strife, and make the breach
wider. Hatred alwayes encreaseth ftrife where it is, and often be¬
gins it where it is not; love alwayes lookes upon great wrongs
as small, and upon mmall ones as none at all. The Church hifto¬
ry reports of Constantine the Great and first Christian Emperor,
that when severall accusations were brought against some of the
Bishops assembled at the Councel of Nice, He would not suffer
them to be urged in publicke, but professed he would rather co¬
ver them with his royall robes, then let them breake out to the
hindrance of the worke, and the scandall of those perlons who
were concerned in them.
Fourthly, Man also is sayd in Scripture to cover sin by the
conversion of the sinner ( James 5. 19, 20.) Bretbren, if any of
you dot erre from the truth, and one convert him, let him kκοw, that
he mhich converteth the sinner from the error of his way, shall save
a soule from death, and sall hide a multitude of sienes; That is, if
any one among you who hath made an outward profession of the
truth, shall turne aside from the rule of the Gospel, whether in

whosoever shall be blessed as an instrument in Gods hand, by

out of that wandering and backsliding condition, This man shall
have the honour (be he who he will Minister or brother) to savt
a soule from deatb, and hide a multitude of fins. Some, I know,
understand these words of the Apostle, as referring to the salva¬
tion of the person who is the instrument of this conversion; his

ment of Timothy in his Ministry (I Tim. 4. 16.) In so doing,

ofthis text runs clearely to the person reduced from the error ot

body.t: his way; Thou foalt save a soule, that is, his soule, and hide a
multitude ef sins, that is, of his sins; as if he had sayd, thou shalt
be a meanes os bringing him to a sight of his sin, and so to hum¬
ble himselfe before Cod and secke the pardon of them, which is
the only true and happy hiding and covering of them.
Thus I have shewed foure coverings of sin, and in all these sen¬
ces, it is good for us, to have our sins covered. Blessed are they
whoie sins are covered by the free favour of God, by the righte¬
ousnesse of Christ, and by the wise charitie of their brethren, ey¬
ther not divulging them, or converting the sinner from them.
But there is a sinfull way in which sin is covered, or there is a
covering of sin, which is both the sin and misery of man, such a
covering of sin as will cover him with shame and confusion of
face for ever. And that’s it which Job disclaimes. He sought and
sought doubtlesse with all his soule to get his sin covered with
the mercy of God, with the righteousnesse of Christ the redee¬
mer, but he durst not make a cover for sin himfelfe, If I covered
my transgressions.
The word notes great or greatest sins, even rebellions and blas¬
phemy; by both which that speech of Elihu (Chap. 34.37.)
is rendred, and our transsation takes the former, For he addeth
rebellion unto his sinne. To rebel is more then barely to sin, Re¬
bellion is impudent and pertinacious sinning. Many sin, who ( in
strict sence) doe not rebel; they that rebel sin vith all their
might. They not only doe evill, but doe it against the light of
good councell givenby others, and against the light of their owne
consciences. How sinfull are they, who adde rebellion to their
sin! Some take it thus here, I have not covtred my transgressions
or my great sins; As if Job had sayd, I have not hid the worst of my
selfe, I have not only not seught to conceale my common fraileties,
but not my foulest spots, and greatest rebellions against Ged. Many
are free to confesse lesser sins, but they prepare coverings for their
grosse enormities. So that if we take the word transgressions, in
this peculiar signification, it much advanceth and advantageth
the sincerity of Jobs heart in this profession.
Yet I suppose we are not tied to that strictnesse of the word in
this place. And we find it sometimes used to expresse ordinary
fins and common faylings in other places of Scripture, (Pre, 70.

0666.head: Chep.31. An Exposition upou thi Book of JOn. Verl. 33.

body.t: 19.) In the multitude of words there rranteth not finne, That is,
there is usually store of sin in store of words, yet we know a slip
of the tongue (for we cannot probably interpret that Scripture ef
meditated evill speaking, a slip of the tongue I say ) is not recko¬
ned among great sins, though no sin considered init selse be litle.
So here I conceave Job intends that he did not cover any sin, whe¬
ther great or litle, when he saith, If I covered my tran (gressions
as Adam.
There's the restriction or modification of the act denyed. Yet
this word Adam may be taken two wayes; First, more narrowly
as a proper name. The first man was called Adam from Adamab,
red eartb, out of which the Lord made or created him (Gen. 2.
7.) And the Lord God formed man of the dust of the ground, and
breathed into his nestrills the breath of life. As Adam was formed
out of the dust of the earth, so from that he tooke his name.
And this sutes elegant y with Tobs purpose, and is also an argu¬
ment that Job was wel acquainted with, and instructed about,
those necessary principles of religion, the state of the first man in
his innocency, as also with his fall from that state, and the sad ef¬
fects and consequents of it. Adam having sinned, imployed that
lit le wit or vaine subtlety he had left to cover his sin, and hide it
from God, as I shall have occasion to shew more particularly, in
the prosecution of this Scripture. Therefore, saith Job, If I ceve¬
red my transgression as Adam, the first man Adam. Whether
Moses had tritten his five bookes before Jobs time is a query of
a difficult, if at all of a possible, resolution; yet however, God was
not wanting to his Church, but eyther by tradition from manto
man, or by immediate revelation from himselfe, continued the
doctrine of the creation and fall of man, with the necessary truths
depending thereupon among his people from Adam to Mises,
which might give ?ob light enough to say even with respect to
that personal act of Adam, I I'have covered my transgreffions as
Adam.
Secondly, We may take the word Adam more largely, that
is, Appellatively, or as a common name applicable to all men;
for every man, since the first man Adam, is an Adam. There are
three words by which man is expressed in Scripture.
First, I/, which signifieth man in his highest excellency and

0667.head: Chap.31. An Expositicu upon the Bock of JOR. Verf. 33.

body.t: dignity, in the quicknesse of his parts and gifts, in the best dresse
or habit of Nature or of Grace.
Secondly, Enosp, which notes man compassed about with in¬
firmity, even weakly, sickly, sad and sorrousull man, or man
though possibly renewed by grace, vet) yet cloathed and bur¬
dened uith the tronblesome issnes of a sinfuss nature.
The third word is that of the text, Adam, and this belong to
all manxinde, or to man as man, whether great or small, strong or
weake, every man is Adam, his body being of the earth earthly.
If I have covered my transgresfions as Adam; That is, as men usu¬
ally doe. Thus the Prophet speakes ( Hosea 6.7.) But they, libe
men, have transgressed thi Covenant. We put in the Margin, like
Adam. And inthe Margin ofthis text in Jeb, we put, aster the

men; That is, as the race and generality of mankinde have hereto¬
fore done and doe to this day. As if he had sayd, I have uot trod
the path, nor followed the course of the world, xho make it their first
busines to sin, and their next to cover and hide their sins.Mr. Brough¬
ton translates fully to this sence of the word; If I'have covered my
sin as every man doth; implying that this is an epidemicall pra¬
ctical disease, infecting all forts and degrees of men. If I cove¬
red my transgressions as Adam,
By bideing mine iviquitie in my bosome.
In these words Job further explaines how he did not cover his
sin, He did not hiac it in his bosome. The word translated to hide,
notes a cunning artificiall hiding, such as hunters or foulers use
when they would take their prey, These lay their nets very close¬
Iy ( for as Solamon saith (Pro. 1. 17.) Surely in vaine is the net
spread in the sight of any bird ) and so the Psalmist expresseth it in

taken; Such a hiding of his iniquity Job denyeth, a close cunning

deth his hand in his bosome, and xill not bring it to his mouth againe,
he had rather starve then worke, and perish rather then be at the
paines to feed himseife. Thus the sinner hideth his iniquity in his
bosome, and will not bring it to his mouth againe; that is, he
had rather be, at least he will venture to be, damned then con¬

body.t: fesse or discover it; He will not bring his bosome sin to his mouth
ina holy confession eyther to God or man. I (saith τ b) havς
not hid
mine iniquitie.
That is, the iniquity which l'am most prone to, and uhich my
heart goeth most after, every man hath some iniquity, which he
may call his speciall iniquity more then any other iniqui y. The
word iniquity in this latter part of the verse, and tran groĩon in
the former are the same in substance; yet this word properly sig.
nifieth that which is crooked or bowed. Holy actions are straight
right, and tend upuard; sinfull actions are crooked and bend
downward. Cain the first borne sinner applyed this word to

13.)Ay punishment is greater then I can beare; ve put in the Mar¬
gin, Mine iniquity is greater, then that it may be forgiven. And
as it notes the crookednes of our actions, so the viliosity of our

David) I mas shapen in (that most crooked and miche pen thing
called) iniquity. This original iniquity as wel as any actuall
though the former lyes clolest and deepest there) must not be
hidden in our bosome; and we may wel conceave that fob had
an ayme at this, when he sayd, I have not covered my trun gressi¬
ons, by hiaing mine iniquitie in
my bosome.
This phrase, To hide iniquity in the bosome, imports the neare st
closing with and loving imbraces of any iniquity. The bosome is
a secret place, and to put a thing in tue bosome, is to keepe it as

fore from the world, is sayd to come out of the bosome of the

body.t: Yet further, Some of the Jewish Rabbins translate, thus, IfI
have hid my sin is my selfe-love, or in the love ef my selfe, or as Mr.
Rroughton, of a selfe-love. With which reading other late learned
Interpreters agree. Some thus; Hiding my six because I loved it,
or out of love to my selse. As selfe love is a sin, so many hide their
sins out of love to selfe. Those things that we love dearely and
have a precious esteeme of, we hide safely; That’s the emphasis
of these latter translations; If I have hid my iniquity because I
loved it, or, Because of my selfe-love; As if Job had assigned two
ethings, which might have prevailed with him to conceale his sin,
mezif he had not feared God; First, the patterne he had from Adam,
or from the dayly practice of most men. Secondly, the love
which man naturally beares to sin. I have not covered my trans¬
gresfions libé Adam, nor hath my love to them overcome me to
hide them.
Againe, When fob saith, he did not cover his transgressions,
nor bide his iniquity in his bosome. We must under stand him in the
full latitude of these words; And so more is intended then ex
pressed; eventhat he acknowledged and confessed his sin As he
did rot proclaime his sin in the market place, so he did discover
it, as in duty he ought, that is, in time, place, and manner conve¬
nient. He not only did not hide his sin, but he acknowledged and
confessedit. As all the negative precepts include their affirma¬
tives, so some negative practices include their affirmatives. Ac¬
cording to which rule of Scripture interpretation, wee may con¬
clude, that when Job sayd, l'have not covered my transgressious, &c.
his meaning was, he did confesse and declare them with sor¬
row and brokennes of heart, that he might give glory to God
ennder a sence of his owne vilenes, and of the riches of his frte
grace in the pardon of them Thus much for the explication and
understanding of this verse; If I have covered my transgressions as
Adam, by hiding mine iniquity in my bosome.
From the whole Observe, First.
Man lovts to hide and seche coverings for his sin.
Satan and our corrupt hearts have no sooner prevailed with us
ro doe evill, but they presently counsell and perswade us to con¬
ceale the evill we have done. Sin enters secretly and suddainely:
It comes like a thiefe to rob and spoyle us of our best treasure.

0670.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upou the Book af IOE. Vert-

body.t: Most sins are committed in the darke, that is, secretly; and all
sins so committed would be kept in the darknes of concealement
and secrecy. Sin is darknesse, and a worke of darknesse; Now
darknesse being so congeniall to sin, sinners must needs love dark¬
nesse. Most of our sins are unknowne to others, yea many of our
sins are unknowne to our selves. Therefore David had no sooner
put this question (Psal.19 12.) N’ho can understand his errours?
But he presently puts up this petition, Cleanse thou me from secret
faults. And these secret faults by him intended in that prayer,
were not such as he had committed out of the eye or sight of o¬
thers, but such as had escaped or were not at all discerned by the
eye of his owne observation. Now, as most of our sins are un¬
knowne to other men, and many of our sins are unknowne to our
selves, soit is the desire of sinfull man, that all his sins might be
unknowne to God. Man, as man, that is, as sinfull man desiroth
that there might be a seale set or a vayle put upon all bis sinnes.
It is as naturall to manto be a sin-coverer as a sin-committer;
And he had rather make some poore shift of his oune to cover it
then goe to God (whose priviledge and gloryit is to cover fin)
to have his fin covered. It was so with Adam the first man, when
he had sinned, how busie was he to hide his sin? It was so with
Cain the second man, when he had sinned, how willing was he
to hide his sin? Cain spilt his brothers innocent blood like water
upon the ground but he would faine have stopped the mouth of
his brothers blood from crying up to heaven. And when God
came to make irquisition for blood, and put he question to him,
where is Abel thy brother? He answered the Lord, first, with a
plaine ly, I kηow not, and, secondly, with a presumptuous query,
Am Imr brethers beeper? What have I to doe with him ? he is
old enough to looke to himselfe. Thus it was with the first, thus
with the second sinner, and so it hath been with sinners ever
since. Doe pot our owne hearts tell us that it is so? Have not
the sons of men been busie in all generations to prepare coverings
for their transgressions? and are they not uponthe same busines
at this day ? If any shall enquire, whence it cometh to passe that
men are thus sinfully diligent in providing covers for their sin?
I answer, the reason ofit ariseth chiefely two uayes.
First, From pride; man hath an high spirit though he doe
low things, things as low as hel; such a thing is sin, even the best
or
2qqq2

0671.head: Chap.31. An Expesition upon the Bocke of Je B. Veri.33.

body.t: or least of it, a low hellish thing, a thing as low as hel; yet sinners
rife up to heaven in high and proud thoughts of themselves; and
therefore they will hide their sin if they can, and when they have
done any foule worke, cover it. The seeming profits and vaine
pleasures ot sin, they like wel, but they are too proud to love the
shame and disgrace that usually attends it. As sin hath that in the
effects of it which may cawe a stout man to tremble, so it hath
that in the nature of it, which may cause an impudent manto
blush. It is a blot a reproach and a dishonour; It debaseth man
inthe eye and opinion of all godly wise and holy men. And the
more wise, holy, and godly any man is, the more are sinners de¬
based in his eye. That’s one part of his character that shall abide
in the tabernable, and duel in the holy hil of God (Psal.15.4)
In his eyes a vile (not a poore but a wicked) person is contemned.
And hence it is, that a wicked person will hide his sin as much as
he can, He likes his sin wel enougb, but he likes not the con¬
tempt and fhame that it exposeth him unto. He hath some care
of his credit, though none of his conscience, and would preserve
his owne honour, while he dishonoureth God. And therefore
had rather run the hazzard of being covered with everlasting
fhame by covering his sin, then take any present shame to him¬
selse by confessingit.
Secondly, This covering of sin ariseth from want of faith;
He that cannot believe his sin shall be covered by God, uill co¬
ver it himlelfe. True confession proceeds from faith, and is one
of the blessed fruits of it. He that saith he hath sinned, and
knoues what he saith, sees wrath due to sin, and himselfe ob¬
noxious to eternal death; unbeliefe as to pardon causeth feare of
punishment: and no marvaile if an unbeliever labour to hide
that, which he sees will be his death. The unbeliever will never
be a confessor, eyther of Gods truth or of his oun sin. Shame and
feare cause men to hide both their sins and themselves; shame bids
the proud man cover his sin, and feare the unbeleever. Or pride
at once bids the same man cover his sin for feare of shame, and
unbeliese bids him cover it for feare of punishment.
Secondly, When Job saith, If I'have covered my transgressi¬
ens as Adam; he intimates that Adam framed covers for his sin,
or chat it is the manner of men to doe so.
Hence obforve.

0672.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition upon tbe Booke of JOR. Verl. 33.

body.t: The sinfull heart of man suggests and finds ont many wayes to
cover sin.
As man hath a mind to hide his sin, so he is dayly imagining
how to hide it. Mans naturall corruption hath not shewed it
selfe more pregnant or fruitfull in any thing then in this (Eccl.7.
29.) Ged hath made man upright (Ot right, God is rightnesse it
selfe, and as he extendeth himselfe into his workes, they are all
right, man especially had the image of Gods rightnes stampt up¬
on him in his first creatton) but they (not only the first, or this
or that man, but all men ]have stugbt out many inventiors; and
those bad ones, very bad ones. There are many honest inventi¬
ons respecting usefull arts and sciences, which man hath found out
by the common light which God hath given But here Selomon
speaks of inventions opposed to uprightnes, and what are they but
evill inventions? And this is one of mans worst inventions to hide
that which is evill, and to make blinds for the covering of his
sin. He hath been most unhappily witty in these inventions.
Mans trade since the fall of Adam, is like that of Adam; What
was his? Moses tells us of mans first invention to hide his bodily
nakednesse (Gen. 3. 7.) The eyes of them both nere open'd, and
they knew that they mere nabed, and they semed fig leaves together,
and made themselves aprons. Before they sinned they were cloa¬
thed with the robe of innocency, but when they had sinned they
cloathed themselves with fig-leaves. A litle after he tells us of
mans second invention ( upon which I shall insist surther hereat¬
ter) to cover the nakednes of his soule. And ever since it hath bin
mans most natural trade to make fig-leafe. coverings, poore shists
and shaddows to hide his soule-nakednesse from the eyes of men,
and if it were possible from the cyes of God too. Wee read in
Scripture of some very witty inventions which women have used
to cover and hide their purposes. I uill instance in three, which
are very remarkeable. First, was not that a witty invention of
Rachil, who having taken away her fathers images, hid them in
the Camels furniture? (Gen. 31. 34.) And the holy story tells us,
hou her wit wrought to keepe the Camels furniture from being
searcht, when her father came into her tent. The second instance
shall be that of Rahab, who to hide the Spies carried them up and
covered them with flax stalks on the roof of the house (Tesp. 2.

0673.head: Chap.31. An Expofitiou upon the Book ef JOB. Verl.33.

body.t: 6.) Take a third in the woman of Bahurim, who used a notable
invention to secure the messengers that went to carry tideings to
David, causing them to goe downe into a well (2 Sam. 17. 18)
And the moman tooke and spread a covering over the welts mouth,
and spread ground corne thercon, and the thing mas not knowne.
And indeed suspition it selfe could hardly suspect that well, which
had such a covering. I mention these, to shew what strange in¬
ventions have been used to cover things, persons, and designes.
Yet these were but grosse, course, and dull pieces of invention
compared with those which the heart of man dayly finds out to
cover his transgressions. Oh how cunning are sinners growne to
cover their sin! What false doores? what trap doores? what
tursings and windings? what labyrinths and meanders what sha¬
dows and vailes, hath the heart of man invented and made to
keepe conveigh or cover sin out of fight? The heart of man is
strangely engaged in these devices, yet of them all we may say as
the Prophet Isaiah doth ot their attempts and devises who would
hide themselves from the judgements of God (Isa.28.20.) The
bed is shorter then that a man can stretch himselfe on it, and the
covering narromer then that he can wrap himselse in it. When sin¬
ners have stretcht their witts upon the very tenters to devise new
covers and cloakes for sin, both they and their sins stand naked
in the sight of God, or ( as we say) they doe all the uhile but
dance in a net; yea they lay themselves the more open to the ju¬
stice of God, by how much they thinke themselves more concea¬
led from his knouledge. And therefore as the same Prophet de¬
nounced a severe threatning against the Jewes, for seeking to shel¬
ter themselves from those stormes which hung over their heads
and were ready to fall upon them by going to Egypt or any for¬
raigne nation for succour. (Isa. 30. 1.) Woe to tbe rebellious
children, saith the Lord, that take counsel but net of me, and that
cover mith a covering, but not of my Spirit, tbat they may adde sin
to sin, or thereby adding sin to sin, that is, adding this sin of
trusting in the creature, particularly in the shadow of Egypt, in a
day of distresse, to all their other sins; Now, I say, as the Jewes
were threatned for seeking such a cover from troubles, so their
case is as dangerous, who seeke or make vaine coverings for their
sin. The Spirit of God hath provided a covering for all our sins,
yet few have an heart to make use of it, But how mad are the

0674.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Book of JOR. Verf. 33.

body.t: most of men to cover one sin with another, to cover sin by that
which is it selfe more sinfull. To all suchthe Lord saith, Woe to
them that cover with a covering, but not of my Spirit; that is, not
with such a covering es my Spirit hath shetoed them and directed
them unto; These indeed ad de sin to sin, The covering is as sin¬
full as the sin which they would cover.
But uhat are those coverings ( disclaimed here by fub) and
which are usual y made by the sons of men to keepe their trans¬
gressions out of sight, or secret?
For answer to this querie, I shall shew you six covers of sin,
all invented and used by sinfull man, and the sixth will give occa¬
