upon the command of man which God hath not commanded.
Children, servants, and subjects must obey, but ’tis in the Lord,
they must not obey against the Lord. The Apostle saith to ser¬
vants, Obey reur Masters in all things (Col: 3. 22.) that is, in all
lamfull things, as the next words expound his meaning, not mith
eye service as men pleasers, but in singlenesse of heart fearing God;
obey vour Masters, but feare God, that is, obey them so tarre as
is corsistent with the feare of God. No Master hath power to
command his servant against the Lord, nor hath any servant li-
berty to ou ey his Muster against the Lord; no man hath power
erther in commanding or obeying, beyond the Law. Wee must
so please men, as not to displease God; if the superior transgres¬
seth the bounds of his pouer in commanding, the inferior trans¬
gresseth the limits of his duty in obeying Neyther doe we in this
ffi

0685.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition upon tbe Booke ef J0R. Verf.33.

body.t: at all let loose the bonds of duty, To cleare which, confider there
are two things in which the du y of an inferior doth consist.
Fust, Subjection to the pouer of his superior.
Secondl, Obedience to the command of his superior; now
in all things which are laufull and answerable to the mind of
God, servants ought both to be subject to the pouer, and to o¬
bey the commands of those that are over them; but in unla vfull
things they must only be subject to their power, not obey their
commands. There is a great difference betueen these two, we
may yeild subjection, and yet resuse obedience, as Casuists deter¬
mine; or which is the same, There may be passive obedience to
the full, where active obedience is not at all, they who are always
subject to the power of others, are not alwayes subject to their
commands. The Apostle Peter (IEp: 2. 18, 20) bids servants
be subject te their Masters mith all feare, not only tothe geod and
gentle, but also to the fromard; but he doth not teach them to o¬
dey their Masters in all things, but rither to suffer fer conscience
sake towards God ( v. 19) Servants are to suffer not only when
they have committed a fault, but they are to suffer rather then
commit a fault, or sin against God. We must serve men for Gods
sake, we must not forsake God to serve men; conscience bids in¬
feriors to be obedient, but they must not be obedient against con¬
science; if it were not sometimes lawfull so refuse obedience to
the commands of those who are above us, the world might quick¬
ly be ruined in duty. There lyes no duty to obey by doing, when
commands are against duty, or of things unlawfull to be done.
There is no disputing the commands of God, and there are no
commands but his, a hich may not be disputed; nor can we be
charged with disobeying any commands ( though we doe them
not) but those which we are bound to obey by doing them,
and those are only the commands of God, and such as subserve
his commands.
Thirdly, Saith another, if I had only a bare command I con¬
fesse that would not excuse me, but the truth is, I was not only
commanded, but threatened, and greatly threatened; if I had not
done it I must have suffered deeply; and surely, God will not hold
a poore creature to so hard a law, as to cordemne him for doing
that uhich he had no mind to doe, but was threatened to doe it,
and muat needs be undone if he did it not; it seemes not only un¬

0686.head: Chap.31. An Expositïon upou the Bekd Io2. Veri 33.

body.t: reasonable, but imcompetible, not only with the goodresse of
God, but uith his Justice, to put that sin upon any mans score,
which he did, not as delighted but as terrified. Yet to the preten¬
ders of this plea, I must say as the Apostle (2 Cor:5. 10.) Know¬
ing the terror ef the Lord me persmads men. Remember the Lord
threatens if you doe ill, and what are all the evills which man
threatens or can inflict, if you doe it not. If the wrath of man ter¬
rifieth you to doe evill, should not the urath of God terrifie you
much more from doing evill? One of the Ancients brings in a
person making this excuse, when urged to excessive drinking;
I did it indetd, but a great man in the company compelled me
to it, a dagger ras set at my breast, with this word, drinke or die,
But the Ansuer given in that particular case may serve for all ca¬
ses. Although ( saith he) the matter be brought to this hard issue,
that it be sayd to thte, cyther drinbe or die, it nere better for tbee
that in preservation and defence of thy omne temperance and sebries
ty, thou shouldest die, then tbat theu sould save thy lose by túy in,
temperance; or it were much more eligible tuat thy body should be
staine siber, then that tby soule should be damn'd drunten. The
Apostles were straitly threatened (Acts 4.17.) not to speake
any more, nor to teach in the name of Jesus, but did they satisfie
themselves and fit doune in slence, because threatened to for¬
beare speaking? read their answer (v. 19, 20.) Whether it be
rigbt in the sight of God, to htarken unto yon more rben unto God,
judge ye; fer ne canxot but speake the things nhich we have seene
and heard. Now if threatenings be no exeuse to us for the for¬
bearing of a good dury, or obedience to an affirmative command,
( which though it oblidge (semper) alwrayes, yet not (ad sem¬
per) to all times, nowr, I say, if they would not ferbeare to dot
good when men threatned) much lesse uill mens threatnings ex¬
cuse ue, if we for feare of them doe evill or transgresse a negative
command, which as it is alwayes binding, so it binds alwayes or
atall times; There's no moment much lesse feason for the doing
of evill, though there may be a season of forbearing to doe that
which is good. There is no necessity of sinning, nor can any ex¬
treamity excuse for doing evill; but there may be a necessitie of
our forbearance at this or that time to doe this or that good du¬
ty, and that necessiry will be admitted by God as a pleadable ex¬
cuie of our forbearance. Elibu chargeth Tob ( Chap. 36 21.)
Sf112

0687.head: Chap.31. An Expasition xpon the Booke of JOR. Verf.33.

body.t: Tuau hast chosen iniquity rather then affliction, whereas indeed
when these two are propoled to our choyce, affliction and trans¬
gression, whether to sin or to suffer, we should without any de¬
hberation or confult upon the po nt, chuse afflictions and suffer¬
inge, yea death it selfe rather chen in quity. Therefore ay not,
l sinned for feare being theeatened with utmost penalties and (X¬
treamities; remember who threatens from heaven, and then you
will not much regard who tbreatens on carth. The three chil¬
dren were threatned uith a fiery surnace ( Dan. 3. 16.) Daniel
himselfe was threatned to be cast into the Lions den (Dan 6.10)
yet as the former would not doe that evill, the wor shipplrg ot the
golden imge, so the latter vould not forbeare to doe that good,
the praying to and worshipping the true God, for all their threat¬
pings.
Fourthly, Saith another of the sons of Adam, true, I have sin¬
ned I have sworne rashly, but such a man provoked me if I have
dose any man vrong or given him ill language it vas upon ill
language fi st received from him, or upon wrong first done to
me, and if I have requited him in his kind, I hope this is no great
matter; In this I may be excused, seeing he began with me, and
urged me toit: I had not uronged him, if he had not wronged
me, nor bad I given him an ill word, if he had not reviled me¬
Thus many wrap up the matter, and cover their transgressions.
I ansver, Can thac which was sinfull in another, make the same
act done by thee sinlesse? vas it sinfull in him to give thee ill lan¬
guage, or was it sinfull in him to doe thee vrong, and will it not
be sinfull in thee also to give ill language, or do wrong! the law
given us of God must be the guide of our actings towards men,
not the actings of other men towards us. That’s a good rule;
Dee to others as you nould be done to by others, that rule will carry
us quite through the world. But this is a false and a most perverse
rule Doe to others, as they have done to you; this is a most unscrip¬
tural rule, that saith, Thou fhalt not give rayling for rayling, aud
mhen theu art cursed thou shalt blesse; that’s the command of
Christ; and shall any looke to be excused for rayling on anotber,
because he rayled upon him first? or shall he thinke to be excu¬
sed for cursing another because himselfe was cursed. Take heed
of these pretendings, 'tis the will of God we should doe good a¬
gainst evill, Can it then be gond te reiurne evill for evill :
ChaF. 31. An Expesition upon tht Bohe of JoS. Verl. 33.
Fifthly, Another will say, true, I have done it, but are there
not many who doe the like or vorse? I am so farre from being
alone in it, that almost all men are with me in it. An I hope that
mhich all men doe, no man shall be blamed for; This is a com¬
mon practice.
It uis the error of the old Pelagians, that corruprion was not
traduced into the nature of man by the fall of the first man, but
that sin is continued by imitation; Children (say they) seeing
their parents or others doe evill takeit up by ex mple; Now,
thongh chis hath been justly condemned as a grosse error, and
the contrary asserted both as a Scripturall and as an exprrimen¬
tall truth, that the whole masse of mankind by nature is stceped
in sinne, and that we have the root of every evill matter in our
selves; yet’tis a truch also, that we doe iil by example, and chat
sin is mightily increased by imitation. What one doth others
are apt to doe, and the most of men goe where thiy see others
goe, rather then where they ought to goe; yea they beginto
conclude they may goe safely enough in a bad way, if they see o¬
thers goe betore them in it
But what though many goe in wrosg wayes, and doe unrigh¬
teous things, yea what though all should goe and doe so, yet that
would not exeuse any one that goeth or doth so. Would it have
been any excuse, thinke you, for Noah to have compli ed uith
that wicked generation, when all flesh had corrupted their way
before God; Noah might have said, I follow the track, I doe as
the rest, all goe this way, and should I stand alone? should I be
singular? Nrah had no such reasonings, he followed the rule not
the example of that age. Thus saith the text ( Gen. 6. 9) Noab
mas a just man and perfict in his generatiens, and Noah wasbed
xith God; That is, he kept close communion with God, let the
world goe whether it would; He was not led away uith tbe
course, nor caryed doune vith the current of the times, nor
would he urite aster their crooked and blotted copy. Lot duelt
in Sodeme, where ten righteous persons were not to be found,
though the preservation of the whole Citie, and the pardon of
them all from present perishing lay upon it Yet Lot preserved
himselse pure, and his rigbteous soule was vexed from day to day,
mith their unlamfull deeds. The Lord gave a speciall Law by Me¬
ses to obviate this mischiefe ( Exod. 23. 2.) Thou shatt not fol¬

0689.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Bock ef IOB. Vers.33.

body.t: Iema multitude to doe evid: Which law doth more then imply,
tlat many would encourage, and fome even warrant chemselves
in doing evill by the example of the multitude. It is somewhat
fficult to breike the ice, and begin: But when many have be¬
gua to us in a way of sin, O how hard is it not to follow? To
follow the most is to follow the worst, for so the most are; and
to follow them as farre as they goe, is to goe to hel, for thither
the most goe. It will be but cold comfort to peristi with a great
company.
Nor is it any whit safer or better to follow the mighty then to
follom the many, yet some thinke themselves very safe, while they
walke in their way, how bad soever the way be. Had we ( say
they) only the multitude to follow, they being rude, and vaine,
it were not so excusable; but we see great men doe it, yea the
wise and learned men of the world doe it, and shall not ue be ex¬
cused for doing that which the Great and wise and learned men
of the world doe? No doubt we shall. Thus they plead to their
owne perdition; “Tis indeed the unhappy priviled ge of Great
ones to have more followers of their worst actions, then of their
persons. Many sin as it were (cum privilegio) under the cloake of
Great mens sinnings. The very errors and mistakes of Rulers may
prove a rule for others to erre and misteke by, and the Authoti¬
ry of their persons puts a kind of authenticknesse upon their most
unwarrantable practices. And therefore ( to note that by the
way) it much concernes those that are above others in place, to
take heed what they doe, especially before their inferiors, because
they are apt to beare themselves high upon the example of those
that are above them. It hath been sayd, Much reverence is due to
children; wee say ( and we say truely) chudren oue great reve¬
rence to their parents, and elders. And ’tis as true, Parents and
Elders should carry it reverently tomards their children, because
the example of a parent, or superior, emboldens children to doe
the like, even to a likenesse in vanitie, whether in speech or beha¬
viour; And as children are ready to take up the ex mple of pa¬
rents, so are all inferiors, the example of those above them. What?
(say they) doe not our Lords and Masters doe these thir gs, and
shall we sticke at them, are we wiser then they? Doe they sweare
and shall we scruple an oath? Are they drunken, and shall rot we
frecly take our cups? are they wantons and fornicaters, and shall

0690.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Book of I0». Verl. 33.

body.t: ve poore underlings forbeare? Doe they prophane the Saboath,
and may not we breake it? Surely, we may, and be blamelesse.
O how desperately are many servants and meane men hardned
and deboyst by example of their Lords and Mastert! The Phari ess
checkt those Officers in the Gospel when they had not attached
and brought Christ to them, because they seemed to have better
thoughts of him then the rulers had ( Joh: 7. 47, 48, 49.) Are
re also deceaved? have any of the rulers or of the Pharisets beleeuid
on him? but this peaple, mho hnoweth not the Law are cursed. As if
they had sayd, What will you take upon you to be better, or to
understand better then your rulers? Will yon take upon you to
believe or be religious beyond their example? Now as some
thinke the faith of inferior persons must be pinn’d upon the rulers
sleeve, and that they must beleeve as their great Masters beleeve,
so, many inferior persons are persuaded they may wel enough
pin the practise of their superiors upon their fleeve, and in all
things without danger doe as they doe.
There are others who beare themselves out in an evill matter
beyond all reproofe, if they see any that professe godlinesse to
doe such things; As they embolden themselves by the falls of
good men recorded in the holy Scriptures, by the drunkennt sse
of Noah, and by the uncleannesse of David, &c. The cloud of
Scripture-witnesses hath a bright side, that is, the gracious actings
of the Saints, and a darke side, that is, the wesknesses and faylings
of the Saints, Now as they goe to the darxe side of the Saints
departed, so also of the living Saints to strengthen themselves in
their wickednesse. But remember the Lord hath not lest us to
live by example, but by rule, therefore never plead example a¬
gainst rule, neither the example of the multitude; nor of the
great, nor of the wise and learned, no nor of the godly and holy
in their departures from the rule. The Apostle himselfe when he
would be imitated, durst not propose himselfe universally to be
imitated, Be ye fellomers of me as I'also am of Christ: if I goe a step
out of the way follow me not there; say not because an Apostle
didit, therefore I may doe it; Wee cannot be excused in follow.
ing the unholy actings of any man, how holy foever he is.
Thus upon the occasion of Adams first excuse, laying his sin
upon his wives perswasion, I have shewed you many other wayes
wherein the sons of Adam treading in his steps, make such like co¬

0691.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upou the Book of IO R. Vert. 33

body.t: verings and excuses for their sin; and from them all it hath ap¬
peared, that neyther perswasions, nor commands, nor threats,
nor injuries and provocations receaved, nor examples given, uill
serve for a covering of our transgre ssions. All such pleas are in¬
valid, nor shall any man be accepted in them; yea ve doe but so
much the more uncover the shame of our nakednesie, by how
much we are the more subtle ard industrious to provide such co¬
verings for it.
Further. (if we look into the history of Gentfis) we may find
another excuse uhich Adam made for his sin, which l shall a litle
consider, for a fuller confirmation of the poynt in hand. Stverall
of the learned both ancient and moderne, have noted ir as a se¬
cond unsafe and altogether unprofitable covering of transgres¬
sion.
If I covered my transgressions asAdam.
As Adam layd his sin upon his wives perswa on, so upon the
dispensation of God; The woman ( saith he, v. 12. ) whom ib u
gavest to be mith me, she gave me ef the tree, and I did eat, As if
he had sayd; Wey am I so prest with this act, as my fault, the eat¬
ing the forbidden tree; for, Lord if theu haast not given me this wo¬
man. I had never donc it, the woman which chou gauest to be mith
me, she gave it me and I did eate; Lerd, nhy diast thou put sach a
snare upon me, why diast thou leave me to such a tempration by the
oman mhich thou gavest me, if any fauli be in tating of this tree,
I must lay it at thy dovre; had it not been for this w man, I might
have done mell enough, surely I had not fallen into this great trans¬
gression, if thou haast not made this moman my com panion. Thus
Adam hoped to cover his sin, and leave the blame of it upon
God himselfe.
And as Adam then, so many at this day cover their transgres¬
sions, and excuse their sins, by putting them upon God. That pre¬
venting Admonion of the Apostle ( James 1. 13.) doth more
then intimate such a cursed plea, alwayes at hand in the heart of
man, Let no man say when he is tempted, Iam temeted of God; As
if the Apostle had said, the mind of man is very apt to conceave
this bad plea for himselfe, and his tongue is as ready toutter it,
even to say, when he is tempted, l am tempted of God, if God
bad not brought me into such a condition, if God had not ser

0692.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition upon the Booke d JOR. Verf. 33.

body.t: things in such a way, I had never been entangled, much lesse over¬
come by this or that temptation. The Apostle in that place gives
warning to all, that they make no such vaine Apologyes, nor goe
about to ease themselves, when they have sinned, by casting their
sin upon God, or by accusing his providence, as the cause ofit,
yet this warning hath not prevented the doing ofit. One of the
Ancients oblerved and reproved this practice as a common error
in his time; Many (saith he) mhen they are derected in any sin, saybcatdicant,
present ly, God hath milled this, er he mould haut things gue teut?
what have I done? xhere is my fault? this thing could not have
been, unlesse it had been the mill of God; for all things fall out ac-
cording to his will, that is, he might hinder and Rop them if he
would, or he might put them into another course if he pleased;
if be morhe none can let, if he let none can morke.
Thus men, presumptuous men are not afraid to charge God
himselfe with their sins, that they may discharge themselves. I
shall give you tuo reasons why they doe so.
First, Man hath a naturall desire to Justifie himselfe, and that
desire is so strong, that he cares not much whom he bespatrerech,
or whom he burdens, so he may but ease and acquit himselfe, nor
cares he whom he wrongs, so he may make his owne wayes ap¬
peare upright.
Secondly, Sin is such an ugly monster that no man uill owne
it,if he can chuse, but had rather lay this child of darknesse at any
mans doore, yea at Gods doore then father it himselfe. And
though there are but few who vill say this plainely, yet many
speake it in parables, or by consequences and inferences. I shall
therefore cleare what I meane and ayme at by giving a few in¬
stances.
First, Saith one, it is my ill fortune, or my fate, that I have
done this evill, such Heathen language is often heard from their
mouthes, who professe Christianity. Now, what is this destiny,
chance, fortune, or fate, which they bable about? uhat doe all
these uncouth words import, but that order into which God hath
put all things, or that issue unto wbich his infinite wisdome hath
disposed all actions and events in this world ? There is no other
chance nor fate, but that which is indeed the counsell and dispen¬
sation of God; and therefore when any cry out, this was our ill
fortune, this was our ill hap, what doe they accuse but the holy
Tttt

0693.head: Chap. 31. An Expofition upon the Booke ef JOR. Vers.33.

body.t: counsels and most righteous dispensations of God.
Secondly, Saith another, it was the unlucky or malignant aspect
of the Starres when I was borne, which drew yea and necessita¬
ted me to take and engage in this wicked course. Many have a
great itch in chis age to consult Astrologers, to find out the positi¬
ons or conjunctions of the Planets in their nativity, or to consider
the influences whether good or bad promising or threatning of
those Starres under whose prædominance they were borne, and
from thence to receave propheticall conclusions, what their crol.
ses, and what their comforts, what their uay, and what their end
in this world fhall probably (say some) or certainly (say others)
be. That ancient father in the place before cited, having reproved
those in generall who charge their sins upon God, brings them in
making this objection. Possibly you who say this, will also say,
u'ho chargeth his sin upon God? He answers, First, by a direct as¬
firmation; Tea ( saith'he) some there are that speake this openly;
As reverend Mr. Calvin and his followers have been falsely char.
ged by the Papists for making God the Authour of sin by theit
opinions and assertions about prædestination; so others from a
prophane spirit and principle speake it out broadly; and are not
afraid to affront God himselfe with these blasphemous imputati¬
cons. But what though some be not so grosse, yet, secondly, there
are too too many, who weave the same web with a finer thred;
and therefore his second answer is; They who say not this, nhat say
they? even this; It was my fate to doe it, the Starres caused me to
doe it; I could not helpe it, I was anavoydably caryed toit. And
ibus (saith he) by a circuit they fetch it about, and accuse God as
the cause of their sins, to whom they vill not come directly and con¬
fesse their sins, that by Christ they may ebtaine the pardon of them,
and peace for their omne poore soules. That wortby of Elder dayes
comes up yet closer to them in fome following passages, Thou
sayest thy unluckie starres have done it; their ill aspects have encli¬
ned thy heart to such fins;but mhat are the starrs? mho made them?
did not God? art they not the worhe of his hands? and who orders them
and their motions? doth not God? there is not a starre moves but by
bis appointment. The starres are Gods militia, his hest, They stirre
not, but by the commandement of God; nom if God made the starres,
and orders the metion of the starres, and thou sayest the starres havs
caused thee to fin; consider, doest thou not say, God made thie to sin?

0694.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon tbe Book of JOR. Vert 33.

body.t: And therefore surely Ged is anjust, and thou art just, because ux¬
lesse he had placid the starres so, thon haast not siuned so. Thus man
blasphemoussy turnes his sin upon God; and while he will not
accuse himselfe for that which he hath done very ill, he accuses
God who made him and all things very good.
Thirdly, Others accuse the times and places in which they
live; I( layd one that was starke nought) live in Rome, where ni
man can be better; I live in times so universally infected, that no
man can escape the infection, nor be innocent. Is not this to ac¬
cuse God also? who was it that cast thy lot to live at such a time,
and in such a place in the world? did not God? hath not he (as
the Apostle speakes, Actt 17.26.) made of one blood all natin¬
ef men, for to duel on all the face of the earth, and hath determined
the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitations:
therefore he that chargeth the place where he lives with his sin,
chargeth God with his sin, who disposeth of all men both as to
time and place, or who hath both their times and places in his
hand, or dispose.
Fourthly, Not a few charge their sin upon their callings, as
if they could not doe or live honestly in them; I know there are
some sinfull or dishonest callings; Therefore as the Apostle ex¬
horts (Tit: 3. 14.) Let all learne to maintaine good workes (or
as we put in the Margin, professe honest trades) for necessary uses,
and avoyd those that are uselesse, and unnecessary. As for law¬
full callings, God hath appointed man to live and labour in them.
Now for any man (when he hath done amisse ) to say, my cal¬
ling put me uponit, or was the cause of my miscarriage, is as
much as to say, God put him upon it. The Apostle gives this rule
to the converted Corinthians (1 Cor:7. 20.) Let every man a¬
bide in the same calling wherein he was called. Some, it seemes, be¬
ing called to the knowledge of Christ, thought they must leave
their worldly callings, and imployments, as if they were sinfull
snares to them, or unnecessary diversions from better things.
Nay, saith Paul, abide in the calling mherein ye mere called, that is,
looke in what honest civill calling the spirituall call of God hath
found you, keepe to that calling still; God doth not call us off
from our imployments and businesse but he calls us to be just and
holy in them. The grace of God doth not set us above commerce
xith men, nor doth our entrance into Gods service, any way ac¬
TELL2

0695.head: Chap-31. Au Expasition upon ibt Booke of JO R. Vert.33.

body.t: quit us from serving one another in our lawfull callings; And
therefore for any man to say, his calling makes him sin, eyther
by doing what he ought not, or by neg ecting what he ought, is
to cast his sin upon God, and to blame Gods ordinance with his
owne disobedience.
Fifthly, Some complaine of their poverty, or of the streights
into œhich the providence of God hath cast them, as the cause of
their sin, of their stealing or murmuring and discontent. These
also rise up against God, and lay the dirt of their filthy hearts
and wayes at the gates of heaven. For thongh there be indeed a
great temptation in such a straitned and afflict ed condition ( as
both Agurs prayer, Pro: 30. 8, 9. and the experiences of many
have taught us) yet it doth not at all necessitate any man to
sin; and such a condition is appoynted us as an occasion for the
tryall of our patience, and dependance upon God in the exercile
of all other graces, not to set our corruptions aworke, or to ex¬
cuse us when we are overcome by them.
Thus we see, that though most forbeare to speake this broadly
and openly, that God is the cause of their sin, yet they doe it by
infcrences, as Adam did, the woman which thou gavest to be mith
me ( sayd he) was the meanes of my fall; and, say they, if we had
been borne under a better planet, if we had lived in better times
and places, or had not been brought into a low condition, where¬
in ve knew not what to doe, we had never done thus. Oh learne
to accuse the naughtinesse and corruption that is in your hearts,
as the fountaine of all your sinfull actings; for kuow, it is not
any farre, it is neyther time, nor place, nor calling, but the wick.
ednesse of your owne hearts, which hath led you into sin, and
andone you.
There is yet a third head of excuse, by which that first trans¬
gression of Adam was intended to be covered; And I may call it
The moman a covering; For, when the Lord saw what sad shists
the man had made to cover his sin, in stead of confessing it; then
he put the Question to the woman also in the 13 th verse; And
the Lord God said to the meman, mhat is this that thou hast done?
end the moman said, the Serpent beguiled me, and I did eat. Here
is no deniall of the fact, the woman confest shee had eaten the
forbidden fruit, but the Serpent beguiled me ( said chee) alas, ifI
bad been let alone l should not have caten, but there was a cun¬

0696.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition upon the Boobe of JoOB. Vert. 33.

body.t: ning Serpent, he came upon me unawares and inticed mee with
faire promises, and so I did eate. This was a truth, the Serpent had
indeed beguiled her; What the woman sayd, was true enough,
that the Serpent had beguiled her, but what shee intended in say¬
ing so, was not true, Namely, that shee uas therefore to be excu¬
sed because so beguiled. Yea this very excuse accused her, and she
was defiled by that which she thought would purge her.
Now as l shewed before, that there is such a sinfull principle
in man to charge his sin on God, so I shall now shew that there
is a common practise among men to charge their sin upon the
Devill. The meere act of charging sin upon God is abominable,
and the intent with which some charge sin upon the Devill is ve¬
ry sinfull. I doe not say that it is sinfull, for any one that hath
sinned to charge his fin upon the Devill, for the Devillis, in
some sence, the authour of all sin, as having brought it first into
the world; he is the father ot lyes, and the furtherer of lyes, as
also of all other sinnes, to the utmost that he can. Now because
the Devill hath so neere and so strong a relation to every sinne,
we may therefore charge all our sins upon him, and doe him no
wrong at all; bat the intent of charging sin upon the Devill may
be very sinfull. To doe it as the woman did it, and as many at this
day doe it with hope to discharge themselves, this is a sin, this is
to cover our transgressions as Eve, and while ue seeke thus to
cleare our selves from the guilt of sin, we fasten and fixe it the
more upon our consciences, and the more provoke God to wrath
against us forit. There are many (as hath been anciently noted)
who wave or avoyd the confession of their sins, and make it their
businesse to accuse, and cry out of the Devill, Oh the Devill, this
subile Serpent, this roaring Lion, he, he hath deceived us, he hatl
prevailed upon us. We mere neither mise enough to discerne his miles,
nor strong enough to resist his ferce. Thus they speake, hoping to
unburden themselves byit.
But let no man thinke to excuse himselfe by accusing the De¬
vill; For though Sathan doth much in causing every man to sin,
yet he cannot force any man to sin; though Sathan tempt us to
sin, and allures the will strongly toit, yet he cannot make auy
man sin whether he will or no. Though Satan may tempt us ube¬
ther we will or no, yet he cannot overcome us in any temptation
unlesse wee our selves will. And untill wee yeild our consent

0697.head: Chap.31. An Expositiou upon the Bok of Jo s. Verl.33.

body.t: which is an act of the will ) the temptations of the Devill, and
bis assaults defile us not, they are indeed our afflictions, and our
troubles, but not our sinnes till they are accepted of, and embra¬
ced by us. So then, the fault is every mans owne; Sathan hath
beguiled you, but did not you consent, did not you accept of the
temptation; it is not his temptation which makes you guilty, but
your admittance of it. As it was sayd long agoe, and may much
more in this slandering age; If to acouse another did mabe him¬
guilty, none could be innocent. So, l may say in this case also, Ffta
be tempted by the Devill would make a man guilty, no man sosuld
be long guiltlesse, even of the mest horrid crimes that ever the Sus
beheld. Jesus Christ himselse had not been without guilt, if to be
tempted makes a man guilty. How did the Devill tempt and as¬
sault Christ! How did he follow him in one houre ( as we may
conceave) with a threefold tempration, besides all the tempta¬
tions which probably followed, the holy text saying, he left bim
for a season. Yet Jesus Christ came off from those thrte and all
other temptations without any touch, without any the least spot
ofsin; He kept himselfe ( so doe beleevers, by him, themselves,
1J0.5.18.) And that micked one touchi him not, that is, left no evill
impression upon him, how much soever he pressed him to evill.
The Prince of this world came, but found nothing in him; he had
malice sufficient in his heart against Christ, but he found nothing
in Christ, to take with his temptation. There being not the least
motion in the heart of Jesus Christ towards a complyance with
the Devill, but an utter abominacion and detestation of him, hee
was not at all hurt with any of his temptations: and so farre as
we keepe off our consent to the Devill, his temptations cannot
hurt us. Ill thoughts springing up in us are our sins, though we
consent not to them; but evill thoughts suggested by Satan are
not our sins till consented to. Therefore take heed of excusing
your selves by charging your lin upon the Devill, and his temp¬
tations; charge it rather upon your selves, and your oune in¬
dwelling corruptions; the Devill doth only strike the fire, your
hearts are the tinder, if your hearts were not tinder, his sparkes
could not kindle upon you; Sathan doth not prevaile over us by
force, but by guile, he insnares us, and winnes our hearts he vex¬
eth us by his wiles, as Moses said the Midianite, did the children
of Israel in the wildernesse. Were the Devill lest to himselfe he

0698.head: Chap.31. An Exposstion upos tbi Book of JOB. Vert, 13.

body.t: would breake us with his power, but he is restrained there, and
hath only wiles and tricks to vex us with He deales uith us like a
Maichivel or an Achitophel, not like a Goliab, or an Alexander.
And hence it is said in the Revelation, He deceiveth ibe nhole
carth: He doth all by craft, he cunningly insnares our affections,
and being a Spirit can insinuate strongly into ours. The Apostle
Peter dealing with Ananias (Acts 5. 3.) expostulates the mat¬
ter with him thus; why hath Sathan filled thy heart to ly to the
boly Ghest; As if he had sayd, Sathan tempted thte indeed, but mhy
hast thou given up tby consent, wby hast thou yeildid so easily to doc
such an abomination? Sathan in a speciall manner takes some men
captive at bis will (2 Tim: 2. 26.) But he leads no man captive
against his will, Sathan leads many captive at his oune will, and
beck, he finds them readv, they are free to come at the first call
of a temptation, yea possibly they are ready to call for a temp¬
tation; but Sathan leads none captive against their oune will
or, take it thus, many are taken captive by Satan at his will, but
Satan cannot captivate the will of any man, whensoever any man
sins, he sins freely. Therefore Satans temptation cannot be an ex¬
cuse to any man, and the hearts of most men are as much in the
temptation, as Sathan himselfe was, and they rise to the baite as
willingly as he casts in the hooke.
Thus I have opened the second observation, wherein it ap¬
peares that the heart of man is very pregnant in finding out and
suggesting variety of coverings for the hiding of sin. And by in¬
sisting upon these three grand heads of excuses practised by our
first parents ( the man excusing his sin by the persuasion of the
woman, as also by the dispensation of God, and the voman ex¬
cusing her sin by the temptation of the Devill, by these I fay) it
appeares what Job meant in this Scripture when he sayd, If Ihave
covered my transgression as Adam. And I might shew you many
other coverings of transgre ssions, taking Adam Appellatively, if
I have covered my transgresfions as men, that is, as the common
sort of men generally doe, who have severall coverings, industri¬
ously, and artificially framed, and wrought to hide their finnes
with; but possibly I have gone too farre already from my me¬
thod of expofition: yet this discovery was so proper to the ex¬
presse words of the Text, that I could not well passe it by, though
it chould be called a digression.

0699.head: Chap.31. An Exposition mpou thi Bock cf I02. Verf. 33

body.t: There are yet other observations which I shall give from this
Text, when l have added only this one word of Caution from all
that I have sayd.
Beware of this practice, the couering of sin, as much as of com¬
mitting it; and know that to cover a sin committed, is to com¬
mit a new one; yea they who make cob. web coverings for their
transgressions ( such are these and all such.lke excuses) will be
forced at last as they (Revel: 6. 16.) to call to the recẽs to cover
them, and to the meuntaines to bide them ( but all in vaine) from
the presence ef bim that sits upon the throne, and from tue wrathef
the Lambe. There is but one covering of transgression which can
stand us in any stead, Jesus Christ our reall Propitiatery. Goe to
Christ, and make him your covering, cover your selves uith his
righteousnesse, that’s a garment large enough and cleane enough
to hide all your sins, and to keepe off all that wrath which sig
hath deserved, and calls for; cover your sins mith the second A¬
dam, but doe not cover your fins as the first Adam; eyther by
the excuses mentioned, or by any other; they are all deceit full,
and too narrow for the purpose. This holy and good man Job,
protested he never made such sinfull artifices the hidings of his
fin.
If I have covtred my transgreffens as Adam, by hideing mire
iniquity in my bosome.
From fubs scope and designe in making this protestation, that
he had not covered his transgressions.
Observe, Thirdiy.
To cover and hide sin is sin ;’tis the adding ot sin to sin.
Iob is purging himselfe from this as well as from any of those
Enormities mentioned and professed against in the foregoing
passages of this Chapter: hee doth not only say, I have not lusted
aster my neighbours wife, nor wrong'd my servants, nor oppres¬
sed the poore, nor put confidence in gold, nor worshipped the
Sun, he (I say) doth not only say, I have not committed these
foule transgressions, but I have not put a fayre covering upon a¬
ny of my transgressions; thereby intimating that to have done
so, had been to commit a greater sin then any of those which he
had not committed. And surely neither our owne sinfull hearte,

0700.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition upon the Booke ef IO R. Vert. 33.

body.t: nor Satan would be so busie to provoke us to cover our sinnes,
vere it not very sinfull. That great enemy sets us about no worhe
but bad worke, black worke, hellish worke: hee knouts wel e¬
nough that to hide a sin committed is to commit a freshi sin, yes
to commit a greater sin then that which we would hide, why else
should he tempt us to hide it? and this is one of the great depths
of Satan, hee perswvades us to hide evill done, pretending our
good by it, or as if he would befriend us; but indeed hee assaults
us as an enemy, and intends us a further mischiefe. The conceal.
ing of sin is the keeping of the Devills councel, and the doubling
of our transgression. Sin is the disease of the soule, and there is
no such way to encrease and make a disease desperate as to con-
ceale it : Silence feeds and cherisheth the diseases of the body;
and so it doth the diseases of our soules. Sin encreaseth two
wayes, by concealement, or by hiding.
First, In the guilt of it : The òbligation to punishment takes
stronger hold upon the soule, and every man is bound the faster
with those chaines of darknesse, by how much the more he la¬
bours to keep his sios in the darke: the longer a sin remaines up.
on the conscience unpardon'd the more doth the guilt of it en¬
crease: now all the while sin is hid, all the while sin is artificially
and intentionally covered, it remaines unpardoned; and therefore
the guilt of it must needs encrease upon the soule.
Secondly, Sin being thus covered encreaseth in the filth and
contagion of it, in the strength and power of it; it gaines more
upon the soule, it growes more master, and more masterly, lust
begins to rage, rave, it commands and caryes all before it, while
wee are so foolish as to kcepe it close and covered. Thus a con¬
cealed sin is greatly encreased both in the guilt and in the power
of it.
If any say, Surely it is not so sinsull to cover and hide sin; sor
doth not the Scripture condemne those that did not hide it?
why doth it rebuke any for not hiding their sins, if to hide sin be
so sinfull? The Prophet seemes to speake that expressely (Isa. 3.
9.) The shem of their countenance testifieth against them (they
were so farre srom hiding their sins in their bosome, that they did
even print them in their foreheads; The hew of their countenance
doth witnesse against them) they declare their fin as Sodome, they
bide it not. Thus the Prophet reproves them, and makes this a
V u u u

0701.head: Chap. 31. An Expofition upen the Booke ef JOR. Verl.33.

body.t: very great aggravation of their sins, that they did not hide their
fins?
I answer, There is a twofold not hiding of sin; Firft, there is
a not hiding which proceede from repentance; Secondly, there is
another sort of not hiding of sinne, which proceeds from imou¬
dence, or thereis a not hiding of sin wvhich proceeds from a broken
heart and there is a not hiding of sin that proceeds from a bra¬
zen face, from a brow of brasse. That’s the meaning of the Pro¬
phet when he reproves those debauched Jewes because they did
not hide their sin, hee reproves them for their impudence, that
when they had done wickedly, they boasted ofit, and held it
forth, they cared not who knewit, therefore saith the text, they
declare their sin as Sedome; they did not declare their sin as tbe
mourners in Sion from an humbled heart and a contrite spitit,
but they declared their sins like the filthy Sodomites. We are like
to have a goodly paterne of repentance from Sodome; where all
were wicked, except Lot and his neerest relations. By two sorts of
men the sin of the world is mightily hightned; First, Some are
so deboyst that they will not hide their fins: Secondly, others
are so hy pocriticall that they use all the courses they can to hide
their sins; Not to hide eur sin through impudence, and to hide it in
hypocrisie, are alite abominable in the sight of God: and that's it
which Tob labours to purge himselfe from, as much as from un¬
cleannesse, oppression, covetousneffe, or any other act of sin be¬
fore specified.
Fourthly, As Job ln speaking this would deny the hiding and
covering of his siu, so hec affirmes the Confession of it, as was
shewed in the explication of the text. So that here is more in¬
tended then exprest; when he saith hee did not cover, his mean¬
ingis, he discover’d his sin; when he saith, hee did not hide it,
his meaning is, hee did disclose it.
Hence observe.
A godly man dotb not orly net hide, but is readr te cenfesse bus
finne.
Hee makes confession that he may be freed from condemna¬
tion; so some understand that ( Isa. 43 26.) Put me in remem¬
brance ( saith the Lord, that is, mind me, both of my promised
mercies, and of thy provoking transgressions) let us plead toge¬

0702.head: Chap.31. An Exposition apou the Bek of 102. Vert 33

body.t: ther: dec lart thou tuat thou mayest be justified. Tbis is a great Go¬
spel truth, though it be questionable, whether inrerded in that
place. A godly man hath secret sins (that is, sins uihich he
Anoues not of ) but he doth not keep his sins secret, hec is ul¬
ling to make them knowne. He doth not cover them from the
knowledge of God, no nor of men, when and as he is bound to
give an account of them. Confession of sin is an indisgencible
piece of true repentance. They who are indeed humbled in the
fight of their sins vill not hide them out of sight; They declare
them alwayes to God, and are not ashamed to declare them ro
man also in a Gospel way. As ’tis sinfull to blow a trumpet, or
proclaime our good workes, so we are not bound to publish our
sins or evill deeds to the world; but when we are called, and see
it a duty to confesse them, we must not hide, but confesse them.
"Tis a great part ofour holinesse to confesse our Iniquities; and
as the holyest man in this world is imperfect and hath sinnes to
confesse; so it is a good degree of his holynesse and pe fection
to confesse his sios. Our blessednesse consists in the remission of
sin (Psal. 32. 1.) Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven,
whose sin ie covered. And therefore we cannot be blessed if our
sins be unconfest (Psal. 32.5.) I said I will confesse mine Iai¬
quitie, and thou forgavest mee the iniquitie ef my sin: the pardon
was given out upon his Confession (1 fob. 1. 9.) If nee canfesse
our fins, God is faithfulland just to forgive us our fins, As if he had
said Sin unconfest shall not be forgiven, He that covereth hu sins
shall not presper; but who so confesseth and forsabeththem (and on¬
ly he) shast finde mercy ( Pro. 28. 13.)
But you will say, is this all that Jub did, barely to confesse
his sin, uhen hee saith, hee did not cover it.
Iansuer, The holy Confession of sin, which is oppos'd to the
covering or hiding of sin; hath three things init.
First, A confession of the fact, or of the thing done; Jospua
said to Achan (Jofh. 7. 19.) Ay Son, give glory to God, and tell
mee, wbat hast thou done? tell mee the story, give mee a narrative
of thy sin. And accordingly hee declared the fact; w'hen I saw
among the spoyles a goodly Babylonisb garment, and two hundred
sherels of silver, and a medge of gold of fistie shekels weight: then I
coveted tbem, and toohe them. Repentant confe ssion begins at the
consession of the fact.
Secondiy,
Vu u u 2

0703.head: Chap.31. An Expesition apon the Book: of IO B. Verf.33.

body.t: Secondly, As there is a confession of the fact, so of the fault,
thar is, that in doing so wee have done amisse, or done sinfully
and foolish!y. When David made a confe ssion or acknowledge¬
ment of that sin, his numbring the people, hee doth not only say,
I have done it, but he saitb, I bave done very foelisply, (2 Sam.23.
10.) Nor did he only confesse that great sin of Adultery, but he
confessed the fault ( Psal. 51. 4.) Against thte, thee only have
sinned, and done this evill in thy sight: I have done this, and in do¬
ing this I have done evill. This is the lise of Gospel repentance.
Some confesse the fact, who yet are not humbled under the sence
of their owne folly and faultines.
Thirdly, There is in Confession not only an acknowledge¬
ment of the fact and fault, but a submission to the punishment;
Confession is a Judging of our selves worthy of death; hee that
confesseth doth as it were put the rope about his owne neck, and
tells the Lord he is as a dead man before him. (True Confession
is a submitting to the lentence of the Judge, yea a judging of our
selves, and a Justifying of God in all, even in his sharpest and se¬
verest dispensations. Thus David (in Psal. 51. 4.) I have done
tvil in thy sight, that thou mayest be justified mhen thou speakest,
and be cleare when thou Judgest; That is, when thou judgest mec
as a father, when thou correctest and chastisest mee ( as God did
wonderfully chastise him for those sins, the sword never departed
from his family) Lord I confesse thouart just in all those sharpe
and severe judgements that l have been threatned with in refe¬
rence to that sin. Daniels heart, was in the same frame while hee
fasted and prayed, and confessed the fins of the people of Ifrael
(Dar: 9 7,8.)O Lord ( saith he) Righteousnesse belongeth unto
thee, but unto us confusion of faces, as at this day, to the men ef fu¬
dab &c. because of their trespasse that they have trespassed against
thee &c.
But some may say, Is there a necessity to make such a confessi¬
on of sin? seeing God is already acquainted with, and knowes
our sins, with all the circumstances and aggravations of them,
what need we Confesse them? why should wee tell that to God
wbich he knows already?
I answer, First, vee doe not Confesse, to informe God of
what he knowes not, but to give glory to God in that which he
hnoxes: So saith fospua to Acban, doe not hide thy sin,but con¬

0704.head: Chap. 31. Ax Exposition upon tbe Booke of JOB. Verl. 33.

body.t: fesse it, and give glery to God; give him the glery of his Justice
and righteousnesse in punishing, and the glory of his patience and
mercy in pardoning. A true gracious confession gives God the
glory of all his attributes, and puis a Crowne upon all his divine
perfections. So then, wee confesse, not to informe God, but to
honour and glonfie him
Secondly, Wee are called to an acknouledgement acd Con¬
fession of our sins to God, that wee our selves may be the more
deeply affected with them; we need not informe God, but wec
have need enough to affest our oune soules: As wee make con¬
fession of the mercies and goodnesse of God, and repeat his kind¬
nesses to us, that our soules may be the more affected uith thant¬
sulnesse for them; So wee are to make confession of our own sin¬
fulnesse, that we may be the more affect ed with the vilenesse and
filthinesse of them, and with godly sorrour for them.
Thirdly, The knowledge which God hath of fin in and by
himselfe, may be a terror to sinners; his knouing of them by us
is only a ground of comfort. God hath no wher e promised to
pardon sin because he kκovs it, but he hath if ue makeit known.
Halesse God know our sins by our confession, he knowes them
only to our condemnation: hee knowes them enough already to
condemne us, though wee dot not confesse them, but he uill not
know them so, as to acquit us unlesse we confesse them. And in¬
deed nothing is knowne properly to God in that capacity as hee
pardons and forgives, but that which is ackrowledged byus.
When a Judge is to give sentence upon persons or actions, hee
rakes notice of nothing but what is made knowne to him as a
Judge; what he knowes in a private capacity is no ground for
him to proceed to sentence upon; every thing must be proved Ju¬
dicially, or witnessed openly in Court, before he gives Judgement,
eyther to acquit or condemne."Tis so in this case; Though all
our sins are knowne to God, yet none of them are knowne to
him as a Judge but what we confesse; and therefore he will not
pardon them or acquit us from them till they are confessed.
Further, That acknowledgement of sin, opposed to covering
and hiding of fin, is
First a confession of all sin; IfI (saith Tob) have hid my trars:
gressions, that is, any of my transgressions; hec doth not say this
or that, but he intends them all together; Ifa man confesse ma¬

0705.head: Chap.31. An Expositien upon the Boos ef IO2. Veri.33.

body.t: ny, and cover but one, all are as if they were covered, as the A¬
postle James speakes about transgre ssion, Hee that becps the wbole
Law, and iffendi in any one poynt, is guilty of ad ( Iumes 2. 10)
So hee that confesseth all his sins, and hides one, bath hid all and
confest none.
But you will say, is it possible for a man to confesse all his
sinnes ?
l answer. Wee may confesse them all as to kinde, though not
as to Individuall particular Acts; for indeed they are more in
numher then the haires of our head; They are innumerable, wee
cannot reckon them up. As wee cannot reckon up all the mercies
of God in the particular acts of them towards us, yet vee may
reckon the species or kinds of the mercies of God to us; So’tis in
the confession of sin. Aaron was commanded ( Levit: 16.21.)
to lay both bis hands upon the head of the live goat, and to cenfesse
over him all the iniquities ef the Children of Israel; and all their
transgressions in all their sinnes.
Secondly, Wee must not hide but confesse our speciall sins in
a speciall manner ( Ex d: 32. 31.) And Mses returned unto the
Lord, and said, O this people have sinzed a great sin, and have made
them gods of gold. Wee have a lixe forme of consession (I Sam:
12.19) And alt the people said unto Samutl, Pray for thy servants
unto the Lord thy God, that xe dy not; for we have added to all oar
fins, this evill, to aske us a king. So saith Pob. If Lhave bid my
transgressims, or, hid mine iniquitie in my boseme, that is, those
transgressions, or thũt iniquity vhich may seeme to beare a grea¬
ter title to mee, or l'toit, then any other sin committed by
me; if I have not made speciall confession of my speciall sinne,
then, &c.
Thirdly, That Confession which is opposed to the coveting
of sin, takes in not only the body of sin, or as I may say, the mat¬
ter of it, but all the severall Circumstances and aggravations of
it. There is an Iniquity of sin, as David speakes ( Psal. 32.5.)
Thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin; hee doth not only say my
sin, out the Iniquitie of my sin, he speaks of the sinfullnesse of sin;
and the Prophet tells Israel, In thy filthinesse is lewdnesse (Ezek:
14. 13.) This lewdnesse or Iniquity of sin ariseth from the con¬
sideration of those circumstances with whicbiit is cloathed. Thus
Evra at once hightens both the mercy of God to the Jewes, and

0706.head: Chap.31. An Expofition upon thi Book of JOR. Verf. 33

body.t: their sinfullnesse against God (Evra 9. 13, 14.) Andaster all
that is come upon us for our evill deedi, and fer our grtat trespasse,
seting that thou our God hest punished us Iisse then our iniquuiet
deserve, and hast given iu such deliverarcẽ as this. As he confes¬
led not only that God had given them deliverance, but fuch a de¬
liverance, yea (saith he) such a delivtrasce as tbis, so we should
confesse not only that we have committed in quity, but such an
iniquity, yea such an iniquity as this, or an iniquity thus and thus
circumstantiated.
Further (to close this observation ) hee that would confesse
fin in opposition to that hiding and covering which Tob here dis¬
avowes, must doe it,
First, Feelingly, as to the weight and smart osit, yea tasting¬
ly, as to the bitternesse and unsavorinesse of it unlesse we have a
tast how bitter sin is, unlesse we are pressed and even sweat in the

There is a vast difference between these two; A special sin and

body.t: OB 31. Vers. 34.
Did I feare a great multitude, or did the contempt
of families terrifie me: that I hept silence, and
went not out of the doore?
MHis holy man Jeb still proceeds to assert and maintaine his
I integrity; In the former verse he hath shewed us, that he
had not covered his transgression as Adam, by hideing his iniquitie
in his bosome. And here he tells us, that he did not feare a great
multitude, nor mas he terrified with the contempt of families, into
a sinfull silence or forbearance to appeare when the duty of his
place called him to come forth and speake in a good cause.I shall
open the particular termes, and then give out their scope and
sence more fully.
Vers.34. Did Ifeare a great multitade?
The word notes more then ordinary feare, even a strong pre¬
vailing feare, which puts the whole man into motion, or into a
commotion rather, into a rout and concussion of the spirits and
powers both of body and soule; Such are the effects of great
feare.
Did I feare a great muliitude ?
Wee may expound it, First, passively, did Ifeare, that is, was
I afraid of, was I put into a trembling fit for feare of a great multi¬
tude? Secondly, the word may be taxen actively, to make asraid,
to oppresse, and breake with violence. He that can breake and
crush all that stand in his way is a man to be feared. And hence
the Scripture saith ( Psal. 89.7.) Ged is greatly to be feared in
the assembly of the Saints. God is such a Majestie, that all, even his
owne people have reason to quake and tremble at his presence or
appearance; and as he is dreadfull in his essentiall Majestie, so in
the providentiall puttings forth and actings of that Majestie.
The Prophet tells us in what a wofull plight the inhabitants of
the earth, the highest ( not excepted) will be, when God deales
with them ( Isa. 2. 19.) They shall goe into the holes of the rockes,
and into the caves of ihe earth, for feare ef the Lord, and for the glo¬

But such families as came to basenes made me shrinke, that I was

body.t: There are three wayes in which men may become the con¬
tempt of the family.
First, by their povertie, and the meanenesse of their condition;
though it be sinfull to contemne the poore, yet ufually the poort
of a family are the contempt ofit.
Secondly, others are the contempt of families, because of the
weaknesse of their parts and gifts, because of their ignorance, and
want of understanding. A mans abilities whether naturall or ac¬
quired, especially gracious abilities raile him up in honour and re¬
spect.
Thirdly, Some are the contempt of families for their ill man¬
ners, for their lewd scandalous and wicked courses, these are wor¬
