cases especially wherein we ought to acknowledge our sin even
before men.
First, In trouble of conscience, when we can get no ease, no
satisfaction by prayer and self. searching, uhen the soule finds no
rest, but the sore runneth and putrifietb, the wound stinketh and
is corrupt, as David spake in his owne case (Psal.38.5.) In this
case it is a dutie to lay open our sin to man. I doe not say, to the
multitude, but unto those who are wise and godly, either Mini¬
sters or Christians. In a troubled darke condition,'tis dangerous
to shut up sorrow in our owne breasts, feare of reproach and
shame from men should not hinder us from discovering the
plague of our heart to those that are discreete and faithfull.
Secondly, If many have taken offence at our sin, if a multitude
are scandalized at what we have done; it is a dutie to acknow¬
ledge and confesse it, even before the multitude; That so our re¬
pentance may be as publicke as our sin hath been, and spread a¬
farre as our fayling hath done.
Secondly, Taking the former clause actively; I could hav¬
made a great multitude afraid, er I could eppresse a great multitade
which reading (as I noted) is much insisted upon by some in¬
terpreters) yet the most contemptible person of any family made
me afraid, if he had Justice on his side, I durst not ( the feare of
God was upon me ) appeare against him, or oppose him in bis
cause. This reading argues much holinesse, humility, and selfe¬
denyall in this righteous man.
And it may teach us;
First, How mach prmer sotver a just and good man bath in bis
hand, he xil not use any of it to the mrong of any the
poorest max.
He that is righteous knoues he hath no power, and finds he
hath no will but to doe righteous things. Laban sayd to facob
Gen. 31.29.) It is in the power ef my band to dee yeu hurt; fo
he bragg'd over jacob; And we doe not finde that Labans spirit
or principle stopped him from hurting Tacob, for (saich he) Tue
God
Yy y y 2

0719.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition apon the Books of JOR. Vert.34.

body.t: God of your fathers spake unto me yesternight, saying, Take thou
beed, that thou speake not to Tacob either good or bad. That is, doc
not speake to him good or bad as to this matter of his returne to
thee, doe not allure him by promises, nor terrifie him by threat¬
nings to desist from his intended journey. Labans spirit was
checked by the Lord not to use his power against Jacob, but it is
not cleare that he had a principle of righteousness and meekness
in him to checke himselfe from doing it. When a man can say,
it is in the power of my hand to doe you hurt, but the Lord hath
given me another heart, I dare not doe you wrong, nor will I op¬
presse you in your right, this is an excellent and a gracious frame.
And this appeared eminently in Joseph (Gen. 50.) His father Ja¬
cob being dead, his brethren were afraid that he would take re¬
venge upon them (v. 15.) And nhen Josephs Brethren saw that
their father mas dead, they sayd, fosepb mill peradventure hate us,
And wil certainly requite us all the evill mhich me did unto him¬.
This foseph our brother is a man in power, and having the com¬
mand of all Egypt, he is able to break the whole multitude of us;
and while we remember our unjust and ill usage of him, what can
we expect but hard usage from him? and therefore they humbly
addressed unto him (v. 16, 17.) And they sent a messenger unto
Joseph, saying, thy father did command befort he dyed, saring, So fhall
ye say unto Joseph, forgive I pray thee, the trespasse of thy brethren
andtheir sin: for they did unto thet evill; And now wee pray thee,
forgive the trespasse of the servants of the God of thy father. And
toseph mept mhen they spake unto him. (It troubled him to be sus¬
pected of revengefull purposes towards them) And Joseph sayd
unto them (v. 19, 20.) Feare net, for am I in the place ef Ged?
As if he had sayd, Vengeance belongs to God not to me,And see¬
ing God hath over-ruled your unkindnes and ill dealing with me,
for the good both of your selves and others, I am so farre from
meaning you any hurt, that I will still doe you good. Thus he
reproved them for the evill which they had done, and releeved
them against all feares, that he would doe them any hurt in the
words following; As for you, ye thought evill against me, but God
meant it unto good, te bring to passe as it is this day to save much
people alive; Nom therefore feare ye net, I mil nourist you and your
litle outs; and he comforted them aud spabe kindly to them. A god¬
ly man is so sencible of the kindnesse of God to him, that he can¬

0720.head: Chap. 31. Au Expesition upon thi Booke of JOB. Verl. 34.

body.t: sot returne unkindnesse where he hath received it, though he
could easily doe it; They indeed know what it is to use power a¬
rigbt, mho when they need not feare what a multitude can do against
them, yet feare to doe wrong to any fingle person. As Paul speakes
of Church.power (2 Cor. 13. 8.) So saith any godly man (what
magistraticall or military power soever he hath) I can doe nothirg
against the truth, but for the trutb. I am for the truth (saith Paul)
there l am a gyant, but I can doe nothing against the truth; I have
neither strength nor understanding for that worke. So saith a
godly man, though I could breake a troope, yet I will not breake
a bruised reed against right; I eannot list up my hand, nor open
my mouth, nor stirre a foote against a righteous man, though in
raggs, or under my feete. And indeed it is ueaknes, not power to
doe any thing against the truth or righteousnesse (Ezek. 16.30.)
How weake art thou seing thou doest these things (what things were
these, the doing were argued weakues? no good I warrant you,
so it followes in the same place) the workes of an imperious u ho¬
riso woman.
Secondly, Note.
It is a high commendation and a strong procfe of the truth and
power of grace, nhen ne have a pomer to doe evil and doe it
not, nor have any heart to doe it.
Many uant nothing but power to doe mischiefe; they have
a heart forit, but they have not a hand. If they could but breake
a troop and oppresse the multitude, whom would they not op¬
presse? whom would they not terrifie? the Lord restraineth them
in their power, else they would ufe it to the utmost. Thou uils
cause thine eart to heare ( saith David, Psal: 10. 18.) To judge
the fatherlesse and the oppressed, that the man of the earth may ro
more oppresse, or (as we put in the Margin) terrifie. The man ef the
earth ( that is, the man who is great and strong upon earth, or in
earthly things) hath an heart to oppresse, there is nothing want¬
ing but leave and opportunity. When once he hath opportunity,
he will not only oppress, but alwayes oppress, he will never make
an end of oppressing, and therefore the Psalmist prays that God
would come and take order with him, that he may no more op¬
presse; As if he had sayd, Lord if thou lettest him alone, he will
oppresse more and more, even his evermore, yea he will not only

0721.head: Chap-31. An Exposition upou the Book of JOR. Vers.34.

body.t: oppresse, but triumph and pride himselfe in his oppre ssions, as be
is described in another Scripture (Psal: 52. 1.) Why boastest thou
tby selfe in mischiefe, O mighty man? (That's a Psalme of David,
wuen Doeg the Edomite came and told Saul, and said unto him, Da¬
vid is come to the house of Abimilech) Why boustest thou thy selfe in
mischiefe, O mighty man ( said David then) The goodnesse of God
endureth continually. (God hath all power in his hand, he could
crush all men as a moth; He is God Almightie, able to destroy
whom he pleaseth, and when he pleaseth, yet the gondnesse of God
endureth continuady. He is good, and he loveth to be doing good;
whereas (v: 3.) Thou lovest evil more then good, and therefore
exercisest thy power in the doing of evil rather then good.
Againe; Taking this interpretation, I could breabe or terrifie a
great multitude, yet the contempt of families terrified me; that is,
if the meanest of the family did but advertise me wherein I had
done wrong, I was afraid to proceed.
Hence observe.
A godly man ù milling to receive counsel or reproofe where there
is cause, from the meanest persens.
He lookes not upon the speaker, but what is spoken; nor doth
he contemne what the contempt of families telleth him, if he tel¬
leth truth. It is sayd in that propheticall promise ( Isa. 11.6.)
The wolf shall duell mith the Lamb, and the Leopard shall lie down
with the Kid, And the Calf and the yong Lion and the fatling toge¬
ther, And a litt le child suall lead them. Here’s a Gracious meta¬
morphosis, They who were wild and fierce as Lions, shall be tur¬
ned into Lambs; They shall have such a tamenesse and mildnesse
of Spirit, that a litle child may lead them. As if the Prophet had
sayd; If the least ( who are able) give counsel, if but a child give
counsel, they will follow him in the way of righteousnesse. As he
that is godly and righely principled, vill not be led out of the
way of truth, holinesse, and righteousnesse, by the dictates or di¬
rections of the most ancient Fathers (Gray hayres command no
reverence but (where they are a croune of glory) as being found
in the wayes of righteousnesse) so if a litle child, or the greenest
head shew him the way of righteousnesse, he cannot but give re¬
verence and followit; or if a litle child shew him where he is
gone out ofthe way, he is convinced and will not goe one step

0722.head: Chap.31. Au Expostlon upon the Book of I02. Vert.34.

body.t: further. Iob professed at the 13 th verse of this Chapter; If I did
despise thi cause of my man servant or of my maid-servant when
they contended mith me, &c. Pob was ready to heare not only his
great Lords and Counsellers, but his common servants; shee that
swept the house, and he that rubed his horse-heels, was not refused
nor rejected by him There is much grace, a bight of grace suewed iu
being nilling to receive counsel or reprorfe from the least and lowest.
Mostly, rich and great men are a terrour to all reprovers, and have
this unhappiness with their greatness, that they may ruine them¬
selves uncontroul’d. Possibly some may mutter at them in secret,
but no man dares speake openly or plainely to them. Tob poynts
at such proud ones (Chap: 21. 30,31.) The micked is reserved
to the day of destruction, &c. Iho fhall declare bis way to bis face?
and who suall repay him what he hath dont? The man is past deal¬
ing with; yon take a Lion by the beard and a Beare by the tooth
when you reprove him. Job was a great man, yet if truth were
spoken by a child or a servant, he hearkened toit; His example
should be our warning, not to despise necessary warnings, what
hand soever brings them to us. If the message be of God, 'tis no
great matter how litle the messenger is. And if our consciences
tell us he speakes truth, and that his finger is upon our soare, let
us not cast it away, nor reject it, lest we be cast away among those
who reject the counsel of God against themselves, who often
sendeth such messages, whether of counsel or reproofe, to us, on
purpose, by persons of least respect, that he may try whether we
respect truth without respect of persons. A godly man will not
say, what’s he that he should be a monitor, that he should tell
me of my faults, or undertake to teach me; If it be a sin that
we are told of, or a duty that we are taught, it is honorable for
us to lay downe our sin and take up our duty, though he be (as
to a worldly account) contemptible, who hath dealt with us a¬
bout eyther.
There is a third interpretation of these uords, which I conceive
to be yet more cleare unto the scope of this text, and that ariseth
from the text as it stands in our translation. Job had been shewing
before what he was, and how he had behaved himselfe in severall
of his relations, as a neighbour, as a husband, as a Master, as a
Magistrate, and as there he professed his Magistraticall integrity,
so here the courage and undauntedness of his spirit, in the dis¬

0723.head: Chap.31. An Expofition upon thi Bock of JO». Vers.34,

body.t: charge of that office. Did I feare (saith he) a great multitude?
or did the contempt of families terrifie me, that I kept filence, and
vent not out ef the doore? As if he had sayd, The violence of the peo¬
ma-ple never hinder'd me from doing my dutie, nor did I at any time goe
cut of my way, lest I should displease the nearest of my owne family,
or the greatest families. It never troubled me wbo opposed me, mhe¬
ther considered fer number, nearnesse, or greatnefse, nhile I mas fer
justice: The contempt of any man did not make me keepe filence,
nor stay me in the least frem doing mbat mas right and equall to all
men.
No man can doe good but he shall have crosse motions, both
from the flesh within him, and from flech without him. We meete
with most rubbs, when we would walke in an even way.It seemes
tob in the discharge of his office, met with many tven with a mul¬
titude ofopposers, especially with opposition from the multitude,
and therefore saith, Did I feare a great multitude?
Hence note.
First, The multitude er generality ef men, are prone to oppose that
mhich is good, and those who doe good.
There is a principle of unrighteousnesse in all men by nature,
and most men in their practice oppose that which is righteous.
Wee find the multitude opposing the greatest good worke that
ever the Lord did, the setting his Son upon his holy hill of Siou.
The whole world of ungodly men, both Princes and people were
up in armes to oppose this glorious worke of God (Psal.2 1,2.)
Why doe the heathen rage and the people imagine a vaine thing: The
kingt of the earth set themselves, and the Princes take counsel to¬
gether, against tbe Lord and agairst bis anoynted, saring, let us
breake tueir bandt asunder. Obedience to Christ is the worlds
bondage, and they will get loose if they can. And as in that, so in
other cases, the people rage and imagine vaine things, when the
best things are in doing. They chat follow the multitude shall
seldome doe any thing that is good. When Moses came downe
from the Mount and charged Aaron with making that Idol, Aa¬
ron by way of excuse tells him the people had pressed him to make
it (Exd: 32. 22.) And Aaron sayd, let not the anger of my Lord
wax hot: thou knowest the people that they are set on mischiefe; for
they sayd unto me, mate us gods, &c. Aaron should not have heard

0724.head: Chap. 31. An Expositiou upon tbi Book ef JOR. Vers.34.

body.t: much lesse feared the maltitude, but he did. Sometimes (I grant)
The voyce of the people is the veyct of Ged: That is, God moves the
multitude by a secret over-powering influence upon their spirits
to cry up and call alowd for that to be done uhich himselfe (in
his wonderfull providences and according to his eternal counsels)
is about to doe. But in most cases, we may say, The voyce of the
pople is the voyce of the Devill. And if you will please the most of
men, or The many, you shall never doe any thing that is pleasing
to God, or profitable unto men. The multitude is an unruly beast.
hurryed by passion, not guided by rule or reason. And as some
excule their doing evill by the urgency of the people, so others
are kept from doing good by the opposition of the people. Saut
(as was shewed more largely upon the former verse) would
needs excuse the miscarriage of that service which God called
him to, by the cry of the people (1 Sam: 15.21.) The people took
of the spoyle &c. As if Saul had sayd, Coula I turne such a torrent,
could I fully execute the Commission mhich God gave me xben the
people mould not consent and cleave to me? They who feare the
people, or resolve to please the people, shall at best, doe the worke
of God to halves, and usually they leave it quite undone, or doc
that which is just contrary to it. Job could say, Did I feare a great
multitude? This was not so much a gallant, as a truely gracious
resolution; and there are but fem who have acted ap to it. The
streame of the multitude doth often carry even Magistrates and
great ones downe with it, to the doing of unworthy and unrigh¬
teous things, or stops them from doing those things which are
honorable and righteous. Every Magistrate is not cloathed vith
Jobs spirit, to be above the sway of a great multitude. Pilate was
carried to one of the worst actions in the world ( though it had
the best and most blessed issue) to passe an unjust sentence upon
Christ ( who was as innocent as innocency it selfe) meerely be¬
cause he feared the multitude (Math: 27. 24.) When Pilate
sam that he could prevaile nothing, lut rather a tumult mas made,
he toche water and mashed his hands before the multitude, saying, I
am innccent from the bleod ef this just person: see ye to it. It is your
cry and your rage that hath prevailed with me, l offered you Ba¬
rabbas to be crucified and Jesus to be released, but nothing (I per¬
ceave) will content you except Jesus dy, therefore take him. See
how this Romane Judge was baffl’d and overcome by the multi¬

0725.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Booke ef J0 ». Vers.34.

body.t: tude to condemne a righteous perfon against the dictate of his
owne conscience, and the light of his judgement. And we read
(Act: 12.2.) How Herod had killed James the brother of fobn mwith
ihe sword, And because he sam it pleased the Jemes, he proceeded
further to tahe Peter also, &c. Thus some doe injustice for feare
of the multitude, and others to gaine the love and good will of
the multitude, care not to be both bloody and unjust.
Secondly, Nore.
A godiy man, especially a godly Magistrate, will doe juast and
righteous things, though ad the morld rise up agairst him¬.
This is the honour of Magistracy, and by this they shew them¬
selves Gods indeed, men acted by the Spirit of God, and acting
in the power of God. Magistrates fhould not yeild no not an
haires breadth through the importunitie of a multitude. It is a¬
gainst the duty of a private Christian to have fellowship with the
unfruitfull workes of darknesse, much more for those that are in
power. It is best to get and keepe the heart so established, as nei¬
ther to doe nor forbeare to doe for feare of the multitude, or for
feare we bring (as we say) fists about our eares, and an old house
upon our heads. We should be resolute in a good cause, though¬
ue purchase to our selves the hatred of the uhole world. And it
is but needfull that we should cast up our account aforehand a¬
bout this thing; for while we set our selves to resist evill ( The
most being every where the worst) we are like to have the whole
world of evill men our enemies. While so many flatter them¬
selves, few or none can digest reproofe, and but a few Justice, from
others.
Againe, Consider the second branch of this verse according¬
to the second acceptation of the word families. The contempt of
families did not terrifie mec- I ( saith fob) neyther feared whole
families, nor the heads or chiefes of families. Some possibly can
trample upon the multitude, and slight the common sort, but
they feare the great ones.
Hence note.
Rig hieous men will doe righteous things, botb in thir publicke
and private capacities, though they provohe the mighty, and
run the haxcird es eteir hortest displeasture.

0726.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upou tbe Bok of IOR. Vers 34.

body.t: Zimri xas a Prince of a chiefe bouse among the Simeonites
( Numb. 25. 15.) yet Phineas was not afraid to provoke that
great family in Israel, but in his zeale for the Lord thrust both
him and Cezli his Harlot thorow the belly and slew them, and
receaved higb commendation from the Lord for doing it. The
day of mans Justice should be like that of the Lords spohen of by
the Prophet (Isa. 2. 12,13.) The day of the Lord of bests suat be
upon every one that is proud and lofty, and upon every one that ut
lifted up, and he shall be brought lon; And upon all ibe Cedars of
Lebanon, that are high and lifted up, and upon all the Oages of Ba¬
shan; And upon all high mountaines, and upon all the hilli ibat art
lifted up; That is, upon those persons who are greatest, highest,
and strongest, like mountaines and hills, like Cedars and Oakes in
the world. God in the execution of his judgements, regardeth
not the greatnesse of men, but impartially powreth vengeance
npon them, nor should men where justice and righteousnesse call
for it; He is not worthy the name or office of a Magistrate, who
cannot (in this sence) contemne the contempt of Families.
Secondly, As the word families, signifieth such as are of neare
relation tous, as some here interpret.
Note.
The feare ef displiasing Rindred and tbose in relation, eften
proves a great obstractien to Justice.
Some would doe right, but there is a kinsman a brother in the
case. We say, It is hard to love and to he wise. Affections pervert
the judgement. And therefore by an ancient Law it was provided,
that no man should be chosen to exercise the office of a Magi-
strate in the Province where he was bred and borne, lest he should
be tempted to favour his hindred and allyes in the forbearance of
Justice, or might seeme harsh and rigorous in doing Justice, ey-
ther against or upon them. It is not easie to see a fault and pun¬
ishit in those that are neare us: and ’tis hardest to see faults in
our selves, because we are nearest our selves. Naturalists observe
that vhen a sencible object is layd neare the sence, the operation
is hindred. There is no man can see himselfe well till he get quite
out of himselfe. And our nearenes to others makes it someurhat
difficalt for us to discerne their faults, but more to censure and
punisha them. Hou hard was it for David to see treason in a son.
Wec

0727.head: Chap. 31. An Expssition apon the Books ef JOR. Vers.34.

body.t: Wce are loth to displease kindred, or to be displeased with them.
It was the commendation of the tribe of Levi (and the Lord ho¬
noured them with the Priesthood for it) that they tooke no no¬
tice of relations in the Lords cause (Dut: 33.8, 9.) And of Levi
he sayd, let thy Thummim and thy Urim be mith thy holy one whom
thos diast preve at Messah, and mith mhom thou didst strive at the
maters of Meribah. Wuo sayd unto bis father, and to his mother,
bave not seene him, naither did hee acknonledge his brethren, nor
Enem his onue children: they observed thy word, and kept thy Co¬
venant. Had these Levites cast off all naturall affection? How is
it then sayd, they did not know father or mother? It was in exe¬
cuting the Lords command, as appeares (Exod: 32. 27.)And
be (that is, Moses) sayd unto them, thus saith the Lord God of Is¬
rael, Put every man his sword by hus side, And goe in and eut from
gate te gate tbroughout the Campe, and stay every uan his brother,
and every man his companion, and every man his neighbour. Now,
when the other Tribes were unwilling to execute this sentence of
God upon their kindred and neare relations, Levi did it, as is re¬
ported in the next words (v. 28.) And the children of Levi did
accordirg to the mord of Moses, aud there fell of the pesple that day
about three thousand men; for Moses had sayd, Consecrate your
solves to day to the Lord, evin every man upon bis son, and upon his
brother, that he may bestom upon you a blessing this day. Levi did
not know father or mother or child so, as to be partiall in or neg¬
lect the execution of the decrec and sentence of God. It is a great
poynt of holy knowledge in such cases not to know father or mo¬
ther or any relations; And it is a truth, that the knowledge of re¬
lations ofcen byasseth us from duty in many cases. When a kins¬
man is in the case, the Law (in some mens opinion) is otherwise.
If Davids heart had not been strongly as wel as sincerely set for
God, The contempt of his wife had cooled his zeale, and made
him ashamed of his Dauncing before the Arke (I Sam: 6. 16.)
That was a Noble resolution of Saul, if it had been well ground¬
ed, when he cast lotts to find out who had eaten contrary to the
oath wherein he had rashly engaged the Army (I Sam: 14. 24,
19) For as the Lord livetb mhich saveth Israel, though it be fona¬
than my Son, he shall surely die. Had Saul done wel in adjuring
the people not to eate till the evening, he had done eminently wel
in resolving not to spare his owne Son for eating, but the former

0728.head: Chap. 31. An Expesition upon the Booke of JOB. Verl. 34.

body.t: being bad, the latter was worse. Be sure you are upon a right
matter, and then the more stiffe and resolved you are against re¬
spect to relations, the better are your resolutions. Personall re¬
lations should suay nothing in a publicke cause, nor should any
notice of persons turne us afide from doing right. The Lord sayd
(Jer: 22. 24.) Thougb Coniah the son of Jeboiakim king of Judab
mere the Signet upon my right hand, yet would I plucke him thence;
that is, though he were as neare to me and as usefull as a Signet is
to man ( for this is spoken only after the manner of men) yet he
shall beare his punishment, and know that he hath grievousl, sin¬
ned against me. This (in proportion) was Jobs honour, he would
not spare Signet-friends, he had rather provoke all the relations
he had in the world, then depart from the rule, and so provoke his
first best friend the Lord, and his next best friend his oune consci¬
ence; God is our best friend, and shall we adventure a contempt
from God to avoyd the contempt of friends? How good & sweet
a friend a good conscience is, none know but they that have it,
nor all they neyther: but to be sure, tis better and easier being
under the displeasure of a thousand families kindreds & :elations,
then under the displeasure eyther of God above, or of our con¬
science in our bosome. Here’s our duty both in publicke and pri¬
vete transactions, never be over-borne by families, eyther not to
doe right, or to doe unrighteously. How upright a man was Tob,
who alwayes did what was right, though against the vote, first, of
the multitude, secondly, of his kindred; thirdly, of great fami¬
lies: All these did not move him at all, nor did they beare the
weight of an haire in the ballance for the turning him out of his
way.
And this is a good patterne for the Ministers of the Gospel;
They should not feare to doe the duty of their place and office;
Theugh, First, The multitude are displeased; though, Secondly,
Their kindred and fathers family contemne them for it, though,
Thirdly, Great men are angry, and are ready to powre out wrath
upon them if they doe. Magistrates and Ministers act like them¬
selves when they are swayed by conscience towards God, not by
humanc concernments or confiderations.

0729.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Book ef JOB. Verl.35.

body.t: O that one would heare ue, behold, uiy desire is, that
the Almighty would answer me, and thãt mine ad¬
versary had written a book.
Surely I would take it upon my shoulder, and binde it
as a crowne to me.
I mould declare unto hine the number of my steps, as
a Prince would Tgoe neare unto him.
OB having given many evidences and proofes of his inte¬
I grity in the foregoing part of this Chapter, sadly, and most se¬
riously imprecating the Judgements of God upon himselse, if his
testimony were not true; he in these three verses shews his assu¬
rance of the goodnesse of his cause, by his willingnesse to have the
whole matter yet more fully heard and examined even before the
purest and most impartiall tribunall. We have two things mott
considerable in this context.
First, Tobs earnest request or petition that he migbt come to
a tryall, O that one mould beare me, my desire ie that the Almighiy
would auswer me (V. 35
Secondly, His profession, with what heart and frame ot spi¬
rit he hoped to appeare and stand forth in the day of his tryall
(v. 36,37.) Surely I mould take it upen my ponlder, and binde
it as a crowne to me; I mould declare te him the number of my steps,
and as a Prince nould I goe neare unto him. These are words of
confidence, like confidence it selfe, yet no groundlesse confidence,
nor the confidence of the wicked, which God will reject, and in
which they shall never prosper.
Vers. 35. O that one would heare mee, or according to the let¬
ter, O that it mere given to me to have a hearer
for me.
tob calleth for a Judge, and doubts not but his Judge uill prove
his Patron; he calls for a Judge to heare him with equity and
moderation of spirit, of which kind of hearing he had found litle
from his friends.

0730.head: Chap.31. Au Expofitios apon thi Bock of JOR. Vert. 35.

body.t: O that one would heare mee.
He speakes indefinitely, as if he vere very indifferent who the
person were, so he were but an indifferent person that had the
hearing of his cause, aay person un byast and un-ingaged should
satisfie him. Some render, O that I'had a Judge to heare mee;
the text is only, O that I had one to heart me, but because ’cis the
business: of Judges to heare and determine causes, therefore it is
well rendered, O that Ihad a Judge to heare me, or a hearing
Judge. The Lord gave command for hearing as wel as Judgirg
(Deut: 1. 16) I charged your Tudges at that time, saying, heare
bet ween your Brethren; There can be no judging without hearing,
therefore a Judge is called a hearer. Thus Abshalon in bis flattet¬
ing and distoyall falutes (2 Sam. 15. 3.) bespake every man he
met, See thy matters are good and right, but there is no man de¬
puted of the King to heare thee: there is not a hearer, that is, there
is not a Judge to heare and determine your case. O that I nere
made Judge in the Land, or the hearer and determiner of diffe¬
rences between you, how readily and how righteously would I
dispatch your causes! And hence the place where Jucges use to
heare causes, is called Tue Auditorie ( Acts 25. 23.) Rhen thεy
mere come in to the hearing place, that is, to the place where causes
were heard and Judgement given. When Tob saith, O that one
would heare me, he intends not an ordinary hearer, or any one that
came next, but a Judge to take cognizance of and make some de-
termination about his case and state: And while Job begs for a
Iudge or a hearer, he doth not appeale from God, as if he vere
unwilling to acquiesse and rest in his Judgement; but he desired
that God would order him such a Judge, or such a hearer as
might doe bim right, according to the integrity of his heart, and
the equity of his cause. And thougn he spake in the former part
of the verse, as if he were content any Judge should end it, yet
we find he draws downe his defire to God himselfe in the latter
part of the verse; My desire is that the Almighty would answer
wet.
O that one vauld hart mes.
There is an Elegancy in the Hebrew text, Grammarians tell us,
that the participle is joyned with a dative pronoune of favour;

0731.head: Chap.31. Au Exposition upon the Bock of IOR. Verf. 35

body.t: O that one would heare me, with regard to my sad case, or with
compassion of my troubled condition; O that he would give me a
hearer sor me; Such a hearer I meane as is affected with and sen¬
cible of my sorrowfull state. Job had been long heard, how many
debates and discourses had there passed between him and his
friends? and yet now he speakes as if he had not been heard to
that day.
Hence observe.
They mhs doe not heare well, dot not heare at all; a matter is
never heard till it be righi ly heard.
And as’tis profitable to consider this, in reference to the hear¬
ing of such controversall debates, as passed between sob and his
friends, so in reference to our ordinary hearing the uncontrover¬
ted doctrines of the Gospel. Many faithfull Ministers of Christ
have preached long, and have had many hearers, who may yet
cry out as Jeb in the text, O that men would heare us! they have
not been heard, though they have had many hearers; few have
heard them, though the y have had a multitude of hearers. How
many Sermons soever you heare, till you heare them to profit,
vou heare them not at all. And how many causes soever the
Judge heareth, till he heareth them with equity and equirinity,
he doth not heare them at all. After Jub had been so long heard,
he had reason to cry out, Otthat one would hrare mee.
Secondly, Note.
A good man defires, and defires carnestly te have his cause
threughly heard, to have it heard te purpose.
As a godly man would have his prayers heard, that is, gran¬
ted, (The Lord is sayd not to heare that prayer, which hee doth
not grant.) he gives God no rest till he hath some hopes or in¬
timations that his holy desires are heard, and answered. So eve¬
ry man in distresse or trouble, every man under hard censures,
slanders, or mis-understandings, longs to be heard, and O how
long and tedious is the time till he hath obtained a desired hear¬
ing ? Tis a great paine not to be heard at any time, but then most
when we our selves are ( as Job was ) in paine. When the body is
in paine, and the minde in paine, when we are wounded within,
and wounded without, O how grieveus and paicesull is it not to

0732.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition upon thi Bocke of IO R. Verf.35.

body.t: he heard, but to have our matters still hanging in suspence, and
no end, no determination made about them! O that one mould
beare mec.
Behold my desire is, that the Almighiy would ansier me.
In this clause Jab pitcheth upon God for his Judge; As if he
had sayd with David (Psal.73.25.) Whom have I in heaven but
thee? and there is none upon the earth that I desire besides thee.
where soall I have a Judge on earthor in heaven but thee? Behold
my desire is, that the Almighty mould ansmer mee.
The word which we trarslate, my desire, is rendered by some,
thus, my signe is that the Almighty weuld auswer me; and so we
put in the Margin of our Bible. They who follow this reading
cerive the word from a roote which signifies, to marke, or to maRe
a figure. So the word is used ( Ezck 9. 4.) Set a marke upon
tbe heads ef these that mourne for the abominations that are commit-
ted in the Land, the word signifies also the uttermest end or terme
of a thing. The Hebrew Alphabet being closed wi h that letter.
They who iosist upon this signification of the word, read not (as
ve) my defire, but my figne er my marbe is that the Almighty
tould ansner me. As if he had sayd, The marke or scope thut I
aime at when I cry, O that one would heare me, is this, ihat the
Almig̨hty would ansirer me: though I setme to speabe at large or at
rvers, yet I have a marke, and the marke I sheete at is ibis, to bave
a hearing from God, O that God mould be the Judge of my innecency
and integrity, against all the false suppositions & mispri,fons uhich
mi friends have had or made of me totbis day.
But I rather adhere to our owne translation, my defireis, &c.
and so the word is derived from a roote which sigrifieth ro nis
or desire; my wist (saith he) or desire is that the Almighiy rrould
answer me. There is a three fold answering.
First, There is an answering to thole who aske questions, for
the resolving of their doubts.
Secondly, There is an answering to those uho make petitions
for the supply of their wants, or the grant of their requests.
Thirdly, There’s an answvering to those that plead against us,
or lay any charge uponus, for the clearing of our innocency, and
wiping away of those objections: in this latrer sence we are to
take it here, O that ibe Almighty monld anfrrer me, that is, chat he
would
A a a a a

0733.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition upon thi Booke ef J0R. Verf.35.

body.t: would undertake and cleare my cause, that he would be Judge,
and witnesse on my side. To ansuer, signifies also to testifie, or
to give a testimony concerning another. Againe, wee answer;
First, in words, when we confirme, acknowledge, and approve,
what another hath sayd or done; Secondly, we answer by our
actions (there is answering by the hand as wel as by the tongue)
when ve doe the thing that is desired of us. O that the Almi,b¬
tie mould answer me. Job having not found an equall Juege on
earth, and knowing that none but God knew the secrets of his
heart, desires that he would be his Judge. So that he calls God
to be his Judge, because he alone was acquainted fully with his
infide, and perfect ly discerned all the motions of his soule, bis ends
and aymes, as wel as the manner of his life. Thus he appealed
from men ( who are usually led by their affectfons, by their love
or hatred) to God, who (from the evidence of things) judgeth
unertingly.
Hence note.
A godly mans defires above all things that God mould heare,
and judge his cause or case.
David made this prayer ( Psal. 26. 1.) Judge me O Lord, sor
Ihave walged in my integrity. And againe (Psal.35.24.) Judge
me O Lord my God according to thy rigbteousnisse, and let them not
rejoyce over me. I have many Judges, many that judge me accord¬
ing to their unrighteousnesse; but ( saith he) Judge me O Lord,
according to thy righieousnesse. Once mort (Plal. 43.1.) Judge
me, O God, and plead my cause against an ungodly natisn. David
desires the Lord to sustaine both the part of an Advocate to
plead his cause, and of a Judge to determine it.
But why doth Tob (or why should any godly man) desire so ear¬
nest ly to have God tojudg him? The reason is, because God is the
best Judge, for first he is the most knowing Judge. They who have
bad causes desire much to come before bad or ignorant Judges,
who cannot looke farre into them, much lesse look thorow them,
they love to come before olind Judges, or if they be seing Judges,
they will doe what they canto put out their eyes, they will blind
them with gifts, as the Scripture speakes, Gifts put out the cyes.
But he that hath a good cause, desires to have a xnowing Judge,
a Judge learned in the Law. And thercfore a godly man must

0734.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upou the Bok of IO ». Verf.33.

body.t: needs desire God to be his Judge, who knoweth him throughly,
who knoweth not only the way without him, but that within him
too, who knoweth not only his actions but his thoughts, who
knoveth not only what he doth, but what he aimes at, the pur¬
poses, intents, and designes of all his actions. Whom should a
godly man desire to judge him in comparison of God, who
knows the frame of his heart, who though he cannot but see ma¬
ny faults, and sinfull faylings in him, yet he knows allo whatsoe¬
ver is good in him, that is, whatsoever himselte hath wrought in
him, and helped him to worke by his Spirit. God knows the
worke of his owne grace, together with the most secret workings
of all that grace. And therefore a godly man desires most of all
that God should judge him. Againe, secondly, he desires it be¬
cause he knows God will be as just in determining his cause, as he
is knowing about his cause; He cannot be turned aside, nor by¬
ass'd by any meanes; no solicitations, no threats, no promises, no
flatteries, no witcheries can in the least draw the Lord off from
that which is right. And as he is a just, and a knouing Judge;
so, thirdly, he is a mercifull Judge, and will award to us accord¬
ing to the tenour of a covenant of grace; hee will not enter into
Judgement with us, upon strict legall termes, upon the termes of
the covenant of works; for then who could desire God to be his
Judge? Enter not into Judgement mith thy servant O Lord, (every
one must say) for no flesb is righteous in thy sight; but a beleever
knows God will judge him npon the termes of the covenant of
grace, and therefore he desireth no other Judge but God. Be¬
hold, my desire is that the Almighty would answer me,
and that my Adversary had mritten a booke.
Whereas some might object against Tobs wish; you, perhaps,
would have the Almighty for your Judge, because you hope he
will favour you; no saich Job, l'am willing that God should know
the very worst of my case; As I desire that God should judge
me, so that my Aaversary should write a booke, and charge me
home. The Hebrew is, the man of my contention. There is a three¬
fold interpretation about this man of his contention.
First, Some by this Adversary or man of cantention, understand
God himselfe, uho had dealt with Tob in outuard dispensations
like an enemy, or an adversary, like a man full of contention.
The
A a a a à 2

0735.head: Chap.31. An Expssition upon tht Bocke of JOR. Vert.35.

body.t: The Lord saith (Isa: 57. 15.) I will not contend fer ever, &c.
I have been long contending, long striving, l have been as an Ad¬
versary to this people for a great while, Bat I will not contend
for ever, least the spirit should faile before me, and the soules that I
have made. Hence some conceave that even God himselse may
here be called Jobs Adverlary, or the man of his contention. So
the Scripture elsewhere expresseth the Lord under the word man
(Exid: 15.3.) The Lord is a man ef marre, the Lerdis his name;
As if he had sayd, the Lord is such a man of warre as is also Lord
and Master of the warre, he wins the day and triumphs in every
battel. The Lord is a fighting man, too mighty for all fighting
men. In which sense, the Lord may be called here a man ef con¬
rentien he can contend and strive, and carry it like an Adversary
eg inst allepponents.
Secondly, Others expound it of his Advocate;“Tis the office
of en Advocate to contend for his Client. O that the Almighty
would ansmer me, and that the man of my contention had mritten a
boote; that is, O that he who is to plead for me and mannage my
cause at the hearing, had drawne up his booke, stated my case, and
layd forth my condition, that the Almighty might proceed to
judgement upon it.
Thirdly, 'Tis taken as we translate for his reall adversary, O
that the max of my contention, or my Adversary who soever he is
that hath or will contend with me, had drawne up his booke, his
booke of accusation, and had filled it with the worst matter that
he could get against me; it should be all one to me what he can
fay against me, while I have the Almighty for my Judge. Thus
he alludes to those who bring in a charge or enditement in wri¬
ting against offenders when they are tryed or arraigned. Such
bookes or bills of enditement are read in open Court before the
Judge the prisoner standing at the bar to receive his Judgement.
O that my Adversary had mritten a booke. From the Elegancy of
the Hebre w, fob calling his Adversary a man of contention.
Observe.
Some men are such lovers of strife, that ihey are men of strife.
They are all for strife, and debate, strife is the very Element
uherein they live, they live in the troubled waters, yea I may
fay, chey live and they loye to live in the very fire of trouble,

0736.head: Chap. 31. Au Expesition upoz the Boke ef IOB. Vert. 35.

body.t: they are men of contention. The good Prophet was so accounted
(Jer. 13. 10.) Woe is me my mother, that thou hast borne me a
man of strife, a man of contention to the mbole tarth, I have neither
lent on usury, nor men have lent te me on usury, yet every one of thim
doth curse me; that is, I medled not uith businesse, I intangled not
my selfe with woridly affaires, l neirher lent nor borrowed, I nei¬
ther bought nor sold, yet I am a man of strise, and contention.
Some though they are nothing but peace in their spirits and spee¬
ches, yet are men of contention to the whole carth, that is, while
they only speake the truth, and hold out the purity of the vayes,
and worship of God, this vexeth all the world of uicked men.
Such are men of strife and contention to the whole earth, every
one wrangles with them, none can beare them. It is said of the
two witnesses ( Reυ: 11. 10.) They tormented the men that dmele
upon the earth. We read of a man ( Rev. 2. 13.) the notation of
uhose name (Antipas) is a man against al men; not that he was
for contention, but he was a man so holy in his life and zealous for
the truth of God, that all men (upon the matter) contended with
him, and he was slaine in the contention. The noble Atbanasius
in the time of the Arrian Heresie, opposed the whole world, he
was a man of contention to the uhole earth. In this sence some
good men the faithfull witnesses of Christ are men of contention
and strife. But many (as sob calls his Adversaries ) are men of
contention in an ill sence, that is, they desire contention and stirre
up strise. Behold ( saith the Prophet, Isa: 11. 11.) Al they ibat
were incensed against thee shall be ashamed and confcunded, they
shall be as nothing, and they that strive mitb thee sball perisp, we put
in the Margin, the men of thy strife; that is, men that are for no¬
thing but strife, or whose strongest bent is to strife, and their am¬
bition to be men of contention. Christ was so conversant with
sorrow, that he is called a man of sorrows (Isa: 53. 3.) And the
spirit of Antichrist is so steeped in fin, that he is called the man of
sin (2Thes:2.3.) And by a like Hebraisme or Elegancy of speech,
They who love to fish in troubled waters, or will be troubling
the waters though they get no fish, are deservedly called men of
trouble, or men of ftrife.
Secondly, When Job saith, O that my Adversary had mritten
a booke, that is, a booke of accusation, a charge, a libell, or an in¬
ditement against me, I wish with all my heart he had brought it
in, let him doe his worst.

0737.head: Chap.31. An Exposition upon the Book of JOR. Verf.36.

body.t: Note.
Wbile our owne boohe ef conscience hath nothing but good in it,
or xhile the booke of our owne conscience is for us, me need not
feare, nor much care mho write beoks against us.
Let our Adversaries write books as large as they will, while we
doe well; let them say their worst while we doe good. It hath
been the distemper of most times, and ’tis of these to write books
of contention, & publish strife, we may say of many (as it was said
of some old Philosophers) They speahe or pen mhole cart ledes of re¬
proach and slander. What is the fence against all this? nothing but
a good conscience, he that can say his conscience writes nothing
but good, and finds the records of that fayre for him, may take
courage and comfort, when men charge nothing but filth and dirt
upon him. Paul had enough to say for him elfe, mhen standing
before the Councel he could say (Act-23. 1.) Men and brethren,
I have lived in all good conscience bifore God, untill this day. And
though as soone as he had sayd so, Ananias commanded to smite
him on the mouth, yet he was wel enough, because bis conscience
did not smite him. He tells us also (2Cer:1.) that though he and
others with him, had been pressed above measure, in so much
(saith he, v. 8, 9.) that me despaired even of life, and had the sen¬
tence of death in our selues : yet (V. 12. ) our rejoycing is this, tbe
testimony ef our conscience. A good conscience is an impregnable
fort, lt feares not the feircest battery of evill tongues, or pers.
Thirdly, Observe.
It is a convincing argument, that a man hath a good conscience
and a good cause, mhen he is milling to be tryed, and to have the
worst laid to his charge.
He that is guilty catcheth at any thing for a covering, and de¬
fires to shadow himselfe that he may escape unseene; faine hec
would keepe his actions and his wayes fayrely mantled over; He
that is honest makes no coverings of what he hath done, nor doth
he feare the discoveries which any man can make of them. He
that is gold cares not to be guilded, nor is he unwilling to be try¬
ed. He saith (as Job in the text) Mr desire is that the Almighty
mould ansmer me, and that mine adversary had mritten a booke.

0738.head: Chap.31. An Expofition upon thi Book of IoB. Verl. 36.

body.t: Vers. 36. Surely I would take it on my shoulder. Mr. Brough¬
ton renders the word of asseveration, Surely, as an
oath; I sweare I mould beare it on my sheulder.
These words are a confirmation of uhat he spake last; as if he
had sayd. When my adversary hath made his booke as bigge and
as heavy as he can, I shall beare it for all that; I would beare it
upon my shoulder. Sin or guilt are a burden which no man is abie
to beare; who can take up any one sin, the least sin, upon hĩs
shoulders, and stand under it? Any ont sin lived in and loved, will
not only over-burden our shoulders, but breabe our baches. But
(saith Tob) let mine Adversary write my faults and faylings, I can
beare the booke upon my shoulders; why? because he knew his
adversary could write no sinfull practise, that he lived in or loved,
or desired to keep in his bosome, as he professed at the 33d verse.
Yea when Tob saith, I would beare it upon my shoulder, he doth not
only intimate it such a burden as would not presse him downe,
nor breake his backe, but that it would be his honour, and that he
should beare that booke as a banner of victory, or as an ersigne
of glory. He was eonfident that whatsoever his adversary could
write, with an intendment to disparrage him, would in the issue
turne to his praise.
There is yet another interpretation of these words, I would
beare it on my shoulder, As if Jobs meaning were; Suppose my ad¬
versary find reall faults in me, and charge me with them upon
due proofe; yet I vill tabe his booke upon my shoulder, aud beare it
patiently as my burden; I will acknowledge and confesse what!
have done amisse, and neither deny or excuse it. The word which
we translate to take upon the shoulder, signifies the taking up of a
heavy burden, and ’tis applyed to the bearing of any punishment;
that’s a good sence, if my adversary doth write my faults indecd,
I will beare his charge upon my shoulder, and take it patiently;
I am ready to submit, as to the dealings and chastenings of God,
so to the reproofes of man. Jab was farre from thinking he could
beare the guilt of his sinne upon his shoulder ( he might as uell
beare the weight of the whole earth as of one fin) only if found
faulty or guilty he would quietly beare the blame. But if his
adversaries booke fhould be found a flander, and his integrity
appeare through all his accusations, what then?

0739.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition upou the Bcok ef I0 ». Verf. 36,

body.t: I weuld bind it as a cromne to me ( saithhe)
The word is plurall inthe Originall, I would ty it for cromnes
to me; so Me. Brougbton renders. Crownes are glorious things,
they are the greatest glory of this world, they are emb’eams of
Soveraignty, or of highest Magistracy and Majesty I mould bind
it as Crownes. The leaves and lines of this booke shall be as so
many peices and Jewels of my Croune, or as many Crownes set
with precious stones. I mould bind it to me as a Crowne, or as
Crownes.
But why doth fob speake thus? had he no si, no faults, that
he saith, I would bind the booke as Crounes to me? did he
thinke nothing could be written of him which he had cause to be
ashamed of ?
I answer; Thougb as some men make garments to cover their
sin, so others cover themselves with sin as uith a garment (Psal.
73.6.) and bind their sin to them as a Crowne glorying in their
shame; yet fub was sarre from eyther of these ungodly tempers:
yea though he had lived like an Angel, yet he knew God might
find just cause enough to charge him with folly. And theretore
in this boasting expression, he only intimates his integrity, that
he was neyther a lover of sin, nor a despiser of goodnesse. Or
uhen Job saith, I mould biud it as Crownes to mee, his meaning is
only this, Though my adversary finde out and hit upon my os¬
fences, yet I shall not be like a common malefactor or condemn’d
offender, no, the very booke of my offences will be not only my
defence, and clearing, but my honour and glory. All that can be
charged upon any man must come under one of these three no¬
tions.
First, Eyther it is false, and that which he never did. (Job¬
friends had charged him with many things which he never did,
with such things as he never contributed so much as a thought
or put a little finger to the doing of them]now that which a man
is falsely charged with, he can easily (at least in the sight of God
and of his owne conscience) discharge himselfe of. And that
which at first was but a calumny, will at last be his crowne.
Secondly, Suppose the fact charged be true, yet if it be
found such as he hath beest humbled for, and repented of, and tur¬
ned from, and unfcynedly begg’d Rrergth against, it fhall not

0740.head: Chap. 31. An Exposition upon thi Booke of JO». Vers. 36.

body.t: turne to his shame. Sins hidden and continued in are our shame,
and will be our confusion, but sins confessed and repented of, are
our comfort and our crowne; we cannot take comfort in any fin,
though confessed and repented of; but we may take much com-
fort that to our knowledge we have no sins, but such as we have
confessed and repented of.
Thirdly, If true,'tis eyther pardoned or unpardoned. Tob
might say, let it be granted, that my adversary hath filled e¬
very page of the booke with such sins as I have indeed commit¬
1.d, yet they are all freely pardoned, God hath fully dischar¬
ged me of them, and given me my ( quietus est or) acquittance
into my bosome. Now then what though my adversary accu¬
seth me, what though he write a booke of accusations against
me; I have already accused my selfe as much before God, and
God hath forgiven me; there is an act of oblivion passed upon
all my transgressions in the court of heaven, The Lord hath said,
that my sins and my iniquities he will Remember no more, then
what doe all these charges amount to? Who shall lay axy thing te
tbi charge of Gods Elect? It ie God that justifieth, rebo is be that
condemneth? It is Christ that dyed. These challenges are univer¬
fall; And though many have both charged and condemned the
very Elect for whom Christ dyed; yet if once a man hath con¬
fessed his fin, & God hath forgiven his sin, all the charges of men
and Devills will be bnt slanders and unseasonable accusatione.
Thus job might triumph over the man of contention, and say,
whatever my adversary can write, is eyther what I have not done,
or if I have done it, I have undone it by confessing it, and God
hath undone it by pardoning it;the Lord hath taken auay my sin
through the blood of the Covenant, and I know that I shall be
Justified. Upon this consideration of Gospel grace, Tob had rea¬
son enough to tell his adversary, that he would beare his booke
of inditement upon his fhoulder, and bind it to bim as a Crowne.
Hence note.
First, wrongfull accusations are matter of honour, rather then
of disgract to the innccent.
There are two sorts of wrongfull accusations, First, when we
are accused of those evills which we never did. Secondly, when
ue are accused for doing that which is good, as if it were evill;
both or eyther of these aceusations are our crowne. It is sayd in

20.10.) I have heard the defaming of many ( that is, many defa¬

The Saints in the primitive times made crownes of all their accu¬
sations, and gloryed in those things which their prophane adver¬

made by their enemies, not done by themselves: or they aceused

body.t: them of that which was not their fault but their glory. They
charged that as sin upon them which was their vertue, and their

are not such disgraces our glory and our crowne? Christ hath

gainst you falsely for my names sake- rejoyce and be excteding glad,
for great is your renard in heaven; That, to be sure, is no lesse then
a crowne far greater and better then all earthly crownes. To that
crowne we must expect to passe ( as the holy Apostle did, 2 Cor.
6.8.) by honour, and dishoneur, by good report, and ill report, as de¬
ceavers and yet true. If there be any truth in ill reports, they are
dirt in our faces, and we have cause to be humbled under them;
but if ill reports be false, we have cause to rejoyce in them, and
they will be crownes upon our heads.
Let me adde these foure good counsels about those evill re¬
ports which may fall upon us. First, if ill reports are true, then
be humbled, Secondly, if false, be comforted; Thirdly, if they
have any thing of truth, or ( not being altogether untrue) have
some very similitude or likenes to truth, then,’tis good for us to
search our hearts and try our wayes more strictly, whether
(though we have not done the thing reported ) we have not gi¬
ven just occasion for such a report; or (though we have not done
that evill) whether we have avoyded all the appearances of that
evill which is reported of us. It was sayd of a virgin, Shee was
shast indeed, but not thought to be so, because shte was more wanton¬
Iy attired then became a chast virgin. Though we are not so ill as
some suspect, yet possibly we are not so good as we would be
thought and ought to be; This should be matter as of present
humiliation, so of future caution. Fourthly, if we have not given
so much as any outward occasion of suspition, yet we shall doe
wel to enquire whether we have not some affect ion to and secret
liking of such sins, this God sometimes punisheth by ill reports,
and makes us see the undue wandrings of our owne hearts, by the
undue wandrings of other mens tongues concerning us.
Againe, Seing Job, though he had many sins, and those such
as his adversary might vorite a booke of, yet could binde the book
of his accusations as a crowne to him.

my stept.
He meanes not corporal steps, but moral, the motions or acti¬

fteps, and every act of these is a step forward or backward, hea¬
ven-ward or hell-ward. So that when Tob saith, I would declare to

But can any man doe that? we may more easily take the num¬
ber of our steps in walking then of our hearts in thinking, of our
tongues in speaking, or of our hands in doing. How then could
Tob say, I would declare unto him the number of my steps, seing they
are innumerable?
I answer; We are not to understand it, as if Job would under¬
take to declare all his particular acts, or every thonght, word, or
deed, which had passed him all his dayes. But first, their kinds,
good and evill, or how he had moved in naturalls, how in civills,
how in spiritualls. Secondly, when he saith, I would declare to him
the number of my steps; his meaning is, I would be exact in disco¬

step. Thirdly, when he saith I mould declare to him the number of

them, but that he would not hide or conceale any one of them;

body.t: Hence note.
A gracious heart hath a very observant eye upen his orrne
wayes.
Job kept an account of himselfe, and of all his wayes, and this
is one of the best accounts we can keepe. Many keepe an account
of their expences, and in-comes; they know what goes out, and
what comes in every yeare, but how few are there that keepe ac¬
count of their lives and conversations, of their thoughts, of their
words and workes, these passe without account; though they
must all be accounted for hereafter. And how shall wee declare
the number of our steps, if we keepe not an account of them?
Tis a great peice of the practice of godlinesse to put the Questi¬
on often to our soules, What have we done? The Prophet ( Jer:
8.6.) sets forth the wickednesse of that age, when no man said,
what have I done? what’s my way? what my steps? what have
I been speaking? what have I been doing? where have my
thoughts been? Only they who have kept an account, are and
uill be willing to give an account. And how sad will it be with
them to be called to an account by God, who have never called
themselves to an account, nor considered how or which way to
makeit? A godly man knowes he must declare his wayes to God
hereafter, and he is ready ( when there is cause) to declare them
to his fellow- brethren here. He cares not (so farre as is fit) who
knowes his whole heart and life. As every one should be ready
(I Pet: 3. 15.) to give a reason ef the hope that is in him mitb
mecknesse, and godly feare; so to give an account of what hath
been done by him, with the same meeknesse and godly feare.
But how shall any man give an account of what he hath done,
tvho keepes no account of what he hath done? David made a
strict search of himselfe, both as to what he hath done, and what
God hath done to him ( Psal:77.5, 6.) I have considered the
dayes of eld, the yeares of ancient times. I call to remembrance my

in my hand, I digged into my heart and life; or as a third gives the
Allusion, I searched as with a fan in mr hand, to finde out what

The word signifies land in Generall, and yet more properly,

By a usuall figure in Scripture, acts of life are ascribed to things
livelesse, and acts of reason to those things which have not fo
